pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1000 wh power station can run a microwave and for how long". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1000 wh power station can run a microwave and for how long?
pages.why_used: The cited pages work out microwave minutes from an assumed 85% of rated capacity, and some say they did no testing. Backup Power Finder lists OutdoorGearLab's usable-Wh figures, but it doesn't give the test load or turn them into microwave time. This page uses energy measured at about 80% of each unit's rated output (a load the size of a microwave's draw) and The Solar Lab's timed 1,479 W run. It converts those into minutes and reheats per charge. It also notes that boost modes (BLUETTI Power Lifting, EcoFlow X-Boost) don't raise the ceiling for a microwave.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's 2,700 W 'Power Lifting' figure, on both the AC180 and the Elite 100 V2, is the maker's limit for pure resistive loads only ('devices consisting of heating elements only'), while the rated output 'remains 1800W'. A microwave is not a heating-element load, so the only number that counts for one is the continuous rating: 2,000 W on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, 1,800 W on the BLUETTI and EcoFlow units, 1,500 W on the Jackery.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 pick rather than changing it. Once boost modes are set aside, the C1000 Gen 2's 2,000 W is the highest continuous rating among the four mainstream picks (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, AC180, EcoFlow DELTA 3, Jackery 1000 v2). The only higher ones are the DJI Power 1000 V2 at 2,600 W and the ALLPOWERS S2000 Pro at 2,400 W. BLUETTI's 2,700 W is a resistive-only mode, so it gives no headroom for a 1,580 W over-the-range microwave. Our Elite 100 V2 row needs one fix: change '1,800 W / 2,700 W' to '1,800 W (2,700 W Power Lifting, heating loads only)' and add a footnote.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns measured usable AC energy into microwave minutes. Using OutdoorGearLab's discharge tests (July 2026), every 1 kWh candidate gives 35–36 minutes at a 1,500 W draw and 17–18 two-minute reheats. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 also has one test at a microwave-like 1 kW load: The Technology Man measured 907 Wh. These numbers show runtime does not separate the candidates, so inverter headroom decides the pick.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and does not change it. Measured usable AC energy puts every candidate at 34.8–36.4 minutes at a 1,500 W draw and 17–18 two-minute reheats, so battery size can't pick a winner. Inverter headroom decides. The C1000 Gen 2 (2,000 W continuous per Anker) and DJI Power 1000 V2 have margin above a 1,500 W draw. DELTA 3 and Elite 100 V2 (1,800 W) have about 300 W of margin. The Explorer 1000 v2 (1,500 W per OutdoorGearLab's spec table) has no margin, which makes it the one to steer away from even though it measured the most usable Wh (910). One extra data point: The Technology Man saw the C1000 Gen 2 overheat after 26 minutes at 2 kW, with the heater placed too close to the unit. That supports staying well under the inverter's limit.

Anker lists the C1000 Gen 2 (ChatGPT's top pick) as not expandable, so it is limited to its one 1,024 Wh battery (about 35 minutes at 1,500 W).

It also shows that neither it nor the DELTA 3 Classic can go past roughly 35 minutes of 1,500 W cooking per charge. A shopper who wants more microwave time should buy the EcoFlow DELTA 3 (1,024 Wh, not the Classic) or the DELTA 3 Plus and add an extra battery. The cheaper Classic cards ChatGPT showed can't be expanded. Separately, ChatGPT's $998 price for the BLUETTI AC180 at BLUETTI-US is the two-unit option; a single AC180 is $499.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'boost' ratings on 1 kWh stations are reduced-voltage modes and not extra continuous power. EcoFlow's X-Boost (2,200 W on the DELTA 3) 'marginally reduces voltage', and BLUETTI limits the AC180's 2,700 W Power Lifting mode to 'pure-resistive heating devices', so for a microwave the continuous AC rating is the real ceiling. Only the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 has 2,000 W of continuous output with no boost mode involved.
angles.decides: This confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick for full-size microwaves drawing about 1,600–2,000 W. Its 2,000 W is a plain continuous rating. The BLUETTI AC180's 2,700 W covers resistive heating devices only, so the AC180 stays capped at 1,800 W for a microwave. The DELTA 3's 2,200 W comes only in X-Boost, which runs at reduced voltage. EcoFlow lists a 1,300 W microwave as an X-Boost example, but that is already below the DELTA 3's 1,800 W continuous rating. So the boost figures should not be used to move the line for the microwave sizes each station can run.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a runtime measured at a microwave-sized load: The Solar Lab ran the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at a steady 1,479 W and it lasted 37.5 minutes, and OutdoorGearLab's usable-energy figures, taken at about 80% of each unit's rated output, work out to about 35–36 minutes at 1,500 W for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (890 Wh each) and about 35 minutes for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 (870 Wh).

Runtime per charge is therefore effectively a tie at about 35–36 minutes or about 17 two-minute reheats at 1,500 W, so the deciding factor is inverter headroom: the Anker's rated 2,000 W against 1,800 W. A 1,000 W-cooking microwave that draws about 1,500 W would leave it no margin. That supports the current page's verdict that it suits only a 700–900 W microwave.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1000 wh power station charges fully from the wall in under an hour". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1000 wh power station charges fully from the wall in under an hour?
pages.why_used: The rival pages, and our own earlier version, repeat Anker's 1,600 W UltraFast figure and the 49-minute claim. None of them reads Anker's US nameplate of 120 V, 12 A max (1,440 W), which is also the code limit for one plug-in device on a standard 15 A circuit. None sets that against EcoFlow's 15 A rating or DJI's 13 A. This page checks each fast mode against what a US 120 V outlet can supply and shows the arithmetic, so it explains why the 49 minutes still fits under an hour at 120 V and why 1,200 W units can't.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the US Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is rated for at most 12 A at 120 V. That is 1,440 W, less than the 1,600 W UltraFast input Anker advertises. On the same 120 V basis the DJI Power 1000 V2 is rated for 13 A (1,560 W) and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 for 15 A (1,800 W). So the model with the highest advertised input has the lowest rated current from a US outlet.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker as the pick and changes how the page should explain it. The 49-minute claim needs only about 1,254 W on average into a 1,024 Wh battery, which is under the 1,440 W nameplate limit. The Solar Lab timed 47 minutes in Ultra-Fast mode (outlet voltage not stated). So the time is believable, but the '1,600 W' headline is not what Anker's US nameplate allows at 120 V. Our '≈13 A at 120 V' circuit warning should be rewritten around the 12 A rating. The EcoFlow is the only one of the three makers I checked whose 120 V rating (15 A) is above its charge wattage (1,500 W). It also had the highest measured charging speed in OutdoorGearLab's test, which favours it as the runner-up.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much wall energy a full charge takes or what that does to the fastest possible time. StorageReview measured 1,180 Wh from the wall to fill the 1,024 Wh EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, about 87 % efficient. Because charging stops at 100 % but the losses still come out of the wall, the fastest possible full charge, with no slow-down near full, is 1,180 Wh ÷ max AC input. That works out to about 44 min for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 at 1,600 W and 47 min for the DELTA 3 Plus at 1,500 W. It would be about 59 min for a 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W, such as the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, which leaves no room to finish in under an hour.
angles.decides: It backs the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick. It has the most headroom: about 44 min is its fastest possible time, against a 49 min claim and a 60 min target, so about 11 min of its claimed charge goes to slowing near full. The DELTA 3 Plus can't beat about 47 min and claims 56. A 1,024 Wh unit capped at 1,200 W (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 TurboBoost) can't beat about 59 min even if it never slowed near full. That rules it out as an under-an-hour answer and explains why BLUETTI only claims 80 % in 45 min. The same check should be run on the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh), whose input cap I couldn't source: unless its charger is better than 89 % efficient, 1,200 W could not fill it in under an hour.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's US page says to wall-charge the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 only with the standard Anker SOLIX AC charging cable, warning that third-party cables may cause damage. The same page rates the AC input at '120V~ 12A Max' while advertising 1,600 W UltraFast, which works out to about 13.3 A at 120 V.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick and adds two conditions to the 49-minute claim: (1) use the supplied Anker SOLIX AC cable, not a spare cord; (2) the maker's own input rating is 12 A at 120 V, yet UltraFast at 1,600 W draws about 13.3 A. Either way, a US shopper needs the station on a 15 A outlet with nothing heavy sharing the circuit. This doesn't change the ranking.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own US spec caps the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2's wall input at '120V~ 12A Max' (1,440 W at 120 V), which is below its advertised 1,600 W UltraFast rate and equals the electrical code's 12 A limit for a single plug-in device on a standard 15 A circuit (NEC 210.23(A)(1)); a US outlet therefore cannot supply the full 1,600 W behind the 49-minute claim.
angles.decides: The finding keeps the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the pick but changes how its claim should be read on a US outlet. Its 12 A input label and the code limit both point to about 1,440 W at 120 V, not 1,600 W. Holding that draw flat would stretch the 49-minute claim to about 54 minutes, which is still under an hour but closer to the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's 55–56 minutes. The 47-minute measured time was taken on UK mains and doesn't carry over to 120 V. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's 1,500 W is about 12.5 A at 120 V, also over the 12 A limit; StorageReview says that rate suits a 20 A circuit and that the app's charge-speed limit is for 15 A plugs. The energy arithmetic sets the floor: StorageReview measured 1,180 Wh from the wall to fill the 1,024 Wh DELTA 3 Plus. A full charge inside 60 minutes therefore needs an average draw of at least about 1,180 W across the whole charge, including the slow final stretch. Modes capped at 1,200 W, such as Anker's normal mode, ALLPOWERS P1800 fast mode and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 Turbo, have almost no margin. That fits the reviews where those modes take about an hour or longer.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OutdoorGearLab (Kenji Mowrey, 2026-07-23) timed the EcoFlow DELTA 3 at a full 0–100 % wall charge in 50 minutes at an average 1,299 Wh/hr, with no app fast mode mentioned, while the same lab timed the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 at 56 minutes in its default mode.
angles.decides: This confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the fastest pick. Two named reviewers each measured 47 minutes with UltraFast on: The Technology Man at about 20 °C, and The Solar Lab. It also sets up a clear second choice for shoppers who won't switch on an app mode. In OutdoorGearLab's single lab, the DELTA 3 filled in 50 minutes on its default charger, which beats the Anker's 56-minute default run there. So the Anker is only fastest with UltraFast enabled. The DJI Power 1000 V2 is borderline: The Technology Man measured under 53 minutes and OutdoorGearLab measured 59 minutes. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 fails the under-an-hour test in OutdoorGearLab's run (almost 2 hours at 563 Wh/hr, mode not stated).

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got lists the Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 (1,024 Wh). Jackery's own US store sells it for $549 today and says it is 'Fully Charged in Just 50 Minutes'. That beats the 56-minute EcoFlow and DJI claims and comes close to the Anker C1000 Gen 2's 49 minutes, which costs $799 at Anker's own US store.
angles.decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 as the fastest maker-claimed full wall charge (49 min, UltraFast enabled in the app). It also makes the price trade-off visible. At maker-store prices the Anker costs $799. The DELTA 3 costs $579 for a 56-minute claim. The Jackery HomePower 1000 v2 costs $549 for a 50-minute claim, but its black version is sold out. The BLUETTI AC180 and Elite 100 V2 cost $499 but are only claimed to reach 80 % in 45 minutes, so they don't meet the 'fully in under an hour' test. The page should add the HomePower 1000 v2 as the value alternative and state its charge conditions once they are sourced.

pages.query: 1000 wh power station bundled with a 400 w solar panel
pages.why_used: The rival pages give only rated Wh and their own 75–85% assumptions. None prints a named lab's delivered-energy figure for any of the 1 kWh kit stations. This page ranks the kits on lab-measured AC energy (BLUETTI AC180 980–1,030 Wh against 850–910 Wh for the EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker units) and adds the low-load result of 530–620 Wh at about 34 W.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the stations' 'max solar input' watts are not comparable: the BLUETTI AC180 is capped at 10 A, so its 2 × 200 W kit reaches 400 W only if the array runs at 40 V or more (series wiring). The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 drops to 8.2 A below 29 V, which allows about 230 W at most, and only Anker's 48 V PS400 panel gets the full 400 W through it, with its 57.6 V open-circuit voltage 2.4 V under the 60 V ceiling.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Each maker's own 400 W kit gets the whole 400 W (AC180 if wired in series, C1000 Gen 2 with the PS400). The finding matters for shoppers who would put a station together with panels bought separately: low-voltage 200 W panels in parallel lose about half their output on the AC180 (10 A cap) and on the C1000 Gen 2 (8.2 A below 29 V). On cycle life, Anker's '4,000 cycles to at least 80%' is the only figure from a maker page I read that names its endpoint. The ALLPOWERS P1800 (cheapest kit, $698) gives no endpoint and its rating differs between stores (US store: 'over 3,000'; a search snippet of the EU page says 3,500+), so the table footnote should say its cycle count can't be compared.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own store sells the AC180 with 400 W of its panels for less when bought as two parts ($769 AC180+200 W kit + $399 SP200L = $1,168, $1.01/Wh) than as its $1,232 'AC180+2*200W' bundle ($1.07/Wh). None states that the Anker C1000 Gen 2 only draws a full 400 W from a panel running at 29 V or more; below that its input tops out near 28 V × 8.2 A ≈ 230 W.
angles.decides: Confirms that both BLUETTI and Anker can take a full 400 W only under a voltage condition, and cuts the BLUETTI row's best price from $1,232 to $1,168 (still about $1.01/Wh against the ALLPOWERS kit's roughly $0.68/Wh on our page, which I could not re-verify today). The value pick stays the same. It adds a buying tip for BLUETTI and a check-the-panel-voltage warning for anyone pairing a 400 W panel with the Anker.

That cap means the AC180 + 2 × 200 W kit, which is in stock at $1,232, can only approach 400 W if its two SP200L panels are wired in series. BLUETTI's own AC180 manual gives no series or parallel instruction, and our page currently says the panels 'go in parallel'.

The AC180 + 2 × 200 W kit, priced at $1,232 on 2026-11-08, gets close to 400 W only when wired in series, and it is also the most expensive kit here. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own 400 W panel for the C1000 Gen 2 kit (PS400, Voc 57.6 V) sits only 2.4 V (4.2%) under the C1000 Gen 2's 60 V solar-input ceiling. Open-circuit voltage rises as panels get colder, so this pairing has the least cold-weather headroom of the kits we list.
angles.decides: This confirms that every listed kit works electrically at the standard 25 °C rating and that no station limits current below its 400 W panel (PS400: 8.33 A at 48 V, within the C1000 Gen 2's 14.5 A high-voltage band). It does not rule out the Anker kit. It adds a winter caveat that applies only to the Anker kit: its panel runs 2.4 V below the input limit. I did not source Voc for the ALLPOWERS SP037 or the EcoFlow 400 W myself today. Rival pages give 45.3 V and 48 V, which would leave about 12–15 V of headroom. If those figures hold, the Anker kit is the one to flag for cold-climate buyers. Anker also lists the C1000 Gen 2 + 400 W bundle as shipping from early December for orders placed after Oct 30.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which 1 kwh power station takes 1000 w of solar through two inputs". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which 1 kwh power station takes 1000 w of solar through two inputs?
pages.why_used: The cited rival lists the DELTA 3 Plus only as 'two 500W MPPT inputs' and gives no volts or amps for either station. None of the results converts the 15 A and 20 A limits into the working voltage a panel string must hold (33.3 V per DELTA 3 Plus input, 50 V for the Elite 100 V2's one input), quotes EcoFlow's rule that a panel exceeding any one limit cannot be used, or carries Notebookcheck's finding that one input makes 1,000 W hard to reach on the Elite 100 V2. This page has all three.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's '1,000 W solar' comes through a single input capped at 20 A under a 60 V ceiling, so the panel string must run at 50 V or more to reach 1,000 W, while each of the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus's two 15 A inputs reaches its 500 W cap from about 33.3 V upward.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick. Its 1,000 W comes from two 500 W inputs, and an ordinary 400–500 W string on each input reaches the cap with room to spare. The Elite 100 V2 is the obvious single-input alternative. On paper it matches at 1,000 W and costs $499, but 1,000 W ÷ 20 A means the string must hold at least 50 V while its open-circuit voltage stays at or under 60 V. That is a narrow window, and Notebookcheck's reviewer said 1,000 W is hard to reach in practice. The page should tell shoppers that the two '1,000 W' figures are not equivalent.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's single 20 A solar input can only reach 1,000 W from a string working at 50 V or more under a 60 V ceiling (1,000 W ÷ 20 A = 50 V), while each EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus port needs only about 33 V for its 500 W (500 W ÷ 15 A).
angles.decides: This supports the DELTA 3 Plus as the answer. The Elite 100 V2 also claims 1,000 W, but on one input it only gets there with a string operating between 50 and 60 V, a narrow window that common portable panels and series pairs can easily miss. Each DELTA 3 Plus port reaches its 500 W anywhere from about 33 V to 60 V, so two ordinary strings can fill it. Before landed losses, both stations take about 1.0 h at a full 1,000 W.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the DELTA 3 Plus's car-charging cable plugs into one of the same two XT60i solar ports, so while it is charging from a car only one 500 W solar input is left. None of them says that each port stops at 15 A either, which means an array needs at least about 33.3 V working voltage, with open-circuit voltage at or under 60 V, to fill a port.
angles.decides: It confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick and adds the conditions. Its two ports reach 1,000 W together only if each array works at 33.3 V or more and stays at or under 60 V open-circuit. Using one port for car charging takes away half the solar input. The single-input BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (12–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W) only reaches 1,000 W from an array working at 50 V or more with open-circuit voltage at or under 60 V. That is a narrow range for real panels, so two inputs are the easier way to get 1,000 W of solar.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow caps each DELTA 3 Plus input at 15 A, so each input reaches 500 W only from a panel string working at 33.3 V or more and staying under 60 V open-circuit. By the same arithmetic, the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's single 20 A input needs at least 50 V of working voltage under a 60 V ceiling to reach 1,000 W, which Notebookcheck says is difficult in practice.
angles.decides: This confirms the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus as the pick and sets what panels the plan needs. To get 1,000 W the shopper needs two separate strings of about 500 W, one per input. Each string must work at 33.3 V or more (500 W ÷ 15 A), have a cold-weather Voc of 60 V or less, and stay at 15 A or less. That rules out paralleling two 20 V-class panels into one input, since EcoFlow's own example (12.9 A × 2 = 25.8 A) is refused, and it rules out putting two 40 V-class panels in series. It also removes the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 as an equal alternative. Its one input needs at least 50 V at 20 A while staying under 60 V Voc, and Notebookcheck works out that two BLUETTI PV350s can't go in series (2 × 46.5 V = 93 V), leaving about 700 W.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured energy balance for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. StorageReview (Dylan Dougherty, Jan 2, 2025) drew 910 Wh out of the 1,024 Wh pack (88.9%) and needed 1,180 Wh in to refill it from 0 to 100% (86.8%). At the full 1,000 W of solar through its two ports, the input side works out to about 71 minutes, which matches EcoFlow's 70-minute claim. Separately, The Solar Lab reports getting 'really close to' 1,000 W with both 500 W ports in use.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick. It is the only candidate where a named tester actually drew close to 1,000 W through two inputs (The Solar Lab, both 500 W ports, Serious 415 W bifacial panels). Its measured efficiency (88.9% out, 86.8% in, StorageReview) means the 70-minute solar claim holds only if the full 1,000 W keeps coming in. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 tested similarly well on capacity (946 Wh at a 500 W load, Techreviewer.de). But it has one DC input (12–60 V, 20 A), so it fails the 'two inputs' requirement. No named reviewer I could open logged its solar watts. It also idles at about 16 W with the inverter on (The Solar Lab), and its AC charging drops to about 500 W below 20% charge.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, a 1,024 Wh station that takes 1,000 W of solar, sells for $499 on BLUETTI US today (2026-11-14), the same price as BLUETTI's 500 W AC180. Volt & Valley shows the two-input EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus at $949, so the second input costs about $450 more, unless the shopper can wire their panels into one 12–60 V string.
angles.decides: This confirms the DELTA 3 Plus for the question as asked. EcoFlow's DELTA 3 series page lists 'two 500W MPPT inputs' for 1,000 W in total, and no other 1 kWh model I checked publishes two inputs that add up to 1,000 W. It also gives the page its price line: the shopper pays about $450 more (EcoFlow's own price wasn't readable today) for two independent inputs instead of the Elite 100 V2's 1,000 W for $499. They give no NAS wattage, no Wh capacity, no headroom against the UPS's output cap and no runtime. This page matches each NAS to a UPS by its measured draw (DXP4800 Plus 64 W peak against the US3000's 120 W cap). pages.query: obd gps tracker
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (RottenWiFi, Vyncs pricing, Bouncie pricing) give driving intervals and prices only. None states how often each tracker reports once the car is parked, what each does when pulled from the port, or that the port keeps powering the tracker with the ignition off; this page has all three from maker documents for every row.

angles.decides: It confirms Spytec Pulse OBD on cost but not on update speed. On cost, Spytec's annual plan is the lowest of the three in year one ($107.40, against $145.98 for Vyncs Basic and $205.79 for Bouncie) and stays lowest through year three ($322.20, $345.96, $437.39). It changes the Vyncs line: Basic's $99.99 a year buys 3-minute uploads, and Basic plus both speed upgrades ($195.98 in year one) costs more than Vyncs Pro ($165.98), which includes them. A shopper who wants second-by-second live tracking is pointed to Bouncie on Bouncie's own claim. The page cannot say where Spytec sits on update interval until that figure is sourced.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the break-even months between the three pricing models: Spytec Pulse OBD month-to-month ($0 hardware, $14.95/mo) is the cheapest way to track a car for up to 7 months, Bouncie only undercuts it from month 17, and on Spytec's annual plan ($107.40/yr) Vyncs Basic does not become cheaper until year 7.
angles.decides: It makes the pick depend on how long the shopper needs tracking. For a short need (a teen's first months, a loaned or stored car, a trial) Spytec Pulse OBD month-to-month wins: $14.95 to start, against $99.64 for Bouncie and $145.98 for Vyncs, and it stays cheapest through month 7. For a year or more, Spytec's annual plan at $107.40/yr beats Bouncie at every horizon ($98.39 less in year 1, $115.19 less over 3 years) and beats Vyncs Basic through year 6. Bouncie is the cheaper choice only against Spytec's month-to-month rate, and only from month 17. On update rate, Vyncs Basic's 3-minute transmit means about 3.25 miles between map points at 65 mph against 0.27 miles for Bouncie; Spytec's interval could not be sourced, so the page should not claim a speed advantage for it.

All three also cover the US, Canada and Mexico, so border driving does not rule out Bouncie, despite what two rival pages say. The pick shifts in three cases. If the OBD port must stay free for another device, Spytec sells a splitter but warns it may stop the tracker reading vehicle data. If an alert on unplugging matters, Vyncs states it has no battery and cannot notify until power returns, while the Spytec Pulse OBD lists a 60 mAh backup battery.

None of them says that Elite's ZU12V trigger excludes floor-rising screens, or that the ZUSBV-RC1 USB trigger (RC1 screens only) is the Kestrel route when a projector has no 12 V output, or which floor-risers ship with their own sync trigger. It lists the CineGrey 4D version (1.1 gain, 70°, 63% ambient light rejection) as 'Not Compatible With Ultra-short/Short Throw or Triple Laser Projectors'.

pages.query: best 2-bay nas for time machine backups from a couple of macs
pages.why_used: Apple's cited page only says 'SMB, not AFP', and the Synology compare pages and roundups name models without explaining that Time Machine keeps filling whatever space the share reports. None of them says where each brand caps each Mac's space: Synology share quotas need Btrfs and ext4 quotas stop at 4 TB, UGREEN caps per shared folder, Asustor per Apple device and QNAP per user, while UniFi documents no cap. This page adds that, sourced from each maker's own pages.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Synology's 14.6 dB(A) noise rating for the DS223 was measured with Synology SATA SSDs, while the DS223j (18.2 dB(A)) and DS225+ (19.6 dB(A)) were measured with hard drives. The DS223's 'quietest' number therefore doesn't apply to the two-HDD Time Machine build ChatGPT told the shopper to buy.
angles.decides: This weakens the DS223's claim to be the quiet pick. With hard drives, which ChatGPT's own plan uses, Synology publishes no DS223 noise figure. The only HDD-based Synology figures are the DS223j at 18.2 dB(A) and the DS225+ at 19.6 dB(A), so the honest comparison is closer than 14.6 vs 19.6. Power figures are also stated on different bases: Synology gives 'access' and 'HDD hibernation' watts, and QNAP gives 'operating (typical)' and 'HDD standby' watts 'with drives fully populated'. Igor'sLAB measured the UGREEN DXP2800 with only one NVMe SSD installed. So no single watt figure ranks these boxes for a 24/7 Time Machine target. The DS223 vs DS225+ choice still comes down to networking and warranty (2 vs 3 years), not quietness.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each 2-bay NAS costs to run per year for Time Machine duty. Using each maker's own access and hibernation wattage over 8 h of drive access and 16 h of hibernation a day, at the EIA's August 2026 US residential average of 18.16¢/kWh, the result ranges from about $9.37 a year (QNAP TS-233) and $10.78 (UGREEN DH2300) through $12.89–15.45 for the three Synology models to $23.33 (TerraMaster F2-425).
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's point that the DS223 is enough for backups only. Its running cost is about $13.52 a year, against $15.45 for the DS225+, so electricity barely separates the Synology models and doesn't change the pick between them. It does mark down the TerraMaster F2-425: its 11 W hibernation figure gives about $23.33 a year, roughly $117 over 5 years, versus $54 for the UGREEN DH2300 and $47 for the QNAP TS-233. That puts the DH2300 ($239.99 + $53.90 ≈ $294 over 5 years) ahead as the low-running-cost choice where a price is sourced. pages.query: which power stations can run 240 volt appliances from one unit
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (Watt & Warden, Power Station Field Guide, StorageReview) mark every single-box split-phase station '240V: yes' and never say that the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus and the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus cut their 240 V outlets while recharging from 120 V. This page lines up each maker's own statement on that condition, adds amps at 240 V, and so separates the units that can keep a well pump running through a long outage with generator top-ups.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got lines up the single-box 240 V units by whether the 240 V outlet stays live while the unit recharges from an ordinary 120 V outlet or generator. Anker says the F3800 Plus's 240 V output 'cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC'. Jackery lists '240V Ports: No Output' for the Explorer 5000 Plus when it charges and discharges at once. BLUETTI says you can 'charge the Apex 300 at 120V without interrupting 240V output'.
angles.decides: Picture a shopper running a 240 V well pump or other load through a multi-day outage while topping up from a 120 V generator or wall outlet. For that shopper the pick moves to the BLUETTI Apex 300, whose maker says 240 V keeps running during 120 V charging. The Anker S5000 may also qualify, but only on The Gadgeteer's word; Anker's own pages say nothing. The F3800 Plus and the Explorer 5000 Plus drop their 240 V output in that situation. The trade-off: the Apex 300's 3,840 W total is only 16 A at 240 V. So a 240 V load over 16 A (a 24 A EV charger, a 20 A dryer element) still needs the F3800 Plus (25 A stated) or the Explorer 5000 Plus (7,200 W, which is 30 A), run on battery only. The footnote finding: '240V: Yes' means 'yes, on battery' for two of the three units ChatGPT recommended.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many amps each unit can deliver at 240 V. Rated watts ÷ 240 V works out to 16.0 A for the BLUETTI Apex 300, 16.7 A for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, 25 A for the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (Anker prints '25A Max') and 30 A for the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus and EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra. So the Apex 300's 50 A-labelled NEMA 14-50R outlet supplies at most 32% of its label.
angles.decides: Shoppers size a 240 V appliance by its circuit amps, so the pick depends on amps at 240 V, not on which outlet the unit has. The Apex 300 (16.0 A) and DELTA Pro 3 (16.7 A) cannot carry a 240 V load above about 16 A, even though each has a 30 A or 50 A outlet. Loads from 16.7 A up to 25 A need the F3800 Plus or a bigger unit, and loads up to 30 A need the Explorer 5000 Plus or the DELTA Pro Ultra. Above 30 A, only the DELTA Pro Ultra X bundle (50 A) does it from one inverter. This makes the Apex 300 the cheapest single-box route only for 240 V loads of 16 A or less. At $1,499 it costs $93.69 per 240 V amp, against $123.30 for the DELTA Pro Ultra.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that two of its single-unit 240 V picks lose 240 V while they recharge. Anker says the F3800 Plus's 240 V output 'cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC'. Jackery lists the Explorer 5000 Plus's 240V ports as 'No Output' during simultaneous charge and discharge. BLUETTI says the Apex 300 runs 120 V and 240 V devices 'even while charging'.
angles.decides: For a well pump or other 240 V load that must keep running while the station is topped up from a 120 V wall outlet or generator, the F3800 Plus and the Explorer 5000 Plus fail on the makers' own pages. The Apex 300 is the only checked unit whose maker says 240 V works while charging, though BLUETTI does not say which charging source that covers. This keeps the Apex 300 ($1,499 at bluettipower.com on 2026-11-17) as the single-box pick for 240 V during recharge. The trade-off is 3,840 W total, about 16 A at 240 V. It also means the page should stop treating every 'single-unit 240 V' station as equal. The F3800 Plus, the $2,999.99 card in ChatGPT's answer, showed 'Sold Out' with no price on Anker's US store today.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus's 240 V output 'cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC', or that the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus's 240 V ports give 'No Output' during simultaneous charge and discharge. Both units take only 120 V AC input. So a single box running a 240 V well pump or dryer goes dead on 240 V whenever it is recharged from a wall outlet or a 120 V generator.
angles.decides: If the plan is to keep a 240 V load (well pump, dryer, mini-split) running while the station is topped up from a 120 V outlet or a 120 V-only generator, the F3800 Plus and Explorer 5000 Plus fail on 240 V. Both have 120 V-only AC input, and the 240 V ports cut out while charging. The F3800 Plus keeps 240 V pass-through only when fed by a 240 V generator through its HPP/generator port (L14-30R bypass up to 6,000 W). The DELTA Pro 3 cannot mix 120 V and 240 V outlets at all. The Apex 300 is the one candidate where a named reviewer (StorageReview) describes 240 V mode staying active on 120 V input, so it is the safer pick for 'recharge while running 240 V'. The page should tell the shopper to check this before trusting any single-box 240 V claim.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts measured inverter idle draw side by side for the single-unit 240 V candidates. The Solar Lab measured about 20 W for the BLUETTI Apex 300, about 45 W for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra, about 58 W for the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus and about 80 W for the original Anker F3800. Left on for 24 hours, that is roughly 0.48 kWh against 1.92 kWh, or about 17% against 50% of each unit's rated capacity.
angles.decides: People who need 240 V from one box usually want it for well pumps, HVAC or sump loads, so the inverter stays on all day. Idle draw then cuts runtime more than the 6,000 W versus 7,200 W ratings that ChatGPT used to rank the units. On the Solar Lab's numbers, the Apex 300 loses about 0.48 kWh a day at idle, against about 1.92 kWh for the original F3800, 1.39 kWh for the Explorer 5000 Plus and 1.08 kWh for the DELTA Pro Ultra. That supports the Apex 300 for long, light 240 V duty. The DELTA Pro Ultra is the pick for heavy starts: it held 9,200 W for about 10 s, while the F3800 held 8,000 W for only 2 to 3 s. The Solar Lab does not say whether it measured idle in 120 V or 240 V mode, so the page should present these as the outlet's figures and not as 240 V figures.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "best 2kwh portable power station for an rv under $900". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What's the best 2kwh portable power station for an rv under $900?
pages.why_used: The rival pages that were cited (RuntimeMath /compare, OutageReadyHQ under $1,000, OutdoorGearLab, BuyerSheet and our 2026-10-31 page) give no measured idle draw for any 2 kWh station, and every runtime table they offer assumes the same usable Wh for every model. This page sets out what named reviewers measured with the AC inverter left on: about 10 W on the Elite 200 V2 (The Gadgeteer), 17 W on the Jackery (The Solar Lab) and 27 W on the DELTA 3 Max (The Solar Lab). It turns each figure into the share of the battery lost per day. Because the AC200L is now discontinued at BLUETTI US, the pick moves to the in-stock Elite 200 V2, which is under $900 and has the best measured idle draw and usable capacity.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, measured to the same 80%-capacity end point, the AC200L it keeps picking has the lowest rated cycle life of the three 2kWh finalists: 3,000+ cycles, against 4,000 for the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 and 6,000 for the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. They also don't say that the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W figure is a 'Power Lifting' mode for resistive loads only, so it is not a surge rating that would start an RV air conditioner.
angles.decides: Among the stations with a built-in TT-30, this points toward the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2: 4,000 cycles to 80% against the AC200L's 3,000+, it's 20.7 lb lighter, and its TT-30R carries a printed 20 A / 2,400 W rating. It also matters because BLUETTI's US store showed the AC200L at $899 but not available today. For buyers who will plug appliances in directly, the finding backs the Elite 200 V2 at $899 (in stock) as the longest-rated battery. That 6,000 is an 80% figure, so it compares like for like. Its 3,900 W mode should not be read as surge headroom for motor loads.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the battery each station's inverter uses per day when it is left on to feed the RV through the TT-30 or an adapter: about 288 Wh/day (14.1%) for the BLUETTI AC200L at BLUETTI's 12 W, 240 Wh/day (11.6%) for the Elite 200 V2 at The Gadgeteer's 10 W, and 216 Wh/day (10.5%) for the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at Anker's 9 W.
angles.decides: It confirms the main finding of this check: the AC200L is not buyable. BLUETTI's US page marks every AC200L variant 'Discontinued', and the store data shows it unavailable at $899, so it can't stay the pick. Among the stations that have a TT-30, the Anker C2000 Gen 2 has the lowest sourced idle draw. Over a day of always-on shore-feed use it keeps 72 Wh (3.5% of 2,048 Wh) more than the AC200L. That backs the Anker as the RV-hookup pick if its price is confirmed under $900. The Elite 200 V2 ($899 on BLUETTI's US store today, 240 Wh/day idle) is the in-stock pick with a confirmed price, but it needs a 5-20P to TT-30R adapter.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own C2000 Gen 2 page lists the BP2000 (Gen 2) expansion battery as its add-on battery for 'up to 4kWh', an 800 W Alternator Charger rated '100% in 3 Hr', and a 10 ms UPS switchover, alongside a TT-30R rated 120 V / 20 A / 2,400 W max. Together those make it the TT-30 model whose maker documents the most RV pairings, now that BLUETTI's US store marks the AC200L and every AC200L bundle 'Discontinued'.
angles.decides: The AC200L is still ChatGPT's top pick in every chat, but BLUETTI's US store now lists the base unit and all its bundles as 'Discontinued'. On 2026-10-31 our page said it was in stock. That makes the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 the TT-30 pick the maker fully documents: a TT-30R at 120 V / 20 A / 2,400 W, one expansion path (BP2000 Gen 2, up to about 4 kWh), an 800 W alternator charger for charging while driving, and a 10 ms UPS. One caveat: Anker's page showed no price today, so the under-$900 condition is still unconfirmed. The Elite 200 V2 at $899 has no RV outlet, and BLUETTI's box list doesn't include an RV adapter, so a TT-30 hookup means buying a separate adapter, which then limits you to that outlet's 20 A.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 2kWh stations with a TT-30 outlet use a floating neutral, so an RV with a Progressive-type EMS or surge protector reads them as an 'open ground' and won't pass power until the shopper adds a neutral-ground bonding plug.
angles.decides: It doesn't change the pick. Both TT-30 picks, BLUETTI AC200L and Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2, have the same issue. Anker says so in its manual, and Mike Sokol says it about BLUETTI as a brand. It adds a needed condition to the 'plug your RV's 30A cord in' plan. Many RVs have an EMS or surge protector that cuts power on an open ground. Those owners need a neutral-ground bonding plug in a spare outlet on the station, or plugged into a splitter alongside the RV cord, or the RV gets no power at all. The fix is the same for every candidate, so it doesn't favour the Elite 200 V2 or Jackery either.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a named reviewer's measured idle draw with the AC inverter on. That draw runs all night under an RV fridge. The Solar Lab measured about 27 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max and about 17 W on the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. The Gadgeteer measured about 10 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 with AC and DC left on. Separately, Notebookcheck got only about 1,600 Wh out of the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at a 200 W load (79%), against about 1,850 Wh at 1,800 W.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. Measured idle draw and low-load capacity count against the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max (27 W idle measured by The Solar Lab) as an overnight RV battery. It is also a caution on the Anker C2000 Gen 2: in Notebookcheck's EU-model test, a 200 W load got only about 79% of rated capacity, so its 9 W idle figure is Anker's own claim. The best measured low-load results belong to the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2: 1.91 kWh discharged (StorageReview) and about 10 W idle with AC and DC on (The Gadgeteer). The top pick, the AC200L, has no independent idle or usable-Wh measurement on the 120 V model. The only figure is BLUETTI's own 12 W self-consumption, quoted by Notebookcheck. So the page can back its runtime claims for the Elite 200 V2 with measurements, but only with maker figures for the AC200L. Illustration, not a measurement: with a 40 W fridge average, 27 W of idle draw makes a 67 W total load against 50 W at 10 W idle. That is about 34% more drain, or roughly 25 h against 34 h from 1,700 Wh.

pages.query: 3d printer for kids
pages.why_used: printingxyz, 3dprinterlab and itechguides give no measured noise for any of these printers. They quote the maker's ratings, such as the A1 mini's '≤48 dB' or the 5M Pro's 50/55 dB, or say nothing about noise. This page puts four measurements from named reviewers side by side: Notebookcheck, Igor's Lab twice and 3DPrint.com. It shows that the enclosed 5M Pro measured a 68 dB average against its 50–55 dB rating, while the enclosed Centauri Carbon 2 measured 44–47 dB. That changes which enclosed printer belongs in a child's room.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the printers' quiet ratings are best-case, mode-dependent figures that aren't comparable with each other: the A1 mini's 'below 48 dB' needs silent mode plus motor noise suppression, the Adventurer 5M Pro is rated 50–55 dB depending on mode, and 3DPrint.com measured the 5M Pro at an average of 68 dB with a 79 dB peak.
angles.decides: It confirms the picks but changes one reason. Enclosed doesn't mean quiet: the 5M Pro's '≤50 dB' (also in our own product name) is its low-noise mode, and 3DPrint.com measured an average of 68 dB with a 79 dB peak. For a printer running in a child's bedroom, the page should say to use the low-noise or silent mode and expect louder bursts. Our 5M Pro product title should drop '≤50 dB' or add 'in low-noise mode'. The temperature row supports Toybox for ages 5–8: its bed is unheated, while the A1 mini has an exposed bed rated up to 80°C and a hotend rated up to 300°C.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Toybox Alpha Four's 75 × 80 × 90 mm build space is 0.54 L, against 5.83 L on the Bambu Lab A1 mini. At the $249 price each page lists, that works out to about $461 per litre of build space for Toybox and about $43 for the A1 mini. None of them says that Toybox refills now cost $15 per 500 g ($30/kg) or that Toybox says other 1.75 mm PLA also works.
angles.decides: It confirms the A1 mini as the best overall pick. For the same $249 starter price it gives about 10.8 times the build volume, which answers the 'outgrown fast' catch. It also changes the Toybox row on our page: its catch currently says 'filament about $60/kg', but refills are now $30/kg, and Toybox says any 1.75 mm PLA works (for example Elegoo at $16.99/kg), so filament cost is no longer a reason to avoid Toybox. Toybox stays the pick for ages 5–8 because of its toy catalog, not because it is good value.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Toybox's own support page says the Toybox takes any third-party 1.75 mm PLA, and that using it 'will not void your warranty'; it rejects any other diameter or material and warns against glitter/speck-filled filament.
angles.decides: This keeps the Toybox Alpha Four as the pick for ages 5–8 and removes the 'proprietary refills' cost objection rivals raise. Running costs are standard 1.75 mm PLA from any brand, warranty intact, or Printer Food at $24.50–$37.80/kg. Two limits to state on the page: Wi-Fi is 2.4 GHz only, and the supported devices are iOS, Android or a web browser. Our 'Catch' cell should read 'Outgrown fast; 75 × 80 × 90 mm' instead of '$60/kg filament'.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Toybox, its pick for younger children, can only join a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network (Toybox: "The printer can't connect to a 5G network") and is set up by linking it to an online Toybox account, with a code the printer shows only once it is connected to the internet.
angles.decides: This confirms the Toybox for ages 5–8, but only for homes with a working 2.4 GHz band and internet access. On a 5 GHz-only network, or a dual-band mesh where Toybox says the 5G network 'will prevent connection', setup can fail. In that case the Bambu A1 mini or the Adventurer 5M Pro is the safer pick. Flashforge added a LAN mode to the 5M series in firmware, so that printer does not depend on a cloud account.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured noise level for any candidate: Igor's Lab measured the open-frame Bambu Lab A1 mini at 55.3 dB(A) from about 40 cm while printing, and Notebookcheck measured the enclosed Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 at 44–47 dB on average with peaks of 54 dB.
angles.decides: Supports the page's enclosed pick for teens and weakens the idea that the A1 mini is a quiet bedroom printer. The A1 mini's measured 55.3 dB(A) is louder than either end of Notebookcheck's 44–47 dB average for the Centauri Carbon 2. The two labs used different distances and methods, and Notebookcheck gave no distance, so present them side by side rather than as a head-to-head result. Because no named lab measured the 5M Pro or Toybox, this does not settle the 5M Pro vs CC2 choice.

It also has Notebookcheck's 150 mm gauge-block result for the Ferret Pro and 3D Printing Industry's reference-block test of the Seal. pages.query: best 3d scanner for reverse engineering
pages.why_used: The rival buyer's guides (invenio3d, TriMech's SHINING 3D guide, 3D Scanner Match) give only headline single-figure accuracies, or no figures at all. None applies the base + rate × length volumetric formula to a real part size, and none says which maker names a test standard. This page works out the error at 300 mm and at 1 m for each scanner from sourced specs, so a shopper can go from their tolerance to a scanner.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the scanners' stated volumetric accuracy into error over a real part length. At 1 m the EinScan Rigil's Laser HD spec (0.04 + 0.06 mm/m) works out to ±0.10 mm, and its IR Rapid spec (0.1 + 0.4 mm/m) to ±0.50 mm. The FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.02 + 0.015 mm/m) works out to ±0.035 mm. That puts the Rigil's laser mode exactly at the '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' limit that ChatGPT's own filter offers, its IR mode far past it, and the UE Pro2 about 3× tighter.
angles.decides: This confirms the higher tier and sharpens the middle one. For parts around 1 m that need ±0.05 mm or better, only the UE Pro2 with photogrammetry meets it on its stated spec (±0.035 mm). The Rigil should only be recommended in Laser HD mode for ±0.1 mm work, and its IR Rapid mode (±0.30 mm at 500 mm) is shape-capture only. The budget picks (MetroX, MetroX Pro, Raptor, Raptor Pro) can only be placed once their mm/m figures come from the maker. Creality's US store pages publish no accuracy figure at all, so the page can't quote one from the store.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a scanner's volumetric-accuracy formula (a mm + b mm/m) into the worst-case error on a part of a stated size; for example, the HandySCAN 3D PRO works out to 0.038 mm on a 300 mm part and 0.080 mm on a 1 m part, and the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry to 0.035 mm on a 1 m part.
angles.decides: It confirms the step-up pick for large parts. Over 1 m, the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.035 mm) holds less than half the worst-case error of the HandySCAN 3D PRO without MaxSHOT (0.080 mm), even though their headline accuracies are about the same (0.02 mm vs 0.030 mm). For parts of about 300 mm or less, the two are within 0.014 mm of each other (0.0245 vs 0.038 mm). That difference matters only below a ±0.05 mm fit tolerance. The budget pick (MetroX vs Raptor) cannot be decided from this run, because their maker formulas could not be opened today (HTTP 429/404).

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which computers the budget picks need. Creality's CR-Scan Raptor manual lists macOS 11.7.7 or later on Apple M1/M2/M3 chips with 16 GB RAM, and on Windows 10/11 64-bit it suggests an i7 7th-gen CPU, an NVIDIA card with 6 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM. Creality sells its Scan Bridge ($299) for the 'Sermoon S1 & Raptor Series' only, and Otter owners must buy a separate version.
angles.decides: For a Mac user, the Raptor is the budget pick that has a maker-documented Apple-silicon path (M1/M2/M3, 16 GB). For a Windows user, Creality suggests an NVIDIA GPU with at least 6 GB VRAM, which adds cost if the PC has integrated graphics. This confirms Raptor versus MetroX as the budget pair, but a full head-to-head needs MetroX's own requirements, which I could not open (see unsourced). On the Revopoint side, the maker's ball-plate listing says its Revo Metro measurement module is 'currently available only for MetroY Ultra and MetroY Ultra CMM models'. So a MetroX buyer gets no Revo Metro accuracy-verification software and should budget separately for inspection software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the per-metre term in a handheld scanner's volumetric-accuracy spec is multiplied by the length of the object being scanned (Revopoint: 'L is the length of the object'). For a reverse-engineering part, the error to expect is therefore base + rate × part length: about 0.06 mm for MetroX vs 0.032 mm for MetroX Pro on a 300 mm part. Creaform measures its figure as sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact; Revopoint gives no test conditions.
angles.decides: This lets the page turn the shopper's tolerance into a pick. With the claimed specs, a part up to about 300 mm can be held near ±0.03-0.04 mm by MetroX Pro (0.032 mm) or HandySCAN 3D PRO (0.038 mm). Standard MetroX at its originally published spec reaches 0.06 mm, which is fine for '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' but not '±0.05 mm precision'. At 1 m the gap widens: MetroX 0.13 mm, MetroX Pro 0.06 mm, HandySCAN PRO 0.08 mm, HandySCAN PRO with MaxSHOT 0.045 mm. On paper this favours MetroX Pro over standard MetroX for anyone at or below ±0.05 mm. It also tells larger-part buyers to add photogrammetry (MaxSHOT or Revopoint's Global Marker mode). One caution: only Creaform states how its figure is measured (sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact). Revopoint's figure has no stated test method, so the two sets of numbers are not measured the same way.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that CNC Kitchen (Stefan Hermann) measured the Creality CR-Scan Raptor with a 100.25 mm ball bar and got 100.24, 100.25 and 100.22 mm. The largest error was 0.03 mm, against Creality's 0.02 mm claim, which is about 0.3 mm per metre. No result states that CNC Kitchen's ball-bar test of the Raptor Pro stayed within about ±0.02 mm with one reading slightly outside spec.
angles.decides: The finding confirms the Raptor as a budget pick for mechanical reverse engineering. It is the only under-$1,000 candidate with a published, named measurement against a reference length: 0.03 mm worst case over 100 mm, roughly at its 0.02 mm claim. It also shows the shopper that real error grows with length (about 0.3 mm/m measured on the Raptor). For the MetroX and MetroX Pro, the only named check is igor'sLAB's statement that the MetroX reaches 0.03 mm on an ideal rectangular block (caliper vs CAD), with no numbers published. So the MetroX's lead in maker-claimed accuracy (0.02 mm + 0.04 mm/m for the Pro) has not been independently measured. The finding does not change who wins at the pro tier, because I found no independent measurements for the Rigil, the FreeScan UE Pro2 or the HandySCAN.

angles.name: Whole category, priced

It also gives no US price for the EinScan Rigil ($4,999 at MatterHackers) or the FreeScan Combo+ ($14,999 at Top3DShop). 3D Scanner Match, the cited buyer page, marks all three 'quote needed'.
angles.decides: This confirms the budget pick and does not overturn it. The MetroX line, from $749 on Revopoint's store, stays the value choice. The next step up costs real money: the EinScan Rigil is $4,999 with no CAD software listed, and its laser volumetric accuracy of 0.04 + 0.06 mm/m is looser than the 0.02 + 0.04 mm/m MetroX Pro figure on our page. The first verifiable US price at metrology grade is the Combo+ at $14,999. The UE Pro2 has no US list price ChatGPT could show, and Creaform sells only by quote. So the page can tell a shopper under about $5k that every listed figure above the MetroX/Raptor tier is either a quote or a Canadian price.

pages.query: best 3d scanner for small objects
pages.why_used: The cited guides say only that handheld scanners need a 'feature-rich subject' and that 'markers matter'. None says the Raptor's 0.02 mm blue-laser mode always needs at least 4 markers in frame (CNC Kitchen), that 3D Printing Industry's Seal test hit trouble on symmetrical parts and had to add reference markers, or that Revopoint sells a marker-topper turntable for featureless objects. This page puts all of that next to each scanner, and it is the deciding factor for small, smooth parts.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the three headline figures it compared on one basis: the MINI 2's '0.02 mm' is single-frame precision and point distance (its accuracy is 0.05 mm), the Seal's '0.01 mm' is an accuracy figure with no test condition and a 0.05 mm resolution, and the Raptor's '0.02 mm' has no condition on any page I could open.
angles.decides: On a like-for-like basis, ChatGPT's 'MINI 2 = 0.02 mm, best for fine detail' compares a point-distance and repeatability figure with the Seal's 0.05 mm resolution and the Raptor's accuracy figure. Comparing accuracy with accuracy, the MINI 2 states 0.05 mm, the Seal 0.01 mm (no condition) and the Seal Lite 0.02 mm. Comparing detail with detail, the MINI 2 states 0.02 mm point distance, the Seal 0.05 mm and the Seal Lite 0.07 mm. This supports our page's split: the MINI 2 for the finest detail (jewelry, 28 mm minis) and the Seal as the all-round pick. It does not settle Seal against Raptor on accuracy, because neither maker's test condition could be sourced.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the MINI 2's closest single frame (52 × 64 mm at 120 mm) covers 3,328 mm², 2.25× less area than the Seal's 100 × 75 mm frame (7,500 mm²), or that a 20 mm part spans 38% of the MINI 2's short side against 27% on the Seal. The price per detail point is also new: the Seal costs $22.70 per point across 1 mm ($454 ÷ 20) and the Seal Lite $15.05 ($215 ÷ 14.3).
angles.decides: It supports the MINI 2 for parts under about 30 mm: its near frame is 2.25× smaller, so a small object fills more of each frame. It supports the Seal and Seal Lite as the value picks. At today's 3DMakerpro store prices the Seal ($454) is $375 under the MINI 2 ($829), and the Seal Lite ($215) is $614 under. ChatGPT priced the Seal at $559.99 and "~$450–$700", which is wrong against the maker store today. I can't confirm or rule out the Raptor and Einstar Vega for tiny parts because I couldn't open their spec pages.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Creality's own US store sells a separate $299 'Creality Scan Bridge' for the Raptor series, on a product page that does not list the Raptor's compatible systems.
angles.decides: It does not change the pick. The MINI 2 stays the default for small objects. The finding only adds a cost note to the Raptor row: its current Creality store price is $879, and Creality sells a $299 Scan Bridge for the Raptor series as an extra. The page should not claim what the bridge does until Creality's manual confirms it.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that these scanners line up their frames by tracking something they can see, and that this fails on the small, smooth or symmetric parts the shopper means. Creality's CR-Scan Raptor blue-laser mode, which ChatGPT picked for small mechanical parts, always needs retroreflective markers with at least 4 in frame. CNC Kitchen found that NIR mode needs no markers but resolves less detail. The MINI 2 needs a marker topper on a turntable for featureless objects, and the markerless Seal had trouble with symmetrical parts and needed reference markers added in 3D Printing Industry's test.
angles.decides: This mostly confirms MINI 2 and Seal for small objects and adds a condition to the Raptor. A small part only takes up a small slice of the scanner's view, and a smooth or symmetric one gives shape tracking little to match. The plan works only with a marker reference (MINI 2 plus the $29.90 marked turntable topper or $19.90 markers in Marker Tracking) or with enough surface detail. The Raptor's 0.02 mm blue-laser mode is the one ChatGPT put forward for small mechanical parts, and it always needs retroreflective markers, at least 4 in frame. A 10–20 mm bracket can't hold 4 markers itself, so they have to go on a marked scan table around it. That means the Raptor is not a markerless pick for small parts. The Seal's marker-free tracking is fine on detailed figurines, but on symmetric or flat-faced parts 3D Printing Industry had to add reference markers.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured accuracy figure from a named tester. 3D Printing Industry measured the 3DMakerpro Seal on a 15 × 20 × 25 mm reference block in turntable mode and got 0.02 mm on X and Z but -0.16 mm on Y, 16 times its 0.01 mm claim. CNC Kitchen measured the Creality CR-Scan Raptor on a 100.25 mm ball bar and got 100.22 to 100.25 mm, at most 0.03 mm off.
angles.decides: This makes the page more trustworthy without changing the ranking. It qualifies the Seal's '0.01 mm' headline: in a named test it held 0.02 mm on two axes but missed by 0.16 mm on the third, on a 25 mm block. That still suits figures and 3D printing but not tight-tolerance small parts. It also gives the Raptor the only artifact-verified result among the candidates (0.03 mm over 100 mm), which supports it as the pick for mechanical parts. The only reviewer figure for the MINI 2 is a general 'within 0.05 mm of CAD' with no per-object numbers. Its 'best for tiny detail' placing therefore rests on maker specs, and the page should say so. Store prices checked today also undercut what ChatGPT showed: Seal $454 and Seal Lite $215, against $559.99 or about $450–700 for the Seal in ChatGPT's answer.

That puts the Seal $375 below the $829 Revopoint MINI 2 and $425 below the $879 Creality Raptor, ChatGPT's #1 and #3 picks. Even with 3DMakerpro's $199 multi-axis turntable, the Seal comes to $653, still under the MINI 2 alone.

The maker's specs give both the Seal and the MINI 2 a 10 mm smallest object (from our page and 3dprinting.com), and the Seal claims 0.01 mm accuracy against the MINI 2's 0.05 mm. Today the Seal also costs $375 less. The MINI 2 keeps its edge only on point distance (0.02 mm) for 28 mm miniatures and jewelry. At $215, the Seal Lite becomes the clear budget pick, well below ChatGPT's 'under $400' bracket. The $879 Raptor and $1,999 Einstar Vega cost much more without a sourced small-object advantage.

pages.query: best 4-bay nas with built-in 10gbe under $700
pages.why_used: No cited rival prices what a working copper 10GbE link costs on each box. They list the QNAP TS-432X at $659 as qualifying without the $69 QNAP cable that takes it to $728, they never price the UNAS Pro 4's $65 SFP+ to RJ45 adapter, and our own page still had the GT at $659.99 instead of today's $559.99. The pick, the UGREEN DXP4800 GT, is not a product we list (UGREEN's GT page returned HTTP 429, so no record was made). Our DXP4800 Plus wins the one-desktop NVMe segment on its PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the QNAP TS-432X's '10GbE' figure (1,181 MB/s read, 887 MB/s write) was measured by QNAP with four Samsung 860 PRO SSDs in RAID 5, or that the SFP+ port ships with no cable or module: QNAP's own DAC is $69 more, which takes the $659 box to $728, over the $700 line.
angles.decides: Five of the six ChatGPT answers seen here (all but the first r1x1 one) put the QNAP TS-432X at $659 as a qualifying 'built-in 10GbE under $700' pick. With nothing in the box to connect the SFP+ port, a shopper buying QNAP's own DAC pays $728, over budget. A shopper on a copper (RJ45) network needs a 10GBASE-T module, and QNAP's store lists only SR and LR optical transceivers as accessories, at no shown price. Its read figure also comes from an all-SSD RAID 5, not the hard-drive array this shopper would fill it with. Normalising both ways keeps the RJ45 UGREEN boxes (DXP4800 Plus, DXP4800 GT) as the picks that work out of the box under $700. The TS-432X becomes a conditional pick: only for a shopper who already has an SFP+ switch or NIC and a cable.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what a working 10GbE copper link costs on each box: the DXP4800 GT gets one for $559.99 with nothing else to buy, but the UniFi UNAS Pro 4 has no 10GbE RJ45 port and its $499 sticker becomes $614 once you add Ubiquiti's listed $549 surcharge-included price and its $65 SFP+ to RJ45 adapter.

It also stops the UNAS Pro 4 from winning on its $499 headline: on an RJ45 network one 10GbE link costs $614 at Ubiquiti's surcharge-included price, or $564 before the surcharge. The Pro 4 only stays cheapest ($512 to $562 with a $13 DAC) for a shopper who already owns an SFP+ switch. The same caveat applies to the TS-432X: it ships with no SFP+ module, so $659 is not the price of a working link. Running the 10GbE link on the DXP4800 Plus costs about $10 a year in extra power.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that QNAP's own TS-432X pages offer only optical SFP+ transceivers (TRX-10GITSFPP-SR, TRX-10GSFP-SR-MLX, TRX-10GSFPP-LR) for the NAS's only 10GbE port, with no DAC cable and no RJ45 10GBASE-T module, or that QNAP says it won't support devices missing from its compatibility list. On an ordinary copper home network, that 10GbE port needs an SFP+ switch, fiber optics, or a module QNAP doesn't support.

pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give peak speeds, maker claims or general warnings about throttling. None of them collects the named long-run tests with duration, room temperature, held write rate and SSD temperature. Those tests are the D1 SSD Plus's 2,550–2,600 MB/s AJA loop and its 15-minute stress test at 30 °C, OWC's one-hour run with no speed drop, the CM642's clean 450 GB write, and the CM850, which had to lose its sleeve to finish. Together they answer 'doesn't throttle on long transfers' directly and cover most candidates.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the long-copy rate next to the headline speed. Makers advertise 3,707–3,900 MB/s from short benchmarks. ASUS's own 30-minute claim for the PA40SU works out to about 1,644 MB/s. PCWorld's 450 GB write on the UGREEN CM642, ChatGPT's 'best for sustained transfers' pick, was slower than a couple of 20Gbps (about 2 GB/s) USB 3.2×2 SSDs, even though the enclosure 'never suffered any thermal related issues'.
angles.decides: The CM642 stays the pick for long copies, but for a narrower reason: in PCWorld's 450 GB test it finished without the thermal dropout that stopped the UGREEN CM850, not because it holds about 3.8 GB/s. On copies of hundreds of GB, the SSD's speed after its cache fills and the copy tool (PCWorld saw Explorer vs FastCopy differences on the PA40SU) limit speed more than the enclosure's fan does. The table should show three numbers for each enclosure: the maker's peak, the host-specific cap (Apple Silicon or Thunderbolt), and any long-copy figure. The footnote should say that a 'no throttle' long write lands around 1.6–2 GB/s.

On 1 TB that is about 12.1 minutes instead of about 6.6, a slowdown that has nothing to do with heat.

That fits ChatGPT's caveat that on long copies the SSD inside, not the 40Gbps link, sets the speed.

angles.decides: This settles the pick for shoppers whose host is Thunderbolt 3 (Intel Mac or older PC): avoid the OWC Express 1M2, which OWC caps at USB 10Gb/s there. Prefer an enclosure whose maker states a Thunderbolt speed: Sabrent EC-U4TN says 2,700 MB/s over Thunderbolt and has a fan. It confirms the existing picks for Apple silicon and USB4/TB4 PCs (OWC: 3,189 MB/s on Apple silicon, 3,836 MB/s on a PC). Two caveats for every pick: use the 40Gbps cable in the box, and don't use an SSD with a heatsink in the 1M2.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that thermal throttling happens inside the SSD itself. The drive's own firmware drops to lower-power states once its composite temperature passes the drive's own thermal-management thresholds. The drive counts each of those events and the seconds spent in them in its standard NVMe health log (Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 transition count and total time). Comparing those counters before and after a long copy is how you tell real throttling from the SLC-cache slowdown that ChatGPT and itechguides could not separate.
angles.decides: This shifts the advice from which enclosure to which enclosure plus which SSD. No enclosure can switch off throttling. It can only keep the SSD under thresholds the SSD's maker sets, and on bus power it has a limited power budget. A Thunderbolt 4 port must supply at least 15 W to accessories, and a plain USB4 port is required to supply half that. That supports the fan model (UGREEN CM642) for multi-hundred-GB copies paired with an efficient Gen4 SSD rather than a Gen5 one. It also gives the page a test anyone can repeat, which rivals lack: log the drive's thermal-management counters during a long copy. If they don't move while speed drops, the cause is the SLC cache, not heat. Caveat: I did not confirm that every ASM2464PD enclosure passes the NVMe health log through to the host. One commenter saw a UGREEN CM850 show up as 'ASMT 2464 USB drive (UAS)' in USBView.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Macworld ran a one-hour Blackmagic test on the OWC Express 1M2 (Thomas Bergbold, Aug 19 2024): the transfer rate did not drop and the case reached about 40 °C. angles.decides: The finding backs the passive pick: the OWC Express 1M2 (one hour, no speed drop, about 40 °C) and the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus (15 minutes at 30 °C ambient, no throttling, 54.8 °C maximum; NAS Compares 2,550–2,600 MB/s write in an AJA loop) both have named long-run tests with no throttling. Its sibling the CM850 lost the drive during that same write with its sleeve on, which shows enclosure cooling matters on the same chip. The page can then say that the one named failure under a long load went to the sleeved CM850 and the passive ZIKE Z666. The finned OWC and TerraMaster bodies and the fan-cooled CM642 held up in every named test.

pages.query: best 8-bay nas under $1500 for a home media library
pages.why_used: The cited pages (WunderTech, ComputingForGeeks, Starry Hope and QNAP's spec sheet) only mark each box yes or no for Plex hardware transcoding, or say 'optional GPU'. None says what each box needs to get it. This page shows that the DXP8800 Plus does it on built-in Quick Sync through Docker. The TS-873A needs a QNAP-supported NVIDIA card that takes no power cable, in one of its two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots, set to QTS mode. The DS1825+ and DS1825neo+ slot is listed for network cards only, and the AS6508T's Atom has no graphics at all. Each step is sourced to Plex, QNAP, Synology, Asustor or Intel.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'Plex hardware transcoding' column means three different things. The UGREEN DXP8800 Plus transcodes on its built-in Quick Sync graphics, but only with Plex in Docker plus Plex Pass. The QNAP TS-873A can transcode only with a bus-powered graphics card such as a GTX 1650 in one of its two PCIe slots, and QNAP says that GPU stops transcoding for QTS while Virtualization Station is using it. The Synology DS1825+ has no graphics-card path at all: its one PCIe slot (x4 link) lists only network cards, so adding 10GbE (E10G30-T1, one RJ45 port) uses the only slot.
angles.decides: Confirms the DXP8800 Plus as the pick for running Plex or Jellyfin on the NAS: it is the only candidate that transcodes out of the box and also has 2× 10GbE built in. It changes how the QNAP should be presented: the TS-873A can transcode, but only by giving one of its two PCIe slots to a graphics card, so a GPU plus 10GbE uses both slots. The DS1825+ stays a storage-only or direct-play pick: its single slot can hold a 10GbE card or nothing else, and no graphics card is listed for it.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the yearly electricity cost of running each 8-bay NAS 24/7. At the EIA 2026 year-to-date US residential rate of 18.19¢/kWh and the makers' own power figures, that comes to $112.16/yr for the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus during drive access ($46.19 with drives hibernated), $95.77 ($29.22) for the Synology DS1825+, $86.15 ($40.90) for the QNAP TS-873A and $106.60 ($59.28) for the Asustor AS6508T.
angles.decides: It confirms the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus pick rather than overturning it. The UGREEN costs about $16–17 a year more to run than the DS1825+ under both maker test states ($112.16 − $95.77 = $16.39 in access; $46.19 − $29.22 = $16.97 hibernated), or roughly $82–85 over five years. That is small next to what the Synology lacks: Quick Sync and built-in 10GbE (it needs an E10G30 card). It does show the TS-873A is the cheapest to run under load, and the AS6508T's high hibernation floor (37.2 W) makes it the most expensive box to leave idle. One caveat: the makers' test conditions are not the same (QNAP tests with all bays filled; Synology and UGREEN don't name their drives). NASCompares, as reported by Starry Hope, measured the UGREEN at about 64–66 W idle with ten drives fitted, which would push its real idle cost toward the access figure.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what QNAP's 'optional GPU' Plex route on the TS-873A actually requires: QNAP's product page says the PCIe Gen3 x4 slots take only entry-level NVIDIA cards that need no power cables (it names the GeForce GTX 1650), a card in use by Virtualization Station stops hardware transcoding in QTS, and Plex's own document says the card must be set to QTS mode, needs Plex Media Server v1.15.1.791 or newer, and only the first card is used.
angles.decides: This confirms the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus as the Plex pick. On the QNAP TS-873A, Plex hardware transcoding means buying a separate entry-level NVIDIA card with no power connector, running it in QTS mode (not shared with VMs), and depending on QNAP's NVIDIA driver packages. One Plex forum user reported GTX 1650 transcoding on a TS-873A failing after a QTS 5.2.3 update with no fix posted. The DXP8800 Plus has Quick Sync on the CPU, so it needs no card. For a media library with transcoding, the TS-873A only makes sense if the buyer accepts the card cost and driver risk. Otherwise it is a direct-play or storage box, like the DS1825+, which has no GPU path at all: its slot list names only 10GbE and 25GbE NICs.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Synology DS1825+'s only PCIe slot (Gen3 x8, x4 link) is listed for network cards only, so no card can give it hardware transcoding. The same results don't say that the QNAP TS-873A gets Plex hardware transcoding only from an entry-level NVIDIA card that needs no power cable, fitted in one of its two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots of a 250 W box, or that a wider card uses up the second slot. They also don't say that the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus's Quick Sync reaches Plex only when you bind-mount the GPU device (/dev/dri) into the Docker container and the server has a Plex Pass.
angles.decides: This confirms the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus as the pick for running Plex or Jellyfin on the NAS. It is the only one of the three that transcodes in hardware with nothing added, and it keeps its 2× 10GbE and PCIe slot free. The DS1825+ has no hardware-transcoding path at all: its slot is listed for 10/25GbE cards only. That makes it a storage-only pick for players that direct-play. The TS-873A can transcode, but only after buying a passively powered NVIDIA card that QNAP supports. That card uses a PCIe slot, and a wider card also blocks the second slot, which is where a 10GbE card would go. The setup also needs a Plex Pass, so the 'optional GPU' route costs more and takes networking headroom away. On every box, Plex hardware transcoding and remote viewing of your own library are paid features, while Jellyfin's are free.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives named, measured numbers for the two boxes it recommends most. NASCompares (Rob Andrews, 2025-07-24) measured the Synology DS1825+ fully loaded with eight drives at 57–62 W idle, 35–38 dBA idle and 290–295 MB/s sequential read over one 2.5GbE port. NASCompares (2024-04-19) measured the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus at 650–700 MB/s over 10GbE, roughly 2.3× faster for media copies.
angles.decides: This confirms the DXP8800 Plus pick rather than changing it. A media library mostly means moving large files. Measured, the DS1825+ tops out near 290–295 MB/s on a single 2.5GbE link (about 580 MB/s peak with link aggregation). The DXP8800 Plus did 650–700 MB/s on 10GbE with no add-in card. Measured idle draw is about the same: 57–62 W for the DS1825+ with eight drives, and about 64–66 W for the DXP8800 Plus with ten drives (secondhand via Starry Hope). So power is not a reason to pick Synology. For a living-room shelf, the measured 35–38 dBA idle with eight drives is a better guide than the 23.8 dB(A) spec. The TS-873A's quiet figures (25 dBA idle, 31 dBA moderate) come from a 2021 test without a full set of drives, so they don't compare directly.
