pages.query: best all-in-one home server under $800 for docker plex and a couple of vms
pages.why_used: None of the rival pages quote Plex's own rule that hardware transcoding "is not currently possible inside of virtual machines". Several of them, and ChatGPT's answers, tell shoppers to pass the iGPU to a Docker VM, which is the layout Plex says won't work. This page uses Plex's and Proxmox's documentation to put Plex in a container on the host and keep the VMs off the GPU. It then compares all-in-one boxes by the RAM they ship with, since that decides whether two VMs fit under $800.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: None of the results ChatGPT got says that Plex's own hardware-transcoding page (last modified 2026-10-27) lists only Intel (Quick Sync/VAAPI) and NVIDIA engines on Linux and mentions only Intel Quick Sync for Docker; AMD appears only in the Windows notes, supported 'as is' and not fully tested. On the stated record, the AMD all-in-ones ChatGPT offered, such as the Aoostar WTR Pro 5825U as 'best for internal HDD storage', have no documented Plex hardware transcoding under Proxmox, Unraid or TrueNAS.
angles.decides: Two corrections decide the pick. (1) Plex transcoding: for the branch where media drives go inside the box, the AMD boxes fall out (WTR Pro 5825U, WTR Max 8845HS, GMKtec K8 Plus) because Plex documents no hardware transcoding for them on Linux. That leaves Intel bay boxes: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at $619.99 with 8 GB included, or the Aoostar WTR Max Intel i5-1235U at $529 barebone with 6 HDD bays, 2× 10GbE and DDR5 up to 96 GB, before RAM. (2) Price on one basis: price every option as configured with 32 GB RAM and 1 TB NVMe, no hard drives. On that basis the 'cheap' $375 MS-01 SE barebone becomes $775 and the MS-01's DDR5 is costlier still: bitdoze priced a 32 GB DDR5 kit at $569.98. So a mini PC with RAM included, or a NAS that ships with RAM, beats a barebone plus retail DDR5 under $800. The table footnote should be: 'Plex HW transcode on Linux/Docker = Intel or NVIDIA only (Plex support, 2026-10-27); barebone prices shown as configured at 32 GB / 1 TB.'

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each candidate costs to leave idling 24/7 at the US average electricity rate. Measured idle draw × 8,760 h × $0.1816/kWh gives about $14/yr for the Aoostar WTR Pro 5825U, $21 for the Minisforum MS-01 i5, $24 for the TerraMaster F4-425 Pro and $39–48 for the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus. Added to today's maker-store price, three years of idle power comes to about $421 (WTR Pro), $532 (MS-01 barebone), $736 (DXP4800 Plus) and $772 (F4-425 Pro).
angles.decides: This supports the split ChatGPT keeps making, with a cost attached. If the drives go in the box, the Aoostar WTR Pro 5825U is cheapest to buy ($379) and to run (8.7 W average idle, about $14/yr). The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus costs about $315 more over three years, though it adds Quick Sync and the UGOS apps. If the media lives elsewhere, the MS-01 i5 at 13.2 W stays cheap to run, but only without an add-in NIC: a ConnectX-5 raised idle to 32.1 W, about $51/yr. Caveat: the reviewers tested with different drive setups. The DXP4800 Plus figure includes WD Red HDDs, the F4-425 Pro figure is SSD-only, and Notebookcheck didn't say which drives were in the WTR Pro. So the NAS gap partly reflects the drives, which the page has to say.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Plex's own support article (last modified 2026-10-27) says hardware-accelerated streaming 'is not currently possible inside of virtual machines', and that Plex lists only Intel VAAPI, NVIDIA NVENC and software x264 as its Linux encoders. The supported layout is Plex in Docker or LXC on the host with /dev/dri bind-mounted, on an Intel Quick Sync chip with Plex Pass. That rules out the 'pass the iGPU to a Docker VM' layout ChatGPT gave in four of its seven answers, and it leaves the AMD Aoostar WTR Pro with no Plex hardware encoder on Linux.
angles.decides: It confirms an Intel Quick Sync box over the AMD Aoostar WTR Pro or Synology DS925+ for Plex. It also sets the layout: run Plex in Docker or LXC on the host, not in a VM, and keep VMs for the other workloads. On the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus that means Plex in UGOS Docker, which our page's 'no iGPU passthrough' VM note already implies. For the MS-01 SE, which ChatGPT kept recommending, Minisforum's own listing says DDR4 (up to 64 GB), not the MS-01's DDR5, and NASCompares confirms there is no SFP+. So the SE is the cheaper compute pick (barebone $375 but out of stock in the US; $775 with 32 GB and 1 TB, in stock), and the shopper should budget DDR4 SO-DIMMs, not DDR5.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Plex's own support article says 'Hardware-Accelerated Streaming is not currently possible inside of virtual machines', while Plex does support bind-mounting the Intel GPU device into a Docker container. That means Quick Sync transcoding belongs in a container on the host (Docker or a Proxmox LXC with /dev/dri), not in the 'Docker VM with iGPU passthrough' layout that ChatGPT told shoppers to build in at least three of the chats.
angles.decides: This confirms the picks more than it changes them. On any Intel box, run Plex in Docker or an LXC on the host and keep the 'couple of VMs' free of GPU work. That way the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus not passing its iGPU to VMs in UGOS stops counting against it, because Plex's supported setup never uses a VM anyway. On the i5-12600H mini PCs (MS-01, MS-01 SE, NAB6 Lite), the iGPU cannot be split between VMs the old way: Intel's GVT-g guide covers only 5th–8th gen, and Proxmox says a device passed to a VM can no longer be used on the host. The page should tell shoppers to put Plex in an LXC using Proxmox's dev[n] device option and not to pass the iGPU to a VM. For the AMD option (Aoostar WTR Pro), Plex's own article lists no AMD hardware transcoding support on Linux, which supports keeping it as the 'bays, not Plex transcoding' pick.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states device-level lab measurements for the 4-bay all-in-one boxes: Notebookcheck measured the Aoostar WTR Pro (Ryzen 7 5825U) at 8.7 W median idle, 46.2 W median load and 10,103 points in Cinebench R23 multi, while KitGuru measured the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at 24.25 W idle on 2.5GbE (30.45 W on 10GbE) with WD Red drives, and Notebookcheck's Geekbench 6.7.1 multi-core averages put the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium 8505 at 5,860 points against 10,748 for the i5-12600H used in the MS-01 and NAB6 Lite.
angles.decides: This puts numbers on the trade-off ChatGPT only describes in words. For VM headroom, Notebookcheck's Geekbench 6.7.1 averages show the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium 8505 at about 55% of the i5-12600H (5,860 vs 10,748 multi-core). Notebookcheck also shows the WTR Pro 5825U at 10,103 Cinebench R23 multi with a measured idle median of only 8.7 W. Together that backs the WTR Pro 5825U as the stronger VM host among the drive-bay all-in-ones, at a low idle draw, though it loses Quick Sync for Plex. The DXP4800 Plus stays the Plex/Quick Sync pick but measures at 24–30 W idle with drives, per KitGuru, and has half the CPU. For the 'media elsewhere' branch, ServeTheHome measured the MS-01 at 25–29 W idle, against IdleWatt's 12 W for the i5. Idle results clearly depend on the test configuration, so the page should present power as ranges with each lab's conditions next to them.
products: Minisforum MS-01 / MS-01 SE / NAB6 Lite / M1 Plus (Core i5-12600H)

On the mini-PC side, only a model sold with RAM at checkout fits. The page should say plainly: price the RAM before you buy a barebones unit.

pages.query: best all-nvme
pages.why_used: ComputingForGeeks and HomelabCompass both list slot widths, but neither gives any processor's total PCIe lane count. ComputingForGeeks also leaves the UGREEN DXP480T Plus's x2 slots as 'generation disputed'. This page uses Intel's own lane counts (20 lanes for the i5-1235U, of which up to 8 are Gen4 on the CPU; 9 Gen3 lanes for the N95 and i3-N305) to settle that question and to show what the extra drives add. It also pairs this with the Asustor FS6806X, which is now under $900 and has 12 Gen4 lanes feeding its six slots.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states load power on a common basis: in the same Liliputing 100 GB-copy test (same reviewer, Ian W Morrison), the UGREEN DXP480T Plus drew about 55 W writing to the NAS and the TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus drew 36.2 W with eight drives, and Asustor's '17.9 W (Operation)' rating for the Flashstor 6 Gen2 is about half of the 32.8 W KitGuru measured during writes.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The F8 SSD Plus and FS6806X draw roughly the same at load (about 33–42 W). The DXP480T Plus draws about 13 W more when writing a 100 GB file (55 vs 41.6 W at peak in Liliputing's tests) and comes with a 140 W adapter, against 90 W and 72 W for the other two. That is the price of its i5 and its x4 Gen4 slots, and it matters only to buyers who care about power under heavy use. At idle the three are within 6.6 W of each other, which works out to about 58 kWh a year left on 24/7. The page can footnote that maker wattage figures can't be compared: Asustor's 17.9 W 'operation' sits between KitGuru's idle and load readings, and TerraMaster's roughly 45 W is a worst case with all eight drives reading and writing.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each all-NVMe box draws at idle for each M.2 slot, or what that comes to per year. From named reviewers' wall-meter idle readings: Asustor Flashstor 6 Gen2 is 13.1 W ÷ 6 = 2.2 W per slot (115 kWh/yr), TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus is 19.7 W ÷ 8 = 2.5 W per slot (173 kWh/yr) and UGREEN DXP480T Plus is 18 W ÷ 4 = 4.5 W per slot (158 kWh/yr).
angles.decides: This adds to the pick rather than changing it. For an always-on box, the Flashstor 6 Gen2 has the lowest idle draw per slot and per year, even with six slots on Gen4 lanes. The F8 SSD Plus gives the most slots for little more power per slot. But each slot is Gen3 x1, so one drive can't fill 10GbE (1.25 ÷ 0.985 = 1.27, so at least two drives striped). The DXP480T Plus costs about twice as much idle power per slot as the other two. You get the i5 and Thunderbolt for that. The three reviewers used different drive setups, so the per-slot figures are a guide, not a ranking from one lab.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Asustor's own memory rule for the Flashstor 6 Gen2 (FS6806X): it has 2 SO-DIMM slots and a 64 GB maximum, and ECC is switched off if a non-ECC module is installed or mixed with an ECC one. Asustor's own spec page and datasheet also disagree on whether the 8 GB module it ships with is ECC.
angles.decides: This settles the main compatibility split under $900. Among the shortlisted boxes, only the UGREEN DXP480T Plus can be linked directly to a PC over a cable: Liliputing ran Thunderbolt 4 direct at about 1.51 GB/s. Asustor says the FS6806X's USB4 ports take only USB4/Thunderbolt 3/4 storage devices and cannot connect host-to-host. A shopper who wants a direct cable to a laptop should take the DXP480T Plus. A shopper who wants ECC should take the FS6806X, but should confirm the stock module is ECC or replace it, because adding an ECC module next to a non-ECC one switches ECC off. Our page also needs two fixes. Asustor publishes the FS6806X lane map (1× Gen4 x4, 3× x2, 2× x1), so 'lane routing unverified' can go. And our FS6806X link (p_id=93) opens the Lockerstor 12R/16R Pro Gen2 page; the right page is p_id=90.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the CPU's PCIe lane budget that limits each box. Intel lists 20 lanes in total for the DXP480T Plus's i5-1235U, and its Gen4 lanes come only from the CPU, which has at most 8 on U/P-series chips. Liliputing's slot map gives those 8 to drive slots 1–2, so slots 3–4, the OS drive and the 10GbE port must run on the Gen3 PCH lanes. Intel's N95 and i3-N305 have only 9 PCIe Gen3 lanes in total, which are shared by up to eight NVMe slots and the 10GbE NIC.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick and does not change it. Even if the DXP480T Plus's slots 3–4 are Gen3 x2, each still moves about 1.97 GB/s, more than one 10GbE port carries (1.25 GB/s raw). Over the network all four slots are limited by the port, not the slot. The lane split only matters for drive-to-drive copies or Thunderbolt transfers inside the box. On the TerraMaster F8 SSD, F8 SSD Plus and F4 SSD, every drive and the NIC share a ceiling of 9 Gen3 lanes. Adding more drives there buys capacity, not more speed per drive, which supports recommending them for capacity per dollar rather than speed.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states any measured figure for the TerraMaster F4 SSD. In its lab review, HWBusters measured 9 W at idle with the unit fully populated and SSDs at 38–39 °C after an hour in a 29 °C room. On noise, it measured 9.1, 18.5 and 24.4 dBA at 1 m (fan on low, medium and full).
angles.decides: This settles the low-power pick under $900. With all four slots filled, the F4 SSD idles at 9 W (HWBusters). That is under half of the DXP480T Plus (about 18 W, Liliputing) and the F8 SSD Plus (19.7 W, Liliputing), and below the Beelink ME Mini with six SSDs (about 16.9 W, NASCompares). HWBusters also measured idle SSD temperatures without heatsinks, which helps a quiet, always-on home box. It does not change the performance pick. The DXP480T Plus has Gen4 x4 bays 1–2 and Gen4 x2 bays 3–4 (Liliputing's lane readout), plus 1.09–1.15 GB/s over 10GbE. HWBusters published F4 SSD throughput only as chart images; it says the 5GbE link was saturated.

pages.query: bone conduction or headphones
pages.why_used: The rival answer runs no search, cites no page, and only ever offers bone conduction for running and cycling. It never says that Bluetooth fails underwater, that IP55 headsets like the OpenRun Pro 2 are not for swimming, or that a swimmer needs IP68 plus onboard MP3 storage. Swimming is the one use where bone conduction is the only answer, and this page names the sets that qualify, with dated prices.

angles.decides: This confirms the split by use, and now with matched numbers. At the same 75% volume, the OpenRun Pro 2 runs 12 h against the Run Plus's 8 h, so for road running the Shokz lasts 50% longer per charge. But the OpenRun Pro 2 and the AeroFit 2 are both IP55, and Shokz says the OpenRun Pro 2 is not for water sports, so anyone who swims must take the MOJAWA (IP68, 2 m for 2 h). The Space One's 40 h with ANC is a 50%-volume figure, so it can't be set directly against the 75%-volume bone conduction numbers. Even so, it is about 3x or more on any basis, which keeps over-ears as the pick for desk and travel.

angles.decides: This confirms the split: bone conduction for workouts, where 30 g and no clamp on the ears matter and 12 h covers about 12 one-hour runs. Over-ear is for long listening days, where 40 h with ANC means about 20 two-hour commutes per charge, at $2.50 per rated ANC hour for the Space One against $5.00 for the Space One Pro, which has the same 40 h. On noise, OutdoorGearLab found the XPeak 2.0's 'Stealth M24' motor was not noticeably quieter than other bikes in its test, despite Lectric's '400% quieter' claim. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Bambu Studio's own PLA profile sets PLA's 'Softening temperature' (temperature_vitrification) at 45 °C but its default Textured PEI bed temperature at 55 °C. Bambu Studio's warning tooltip fires when the bed is at or above the softening temperature and tells you to open the front door and/or take off the upper glass to avoid nozzle clogs. Textured PEI at Bambu's own 55 °C default is 10 °C over the 45 °C softening value, so Bambu Studio will tell you to open the door or lift the lid. pages.query: best cassette deck
pages.why_used: StereoNET (cited in all three chats) lists the W-1200 only as having 'noise reduction'. Tape Lab gives no specs. Home Audio Advice says the W-1200 'includes Dolby B noise reduction', which implies it records with Dolby B. None of them says that both new decks have one shared record/play head and that their noise reduction works only on playback, so no tape they record carries Dolby encoding. Nor do they say that neither deck can record on metal tape, or that the vintage picks have separate record and playback heads with separate Dolby encode and decode circuits. That is the reason behind the 'buy new or buy vintage' split, and this page puts it into the table for six decks.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on the same WRMS scale the new TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII are rated at 0.25% wow and flutter. That is 11–13 times the 0.019% to 0.022% the Nakamichi Dragon and Sony TC-KA7ES are rated at. The new decks' frequency response is also quoted at a looser ±4 dB and stops at 15 kHz, while the vintage decks reach 22 kHz at ±3 dB.
angles.decides: It confirms the split pick and puts a number on it. For playback fidelity, a serviced vintage 3-head deck is in a different class: rated speed stability is 11–13 times better on the same WRMS basis. On paper, though, S/N is not the gap: the TEAC's 59 dB A-weighted and the TC-KA7ES's 57 dB with Dolby off are about the same. For the 'buy new' pick, the TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII have identical makers' deck specs (0.25% WRMS; 30 Hz–15 kHz ±4 dB on Type II tape; Dolby B-equivalent playback NR only). So the choice between them comes down to price, the remote, and rack mounting, not sound. Footnote for the table: the Revox B215's '0.1%' is a DIN 45507 peak-weighted maximum, not WRMS, so it can't be ranked against the 0.25% WRMS figures. Reviewers measured it at 0.01–0.042% RMS.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the new TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII are rated at 0.25% WRMS wow and flutter. That is about 13 times the Nakamichi Dragon's rated 0.019% WRMS (0.25 / 0.019 = 13.2) and 6 to 25 times the 0.01–0.042% RMS that reviewers measured on the Revox B215.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's split and puts a number on it. If sound quality is the goal, a serviced vintage 3-head deck is the pick, because the W-1200 and 202MKVII flutter is roughly an order of magnitude higher. If the goal is warranty, dubbing and USB digitizing, the W-1200 is still the new-deck pick: it is lighter and has a remote. Both new decks share the same 0.25% transport rating and 48 kHz/16-bit USB, so the choice between the two comes down to rack ears versus home use, not sound.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that both new-production picks, the TEAC W-1200 and the Tascam 202MKVII, cannot record Type IV metal tape and cannot record with Dolby-style noise reduction. Their noise-reduction switch only cuts hiss on playback. So a shopper who wants to make Dolby-encoded or metal-tape recordings needs a vintage deck.
angles.decides: This backs up ChatGPT's split, with a reason the rival pages don't give. The W-1200 and 202MKVII are the right picks for playing old tapes and digitizing them over USB. They record only Type I and II tape, and their noise reduction can't be applied while recording. Shoppers who want to record at full quality, using metal tape or Dolby noise reduction, need a serviced vintage 3-head deck. A wiki lists the Sony TC-KA7ES with Dolby B, C and S and Type I/II/IV tape, but I did not get a maker document for it. Between the two new decks, the 202MKVII's maker page lists current Windows 11 and macOS releases. The W-1200's manual lists systems only up to Windows 10 and macOS 10.13, as of November 2017.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the two new decks it recommends (TEAC W-1200, Tascam 202MKVII) have one combined record/playback head per well and a noise-reduction circuit that works only on playback. TEAC's manual says it 'cannot be used when recording to achieve a noise reduction effect like Dolby B', and neither deck records on metal tape. So every tape these decks make carries no noise-reduction encoding. The vintage picks have separate record and playback heads and separate Dolby encode and decode circuits (Nakamichi's 'Double Dolby', the Revox B215's four Dolby B/C ICs).
angles.decides: This confirms the split ChatGPT only hinted at ('not as high-fidelity'), and it gives the physical reason. For playing and digitizing existing tapes, the W-1200 or 202MKVII works: Dolby B-equivalent decode on playback, USB at up to 48 kHz/16-bit, Type I/II/IV playback. For making new recordings at the best quality, the new decks can't do it. They record un-encoded on Type I/II only, with no off-tape monitoring. A shopper who wants to record needs a serviced 3-head deck with record-side Dolby: Nakamichi CR-7A or Dragon, Revox B215, Sony TC-KA7ES (Dolby S). Pick the W-1200 for a buy-new playback and ripping deck. Pick the CR-7A or B215 for recording.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for any deck sold new today: HomeTheaterHifi's John E. Johnson Jr. measured 0.52% RMS wow and flutter on the TEAC W-1200, recording and playing back his own test tones. That is twice TEAC's 0.25% spec. On the same tones the 1 kHz distortion was 1.9–2.6%, and the response on Type I tape was down 10 dB by 10 kHz.

The W-1200 stays the best deck you can buy new, and the Tascam 202MKVII uses the same transport and lists the same 0.25% spec, so the measurement does not separate the two. pages.query: cd player with bluetooth
pages.why_used: The cited pages list no transmit codecs for any portable player (macmyths and rottenwifi say outright they have none; howtovr names only SBC for one boombox), and none says the standard FiiO DM13 can't transmit. None explains that AirPods and AAC/LDAC headphones end up on SBC whichever player sends to them. This page shows, for each candidate, which codec it sends and which codec common headphones actually receive, based on the maker spec pages and the Bluetooth SIG A2DP spec.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a 'Bluetooth' spec on a premium portable CD player can mean the wrong direction or the wrong SKU: FiiO's own DM13 page says the standard DM13 cannot transmit Bluetooth (only the DM13 BT sends to headphones, in aptX HD, aptX LL, aptX or SBC), and the Shanling EC Play's LDAC works only when it receives from a phone, because it sends to headphones in SBC only.
angles.decides: This confirms the FiiO DM13 BT as the premium pick for someone sending CDs to Bluetooth headphones or a speaker. It transmits aptX HD and aptX LL, while the EC Play sends SBC only. It also adds a buying rule: the listing must say 'DM13 BT', because the standard DM13 has no transmitter. The EC Play is the better choice only if the shopper wants to stream from a phone into the player (LDAC receive) or needs the longer 12 h rating. For the cheap tier, the battery figures normalised to Wh show the Coby CD201 carries about 39% of the DM13's stored energy (5.55 vs 14.25 Wh), so its 6 h rating is the one to treat with caution.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: None of the results ChatGPT got turns a battery rating into full CDs per charge. Worked out from the makers' own figures, the Shanling EC Play plays about 9.7 full 74-minute discs per charge and the FiiO DM13 about 8.1. Neither maker gives a runtime with Bluetooth transmit on, so both counts are for wired listening.
angles.decides: This supports keeping the battery claim on the pick modest and labelled as wired. The DM13 rating of 10 h or more (about 8 full CDs) was measured at 32 Ω wired with the display off. FiiO publishes no Bluetooth figure, so our current cell saying '10 h rated, ~8 h measured' should name its conditions and its measurer, or the '~8 h measured' part should come out. On rated figures, the Shanling EC Play gets more discs per charge (about 9.7 vs 8.1) from a smaller battery (3,450 vs 3,750 mAh) and weighs less (418 g vs 450 g). It transmits SBC only, while the DM13 transmits aptX HD and aptX LL. The runtime point favours Shanling and the codec point favours FiiO, so the pick turns on whether the shopper's headphones support aptX.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the FiiO DM13 sends only SBC and aptX codecs (no AAC or LDAC) and comes in a 'Standard version' that cannot send Bluetooth at all. So AirPods (AAC/SBC) or an AAC/LDAC headphone such as the soundcore Space One gets plain SBC from it, the same as from the SBC-only Shanling EC Play.
angles.decides: The DM13's aptX HD / aptX Low Latency edge over the Shanling EC Play (SBC-only transmit) is real only with aptX-capable headphones. With AirPods or an AAC/LDAC headphone like the soundcore Space One, both players send SBC, so the pick should rest on battery, anti-skip and price, not codec. The shopper must also buy the DM13 Bluetooth version, because FiiO says the Standard version cannot transmit. The Panasonic SC-PM270 and GPX BCB119B-type boomboxes only receive from a phone. For wireless headphones, only the DM13 BT, the EC Play, or a transmitter like the 1Mii B06TX on an existing player qualify.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Bluetooth A2DP standard makes SBC the only codec every transmitter and every headphone must support (Bluetooth SIG, A2DP 1.4 §4.2.1). Better codecs are optional and work only when both ends share one. The FiiO DM13 sends aptX, aptX HD, aptX Low Latency and SBC but not AAC, so AirPods Pro 3 (AAC and SBC), soundcore Space One (SBC, AAC and LDAC) and Marshall Major V (SBC, AAC and LC3) all fall back to SBC. That is the only codec the Shanling EC Play transmits.
angles.decides: This confirms the plan works: any transmitting CD player will play through any A2DP headphone or speaker, because SBC is mandatory on both sides. It changes how to pick between the DM13 and the EC Play. The DM13's aptX HD only matters with headphones that also take aptX HD. With AirPods, soundcore Space One or Marshall Major V, both players send SBC, so that codec advantage disappears. The choice then comes down to battery (DM13 10 h rated, EC Play 12 h), skip protection and price. The EC Play's LDAC and AAC only work in its receive mode (phone to player), not when it sends CD audio.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Audio Science Review (NTTY) bench-tested the FiiO DM13. That test found 0.0015% THD+N, 98 dB dynamic range and 10 h of battery life, and the player passed physical dropout test discs up to 3 mm. That makes it the only candidate whose skip resistance and runtime anyone has measured.
angles.decides: This backs the FiiO DM13 as the pick for someone who will carry the player around. It is the only candidate with a named lab result on skip resistance (dropout test discs) and on battery life (10 h on the ASR bench). Rivals only repeat buffer seconds from the box. Two cautions apply. First, ASR tested the non-Bluetooth DM13, so nothing has been measured on the Bluetooth link of the DM13 BT. Second, runtime reports for the DM13 run from just over 8 h (HomeTheaterHifi) to 10 h (ASR). The table should say '8–10 h measured, by source' rather than '~8 h'.

pages.why_used: The cited Home Welder and Woodworking Projects pages only say a pedal is 'included' or 'sold separately'. Neither says which pedal plugs into which machine, that LOTOS and PrimeWeld spare pedals are locked to particular models, or that YesWelder's pedal option costs less than its bare welder. This page prices every AC/DC pick with its pedal and lists each pedal's plug and the maker's compatibility list.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that how bright a laser looks equals its power times the eye's sensitivity at its wavelength. By the CIE 1988 photopic table, the eye's sensitivity is 0.710 at 520 nm and 0.885 at 532 nm (green) but 0.107 at 650 nm (red). That makes a green laser look about 6.6–8.3× brighter than a red laser of the same power. Because the laser class caps power (Class 2 at 1 mW, Class 3R at 5 mW), a green Class 3R laser can look about 5× brighter than a green Class 2 laser like the Klein 56074, and about 33× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 laser.
angles.decides: This confirms that the main pick should be a green Class 3R light (the US Wuben X5 3R or the US Olight ArkPro) for anyone who wants to point at things at a distance or in daylight. The arithmetic: the 5 mW Class 3R cap × 0.710 = 3.55 brightness-weighted mW. A Class 2 green like the Klein 56074 (<1 mW) gives under 0.71, and a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 gives 0.107. So ChatGPT's 'Best for work' Klein 56074 has at most a fifth of a 3R laser's visible brightness, and its red budget picks (Hyper Tough, Coast PM50R, Fenix E06R, Klein 56040) are far dimmer still. The same arithmetic means a Class 1 green at the 0.39 mW our page lists for the Wuben X5 Class 1 (0.39 × 0.710 = 0.277) would still look about 2.6× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red. That gives the X5 Class 1 a sourced reason to rank above red lasers for workplaces that ban Class 3R.

Angle C is also the most complete: the 'MacBook: two extended screens' cell is sourced for every row, while the charging-source angle (A/B) has no sourced adapter rating for the T722 or the TESmart docks.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the AV Access KD-E10's '100 W laptop charging' only works when you plug your laptop's own charger into the dock, because its included adapter is 12 V / 3 A (36 W) and just runs the dock. The iDock M10, which is also labelled '100 W', ships with a 20 V / 6 A (120 W) adapter and sends power to the laptop over its included dual-head cable.
angles.decides: For a Windows-laptop shopper choosing between the two AV Access docks, the KD-E10 ($169.99) is not a one-cable dock. You still need the laptop's charger at the desk, plugged into the KD-E10. The iDock M10 ($289.99) powers the laptop from its own 120 W adapter. On a Mac the KD-E10 also mirrors its two screens. The AV Access KD-E10 lists '100 W' PD, but its brick is 12 V × 3 A = 36 W, the dock itself can draw up to 33.12 W, and AV Access says to plug in the laptop's original adapter as well. The M10's own 120 W brick covers 100 W PD, and on M4/M5 or Pro/Max Macs it runs two extended screens, which works out to $289.99 / 2 = $145 per extended screen. The KD-E10 at $169.99 still makes sense for a Windows laptop if the shopper keeps their laptop charger at the desk anyway. Our own table should change its KD-E10 'Laptop charging: 100 W' cell to '100 W pass-through (needs your laptop charger)'. The iDock C10 supplies 60 W from its own brick. That is 60 / 140 = 43% of a 140 W MacBook Pro charger's rating, and AV Access itself sends 140 W laptops to the KD-E10 or the original adapter.

pages.query: best lifepo4 battery charger
pages.why_used: Clamp & Crank works out dollars per amp only for the NOCO GENIUS10 and prices no LiFePO4-only charger. PowerGearGuide, Epic Van Life and RV Parts Giant print no prices, and the Victron and NOCO spec pages carry none. This page puts cost per amp beside refill time and charge voltage for all seven chargers, at today's prices.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the four picks' lithium charge voltages side by side. Victron's Li-ion mode stops at 14.2 V and then holds the battery at 13.5 V with no float, while the Redodo and LiTime 20 A chargers go to 14.6 V and then shut off. Peak charging power is about 213 W for the Victron 12/15 (15 A × 14.2 V) against about 292 W for the 20 A units (20 A × 14.6 V), and Victron gives full rated output only up to 30 °C.
angles.decides: Confirms the 20 A, 14.6 V pick (Redodo 20A at $82.99 today) for a shopper who wants a 12 V LiFePO4 battery filled fast and full. It delivers about 37% more power than the Victron 12/15 and charges to 14.6 V, then shuts off. The Victron fits a battery left connected for months, as on a boat: it charges more gently to 14.2 V and then holds at 13.5 V. It is not the 'faster 15 A' choice its amp rating suggests. Separately, our table's Victron row 'Wakes a shut-off BMS: Not stated by the dealer' should change: Victron's own product page says the charger revives a battery 'even from 0 volts'.

For US buyers it narrows the Victron choice to the 120 V version. Redodo 20A is $82.99 today, which keeps it as the budget 20 A pick over LiTime ($102.99 on our page, 2026-11-06).

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got ties Victron's under-voltage-protection reset to lithium batteries. Victron's own manual says the Blue Smart IP65 resets a tripped UVP on a Li-ion battery and starts charging. Its Li-ion mode also stops at 14.2 V with float disabled, and Victron warns not to charge Li-ion below 0 °C but describes no automatic low-temperature cut-off. None of them turns any NAS's wattage into a yearly cost for a server that stays on all the time, and none warns that the makers test with different numbers of drives. This page converts each maker's access and hibernation watts into kWh and dollars per year and checks them against what reviewers measured with two drives.

Its 5.24 W maker figure was measured with one 2 TB drive, and OCinside's two-HDD RAID 1 test came out at about 7 W idle (as reported by starryhope), so its low figure holds up with two drives. The QNAP TS-264 looks about 3x worse on paper (18.288 W against 6.08 W for the DS225+), but QNAP tested with both bays full and the others didn't, so part of that gap is the test, not the hardware. At the spec-sheet disk-standby figures, 24/7 use comes to about 46 kWh/yr (UGREEN), 53 kWh/yr (Synology), 111 kWh/yr (Asustor) and 160 kWh/yr (QNAP). pages.query: which nas is best for running nextcloud as my own cloud
pages.why_used: The rival pages that were cited (racksandwatts, esp32, the AIO readme) give only CPU names and RAM. None has a benchmark, so nothing shows that the DS925+'s 'AMD Ryzen', presented as the premium choice, is the slowest per core on the shortlist. This page adds PassMark single-thread and CPU Mark scores for all six candidates, plus a Docker Engine/API column that turns 'Docker support' into a comparable figure.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the Docker Engine version each NAS OS ships, or how that compares with the Docker API v1.44 that Nextcloud AIO uses by default. UGREEN UGOS Pro (29.6.2, API ≤1.55), ASUSTOR (29.6.2), QNAP Container Station (27.1.2, API 1.46) and TerraMaster TOS (27.2.1, API 1.47) all meet it. Synology DSM Container Manager (24.0.2, API 1.43), on the DS925+ and DS225+, is the only one below it. AIO's Docker socket proxy and AppAPI fail there unless you override the API version, which the AIO maintainers say they don't support or test.
angles.decides: This backs the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 as the pick for running Nextcloud AIO as shipped, and it weakens the DS925+, which ChatGPT called the 'best software experience' or 'best overall'. On DSM, AIO needs the DOCKER_API_VERSION override that the maintainers don't support, or the Docker Socket Proxy (needed by AppAPI/ExApps) turned off. Synology has kept Container Manager on Docker 24.0.2, which reached end of life in June 2024, through its August 2026 package update. QNAP and TerraMaster meet 1.44 but run older engines than UGREEN and ASUSTOR. Footnote for the table: the 'Docker support' tick every rival shows is not equal across brands.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what it costs to keep each NAS running all day and night, which a Nextcloud server must do: at the US average home rate of 18.16¢/kWh (August 2026), the makers' own power figures come to about $60 a year for the Synology DS925+, $64 for the QNAP TS-464 and $27 for the Synology DS225+ with the drives awake, versus $20, $34 and $10 with the drives asleep.
angles.decides: This confirms the shortlist rather than changing it. The QNAP TS-464 costs the most to run in the makers' own figures: 40.5 W typical against 37.9 W for the DS925+ while drives are being accessed (about $4 more a year), and 21.6 W against 12.3 W with drives asleep (about $15 more a year). So its $639 price edge over the DS925+ ($829.99 at Micro Center in ChatGPT's answer) shrinks a little over 5 years. The DS225+ is by far the cheapest to run, about $27 a year, but tops out at 6 GB of RAM, short of the 16 GB ChatGPT recommends. Nextcloud's background jobs every 5 minutes tend to keep the hard drives from sleeping unless its data sits on SSD, so the drives-awake figure is the realistic one. That makes 'put the database on NVMe' a running-cost point as well as a speed point. For the DXP4800 Plus I could only source a reviewer's idle reading (KitGuru, 24.25 W, about $39 a year), which isn't comparable with the maker figures.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, as of November 2026, Synology's Container Manager still runs Docker Engine 24.0.2, which tops out at Docker API 1.43. That is below the v1.44 that Nextcloud AIO's own code calls by default, so on the DS925+ or DS225+ AIO only runs if you override the API version, a setup AIO's maintainers say they don't support. The UGREEN DXP models (29.6.2), Asustor (29.6.2), TerraMaster (27.2.1) and QNAP (27.1.2) all ship engines at or above 1.44.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's choice of the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 over the DS925+ for Nextcloud AIO. UGOS Pro's Docker 29.6.2 meets AIO's default API with nothing to configure. On the DS925+ (and DS225+) the shopper has to run AIO with DOCKER_API_VERSION overridden on an engine that went end-of-life in 2024, and also mount Synology's own socket path. Container Manager's GUI can't manage AIO, so it's run over SSH or a scheduled task, and AppAPI/External Apps errors have been reported. The DS925+ can still put its database on NVMe, but only with Synology-verified SSDs for an M.2 pool. QNAP, TerraMaster and Asustor all clear the API bar. In UGREEN's cheaper home line, the DS2300 should read DH2300: it has no official Docker, so it drops out for AIO, while the DH4300 Plus does officially support Docker.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Nextcloud All-in-One calls the Docker Engine API at a pinned v1.44 by default, while Synology's Container Manager is still built on Docker Engine 24.0.2 (newest build 24.0.2-1707, 2026-11-05), whose highest API is 1.43. On the DS925+ and DS225+, AIO therefore needs an SSH install with a DOCKER_API_VERSION override that Nextcloud says it does not support. UGREEN's UGOS Pro ships Engine 29.6.2, which needs no override.
angles.decides: It confirms UGREEN (DXP2800 / DXP4800 Plus) as the pick for Nextcloud AIO and pushes the Synology DS925+ down. DS925+ owners can't use AIO's default, supported setup from the Container Manager GUI. They need SSH or Task Scheduler as root, a custom socket path and DOCKER_API_VERSION=1.43, which the AIO readme says is not supported or tested by the maintainers. One DSM owner on Container Manager 24.0.2 reported the AIO mastercontainer warning that 'only v1.44 is officially supported' and AppAPI failing in a loop. QNAP (Engine 27.1.2) and TerraMaster (27.2.1) are above API 1.44, so the default works there. Shoppers who stay on Synology should be told to plan for the override, or to use the community nextcloud/docker image with Compose, which doesn't drive the Docker API.

It also clears a v3 risk: v3's NumPy needs x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2) or the classifier crashes with SIGILL, and Intel lists SSE4.2 for both the J4125 (DS225+, DS224+) and the N5105 (AS5402T), so those budget Celerons are safe.

pages.query: best nas for photographers with 10 tb of raw files who edit in lightroom
pages.why_used: Fstoppers and Camera Lookout, the two rival pages cited for this question, repeat Synology's 522/565 MB/s headline and give 2.5GbE's raw ceiling. Neither works out what one editing computer actually gets. This page does that from the makers' test notes and MightyGadget's hard-drive test: 500–600 MB/s from the DXP4800 Plus over 10GbE against 295 MB/s on one 2.5GbE link, about 2× rather than 4×. It also gives QNAP's own measured drop to 275 MB/s with small files.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' MB/s headlines into what one editing computer actually gets: Synology's 522 MB/s for the DS925+ is more than one 2.5GbE link can carry (312.5 MB/s raw), so one Mac gets about 295 MB/s, the figure QNAP measured on a single 2.5GbE link. A 10GbE box with four hard drives in RAID 5 gives one client 500–600 MB/s in MightyGadget's test. That is about 2× faster, not the 4× the port speeds suggest, and QNAP's own chart shows a single 10GbE link falling to 275 MB/s when the files are 1 MB each.
angles.decides: This supports the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus ($619.99 at UGREEN's store on 2026-11-08) as the pick for one photographer editing on one computer. For large transfers such as imports, exports and preview builds, its built-in 10GbE port with four HDDs in RAID 5 gives one client about 500–600 MB/s, roughly twice what a DS925+ can give one client (about 295 MB/s, with no PCIe slot to upgrade). The DS925+'s 522/565 MB/s needs both ports and several clients, which a single editor will not see. The QNAP TS-464 can reach 10GbE speeds, but only by using its one PCIe slot (Gen 3 x2) for the card. The footnote: 10GbE helps with batch work, not opening one RAW file at a time. With 1 MB files, QNAP's own single 10GbE link read 274.94 MB/s, about the same as one 2.5GbE link with large files. So a shopper who edits from local copies and only archives to the NAS can stay on 2.5GbE.

pages.query: best nas to run pi-hole or adguard home plus a wireguard vpn for the house
pages.why_used: None of the cited pages (Synology's Container Manager page, UGREEN's DXP2800 page, the racksandwatts guides) says that DSM 7.3 runs Linux 4.4.302+ while WireGuard entered the kernel in 5.6. That means the 'run WireGuard in a container on the DS225+' route fails on stock DSM. This page sets each NAS OS's WireGuard route and kernel next to the deciding specs, and the pick rests on UGOS Pro's 6.18 kernel.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' low idle figures are drive-hibernation numbers taken under different setups (UGREEN: one Seagate 2 TB drive; QNAP: all bays filled; Synology: setup not stated), or that UGREEN says Docker containers and always-active databases keep the drives from hibernating. So for a 24/7 DNS and VPN box the figures that compare are the drives-active ones: DXP2800 16.38 W, DS225+ 16.98 W, TS-264 29.086 W.
angles.decides: This backs the DXP2800 as the NAS pick, and it adds a cost against the QNAP TS-264, the only maker-confirmed native WireGuard server among the candidates. With containers running, the drive-asleep figures (5.24 / 6.08 / 18.288 W) don't apply, because UGREEN itself says Docker containers and always-active databases block hibernation. The like-for-like figures are 16.38 W (DXP2800), 16.98 W (DS225+) and 29.086 W (TS-264). That works out to about 143 kWh, 149 kWh and 255 kWh a year. So the TS-264's built-in WireGuard costs about 111 kWh a year more than a DXP2800 running WireGuard in a container. The DS225+ has nearly the same power draw as the DXP2800, but its makers' page lists no M.2 slot, so containers can't be moved off the hard drives to let them sleep. Its VPN Server also has no WireGuard. Both points favour the DXP2800 or TS-264 for anyone who wants the drives to sleep. Also normalised: native WireGuard on the stock OS. QNAP QVPN: yes (QNAP's own page). Synology DSM VPN Server: no (OpenVPN, L2TP/IPsec, PPTP only). UGREEN UGOS Pro: OpenVPN and WireGuard according to VPN Tracker only; no UGREEN page found.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the yearly electricity cost of leaving each candidate on 24/7 as the house DNS and VPN box, worked out from each maker's rated idle draw at the 2026 US average residential rate (EIA, 18.19 ¢/kWh year to date). The range runs from about $5 a year for a Raspberry Pi 5 to $10 for a Synology DS225+ with its disks asleep, $20 for an Asustor AS5402T and $29 for a QNAP TS-264 with its drives in standby.
angles.decides: Running 24/7 is the whole job here, so yearly power cost is the real gap between candidates. With disks asleep, the DS225+ (6.08 W, about $9.69 a year) and DXP2800 (about 7 W, about $11 a year) cost about the same to run. The QNAP TS-264 (18.288 W in disk standby, about $29 a year; 29.086 W operating, about $46) costs roughly 3× as much. Over 5 years that is about $146 to $232 for the QNAP against about $48 for the DS225+, which cancels a large part of the QNAP's main advantage, its native WireGuard server. A Pi 5 at about 3 W costs about $5 a year. That supports ChatGPT's advice to use a separate small box if the shopper doesn't need storage. One caution that is my own inference, not something a source said: the DS225+ has no NVMe storage pool (racksandwatts spec list), so Pi-hole or AdGuard containers would sit on the hard drives. Constant query logging could then stop the disks from sleeping, which moves it toward its 16.98 W access figure (about $27 a year). The DXP2800 can keep containers on NVMe.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which NAS operating systems have a maker-documented WireGuard server. Only QNAP and Asustor document one. QNAP's QVPN Service 3.0 offers it on x86 models only, and the TS-264 is x86. Asustor's VPN Server 1.1.0.r327 adds it, and Asustor's own App Central AdGuard Home package covers the Nimbustor 2 Gen2's AS54 series, so that NAS can run DNS filtering and WireGuard without Docker. Synology DSM 7.3 and TerraMaster TOS 6 list only OpenVPN, L2TP/IPsec and PPTP, and UGREEN has no maker document for its WireGuard server.
angles.decides: This changes the pick for a shopper who wants both services as maker-supported apps, with no Docker, macvlan or port-53 workarounds. The Asustor Nimbustor 2 Gen2 (AS5402T, AS54 series) is the only candidate where the maker's own App Central lists both a WireGuard VPN Server and AdGuard Home for its series. The QNAP TS-264 has a documented WireGuard server, but DNS filtering still goes through Container Station. Our current page says the AS54 series is not on Asustor's VPN Server list. That is wrong: the list I read on 2026-11-08 includes AS54. On the Synology DS225+ and TerraMaster F2-425 Plus, WireGuard needs a container or a community package. The UGREEN DXP2800's built-in WireGuard is backed only by VPN Tracker, a VPN software vendor. The DXP2800 can stay the best-hardware pick, but not the 'it's built in' pick.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Synology DSM runs Linux 4.4.302+, while WireGuard entered the mainline kernel only in Linux 5.6, so the 'WireGuard in a container' route ChatGPT suggested for the DS225+ (wg-easy or linuxserver/wireguard, both of which rely on the host's kernel module) has no module to use on stock DSM.
angles.decides: This moves the DS225+ out of 'best overall' for this plan. Pi-hole or AdGuard Home in Container Manager is fine. A WireGuard server, though, needs either an unofficial third-party kernel module (gpopesc build, tested only on a DS920+, 'at your own risk' class), Synology's native OpenVPN instead, or a userspace tool such as Tailscale. Gluetun is a userspace VPN client, so it does not provide a home VPN server. The UGREEN DXP2800 is confirmed as the pick: UGOS Pro 1.19.1 moved to kernel 6.18, well past 5.6, so wg-easy can use in-kernel WireGuard. TerraMaster says TOS 6 is built on Linux 6.1 LTS, which is past 5.6, but one TOS 6 beta owner reported the system actually ran 5.15.59 with WireGuard not working. QNAP (QVPN) and GL.iNet ship WireGuard as a built-in server and avoid the question.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured idle power for any of the candidates. ComputerBase measured the UGREEN DXP2800 at 18.6 W idle with two HDDs and 7.3 W with the HDDs in standby, and the same lab measured the J4125 Synology DS224+ at 18.6 W idle and 3.5 W in standby. PC-WELT measured the QNAP TS-264-8G at 26.5 W idle. ServeTheHome measured the GL.iNet Flint 2 at 5.6 W idle, and CNX Software measured it at 834–889 Mbps as a WireGuard server. For an always-on DNS + VPN box that is a 3–5× gap in power draw.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's own caveat that a router or Pi beats a NAS if the shopper needs only DNS + VPN, and it puts numbers on it. In ServeTheHome's test the Flint 2 idles at 5.6 W, about 49 kWh a year (5.6 W × 8,760 h). CNX Software measured it at 834–889 Mbps in WireGuard server mode. Jeff Geerling measured a Pi 5 8GB at 3.2 W, about 28 kWh a year. A DXP2800 whose HDDs keep spinning idles at 18.6 W in ComputerBase's test, about 163 kWh a year. For a shopper who also wants storage, the DXP2800 remains the NAS pick: ComputerBase measured it level with the Synology DS224+ at 18.6 W idle, and PC-WELT measured the QNAP TS-264 at 26.5 W idle, so it doesn't cost more to run. One condition goes with that pick: put the AdGuard/Pi-hole and WireGuard container data on the NVMe slot, not the HDD volume. Otherwise the HDDs can't reach the 7.3 W standby state.

pages.query: best nas to run proxmox or several virtual machines in a home lab
pages.why_used: The pages these answers relied on (Proxmox's requirements, QNAP's spec sheet, homelabpicks, computingforgeeks) give spec-sheet wattage at most. None of them measured wall power for the NAS and mini-PC hosts they recommended, and the one measured figure in reach (Notebookcheck's DXP6800 Pro review) was never cited. This page puts Notebookcheck's 11.8–15.9 W N5 Pro idle beside the DXP6800 Pro, DXP4800 Plus and MS-01 figures, and that comparison decides which box to run around the clock. It also adds the ZFS RAM arithmetic and the passthrough layouts owners reported.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Minisforum N5 Pro's three M.2 slots share four PCIe 4.0 lanes, split x1/x1/x2 (ServeTheHome), with the OS on one of the x1 slots, or that its 'x16' slot is wired x4. So the mirrored NVMe VM pool every ChatGPT answer recommends would run on an x2 and an x1 link, about 2 GB/s each way at most, while the QNAP TVS-h674's two M.2 slots are each Gen4 x4.
angles.decides: This confirms the N5 Pro as the CPU and RAM pick (12C/24T, 96 GB ECC) but changes how to build it: put the VM pool on an NVMe card in the x4 slot, or accept roughly 2 GB/s per drive. A shopper whose priority is fast mirrored NVMe VM storage with a free x16-length slot should look at the QNAP TVS-h674 (2× M.2 Gen4 x4, plus Gen4 x16 and x4 slots), at a much higher price. It also turns 'three NVMe slots' into one boot slot plus two narrow data slots, which matters for the 'two NVMe drives, mirrored' layout in all three ChatGPT answers.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works Proxmox's own memory rule (2 GB for the host plus 1 GB per TB of used ZFS storage) through for these 64 GB-ceiling NAS boxes. Done, it leaves 42 GB for guests with 20 TB of used ZFS data and 22 GB with 40 TB, so a full 6-bay pool takes about a third of the RAM before any VM starts.
angles.decides: This tempers the all-in-one pick. On any 64 GB-ceiling box (DXP4800 Plus, DXP6800 Pro, TVS-h674), filling the bays with a big ZFS pool cuts guest RAM to 22–42 GB, so 'several VMs plus TrueNAS-style ZFS' fits only with a modest pool or with VMs kept small. Per thread, the DXP6800 Pro is the cheapest UGREEN at $91.67, versus $103.33 for the DXP4800 Plus. For many VMs on top of a large pool, it points toward a box with a higher RAM ceiling. Intel lists 96 GB for the DXP4800 Pro's i3-1315U, but UGREEN's own ceiling for that box isn't sourced.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that UGREEN NASync boxes have a BIOS watchdog that keeps rebooting a non-UGOS OS such as Proxmox, TrueNAS or Unraid until it is turned off in the BIOS (Ctrl+F12 at the UGREEN logo), or that UGREEN's policy leaves the hardware warranty unchanged when you install a third-party system.
angles.decides: This confirms the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP6800 Pro as the all-in-one Proxmox pick. Bare-metal Proxmox works once the watchdog is off, and per UGREEN's policy as the Debian wiki quotes it, the hardware warranty is unchanged. By contrast, homelabpicks says TerraMaster voids the warranty when you install another OS, and QNAP's TVS-h674 page lists only QTS and QuTS hero and says to use only QNAP memory. Where Proxmox is the main goal, this tips the choice toward UGREEN over TerraMaster.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, ChatGPT's 'favorite all-in-one', splits its six bays across two SATA controllers (Intel Alder Lake-P AHCI at 00:17.0 plus an ASMedia ASM1164), while the DXP4800 Plus puts all four bays on a single ASM1164, so a TrueNAS VM under Proxmox gets every bay with one passthrough on the 4800 Plus but needs two on the 6800 Pro.
angles.decides: If the shopper's plan is Proxmox bare-metal with a TrueNAS VM that owns the drives, the DXP4800 Plus is the clean fit: one ASM1164 holds all 4 bays, and an owner passed it from the Proxmox GUI. On the DXP6800 Pro (and the DXP8800 Plus) one controller passthrough covers only some of the bays. You either pass both controllers, fall back to per-disk passthrough (an owner saw TrueNAS SCALE refuse a RAIDZ because the vDisks lacked unique serials), or let Proxmox run ZFS itself. On any UGREEN, the BIOS watchdog has to be turned off first or the box reboots about every 3 minutes without UGOS.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Notebookcheck measured the Minisforum N5 Pro (Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370, 12C/24T) idling at 11.8–15.9 W. pages.why_used: The cited Synology spec and KB pages say only that immutable snapshots exist 'on supported Synology models'. This page shows which NAS keeps a snapshot of the Veeam/Macrium SMB share that the share login saved on every PC can't delete: Synology's immutable snapshots, QNAP's that work only on QuTS hero, and the locks on Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN that only stop automatic cleanup.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the word 'immutable' or 'lock' means different things across NAS brands. On the Synology DS225+, an immutable snapshot can't be deleted by anyone until its protection period ends. On the QNAP TS-264 the same protection exists only after a switch from QTS to QuTS hero h6, and then deleting a protected folder needs a Secure Deletion USB key. On Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN, a 'locked' snapshot is only skipped by automatic cleanup and can still be deleted by hand. A third-party UGREEN API client found that a locked snapshot 'is deleted just the same' through the API. This matters because Veeam Agent and Macrium write to an SMB share whose credentials sit on every PC.
angles.decides: This confirms the Synology DS225+ as the pick when the backup target is an SMB share written by Veeam Agent Free or Macrium. Its product page says it supports immutable snapshots, so a ransomware-hit PC holding the share password can't delete the snapshot behind the backup files. The QNAP TS-264 can match this, but only after a switch from its default QTS to QuTS hero h6.0.2 (TS-264 is on the applicable-models list). The cells for the Asustor AS5402T, TerraMaster F2-425 Plus and UGREEN DXP2800/DH2300 should read 'lock (stops automatic cleanup, can still be deleted)', not anything that suggests immutability. angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Veeam Agent for Windows cannot wake a PC that uses Modern Standby for a scheduled backup and does not start scheduled backups while the PC is in Modern Standby, and that Veeam Free allows only one backup job. They also don't state that the NAS makers' own image agents need BitLocker turned off before backup (QNAP HDP PC Agent) or decrypted (Synology ABB on DSM 7.3), while Veeam only needs the volume unlocked.
angles.decides: This confirms that a basic SMB NAS is enough when the PCs run Veeam Agent Free. Veeam supports a network shared folder target, a daily schedule and unlocked BitLocker volumes. The Modern Standby limit applies whichever NAS you buy, so the page should tell shoppers to leave the PCs awake or plugged in at the backup time, or to use the backup-on-lock or log-off triggers. It weakens the argument that 'Synology Active Backup for Business may eliminate your need for Veeam or Macrium', and the same goes for QNAP's HDP PC Agent. On BitLocker-encrypted PCs, both makers tell you to decrypt or turn BitLocker off first, and both say BitLocker has to be turned back on after a full restore. So for encrypted PCs, Veeam to a share on any Btrfs NAS (DS225+, DXP2800, TS-264) is the cleaner route than the NAS maker's agent. If shoppers buy a DS225+ or DS425+, they can fit their own hard drives on DSM 7.3. M.2 pools and cache still need drives from Synology's list.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Windows 11 24H2 Pro requires SMB signing and blocks guest access to shares. Because of that, the Veeam Agent (or Macrium) target has to be a NAS share that allows signing, opened with a named NAS user account. If you skip credentials, Veeam connects as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Also, Veeam's scheduled nightly job won't start on a PC that is sleeping in Modern Standby.
angles.decides: It confirms the plan rather than changing which NAS to buy. Every candidate runs a Samba-based SMB server, so each can work, as long as you create a NAS user per PC (or one backup user), give it Full Control of the share, enter those credentials in the Veeam or Macrium job and in the recovery media, and leave guest access off. What really decides whether 'nightly' happens is the PCs, not the NAS: on a laptop or desktop that sleeps in Modern Standby, Veeam won't start the scheduled job, so set 'Backup once powered on' or keep the PCs awake. With Veeam Free, each PC gets exactly one backup job, has no synthetic fulls, and keeps 7 days of restore points by default. That favours a NAS with Btrfs snapshots underneath for longer history, which points to the DS225+/DS425+, DXP2800, F2-425 Plus or AS5402T over the ext4-only DS223j.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how fast these NAS boxes actually take a Windows image. Blackvoid timed Synology Active Backup for Business making the first full backup of a Windows 11 PC to a DS225+: 60.3 GB in just under 12 minutes (85 MB/s), stored as just over 40 GB after deduplication. The QNAP TVS-h674T ($417/bay) and TVS-h874T ($386/bay) are the exception: their built-in LAN is only 2× 2.5GbE (590 MB/s measured), so Thunderbolt is their only fast link without buying a card. QNAP (20 Gbps cap), UGREEN (DXP480T Plus, DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus on UGOS 1.2.0.2121 or later) and, per its help page, TerraMaster's TOS all do. pages.query: noise cancelling headphones with mic

None of them gives a noise-cancelling score out of 10 for the Sony or the Bose. This page sets SoundGuys' noise-cancelling scores side by side for all six candidates (Space 2 Pro 8.8, Sony and Bose 8.7) and adds the reader mic polls. Angle E is the only one complete for every row: angles A and B have no talk time for the Bose, and C and D cannot say whether the Bose mic works over USB.

The makers' talk times with ANC on reverse the headline battery order: Jabra Evolve3 85 is up to 21 h and Sony WH-1000XM6 is up to 24 h. Their music figures (55 h vs 30 h) point the other way, and those are what SoundGuys prints. Bose publishes no talk time, and Bose's own footnote gives 24 h of music at full noise cancelling against a 30 h headline.

On a call with ANC on, Sony rates 24 h and Jabra 21 h, despite Jabra's 55 h vs 30 h music headline. On ANC-on talk time the Jabra is a draw at best. The case for it is still mic clarity (SoundGuys: 'sounded the clearest of the tested mics'), the Link 390 dongle and Teams/Zoom certification, not endurance. The table should have a 'talk time, ANC on' column, and the footnote should say that music hours overstate call hours by 6 h (Sony) to 34 h (Jabra).

At 4 h of calls a day that is 6.0, 5.25, 5.25 and 5.0 workdays, so the Jabra Evolve3 85's 55 h headline drops to 38% on calls while the Sony keeps 80%.
angles.decides: This confirms the Sony WH-1000XM6 as best overall for a call-heavy buyer. It has the lowest music headline here (30 h, against Jabra's 55 h) yet the most talk time (24 h), so it lasts longest in meetings. It also stops battery from being a reason to pay the Evolve3 85's ~$649 MSRP (the figure ChatGPT showed): on calls it matches the Evolve2 85 at 21 h. The $199.99 Space 2 Pro gets within one workday of the Sony (5.0 vs 6.0 days at 4 h/day). The Bose QC Ultra (2nd Gen) cannot be ranked on this, because Bose publishes no talk time.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that when the Sony WH-1000XM6 runs on its supplied cable, its Bluetooth is turned off and Sony tells you to answer calls on the phone and speak into the phone's microphone, so the headset's own mics only work for calls over Bluetooth. Among the over-ears compared, only the Jabra Evolve2 85 gives a laptop a separate path for calls: a Jabra Link USB Bluetooth adapter, sold in USB-A or USB-C and in Microsoft Teams or UC versions.
angles.decides: This settles the pick for a shopper who calls from a PC. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and the soundcore Space 2 Pro can only carry laptop calls over Bluetooth Hands-Free (Sony says to pick 'Headset (WH-1000XM6 Hands-Free)' and warns that the Stereo/A2DP choice may make a video call unavailable). The Jabra Evolve2 85 adds a dedicated USB adapter, and its MS version is Teams-certified. So the Jabra is the pick for PC and Teams calls, and the Sony and soundcore suit a phone plus a laptop over Bluetooth.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a classic-Bluetooth headset can only use its mic through the Hands-Free Profile, which plays audio in mono at lower fidelity than A2DP. Microsoft says only LE Audio headsets, on Windows 11 24H2 with an updated Bluetooth driver, keep stereo playback while the mic is in use. That makes the PC connection (LE Audio, a mic over USB-C, or a USB dongle) the thing that decides how laptop meetings sound.

The Jabra Evolve2 85 (supplied Bluetooth USB adapter) and the Sony WH-1000XM6 (LC3 and LE connections, per SoundGuys) have a route around the Bluetooth hands-free mode. The Sony route only works on a Windows 11 24H2 PC with LE Audio hardware and an updated driver. The soundcore Space 2 Pro lists only AAC, SBC and LDAC, so on a PC it falls back to HFP mono whenever the mic is on. Bose's page says USB-C carries playback but does not say the mic works over USB, so the Bose falls back to HFP on Bluetooth calls unless its USB mic is confirmed. The page should add a 'calls on a PC' column (LE Audio / USB mic / dongle / none), not just mic counts.

pages.query: open ear or earbuds
pages.why_used: ChatGPT tells people who wear headphones 6–8 hours a day to buy open-ear, but it gives no battery figure for any model and doesn't say which mode a rating assumes. This page shows how each pair does over an 8-hour day in the mode people actually use. ANC on, call mode and Bose's Immersive Audio each leave a pair short of a workday. Open-ear pairs played in music mode have hours to spare.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the in-ear Liberty 4 Pro's '10 h' battery rating is with noise cancelling off. Headphonecheck ran the same test (AAC, high volume) on all three. It measured 6.5 h for the Liberty 4 Pro with ANC at maximum, against 9 h for each of the open-ear AeroFit 2 and Bose Ultra Open. So once you use the noise cancelling that is the reason to buy in-ear, the open-ear models run about 38% longer per charge.
angles.decides: The finding backs the open-ear pick for the 'wear it 6–8 hours a day' shopper, and shows the in-ear advantage is conditional. An in-ear pair outlasts open-ear only with ANC off (Liberty 4 Pro 10 h vs 9 h, Headphonecheck). With ANC on, the in-ear falls below a full workday (6.5 h Headphonecheck; 5 h 42 min SoundGuys), while AeroFit 2 and Bose Ultra Open each reach 9 h on the same test. Bose's spatial-audio mode is the exception among open-ear models: 4.5 h by Bose's own figure, 5 h by Headphonecheck. Footnote for the table: battery hours = same lab, same codec, same 'high volume'; in-ear shown with ANC on, Bose shown with Immersive Audio off and on.

For in-ear, it confirms that ANC costs a full workday on one charge (Liberty 4 Pro measured 5.7 h with ANC on). Our page's Bose row is out of date. Shokz claims an average 14 dB reduction for the OpenFit Pro. Also, our page's Bose link returns 404. pages.query: best portable monitor that sits above a laptop screen
pages.why_used: The cited reviews and guides (Macworld's Float 2 Pro review and Mac guide, Fstoppers, Wired and Mobile Pixels' Black Friday post) never say that the Xebec Snap's USB-C link is DisplayLink, or that Xebec's own help centre warns Netflix, Prime and Disney+ can play black with sound on it. This page sets that against the Float 2 Pro's driver-free DP Alt Mode link and adds both makers' store prices from 2026-11-13.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Xebec Snap's 'USB-C' video link is DisplayLink. Xebec's own help centre warns that protected video in Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime, HBO, iTunes, YouTube TV and Udemy may show a black screen with the sound still playing while DisplayLink screens are connected. The Duex Float 2 Pro uses native USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode with no driver.
angles.decides: This backs the Duex Float 2 Pro for 15–16" laptops, since it plugs in and works with no driver and protected video plays. It also adds a real caveat to ChatGPT's 'for smaller laptops' alternative, the roughly $708 Xebec Snap + Stack-Up Mount. That setup needs the DisplayLink driver and macOS 11 or later, and Xebec itself says streaming services may show a black picture on it. So a 13–14" laptop owner who wants Netflix or Prime on the upper screen should not take the Xebec.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much laptop battery each stacked screen uses per hour. Both are bus-powered with no battery of their own. The Duex Float 2 Pro in Limited Power Mode (7.5 W) uses about 7.5% of a 16-inch MacBook Pro's 99.6 Wh battery per hour. A Xebec Snap screen (about 16.5 W) uses about 31% of a 13-inch MacBook Air's 53.8 Wh per hour, which would flatten that battery in about 3.3 h on the screen's load alone.
angles.decides: It confirms the Duex Float 2 Pro for 15–16-inch laptops away from a wall outlet: in Limited Power Mode it uses about 7.5–11%/h of a 16-inch MacBook Pro or 15-inch MacBook Air battery. It qualifies ChatGPT's Xebec suggestion for 13–14-inch laptops: unplugged, each Snap screen uses about 23–31%/h of a 14-inch MacBook Pro or 13-inch MacBook Air battery and roughly doubles a MacBook Air 13's carry weight (+2.5 lb on a 2.7 lb laptop). So it suits people who plug in (the bracket passes power through), not battery-only travel.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Xebec's help center says Snap pass-through charging may not start at all with a charger above about 100 W. A 16-inch MacBook Pro ships with Apple's 140 W adapter, so on that laptop, which is the size Xebec's stacked setup is pitched at, the owner needs a separate 45–100 W charger. Xebec also says DisplayLink screens can show black video for Netflix, Disney+, Prime and YouTube TV.
angles.decides: Confirms the Duex Float 2 Pro as the pick for 15–16-inch laptops. It drives the screen natively over DP Alt Mode USB-C (no DisplayLink, so no streaming black-out), and Macworld names the 16-inch MacBook Pro as its best fit. It also adds a caveat to the Xebec Snap + Stack-Up row: on a 16-inch MacBook Pro the bundled 140 W charger is above Xebec's ~100 W pass-through ceiling, protected streaming may go black on the stacked screen, and the Stack-Up Mount holds only one stacked screen (one per bracket, left wing only). That narrows Xebec to 13–14-inch laptops whose own chargers are 100 W or less, which is the size ChatGPT already steers it to, and now with a sourced reason.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, in the maker's own words, that the Duex Float stands on its own fold-out base with the laptop placed in front of it and that the magnets are optional. The lid and hinge do not carry its 2.9 lb. That one fact undoes both the hinge-strain warning ChatGPT repeated from Fstoppers and its 'best suited to 15–16-inch laptops' limit.
angles.decides: This confirms the Duex Float 2 Pro as the pick and widens who it suits. Its own base carries the weight, so a thin lid or a 13–14-inch laptop is not ruled out by hinge load. Mobile Pixels' Duex Float FAQ answers 'Will the Duex Float work with 12.5'', 13.3'' or 14.1'' laptops?' with 'Yes'. The real conditions it has to meet are: (1) a USB-C port with DP Alt Mode for the single-cable setup, otherwise mini-HDMI plus a separate power cable; (2) running from the laptop alone caps brightness (80% in Limited Power Mode per Macworld) until a 15 W+ PD charger is added; (3) it can't be used with a laptop stand, because the Float would sit lower than the raised laptop. ChatGPT pointed small-laptop owners to the Xebec Snap with Stack-Up Mount (about $708), which mounts on a lid bracket, so the weight logic actually points the other way.

pages.query: portable projector with screen
pages.why_used: The cited rivals list lumen ratings and battery hours as separate figures. None works out how bright the picture is on a given screen (lumens × gain ÷ area, against SMPTE's 16 ft-L target), and none says the advertised battery hours are rated in a dimmed Eco mode, which ProjectorCentral measured at 151–154 lm on the MoGo 4. This page does that math for each projector on one 120-inch, 1.1-gain screen.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Yaber T2 Plus, its pick for watching where there is no outlet, turns its brightness setting down from 100 to 60 when running on battery, so its brightness rating and its roughly 2.5-hour battery figure do not apply at the same time.
angles.decides: This confirms that for a battery-powered screen setup, the battery column cannot be read alongside the brightness column. The T2 Plus runs at a reduced brightness setting (60 of 100) on battery. Its brightness also appears as 450 ANSI lumens in reviews but as 350 ISO lumens on Yaber's own listing (this listing figure is from search output; I could not reopen the page). The page should footnote that battery hours are at reduced brightness. For outdoor screens of 100 to 120 inches, plug-in models with higher ratings (Aurzen EAZZE D1 MAX at 1,000 ANSI lumens; Vankyo H500R at 330 ANSI lumens) are the better pick when an outlet or power station is available. Battery models are the pick only when there is no power at all.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how bright each bundle's projector makes its own included screen in foot-lamberts: the Fugoo kit ChatGPT kept recommending lights its 120-in screen to about 5.9 ft-L, roughly a third of the 16 ft-L dark-room target, which suits a picture of about 73 in. The JMGO PicoPlay+ gives about 15.2 ft-L on its 100-in screen, close to the target.
angles.decides: It changes the pick. The cheap kits ChatGPT leads with (Fugoo $149.99, and our own Aurzen D1 + 120-in screen at 5.15 ft-L) only reach the 16 ft-L dark-room target at about 68 to 73 in, so their 120-in screens are mostly for show. The Vankyo H500R is rated by its maker for up to 80 in, yet the H500RS bundle comes with a 100-in screen (11.1 ft-L). The JMGO PicoPlay+ (450 ISO lm, 100-in screen, 15.2 ft-L, 3 h battery) is the only bundle shown that fills its own screen at the target and also runs one full film without a wall plug. The ETOE Seal Pro (23.4 ft-L at 120 in) and our Aurzen D1 MAX (25.7 ft-L at 120 in, gain 1.1) are the plug-in picks for a full 120-in screen. The Seal Pro draws 180 W and weighs 10.4 lb, so it is only nominally portable.

pages.query: biggest power bank allowed on a plane
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages are all rule pages (FAA PackSafe, the IATA power-bank guidance, 49 CFR 175.10 copies, American Airlines restricted items). None names a power bank or says how much energy a 99 Wh bank actually delivers, and none says that one of them cuts out from heat at laptop loads. This page adds lab-measured output: Techtest.org for Anker, EcoFlow and UGREEN, and ChargerLAB for AOHi. That evidence moves the pick to the Anker Prime 26K (99.75 Wh, up to 89.8 Wh measured, steady 140 W). Anker is not a product we can link (amzcheck returned no Amazon listing), so our AOHi Future Starship takes the phone/tablet segment it honestly wins and our UGREEN 145W takes the budget/light segment.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers of the biggest carry-on banks rate their cells at 3.6 V rather than 3.7 V. At 3.6 V the largest pack under 100 Wh is about 27,777 mAh, not 27,000 mAh. So the 27,600 to 27,650 mAh banks (AOHi Future Starship 99.36 Wh, Anker Prime A1340 99.54 Wh, EcoFlow RAPID Pro 99.54 Wh) need no airline approval, even though ChatGPT's 3.7 V table would put them at about 102 Wh and in the 'approval required' row.
angles.decides: It confirms the page's picks. The largest banks that need no approval are the ~27,600 to 27,650 mAh class, labelled 99.36 to 99.54 Wh, not '27,000 mAh' as ChatGPT says. The column the page should show is the printed Wh figure, not mAh. Separately, the UK CAA page (effective 27 March 2026) still allows 100–160 Wh with operator approval, two power banks per person, and no recharging on board. That contradicts ChatGPT's line that 2026 IATA guidance caps power banks at 100 Wh, so the AOHi 40K (146 Wh) stays as the 'needs airline approval' row.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that every power bank that skips airline approval stops at about 99.5 Wh, so 'biggest' is a tie and the real differences are cost per Wh ($1.20/Wh for the AOHi Future Starship at $119 vs $1.77/Wh for the EcoFlow RAPID Pro at $175.99) and how much reaches a laptop (about 81 of the RAPID Pro's 99.54 Wh in Macworld's MacBook Pro 14 test, roughly 82%).
angles.decides: This confirms the page's angle: pick a bank of about 99 Wh. Capacity is capped at the same level for every candidate, so the pick comes down to price and weight per Wh. The AOHi Future Starship 240W gives the most Wh per dollar at $1.20/Wh. The EcoFlow RAPID Pro costs about 47% more per Wh ($1.77) and weighs 1.54 lb. Anker's current Prime 26K 300W is the lightest bank I could source (1.32 lb), but anker.com US only listed it bundled with a charging base at $329.99. Our page's Anker row points to a URL (a1340) that returned 404 today. Going over 100 Wh (the AOHi Starship 40K, $179) needs airline approval for a bank ChatGPT's answer says some airlines now cap at 100 Wh, so it should stay a footnote.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Delta caps each power bank at 100 Wh 'with no exceptions' and allows at most two. Delta keeps the 101–160 Wh airline-approval route for spare batteries only. That means a 146 Wh power bank such as the AOHi Starship 40,000 mAh is barred on Delta even if the passenger asks for approval.
angles.decides: This confirms that the pick has to stay under 100 Wh. It also argues for moving the AOHi Starship 40,000 mAh (146 Wh) out of the main table, or labelling it 'not allowed on Delta (or American, per ChatGPT's reading of AA's page) even with approval'. The page's 'needs airline approval' label understates the limit. Separately, Anker's US URL for the A1340 27,650 mAh 250W, which the current page lists, now returns 404. Anker's US store is selling the Prime 26K 300W (A110A, 26,250 mAh / 99.75 Wh, $229.99, in stock) in its place.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 100 Wh test is applied to the Wh rating printed on the case, which the rule calculates as rated amp-hours times the cell's nominal voltage. The top 99 Wh packs use 3.6 V cells, so about 27,700 mAh is the real ceiling, not the 27,000 mAh that ChatGPT's 3.7 V table gives.
angles.decides: This confirms that the biggest bank allowed with no approval is the one with the highest Wh on its label below 100. The 27,600 to 27,650 mAh class qualifies: AOHi lists its pack at 99.36 Wh, and the Anker and EcoFlow 27,650 mAh packs work out to 99.54 Wh at 3.6 V (our page's figure; I could not confirm it on their pages today). mAh alone can't sort them, because the same mAh at 3.85 V would be over 100 Wh. Above 100 Wh up to 160 Wh you need the airline's approval, for example for the AOHi Starship 40K. Since 27 March 2026, ICAO rules also cap each person at two power banks and forbid recharging them on board.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how much power a bank just under 100 Wh actually delivers. In ChargerLAB's lab test, the AOHi Future Starship 240W (99.36 Wh) gave out about 79–90 Wh at 15–45 W but tripped its temperature protection after 10 minutes at 140 W, having delivered only about 24 Wh. In Techtest.org's test, the EcoFlow RAPID Pro (99.54 Wh) delivered about 85.5 Wh at that same 28 V/5 A (140 W) load.
angles.decides: It changes the lead pick on our current page. The AOHi Future Starship 240W is listed first, but ChargerLAB's test shows it cannot sustain its advertised 140 W, or even 100 W. At 100 W it stopped after 23 minutes with 35.52 Wh delivered. That matters most to the shopper this query brings, who wants the biggest airline-legal bank, usually to run a laptop. In Techtest.org's test the EcoFlow RAPID Pro held 100 W and 140 W loads all the way to empty (84.2 Wh and 85.5 Wh). Present them side by side with each lab named, not as one benchmark. For the lower-cost slot, Techtest.org measured 74.3–80.4 Wh from the UGREEN 145W 25,000 mAh and weighed it at 508 g, which suggests that slot doesn't need a full 99 Wh bank.
