pages.query: power bank for laptop
pages.why_used: Macworld (cited) says only that a 16-inch MacBook Pro needs a 140 W PD 3.1 bank. It mentions the MagSafe 3 cable once, in passing, gives no model-year limit and no measured loss. None of the results states Apple's rule that 140 W over a USB-C cable works only on the Nov 2023 and later 16-inch, or ChargerLab's measurement on a power bank: 130 W through MagSafe 3 versus 90 W through a USB-C to USB-C cable. D is chosen over C because its measurement was taken on a power bank, not a wall charger.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy these power banks actually deliver out of their rated Wh. Anker itself says its 90 Wh Laptop Power Bank A1695 delivers only about 63–70 Wh, and on the same 26,250 mAh pack it estimates a 30–45% loss. Techtest.org measured the Prime 26K delivering 79.6–89.8 Wh (80–90% of its 99.75 Wh) and an earlier UGREEN 145W revision delivering 74.3–80.4 Wh (80–87% of 90 Wh). The rated 90/91.25/99.75 Wh figures only predict laptop recharges once you apply the same delivered-energy method to every model.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than overturning it. On a delivered-energy basis the $79.99 UGREEN 145W (80–87% measured on the 2023 100 W revision, about 74–80 Wh) and the $229.99 Anker Prime 26K (about 80–90 Wh measured) are about 10 Wh apart. That is a small energy edge for almost 3× the price, so the Prime's case rests on two 140 W ports and 48-minute recharge, not capacity. Anker's own '63–70 Wh usable' for the $119.99 A1695 should not be set against other makers' raw cell Wh as if it were a worse battery. It is the only maker in the set that publishes a usable figure, and Techtest's measurement of the Prime suggests Anker's loss estimates run pessimistic (its 30–45% loss on 99.75 Wh implies about 55–70 Wh vs 79.6–89.8 Wh measured). The table footnote should say this.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many watt-hours each bank actually puts into a laptop, or what that comes to per pound and per dollar. Macworld's MacBook Pro test scores work out to about 87.5 Wh for the Anker Prime 26K ($2.63 per delivered Wh, 66 Wh/lb) and about 64 Wh for the Anker 25K 165W ($1.86 per delivered Wh, 49 Wh/lb). Anker's own figure for the 25K 165W is 65 Wh, which agrees and means less than one full charge of a 70 Wh 14-inch MacBook Pro.
angles.decides: It argues against ChatGPT's Anker 25K 165W card. That bank turns its 90 Wh rating into about 64–65 Wh at the laptop, which is not a full charge of a 70 Wh 14-inch MacBook Pro. The Anker Prime 26K delivers about 87.5 Wh, a full charge plus about 25%. Per dollar, though, both Ankers are beaten by banks Macworld scored 119–120% at under $90 (INIU Cougar P64, EcoFlow RAPID Pro 27K). The UGREEN 145W keeps the best figures on rated specs ($0.89 per rated Wh, 81 rated Wh/lb), but no reviewer has measured what it delivers, so its value pick stays provisional until it is tested.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that USB-C-to-USB-C fast charging (140 W) of a 16-inch MacBook Pro only works on the Nov 2023 model and later; Apple lists Apple's USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable as the only fast-charge route for older 16-inch models. MacRumors reports the 2021/2022 16-inch models are capped at 100 W over USB-C, and ChargerLAB measured an M1 Max 16-inch at 89.88 W over USB-C versus 130.02 W over MagSafe 3. So a 140 W bank's built-in USB-C cable cannot fast-charge those older 16-inch machines.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro from Nov 2023 or later, any 140 W port bank (UGREEN 145W, Anker Prime 26K) works with a 240 W / 5 A USB-C cable. For a 2021 to early-2023 16-inch Pro, the pick must be a bank with a free USB-C port that reaches 140 W, used with Apple's USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable. Built-in-cable banks (Anker A1695, capped at 100 W on every cable; the Baseus FC41's built-in cables) then charge at about 100 W at best. For a 14-inch Pro or MacBook Air, Apple lists 96 W (or 67 W for the 13.6-inch Air) over plain USB-C as fast charge, so the 100 W Anker A1695 is enough and 140 W adds nothing.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 16-inch MacBook Pro only takes the full 140 W through Apple's USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable, or through Apple's 240 W USB-C cable on the Nov 2023 and later models. ChargerLab measured that an M1 Max 16-inch on a 140 W power bank drew about 130 W through MagSafe but dropped to 90 W on a USB-C to USB-C cable.
angles.decides: This confirms the 140 W picks (UGREEN 145W, Anker Prime 26K A110A) only for 16-inch MacBook Pro owners who also use a USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable, or Apple's 240 W USB-C cable on a Nov 2023 or later 16-inch. With an ordinary USB-C to USB-C cable, a 2021 16-inch gets about 90 W in testing. In that case a 100 W bank like the Anker A1695 or the Baseus FC41's 100 W port performs about the same, for less money and weight. Every 14-inch Pro and every Air fast-charges over any USB-C charge cable at 96 W or more, so 140 W adds nothing for them.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives an output-port measurement in Wh, or a sustained-power measurement, for the candidates. techtest.org's electronic-load tests found these numbers. The Anker Prime 26K 300W delivered 79.6–89.8 Wh of its 99.75 Wh rating and held a constant 140 W. The Anker 25K 165W (A1695) averaged 74.2 Wh of its 90 Wh rating, and when asked for 100 W it fell to about 65 W once the battery was down to roughly 25%.
angles.decides: This confirms the Anker Prime 26K 300W as the pick for power-hungry laptops. In a named lab test it delivered the most Wh and held 140 W steadily. It also weakens the Anker 25K 165W ($209.98 in ChatGPT's answer, $119.99 on our page). In the same lab it gave the fewest Wh of the three tested, and it can't hold 100 W through the whole battery. The UGREEN 145W value pick measured 74.3–80.4 Wh, which is better than the A1695. But that test is of a 2023 unit whose top USB-C port was 100 W, so it should not be used for a 140 W version without first checking the model.

pages.query: best power bank for steam deck
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (gamingonbatteries 'Compared for Real Playtime', vgkami, itechguides) say their playtime and capacity figures are calculated or taken from listings. None gives a named reviewer's measured delivered Wh or throttling result for any bank, and none gives a measured Steam Deck draw. This page ranks the banks by Techtest.org's measured Wh, turns that into Deck OLED hours at The Phawx's measured 24 W, adds the 15V⎓3A per-port check, and flags the throttling Techtest measured on the 45 W INIU Carry that ChatGPT recommended.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the maker's own rule for turning a label mAh into deliverable capacity. Anker's support FAQ says that rule is cell mAh × 3.7 V ÷ 5 V × 82% boost efficiency. Applied to the picks, a 20,000 mAh bank delivers about 60.7 Wh and the 24,000 mAh Anker 737 about 72.8 Wh. Against a 50 Wh Steam Deck OLED that is about 1.2 and 1.46 full charges before the Deck's own charging losses.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and doesn't change it. Using the maker's own 82% figure, every 20,000 mAh candidate (INIU P62-E1, UGREEN 20K, Baseus Blade H1) works out to about 1.2 OLED charges, and the 24–25K banks to about 1.45–1.5. That matches the 'about 1.2 / about 1.5' column already on our page. Capacity therefore doesn't separate same-size banks, and price, weight and built-in cables decide the pick. One price note: the UGREEN 25K 165W with built-in cables that ChatGPT showed at $74.99 is $109.99 on us.ugreen.com today, so ChatGPT's 'best value' framing for it is out of date.
products: UGREEN Nexode 25,000 mAh 165 W with Built-in Cables
UGREEN Nexode 20,000 mAh 165 W with Retractable USB-C Cable

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a maker's own usable-output figure into Steam Deck OLED terms. Anker's A1695 is rated at 63–70 Wh usable, which is 1.26–1.40 full OLED charges, about 3.8–4.2 extra hours at Valve's heaviest rate (3 h per 50 Wh) and $1.71–$1.90 per usable Wh at $119.99. UGREEN's 20,000 mAh 100 W is rated at 11,300 mAh at 5 V (56.5 Wh), which is 1.13 OLED charges, about 3.4 heavy-load hours and $1.42 per rated-output Wh at $79.99.
angles.decides: It supports the cheaper pick: the UGREEN 20K 100W costs less per usable Wh ($1.42) than the Anker 25K ($1.71–1.90). Paying the extra $40 for the Anker gets you about 0.13–0.27 more OLED charges, which is about 0.4–0.8 more heavy-load hours. For a Deck-only buyer the Anker is worth it only for the built-in cables. The usable-Wh basis also shows that no bank under 100 Wh gets near two full OLED charges. Our current page's 'about 1.5' for the 25K banks is too high and should read about 1.3–1.4.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Steam Deck fast-charges only by asking for USB PD's 15 V / 3 A level and cannot use 20 V, so a power bank that offers 5 V and 20 V but no 15 V level charges it at 5 V / 15 W, whatever its total wattage.
angles.decides: It adds a spec-sheet check rather than changing the pick. The port the Deck will use must list 15V⎓3A. A big 100 W, 140 W or 250 W total doesn't count without it. Anker's US page lists 15V⎓3A on both USB-C ports of the Anker 737 (A1289), so it passes. I couldn't open the maker pages for the INIU Cougar, UGREEN Nexode 100W, Baseus Blade H1, Anker Prime A1340 or Anker A1695 (rate-limited or 404), so they still need a 15V⎓3A line before the page can say they pass. ChargerLAB's tests also cap expectations: Valve's own 45 W adapter gave about 39 W, and about half of 10 power banks gave about 35 W, the rest 15–25 W. Telling shoppers to buy 65 W+ for headroom therefore makes no difference to the Deck.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Techtest.org (Michael Barton) measured the INIU Carry 20,000 mAh 45 W (P51L-E2) throttling to about 27 W under sustained load, and to 17 W when charging a laptop. ChatGPT picked this $36.99 bank as having 'enough output for the Deck'. The Phawx measured the Steam Deck OLED drawing 24 W in Cyberpunk 2077, so that leaves almost nothing to charge the Deck while playing. Also missing from every result: Techtest's measured delivered Wh for the main candidates, which runs from about 58 to 90 Wh.
angles.decides: It knocks out the INIU Carry 45 W (P51L-E2) as a pick for charging while playing. Its 45 W rating does not hold: Techtest measured it throttling to about 27 W from heat, close to the Deck OLED's measured 24 W draw. It also ranks the bigger banks by measured energy rather than mAh. Anker Prime 26K 300 W delivered 79.6–89.8 Wh. Anker 737 averaged 74.6 Wh, peaking at 78.0 Wh at 20 V/3 A. Anker A1695 averaged 74.2 Wh. UGREEN 25K 165 W (PB552) averaged 72.6 Wh. UGREEN 20K 165 W retractable (PB726) delivered 62.5–66.4 Wh. UGREEN 20K 130 W delivered only 54.8–64.7 Wh, falling as load rose. So the 25 K-class banks give about 10 Wh more usable energy than the 20 K UGREENs, roughly 25 extra minutes at 24 W. The UGREEN 25K 165 W gives about the same measured energy as the Anker A1695 and is listed for less. One limit: Techtest found the UGREEN PB552 throttled from 140 W to 65 W at about half charge, but 65 W is still above the Deck's 45 W.

pages.query: power bank with ac outlet
pages.why_used: None of the rival pages gives the AC outlet ratings of the flight-legal AC power banks (Sherpa 100AC 110 V × 0.9 A = 100 W max, modified sine; Omni 20+ modified sine) or checks them against a device maker's threshold. ResMed sets 150 W continuous as the minimum inverter for newer CPAPs. This page uses that line to split the flight-legal 100 W banks from the 200 W+ power stations, on the CPAP follow-up the shopper keeps getting asked.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No rival result ChatGPT got states that both flight-legal AC power banks it recommends, the Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC and the Omnicharge Omni 20+, have modified-sine outlets according to their own makers. That goes against ChatGPT's own advice to buy pure sine. The $119 BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini is pure sine and is rated 3,000+ cycles to 80%, while Goal Zero rates the Sherpa only for 'Hundreds of Cycles' and doesn't say to what capacity.
angles.decides: It confirms the Sherpa 100AC or Omni 20+ for a laptop on a plane. A laptop's own power brick normally runs fine on modified sine, so a Sherpa buyer loses nothing. But a shopper who follows ChatGPT's pure-sine advice, or who plugs in a CPAP machine or anything motorised, can't get pure sine in the under-100 Wh class from either maker. Their maker-sourced option is the Elite 10 Mini: pure sine, 128 Wh, LiFePO4, rated 3,000+ cycles to 80%, $119 on 2026-11-14. That's less than half the Sherpa's roughly $250, which comes from our old page; I couldn't re-check it today. The catch is that it's over 100 Wh and won't fly as a normal carry-on. The table footnote: '100 W' on the Sherpa is a maximum (110 V × 0.9 A, about 99 W), not a stated continuous rating, and none of these makers publishes a surge figure.

If the shopper flies, the Sherpa 100AC (95 Wh) still wins, and the page should say they pay about $2.63/Wh for the airline-legal size against $0.93/Wh for the Elite 10 Mini. If the bank never goes on a plane, the Elite 10 Mini gives 35% more Wh, twice the AC wattage (200 W vs 100 W) and LiFePO4 cells for less than half the price. That makes it the value pick for car, desk or outage use. Omni 20+ ($249) sits at the Sherpa's price point, so it competes on weight, not on $/Wh.

pages.query: best power banks for flying
pages.why_used: RuntimeWise and the rules pages give the 100 Wh limit and a generic mAh × 3.7 V conversion, but none gives a real bank's printed Wh. None shows that makers rate cells at 3.6–3.8 V, so 27,600–27,650 mAh banks print under 100 Wh while a 3.7 V estimate puts them over, and Anker's 26,250 mAh holds as much as EcoFlow's 27,650. This page lists the printed Wh and the implied voltage for each bank, adds the measured delivered energy, and points buyers to the largest bank they can legally carry.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that makers turn mAh into Wh with different cell voltages: Anker's 26,250 mAh Prime is rated at 3.8 V (99.75 Wh), while EcoFlow's 27,650 mAh RAPID Pro (99.54 Wh) and AOHi's 27,600 mAh Future Starship (99.36 Wh) are rated at 3.6 V. All three are under the 100 Wh limit, but ChatGPT's 3.7 V table would put the two larger banks at about 102 Wh, and only the Wh printed on the label settles whether a bank can fly.
angles.decides: The finding confirms that the largest banks you can fly with are the 99.x Wh ones (EcoFlow RAPID Pro, AOHi Future Starship, Anker Prime 26K), even though ChatGPT's 3.7 V table would rule out anything over about 27,000 mAh. It also means the page should compare banks by label Wh and by delivered energy, not by mAh. Footnote for the table: Anker's 26,250 mAh at 3.8 V and EcoFlow's 27,650 mAh at 3.6 V are almost the same energy (99.75 vs 99.54 Wh), so the extra 1,400 mAh on EcoFlow's box adds nothing. Second footnote for laptop users charging on a plane: the '140 W' port rating is not sustained power. ChargerLAB's AOHi discharge at 100 W stopped on temperature protection after 23 minutes, having delivered 35.52 Wh of the 99.36 Wh label.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy per pound a specific power bank carries, or how much energy the usual two-bank airline limit lets you board with: 2 × 99.75 Wh = 199.5 Wh weighing 1.32 kg (2.64 lb) with Anker's Prime 26K, against 2 × 72 Wh = 144 Wh weighing 582 g (1.28 lb) with Nitecore's NB20000 Gen3, which at 112 Wh/lb carries about 1.5× the energy per pound of the Prime 26K's 75.6 Wh/lb.
angles.decides: Many airlines cap you at two power banks, and RuntimeWise lists seven, Emirates included, that ban recharging a bank from seat power. The energy you board with is therefore close to all you get, so total Wh within the bank limit, and its weight, is the number that matters. For phones and tablets, the Nitecore NB20000 Gen3 gives the most energy per pound among the banks I could source (two of them: 144 Wh for 582 g). For laptops, two Anker Prime 26K banks reach the highest total, 199.5 Wh, but cost 618 g more for 55.5 Wh more. On Emirates (one bank), the best you can carry is the Prime 26K's 99.75 Wh. The finding backs a split pick: a light high-density bank for phones and a 99.75 Wh bank for laptops. It does not support ChatGPT's single answer of a 20,000 mAh bank.

So the reason ChatGPT gave for its top pick, charging a laptop from the bank on a long-haul flight, is the one use the rules now discourage or ban.
angles.decides: It changes the basis for the pick. While flying, the bank mostly cannot be used: it can't be recharged from seat power, and on ICAO-aligned carriers it shouldn't charge a laptop either. So the high output rating (165–300 W) buys little on the plane. What decides the pick is a printed rating of 100 Wh or less (Delta allows 100 Wh each 'with no exceptions'), stowage under the seat, and enough capacity for layovers and the destination. The page should say 'charge your laptop from seat power and use the bank between flights' rather than 'long-haul laptop bank'. That favours a cheaper 20,000 mAh / 72–74 Wh unit (UGREEN 35524, INIU P62-E1, Baseus Blade H1) over $180–230 300 W banks for flying-only buyers. The Anker Prime 26K's 99.75 Wh also shows that mAh × 3.7 V is not the airline figure. At ChatGPT's 3.7 V it would come to 97.1 Wh, but Anker prints 99.75 Wh, which works out to about 3.8 V. Only the printed Wh counts.

pages.query: best portable power station for a 12v fridge for 3 days
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages list capacity, port counts and the DELTA 2 Max manual's car-outlet spec. None gives a measured idle draw for the 2 kWh candidates, and none works out what that draw costs over 72 hours. This page gives The Solar Lab's measured idle and efficiency for six stations, the 72-hour loss and the fridge average left after it. It also says the Anker SOLIX S2000 has no 12V socket.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX S2000, its #2 pick for a 12 V fridge, has no 12 V car output at all. Anker's spec table lists only USB-C (100 W + 15 W), USB-A (12 W) and AC outputs. On the S2000 a 12 V fridge has to run from the fridge's AC adapter with the inverter on, and Anker rates that state at 6 W 'Active Idle Power'. Over 72 h that is about 432 Wh of overhead before the fridge draws anything.
angles.decides: The S2000 should come off a 12 V-fridge list, or be shown as AC-only with an idle penalty. Of the ~2 kWh units, the ones that hold the pick are those with a real 12 V car port: Anker's C2000 Gen 2 (12 V / 10 A), EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max and BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. A normalised idle column also matters for 3 days. Makers state idle three different ways: Anker S2000 gives 'Active Idle 6 W / System Standby 2 W', Anker C2000 Gen 2 gives '9 W idle' with no conditions, and Jackery gives no figure, but The Solar Lab measured about 17 W with the inverter on. Over 72 h those figures range from about 144 Wh to about 1,224 Wh. That is the footnote: run the fridge from the 12 V port with the inverter off, never from AC.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the battery the station uses on itself over 72 hours. That ranges from about 360 Wh (DELTA 2 Max with AC off, 5 W × 72 h) to about 1,944 Wh (DELTA 3 Max with the inverter left on, 27 W × 72 h, 95% of its 2,048 Wh). None of them says that Anker's SOLIX S2000, ChatGPT's #2 pick, has no 12V car-socket output.
angles.decides: 1) The Anker SOLIX S2000 should come off the list as a 12V-fridge pick. Its fridge would have to run through the AC inverter and the fridge's own AC adapter. 2) Over 3 days, the station's own draw matters as much as its capacity. At an average fridge draw of 20 W, the DELTA 2 Max with AC off lasts about 82 h. The Elite 200 V2 lasts about 70 h (its 9.5 W idle figure doesn't say whether the inverter was on). The Jackery 2000 v2 with the inverter on lasts about 55 h, and the DELTA 3 Max with the inverter on about 44 h. So the page should give a rule, 'switch AC off and run the fridge from the 12V socket', and rank stations by measured idle draw with AC off.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got names the one expansion pack that fits the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (Anker SOLIX BP2000 (Gen 2), up to 4 kWh) together with its 12V⎓10A car-charger output and Anker's own claim of 9 W idle draw and 7 days on a portable fridge.
angles.decides: The C2000 Gen 2 confirmation is weak: its 12V port is the standard 10 A socket a compressor fridge needs. The BP2000 (Gen 2) is the only pack Anker names for it, so a shopper who wants more than 3 days with no sun knows which battery to add. The pick still depends on the unsourced auto-off check below. If BLUETTI's DC ECO mode or EcoFlow's 12V DC timeout can turn the car port off between compressor cycles, the page has to tell shoppers which setting to change for a 72-hour run.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a power station can switch its own 12 V car port off under a light load. Jackery's Explorer 2000 Pro manual turns the Car Port off after 12 hours at 2 W or less, and it stays off until someone presses the button.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. As Jackery words the rule, the port only shuts off after 12 continuous hours at 2 W or less, and a compressor fridge that is running breaks that each time the compressor starts. The risk to a 3-day unattended run is mainly in cold weather or with the fridge switched to standby. The page can add a practical step: before leaving, find and turn off any low-load or ECO auto-off for the 12 V port. I could not source the matching setting for the Elite 200 V2 (DC ECO), DELTA 3 Max / DELTA 2 Max, C2000 Gen 2 or Explorer 2000 v2.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the measured no-load idle draw of the candidate stations. The Solar Lab measured these with the inverter on: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 9.5 W, EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max 13.6 W, Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 17 W, Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 18 W and EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max 27 W. Over a 72-hour fridge trip that is roughly 680 to 1,940 Wh lost before the fridge draws anything. No result says either that the Anker SOLIX S2000, ChatGPT's #2 pick for a 12V fridge, has no 12V car socket.

At The Solar Lab's inverter-on idle figures, the DELTA 3 Max (ChatGPT's top pick) could lose about 1,944 Wh over 72 h, nearly its whole 2,048 Wh. The Elite 200 V2 would lose about 684 Wh. The Elite 200 V2 also has the best measured efficiency, 94% against the DELTA 3 Max's 79%. That supports the Elite 200 V2 as our #1 pick among stations that have a 12V socket. The Anker S2000 has the lowest idle of all (6 W, or 2 W with the inverter off), but it has no 12V car socket. It should be dropped from a 12V-fridge list or marked as AC-adapter only. Whatever the station, shoppers should switch the AC inverter off and run the fridge from the 12V port.

pages.query: best portable power station for a travel trailer

That shows the Jackery HomePower 3000 loses 6% of its battery per day to standby where the others lose 12% to 32%.

A shopper who wants the trailer's 30 A panel to act like shore power should pick the HomePower 3000 (30 A, 3,600 W, $1,499 as the Solar Generator listing on jackery.com) or the DELTA Pro 3 (30 A plug limit, 4,000 W). The cycle-life column barely moves the order: the AC200L is the shortest-lived at 3,000 cycles to 80%, and Jackery's 4,000 cycles are counted to 70%, a looser end point than the others' 80%.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out cost per usable watt-hour from a measured discharge, or hours to refill from each station's own maximum solar input. On those numbers the BLUETTI Elite 300 ($1,199 at bluettipower.com; StorageReview measured 2.67 kWh delivered from its 3,014 Wh battery) costs about $0.45 per delivered Wh and refills in about 2.5 h at its 1,200 W solar limit. The Elite 300 delivers more energy per dollar than the C2000 Gen 2 or the HomePower 3000, it is about as light per Wh, and it refills from solar in about the same time while holding about 47% more energy. ChatGPT's #3 pick, the BLUETTI AC200L, is marked 'Discontinued' on BLUETTI's own US store, so it should drop out. A $0.44/Wh figure for it is moot. The C2000 Gen 2 still wins if the shopper's priority is the lowest total weight (41.7 lb) for a light trailer.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got cites a maker document on how a station's neutral is wired. Jackery's own HomePower 3000 (JE-3000B) spec FAQ answers the question 'is the neutral floating or bonded?' with 'floating', and the same FAQ calls its 120V/30A TT-30 port 'an auxiliary power input for small camper vans and trailers'. That matters for a trailer with a hardwired EMS or surge protector that checks for a missing ground.

Jackery documents the HomePower 3000 (ChatGPT's 'best balance' pick) as floating neutral and not expandable ('battery packs: Not supported'). An owner whose hardwired EMS checks for a ground should expect an open-ground fault, and Jackery offers no expansion path. For the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (ChatGPT's #1), Anker's page puts the TT-30R at 20 A / 2,400 W. That is below the 30 A the trailer's inlet implies, even though Anker's headline says 'Power Your Entire RV' and claims the unit runs 'most window and RV A/Cs'.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which fix the EMS side recommends when a trailer's EMS sees a power station's floating neutral as an 'open ground' and cuts power: Progressive EMS support says to remove or bypass the EMS, says not to put a neutral-ground bonding plug in a power station, and offers a permanent bypass switch for EMS units built into the RV.
angles.decides: This confirms the picks rather than changing them. For a trailer with a hardwired EMS (common on newer trailers), any of the candidates may lose power the moment it is plugged into the shore cord, because the EMS reads the station's floating neutral as an open ground. The page should say the plan needs either a plug-in EMS that can be left out or a bypass switch on a built-in one. A bonding plug is disputed: Progressive EMS support (via AIR GEAR) says don't, while Mike Sokol shows how. I found no maker statement saying any candidate bonds neutral to ground, so this does not separate the picks.

pages.query: best portable power station for a window air conditioner
pages.why_used: The two cited pages size stations from spec sheets. BuyerSheet applies a flat 85% to every model and GeneratorChecker a flat 0.70 derate. Neither gives a named reviewer's measured AC efficiency or idle draw. Those measurements run from 79% to 94% and from 9.5 W to 27 W, and they move the top 2 kWh pick from the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max to the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2, about 0.7 h more runtime on a 5,000 BTU unit.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's only above-rated output figure for the Elite 200 V2 (3,900 W 'Power Lifting') is limited by BLUETTI to 'pure resistive loads' like kettles and hair dryers. That means it is not a compressor-start surge. BLUETTI's US page publishes no surge figure at all, while Anker states '4,000W peak' with no duration.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. Every candidate's continuous rating (2,400 to 2,600 W) is already above the 1,300 W (StationHours) to 2,100 W (BuyerSheet) start-up spike these pages assume for a 5,000 BTU unit. So on the maker pages I could open, no candidate needs its boost or peak figure to start the compressor. For the table this means: compare stations on continuous watts, mark the Elite 200 V2 surge as 'not published (3,900 W is resistive-only Power Lifting)', and write Anker's 4,000 W as 'peak, duration not stated'. Don't add the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W to a surge column the way StationHours does.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what each station's own solar kit does while the AC is running. Take a 5,000 BTU window AC at its rated CEER of 11 (about 455 W while cooling). The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 2×200 W kit ($1,499) has 400 W of panels. In full sun those panels cover more than the AC's average draw at 50% duty (268 W from the battery), so the battery still gains about 132 W. With the compressor on all the time, the battery loses 135 W, which stretches a full charge to about 15 hours instead of 3.9. None of these results gives cost per usable Wh either.
angles.decides: This supports the 2 kWh class (Elite 200 V2 or C2000 Gen 2) as the value pick when the shopper adds a 400 W solar kit. With a 5,000 BTU AC running half the time, the 400 W kit keeps the Elite 200 V2 charging during full sun, so daytime cooling has no hard limit and the battery is left for the evening (about 7.7 h at 50% duty). Without panels, neither 2 kWh unit gets a 5,000 BTU AC through a full 8-hour night even at 50% duty: the Elite 200 V2 gets about 7.7 h and the C2000 Gen 2 about 7.65 h. That is the case for a 3 kWh station (Elite 300 or DELTA 3 Ultra), but I did not source those two this session.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a 230 V window AC, the 18,000 BTU class sold as 230 V-only (Midea MAW18S2WWT: 230 V, 10 A), needs a 240 V station. Of the stations on our page, Anker's own page shows 240 V only on the SOLIX F3800, which delivers it through a NEMA 14-50 and an L14-30 outlet (6,000 W max at 240 V) and has no NEMA 6-15 or 6-20 receptacle.

Of the stations on our page, only the Anker SOLIX F3800 (or F3800 Plus) has a 240 V outlet on its maker page, and the shopper still needs a cord or adapter from the 14-50R or L14-30R outlet to the AC's 6-15P or 6-20P plug. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 300's advertised 4,800 W figure is 'Power Lifting', a mode meant only for resistive loads in which real output stays at 2,400 W and which gives no extra startup allowance for motors or compressors; so a fixed-speed window AC's startup surge has to fit under 2,400 W on that unit.
angles.decides: This narrows the Elite 300's headroom but does not rule it out. Its real ceiling for a compressor is 2,400 W, while generatorchecker.com estimates about 2,010 W to start a fixed-speed 8,000 BTU Frigidaire FHWC084WB1 and buyersheet.com assumes about 2,100 W. That leaves roughly 300–390 W of margin. The page should show '2,400 W (4,800 W Power Lifting, resistive only)' rather than any '4,800 W surge' label. It should rank units with a true peak rating, such as the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (2,400 W, peak 4,000 W, no SurgePad mode on its page), ahead of the Elite 300 when the shopper has a fixed-speed (non-inverter) AC. Inverter window ACs, which generatorchecker.com estimates at 1.1–1.5x running watts to start, are unaffected.

The Solar Lab measured AC efficiency and idle draw for three 2 kWh stations: ChatGPT's 'best overall' EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max at 79% and about 27 W, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at about 89% and about 18 W, and the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 at 94% and 9.5 W. Applied to the rated batteries, that is about 1,620 Wh usable on the DELTA 3 Max against about 1,950 Wh on the Elite 200 V2, roughly 20% more air-conditioner runtime from a battery of about the same size.

Two labs agree on the Elite 200 V2: The Solar Lab measured 94% efficiency and APH Networks drained 2,028 Wh (97.8% of rating) at about 987 W. The DELTA 3 Max measured 79% efficiency and about 27 W idle, the worst of the three. At an assumed 450 W (5,000 BTU) draw with no compressor cycling, that works out to about 4.3 h for the Elite 200 V2, about 4.05 h for the C2000 Gen 2 and about 3.6 h for the DELTA 3 Max. Idle draw adds to the gap because a window AC's compressor cycles off and the inverter keeps drawing. Over an 8-hour night that is about 216 Wh at 27 W against 76 Wh at 9.5 W. In the 3 kWh tier, Notebookcheck's Elite 300 test (88% at about 200 W, over 92% at 1,800 W) and The Solar Lab's idle figures (Elite 300 15 W, DELTA 3 Ultra 22 W with 82% efficiency) also lean toward BLUETTI. pages.query: power strip with usb ports

ChatGPT's answer says only that laptops 'benefit from 65W or higher'. The cited Tom's Guide body would not load, so it is unchecked. This page puts the hours, worked out from Apple's 53.8 Wh battery figure, into every row. The overall pick (Anker 351) is not a product we list. Using Apple's 53.8 Wh 13-inch MacBook Air battery, the 20 W strips (Anker 351, TESSAN PS07, TESSAN Tower) need at least 2.7 h and the Anker 12-in-1 needs 1.5 h, or 2.7 h once a second port is in use. pages.query: quiet gaming controller
pages.why_used: Shoppers asking for a quiet gaming controller need to know which buttons are actually silenced. The cited rivals don't say: HLPLANET's G7 page only labels face buttons 'Membrane (Quiet/Soft)', and the Reddit threads and Super Nova manual carry owner opinion or bare specs. None goes input by input through what each maker's 'quiet' covers. None quotes EasySMX's own 'tactile microswitch' D-pad wording for the X05 Pro, and none sets out that the Chitu 2 Silent Edition swaps every button and the stick rings to silicone.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers mean different buttons by 'quiet': EasySMX's own X05 Pro page doesn't say which buttons are damped and calls the D-pad a 'tactile microswitch', which contradicts the 'silicone-damped D-pad' ChatGPT gave as its top pick, while GameSir limits 'silent' on the Super Nova to the ABXY buttons and lists a membrane D-pad.
angles.decides: This confirms the X05 Pro as a pick but corrects what it is quiet at. EasySMX does not stand behind a damped D-pad: the product page says tactile microswitch and the January 2026 press release says metal dome. The only named reviewer, Ban at Retro Handhelds, calls the D-pad 'a really quiet clicky', not silent. For D-pad-heavy play (platformers, fighting games), the Super Nova is the safer quiet choice on the makers' own specs: GameSir lists a membrane D-pad and The SixthAxis says the buttons are membrane 'across the board, including the D-pad'. Its quiet claim, though, covers ABXY only. The page's 'What is quiet' column should show the maker's scope and the reviewer's observation as separate entries per product, with the footnote explaining that 'quiet buttons' is not a standard spec.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how many late-night sessions each quiet pick lasts on one charge. At a stated 2 hours a night, the EasySMX X05 Pro lasts 3 nights (HLPLANET: about 6 h), the standard Mobapad Chitu 2 about 7 (HLPLANET: about 15 h) and the GameSir Super Nova 9 (Wccftech: 18 h).
angles.decides: This confirms the X05 Pro as the quietest-for-the-money pick, but with a cost the page should state. Its measured runtime is the shortest of the quiet candidates: 3 nights at 2 h, against 9 for the Super Nova. A shopper who plays wireless at night and doesn't want to charge every few days should look at the Super Nova (it ships with a charging dock) or the Chitu 2. Wired or 2.4 GHz-dongle play near the PC makes this moot. Separately, EasySMX's own X05 Pro page describes the D-pad as 'tactile microswitch'. That contradicts ChatGPT's 'silicone-damped D-pad' line, so the page should say only the face buttons are maker-confirmed as silicone-damped.
products: Mobapad Chitu 2 HD (standard; Silent Edition shares the 1,000 mAh battery per our page)

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got lists, from each maker's own pages, which quiet pad fits which platform: EasySMX's store sells the X05 Pro for 'PC, Switch, mobile and other handheld consoles' with no Switch 2 claim, Bluetooth polling of only 125–250 Hz and a D-pad described as a 'tactile microswitch'. EasySMX's S05 Pro is the model that combines silicone-damped buttons with stated Switch 2 compatibility and one-button wake-up. The GameSir Super Nova is Bluetooth-only on iOS and needs controller firmware 1.13 or later to wake a Switch 2.
angles.decides: This splits the pick by platform, which is exactly the platform question ChatGPT asked the shopper. PC or Steam Deck: the X05 Pro stays the pick, but over its 2.4 GHz dongle or a cable (1000 Hz), not Bluetooth (125–250 Hz). Also stop saying its D-pad is damped: EasySMX itself calls it a tactile microswitch. Switch 2: the X05 Pro's maker page makes no Switch 2 claim. EasySMX's own S05 Pro ($54.99) states Switch 2 compatibility, one-button wake-up and silicone-damped buttons, so it, or the Mobapad Chitu 2 Silent Edition, should be the Switch 2 cell. PS5: the DualSense is the only candidate. On PC its haptics need USB and its mic works only on Windows. Xbox: the GameSir G7 SE (wired) is the only quiet option. Neither EasySMX pad works on Xbox or PlayStation.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that rumble, not button switches, can be the loudest thing a controller makes. EasySMX's own explainer says 'Strong rumble can create greater room noise than the buttons'. Both quiet picks let you turn it down without a PC: the X05 Pro uses M + Left Stick (Level 0 to 4), and the PS5 has Vibration Intensity and Trigger Effect Intensity under Settings > Accessories.
angles.decides: Keep the EasySMX X05 Pro as the top pick: EasySMX says it 'uses redesigned button mechanics and silicone damping' and Retro Handhelds lists its face buttons as 'Optimized Quiet' membrane. The page should add one setup line, though: quiet buttons don't help if rumble stays strong. On the X05 Pro, press M and push the Left Stick down to lower vibration. For the DualSense, set Vibration Intensity and Trigger Effect Intensity to Off in PS5 Settings > Accessories > Controllers. That keeps the DualSense as the quiet PS5 pick and fixes the trigger-noise caveat ChatGPT left open. The microswitch vs membrane split also backs leaving microswitch pro pads out (GameSir G7 Pro, Cyclone 2).

Gamepadla measured wired button latency at 4.95 ms for the EasySMX X05 Pro, 6.14 ms for the Mobapad Chitu 2, 3.00 ms for the GameSir G7 SE, 7.32 ms for the GameSir Super Nova and 7.8 ms for the DualSense. For the quietest choice, Eric Hauter at Gaming Nexus called the X05 Pro 'definitely the quietest' of the controllers he owns. pages.query: best rechargeable aa batteries
pages.why_used: Neither page that was cited (Digital Camera World and the Which? sample), nor any of the top uncited results, says that eneloop's 2,100 cycles and eneloop pro's 500 come from the old, shallow JIS 2013 test. None gives Panasonic's own full-drain JIS 2019 figures of about 600 and about 150. This page ranks each cycle claim by the test behind it and pairs it with how much charge each cell keeps in storage, which answers 'which last longest' directly.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Panasonic's own figures under the current JIS C 8708:2019 test are about 600 cycles for eneloop AA and about 150 for eneloop pro AA. That test drains the cell fully before each recharge. The widely quoted 2,100 and 500 come from the old JIS 2013 test, which uses low current and never empties the cell, so they cannot be lined up against Tenergy's 1,200 or IKEA's 500, which name no test at all.
angles.decides: It backs eneloop standard as the long-life pick: on Panasonic's own like-for-like full-discharge test it lasts about 4 times as many cycles as eneloop pro (600 vs 150). It weakens eneloop pro for camera flashes, because flash use drains cells fully, which is the case where the 150 figure applies, not the 500. It also means the page's 'Cycles (maker)' column cannot rank eneloop's 2,100 against Tenergy's 1,200 or LADDA's 500: those makers cite no test. The only independent full-discharge number I found is from Which?: LADDA 2450 'lost about a third after 200 cycles'. The column should footnote the test, or show eneloop as 600 / pro as 150 (JIS 2019).
products: Panasonic eneloop AA / eneloop pro AA

The XTAR 1.5 V lithium costs about $7 a cell and only makes sense for devices that misread 1.2 V NiMH.

pages.query: rechargeable aa batteries for solar lights
pages.why_used: The cited pages say only that bigger cells 'can take 3-10 days of direct sunlight' to fill (Ideal Garden Lights) or list mAh with no charge input (Tenergy). This page works it out from a typical 2 V 100 mA path-light panel (about 600 mAh per sunny day): 1.7 sun-days for 1,000 mAh, 2.2 for 1,300 and 3.2 for a 1,900 mAh eneloop. That turns 'match your original capacity' into a number a shopper can check, and it also covers why a 1.5 V lithium AA can never be charged by a roughly 2 V panel.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that none of the cycle counts quoted for solar-light AAs can be compared. Tenergy's 2,000 cycles for both Solla packs and Panasonic's 'up to 2100 times' for eneloop are printed on the maker pages with no test method, depth of discharge or standard, and Tenergy's -4 to 122 °F is a 'working temperature' that does not say whether it covers charging.
angles.decides: It weakens the 'more rated cycles = longer life' reading of our current table, where eneloop shows 2,100, Solla 2,000, EBL 1,200 and Brightown/Lightalent 1,000. Neither of the two figures I could source names its test, so the column should carry a footnote: 'maker figure, test method not stated'. It should not rank cells by it. If the Panasonic 2017-revision figure (about 600 cycles under IEC 61951-2:2017 7.5.1.4, against 2,100 under the 2011 edition's 7.5.1.3) is confirmed on a Panasonic page, eneloop's cycle advantage over Solla goes away. The pick would then rest on what is sourced: Solla ships pre-charged and makes the only solar-specific overcharge/over-discharge claim, and eneloop states 70% charge retained after 10 years. That confirms Tenergy Solla 1000 as the pick for typical 600–1,000 mAh lights.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out, for each AA capacity, how many sunny days a typical garden-light panel needs to fill it. A 2V 100 mA panel with about 6 h of sun gives roughly 600 mAh a day. On that basis a 1,000 mAh Solla needs about 1.7 sun-days, a 1,300 mAh cell about 2.2 and a 2,000 mAh eneloop or Brightown about 3.3. The light only drains about 600 mAh a night, so capacity above one day's harvest is buffer for cloudy nights and does not make the light brighter or run longer.
angles.decides: It backs ChatGPT's 'don't oversize' warning with a number and makes it a rule of thumb. For a common 600 mAh, 2V/100 mA path light, 1,000–1,300 mAh is the most a single sunny day can nearly or fully refill (1.7–2.2 sun-days). 2,000 mAh cells (eneloop, Brightown) need 3+ sun-days, so in short winter days they mostly sit partly charged. By cost per Wh from the makers' own stores, the Tenergy Solla Premium 1300 20-pack ($0.88/Wh) and the Solla 1000 24-pack ($0.90/Wh) beat the 12-packs. EBL's own store, at $3.75 a cell for a 4-pack, is the poorest value. So for most lights the pick is the Solla 1000 (24-pack) or the Solla Premium 1300 (20-pack), not a 2,000 mAh cell.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states why a 1.5 V lithium 'rechargeable' AA can't work in a solar light: XTAR says its 1.5 V Li-ion AA (a 3.6 V cell behind a buck regulator) needs a 4.75–5.5 V charging voltage, while a garden-light solar cell puts out about 2 V open-circuit in bright sun, so the light's own panel can never recharge it. Only a 1.2 V NiMH cell can be charged by that panel.
angles.decides: It rules out 1.5 V lithium rechargeable AAs, including the XTAR 1.5 V AA 4,150 mWh that Dealectric lists, for solar lights: the panel can't reach their charge voltage, so they would drain and stay flat. That leaves 1.2 V NiMH as the only workable chemistry and supports the Solla, EBL and eneloop rows. At 20 mA a 600 mAh cell takes about 30 h of full sun and a 2,000 mAh cell about 100 h, so 1,000–1,300 mAh cells fit small lights better than 2,000 mAh ones. That backs ChatGPT's 'match the original capacity' advice and the 1,000/1,300 mAh Solla picks over eneloop or Brightown 2,000 mAh for typical path lights.

pages.query: best replacement dvr for my existing analog security cameras
pages.why_used: The Dahua and Hikvision pages that were cited cover video formats and resolution. None of them says how the cameras get their power. If the old DVR powered the cameras through the coax, they stay dark on an ordinary hybrid DVR such as the cited XVR7208A-4K-I3, which runs on 12 VDC 5 A and lists no camera power. Dahua's PoC XVR names only HDCVI PoC cameras as the ones it powers. This page puts that check before the pick and adds US maker-store prices.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, across brands, that a '4K' DVR records 4K coax cameras at only 7–15 fps per channel: Viewtron VT-DVR-8 does 7 fps at 4K/8MP, and Dahua XVR7208A-4K-I3 does 15 fps on TVI and AHD. Dahua's 30 fps at 4K needs CVI cameras and Encode Enhancement turned on, and covers only channels 1 and 5. Older CVBS cameras stay at 960H on any of these recorders.
angles.decides: The footnote changes the pick by camera type. GL.iNet's own blog adds a second point for shoppers who want to reach their home server: at 288 ms round trip, a GL.iNet case saw 47.3 Mbps through WireGuard against 455 Mbps without it. pages.query: best triple-screen laptop extender for a 16-inch laptop with 19201200 panels
pages.why_used: The cited roundups and answers repeat the warning that base M1/M2 Macs support only one external display, and they offer driver-based extenders as the fix. None of them says that every Apple-silicon 16-inch MacBook Pro drives at least two external displays natively. None says that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' units block protected video on every screen. This page adds Apple's display counts per chip, FOPO's own driver and Mac statements, and Plugable's HDCP documentation.

angles.name: Normalise

The 'base M-chip supports one external display' caveat therefore does not apply to a 16-inch Mac, and a driver-free extender with two added screens runs both screens independently without the UsbDisplay/DisplayLink-style driver.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro: 3 external displays; M5 Max: 4), the driver-free dual-16-inch extenders work with both screens extended and no driver. These are the FOPO S11 at $399.99 and the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite. That removes the Mac reason our page gives for picking the driver-based S788. The S788 is still the choice only for a buyer who wants three added screens, which makes four displays in total, not a triple-screen setup. For a laptop + 2 'triple' setup, the pick shifts toward the S11 or Dual Lite. The footnote for the table is: 'Triple' in product names is not a fixed count. FOPO S11 means laptop + 2 screens. FOPO S788 'Triple' means 3 added screens, so 4 displays. INVZI MagHub 'Quad Max' means 3 added screens.

I couldn't open a page to confirm the INVZI price, though. The S9G is cheapest at $150 per screen, but that price comes from UPERFECT's blog, not FOPO's store.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that no 16-inch MacBook Pro ships with a base chip: Apple's spec sheets say the 16-inch M1 Pro (2021) drives up to two external displays and today's 16-inch M5 Pro and M5 Max drive up to three and four, so the base-chip limit of one external display, which ChatGPT and UPERFECT gave as the reason to buy a driver-based extender, never applies to a 16-inch Mac.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro owner, this confirms a driver-free dual-panel extender (two 16-inch 1920×1200 screens over USB-C or HDMI, like the INVZI MagHub Dual 16 or FOPO S11 that ChatGPT showed). It also removes the Mac-chip argument for a driver-based unit like the FOPO S788 or INVZI MagHub Trio 16, which would add a USB display driver and an extra power supply for no compatibility gain. Pick driver-based only when a Windows 16-inch laptop has fewer than two video-capable outputs. The page should open its compatibility table with: '16-inch MacBook Pro, any Apple-silicon generation: two native external displays, so driver-free works.'

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that every 16-inch Apple-silicon MacBook Pro natively drives at least two external displays, so base-chip workarounds don't apply to a 16-inch Mac, or that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' extenders (DisplayLink, Silicon Motion InstantView) block HDCP-protected video such as Netflix and Prime Video on every screen of the Mac, including the built-in one, while they are connected.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro, the Mac caveat that pushed ChatGPT toward driver-based extenders doesn't apply. The 2021 M1 Pro already drives two external displays natively, and the current M5 Pro drives three. So a driver-free two-screen extender is the pick, as long as each screen gets its own native video output: the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite (USB-C plus mini-HDMI per its Best Buy listing title) or the FOPO S11. Driver-based units (FOPO S788, MagHub Trio 'Driver Required') add a third screen. On a Mac they cost you protected streaming on all screens, and on macOS 15 and later the Screen Recording permission they need may have to be renewed periodically. Only someone who needs three external screens, or has a laptop without two video-capable outputs, should take that trade.

On a 13-inch Air the Trio 3 Pro hangs 4.13 lb off a 2.7 lb laptop, 53% more than the laptop weighs, and the bag weight comes to 6.83 lb. angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a MacBook Air with an M4 or M5 still needs Xebec's separate Mac Adapter (with DisplayLink) to run the Tri-Screen 3. Xebec's help center says Macs with Thunderbolt ports are 'Not compatible — Mac Adapter required.' On the same M4/M5 Air, Macworld ran the Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro without any driver, using one USB-C cable per screen.

It also runs through DisplayLink, which Macworld says caps at 60 Hz and blocks protected content on every screen. The Trio 3 Pro uses the Air's native two-display support over its two Thunderbolt ports with no driver, though that fills both of the Air's USB-C ports and leaves only MagSafe for charging. For M1, M2 and M3 Airs, every candidate needs software or a dock: the Trio needs Mobile Pixels' driver, the Xebec needs its Mac Adapter, and Kefeya says a docking station is required. So the pick should be split by chip, and the Xebec's 'Mac adapter needed' warning must not be limited to older Airs.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that macOS does not support DisplayPort MST for extended displays, so one native USB-C video cable can only carry one extended screen to a Mac. On an M4 or M5 MacBook Air, a driver-free triple extender therefore needs both Thunderbolt ports, one per screen, with MagSafe left for charging. For the same reason, Xebec says the single-cable Tri-Screen 3 needs its DisplayLink Mac Adapter on every Mac, not only on M1, M2 and M3 models.

Its two USB-C cables, one per screen, drive both screens natively with no driver: Macworld's Simon Jary says Macs above plain M1 and M2 run both screens 'without the software download', and Apple specs two external displays plus the built-in screen. The Xebec Tri-Screen 3 runs on a single cable, so it stays tied to the $59 DisplayLink adapter and its driver even on an M5 Air. That makes it a weaker buy for new Airs and moves it to the 'M1–M3 or must-be-one-cable' slot. On M1, M2 and M3 Airs every candidate needs a driver either way, so the finding doesn't change the pick there.

pages.query: trolling motor with battery

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the headline watts on these motors are battery-draw figures you can compare directly (rated watts × maker runtime ≈ pack Wh), or that the extra watts are not: ePropulsion's kLite 750 '750 W' boost only works above 50% charge, which caps it at about 15 minutes (its own table), the eLite's 750 W Sport mode runs 1 minute at a time, Newport's '600W' is a peak figure, and every maker's 'HP equivalent' works out to about 3 hp per kW when 1 kW is only 1.34 mechanical hp.
angles.decides: It confirms the kLite 750 as the kayak pick on fair terms. Taken at sustained power, the kLite (500 W nominal) and Newport NK180 HD (600 W peak, 25 A at 24 V) are close. The kLite's 750 W boost is a burst of about 15 minutes and should not be read as more power than the Newport. It also says to compare the Spirit 1.0 Plus (1,000 W) and Torqeedo Travel S (1,100 W input) by watts and Wh, not by their matching '3 HP' labels, which mean the same thing as Newport's '1.8 HP' at 600 W. Cycle life cannot be compared one-to-one: the kLite gives 800 cycles to 80% state of health, while the Spirit Battery Plus manual gives 500 cycles at 80% depth of discharge.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states price per Wh or Wh per pound carried. At today's prices the ePropulsion Spirit 1.0 Plus costs $2.35 per Wh against $3.15 for the Torqeedo Travel S that ChatGPT showed. The Spirit also carries 28.9 Wh per lb against the Travel S's 24.7 Wh per lb: 196 Wh more for $399 less, and the total weight is only 0.3 lb higher.
angles.decides: For dinghies and jon boats this changes ChatGPT's pick. The Spirit 1.0 Plus with its battery gives 1,276 Wh for $2,999 at 44.1 lb. The Torqeedo Travel S gives 1,080 Wh for $3,398 at 43.8 lb. The ePropulsion runtime table also shows 5:00 at 250 W (4.4 mph). For kayaks, the eLite ($3.44/Wh, 21.7 Wh/lb) beats the kLite 750 ($4.23/Wh, 19.5 Wh/lb) on both numbers. The kLite's case is its kayak-specific mount and longer test runtime at 4 mph. The Newport NK180 HD bundle is the cheapest energy here at $1.78/Wh, with a separate battery. Its bundle price equals motor, battery and charger bought separately. The NT300 bundle ($2,767.97) costs $807.99 more than its motor plus 36V 30Ah battery bought separately ($1,959.98).

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the ePropulsion eLite and kLite 750 cannot run directly from an external battery. Their Range Extension Kit only lets a 12 V third-party battery recharge the built-in 378 Wh pack at up to 100 W. The Spirit 1.0 Plus does take external batteries directly (39–60 V input), and the new 44 V Torqeedo Travel batteries are not on the compatibility list of the older 29.6 V Travel 1003/1103 battery.

A shopper who buys a kLite 750 or eLite and adds a 12 V LiFePO4 battery (for example the Redodo 12V 50Ah we already list) gets a slow on-water recharger, not more power. ePropulsion's own extended-range figure is 378 Wh + 691 Wh = 1,069 Wh, and the external battery flows in at no more than 100 W, so refilling the 378 Wh pack takes at least 3.8 h. A shopper who wants to swap in a bigger separate battery should look at the Spirit 1.0 Plus, whose external-battery input accepts 39–60 V and for which ePropulsion recommends its E-Series packs. Owners of an older Torqeedo Travel 1003/1103 should not expect their 915 Wh battery to carry over to the new Travel S, because the new packs are 44 V. The traditional 12 V Redodo batteries on our page do not plug into any of these integrated motors.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Minn Kota's own rule for a motor plus a separate lithium battery: the battery's continuous discharge rating must cover the motor's max amp draw, otherwise the battery management system restricts power and the motor 'may shut off or perform erratically'. Minn Kota also says brushed motors on lithium should be held to 85% speed (Speed 8.5).

The Redodo 12V 50Ah Bluetooth trolling battery is rated 60 A continuous for 30 minutes, so it clears that check and the row can stay. Redodo's general-purpose 12V 50Ah has a 50 A BMS, which leaves no margin at full throttle on a 55 lb motor, so it should not be swapped in. The page should also tell readers with brushed Minn Kota motors to cap speed at 85% on lithium, per Minn Kota. The integrated ePropulsion units avoid the whole question because the motor and BMS come matched.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured on-water speed. Cruising World timed the Torqeedo Travel 1103 S at 4.3 kn and the ePropulsion Spirit 1.0 Evo at 4.2 kn on the same 8 ft inflatable, and a 2.5 hp Mercury gas outboard reached only 4.6 kn on that boat.

A 1 kW motor with a clip-on battery (Spirit 1.0 Plus, which ePropulsion says floats) tops out at about 4 kn on a dinghy in two independent tests, Cruising World and Yachting Monthly. pages.query: best usb xlr microphone
pages.why_used: The cited rivals recommend USB/XLR hybrids so the buyer can 'upgrade to an audio interface later', but none of them says what each mic keeps once it is on XLR. The MV7+'s auto gain and denoiser stop working on XLR, though both of its outputs run at the same time. The PodMic USB's XLR port goes dead while USB is plugged in, and over XLR it loses APHEX and headphone monitoring. The XLR sensitivities show how much more interface gain each mic needs. This page states all of that from Shure's manual, Thomann, Podcastage, ComputerBase and the makers' spec sheets.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each hybrid mic actually keeps when you move it to an audio interface over XLR. The Rode PodMic USB's XLR port goes dead while USB-C is plugged in. In XLR mode it also loses APHEX processing and its headphone jack, and a Behringer UMC204HD had to be turned all the way up to drive it. The Shure MV7+ runs USB and XLR at the same time, and its XLR feed is unprocessed.
angles.decides: If the shopper plans to move to an interface later, which is the reason ChatGPT gave for buying a hybrid, the PodMic USB's 'value' pick gets weaker. Over XLR it is a plain dynamic mic with about 1.4 mV/Pa output and none of the features ChatGPT credited it with. ComputerBase had to max out a UMC204HD to drive it, with audible noise. The MV7+ gives a 2 dB hotter XLR signal (1.78 mV/Pa) and can feed a processed USB stream and a raw XLR stream at the same time, for example a recorder plus a stream. That backs the MV7+ for anyone who will really use the XLR side. For USB-only buyers the PodMic USB pick still holds.

angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The Q9U and PodMic USB come out about the same in XLR mode (both -57 dB, about 1.4 mV/Pa). Either way, a shopper who wants the XLR upgrade needs an interface with about 58 dB of clean gain or an inline booster. I couldn't source the MV7+ XLR sensitivity, so I can't rank it on this figure. The page should add a 'gain needed via XLR' column next to 'Outputs'.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Shure's MV7+ manual says XLR audio is not affected by software settings, so Auto Level, the denoiser and the other MOTIV features drop out once the mic goes into an interface. The results also don't give the makers' XLR sensitivities, which show the Samson Q9U (−57 dBV/Pa) needs about 6 dB more preamp gain than the Maono PD400X (−51 dBV) and 2 dB more than the MV7+ (−55 dBV/Pa).

It also adds a warning: ChatGPT's reason for picking it (auto gain and denoising) disappears when the shopper 'upgrades to an audio interface', because Shure says software settings don't affect XLR audio. Over XLR, the PD400X's hotter −51 dBV output suits a low-gain interface better than the Q9U's −57 dBV/Pa. pages.query: which ecoflow power station should i buy

None of them separates the fixed DELTA 3 Max, DELTA 3 Ultra and DELTA 3000 Gen4 from the expandable Plus and 3800 Gen4 versions, or mentions EcoFlow's short list of models that can auto-start the Smart Generator. That choice has to be made before buying, because a fixed unit stays at its built-in capacity for life.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that each EcoFlow lists three different wattages (rated continuous, surge, and X-Boost), or that EcoFlow's own manual says X-Boost works by limiting voltage, is 'more suitable for heating devices' and does not work with appliances that have strict voltage requirements, while the US store copy lists X-Boost figures beside refrigerators, washers, circular saws, laptops and air conditioners. A motor appliance has to fit inside the rated figure (1,800 W on DELTA 3 Classic, 2,400 W on DELTA 3 Max, 3,000 W on DELTA 3 Max Plus, 3,600 W on DELTA 3 Ultra), not the X-Boost figure (2,600 / 3,400 / 3,800 / 4,600 W).
angles.decides: It changes which size to buy for anyone who wants to run a motor or electronic load above a model's rated output, such as a window AC, well pump, washer or saw. EcoFlow's own manual limits X-Boost to heating devices and excludes appliances with strict voltage requirements, so the X-Boost number does not count for these loads. The shopper should pick by rated continuous watts, with surge covering only the start-up spike. For a 2,000-2,400 W motor load, the DELTA 3 Classic (1,800 W rated, US$479 on the product page today) is too small even though its 2,600 W X-Boost figure looks big enough. The shopper needs at least the DELTA 3 Max (2,400 W, from US$879 per the store's search listing; the search tool did not split Max from Max Plus) or the Max Plus (3,000 W, US$1,149). For kettles, hair dryers and heaters, X-Boost does let the smaller unit run them, at reduced heat. Two smaller points: EcoFlow's US pages now state lifespan as '10 years' instead of cycles to a stated percentage, so cycle-life figures can't be compared across the range. Switchover time is 10 ms on the DELTA 3 family against '<30ms EPS' on the still-sold RIVER 2 Pro and RIVER 2 (240), which matters for a desktop PC or NAS.

pages.query: which enclosed 3d printer heats up the fastest
pages.why_used: The cited rivals give QIDI Plus4 warm-up times only from QIDI's own blog, a retail listing and an anonymous owner, and they list Bambu times as not published. This page names who timed each chamber and how (thermocouples, bed on or off, a 230 V unit). It also adds two things from QIDI's own firmware: the Plus4 caps its chamber heater at 40%, and it waits for the bed before heating the chamber.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 'up to 65 °C' chamber rating hides a 1.85× spread in heater power per litre of build volume across QIDI's current enclosed printers. The figures, from QIDI's spec sheets, are Plus5 550 W ≈ 17.9 W/L, Q2 280 W ≈ 15.0 W/L and Max4 500 W ≈ 9.7 W/L. Creality's K2 Plus heater only switches on when the chamber is set above 40 °C. Bambu publishes no chamber-heater wattage for the H2D or H2S.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's top pick, the Plus4, is listed as discontinued (desktop3dprinters.us). After normalising, the QIDI Plus5 ($699 at QIDI US) has the most stated chamber-heater power per litre among current models. It also has the only maker-stated steady-state figure (500 W for ABS at 25 °C ambient) and a bed QIDI says runs at full power for 3–5 minutes during warm-up. That makes it the best-supported current answer for chamber heat-up. The Max4 has the same 65 °C label but about half the heater power per litre, so 'same max temperature' should not be read as 'same warm-up'. The K2 Plus's 60 °C rating comes with a heater that only runs for setpoints above 40 °C. None of this is a measured head-to-head time; it ranks stated heater power only.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states chamber-heater watts per litre of cabinet. On that measure the QIDI Plus5 is highest (550 W ÷ 136.2 L = 4.04 W/L), well ahead of ChatGPT's pick, the Plus4 (400 W ÷ 135.3 L = 2.96 W/L), and ahead of the Q2 (3.22 W/L) and Max4 (2.53 W/L).
angles.decides: This changes the pick ChatGPT gave. It named the Plus4 for fastest chamber heat-up, but by the maker's own figures the Plus5 puts 1.37× as much chamber-heater power into almost the same size cabinet (4.04 / 2.96 = 1.37). The Plus5 should therefore warm its chamber fastest of the QIDI line, and Dealectric lists it. This is a power-density proxy, not a measured time. Bambu (H2S, X2D, H2D) and Creality (K2 Plus) don't publish chamber-heater wattage, so the ratio can't rank them; the page should say so rather than guess.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that QIDI's current Plus4 firmware limits the 400 W chamber heater to 40% duty (max_power 0.4, roughly 160 W) and holds chamber heating until the bed reaches temperature, while the QIDI Q2 firmware lets its 280 W chamber heater run at full power (max_power 1). That makes the '~5–8 min' Plus4 chamber figure ChatGPT used a poor guide to a Plus4 running current firmware.
angles.decides: It weakens ChatGPT's pick of the Plus4 for 'fastest chamber heating'. On current firmware the Plus4's usable chamber heater power (0.4 × 400 W ≈ 160 W) is below the Q2's uncapped 280 W, and the Plus4 heats bed and chamber one after the other rather than together. Any warm-up time for the Plus4 should name the firmware and power setting. The fast 5–8 min figures come from before the cap or from unstated conditions. This finding does not by itself prove the Q2 heats its chamber faster, because the Q2 has a smaller chamber and nobody has published a timed Q2 test.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that on US 110–120 V power each printer's heaters share a smaller power budget. Bambu rates the H2S at 1,170 W max at 110 V against 2,050 W at 220 V. Creality says the K2 Plus chamber may not reach its 60 °C target at 110 V when the room is below 15 °C. The QIDI Plus4 has a separate 400 W chamber heater on top of its 450 W machine rating.
angles.decides: This supports the QIDI Plus4 as the pick for fast chamber heating in a US home. Its 400 W chamber heater has its own power rating on top of the 450 W machine rating. Bambu's H2S is limited to 1,170 W in total on 110 V. Creality itself warns the K2 Plus chamber may not reach 60 °C at 110 V in a cool room. Shoppers on 120 V should expect Bambu and Creality warm-ups to be slower than figures measured on 220 V.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got names who timed any chamber or says how. CNC Kitchen (Stefan Hermann) put thermocouples in a European 230 V Bambu Lab X2D and measured a real 65 °C in about 20 minutes with the chamber heater alone. He says running the heated bed too roughly halves that, and US 110–120 V units will likely take longer. On the H2D he timed about 10 minutes to 60 °C with bed and heater together, also on a 230 V machine.
angles.decides: This partly undermines ChatGPT's pick. The only named, instrumented chamber timings I could open are for the Bambu Lab X2D and H2D. The QIDI Plus4's '5 minutes to ~60 °C' is from QIDI's own blog and names no tester or conditions. So the Plus4-vs-X2D comparison sets a vendor claim against a heater-only thermocouple test on a 230 V European unit, which is not a fair head-to-head. With the bed on as well, CNC Kitchen's numbers put the X2D at roughly 10 minutes and the H2D at about 10 minutes to 60 °C. Both figures come from 230 V machines, and a US shopper's 120 V unit is likely slower. The page should say plainly that no named reviewer has timed the QIDI Plus4, QIDI Plus5, Creality K2 Plus or Bambu H2S under the same conditions, so 'fastest' cannot be crowned from measurements.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that CNC Kitchen measured the Bambu Lab X2D's chamber with thermocouples, finding it reached a real 65 °C in about 20 minutes on the heater alone and in roughly half that with the bed also heating, which is the only thermocouple-measured time to the full 65 °C among the candidates; the X2D is also $589 at 3D Universe today, $60 less than the QIDI Plus4's $649 at QIDI US.
angles.decides: This narrows ChatGPT's Plus4 pick rather than confirming it. With the bed running, the X2D reaches a real 65 °C in about 10 minutes (CNC Kitchen: 'roughly half' of 20 min). The Plus4's best owner figure is under 10 minutes to a 60 °C reading on a sensor that read high, with print-ready at 16 min 30 s. So the two are about level on chamber heat-up, and the X2D's figure was measured more strictly. The X2D also costs $60 less today ($589 at 3D Universe against $649 at QIDI US). The page should call the Plus4 and X2D a near-tie on chamber heat-up, say the X2D's time is the better-measured one, and note it is cheaper today. QIDI's own pages give heater wattage (Plus4: 400 W) but no heat-up time.

pages.query: which solar generator with panels included recharges the fastest from its own panels
pages.why_used: The cited rivals rank 200–400 W bundles: Trek4Tech's fastest takes 5.4 h, with no prices and no ALLPOWERS kit. RuntimeMath's fastest pairing is a station and panel bought separately. None of them lists the P1800 + 600 W bundle or gives each kit's hours to full from its own panels. angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180 + 2×200 W kit gets its full 400 W only if the two SP200L panels are wired in series. The AC180's solar input is capped at 10 A (12–60 V). Each SP200L's short-circuit current (Isc) is 10.8 A and its open-circuit voltage (Voc) is 24.6 V. Wired in parallel, the pair therefore cannot deliver more than about 246 W, so a full charge takes at least 4.7 sun-hours instead of 2.9. In series the pair is 49.2 V Voc, which is under the 60 V limit, so all 400 W can reach the battery.
angles.decides: This does not change the fastest pick on panel-to-battery ratio. That is the ALLPOWERS P1800 kits: 1,024 Wh with 600 W of panel, about 1.7 h at rated panel watts, or with 400 W, about 2.6 h. The P1800's solar input is 650 W, which is above both panel sizes. The finding sets a condition on the next-fastest kit. The BLUETTI AC180 + 2×200 W ($1,232) is about 2.9 h only in series and at least 4.7 h in parallel, which would put it behind both P1800 kits by a wide margin. The Elite 200 V2 has a 20 A input, so its 2×200 W kit (about 5.2 h) is not affected much by wiring. The page should give 'wire in series' as the instruction for the AC180 kit.

pages.why_used: The cited rivals rank the Kobra S1 quietest on Anycubic's own ≤44 dB and carry no independent reading of it; none names a tester, date and distance beside each figure. This page adds igor'sLAB's 59.6 dB(A) for the Kobra S1 (and its 64.7 dB(A) P1S reading at 40 cm), credits the CC2's 44–47 dB to Notebookcheck, and adds Anycubic's own 48/55 dB rating for the bundled ACE 2 Pro.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the quiet-mode figures behind its ranking come from three different test setups that cannot be lined up. Only Bambu gives a distance (P2S: under 50 dB in Silent Mode at 1 m). Elegoo's 45 dB for the Centauri Carbon 2 is a lab reading in Silent Mode with the auxiliary part-cooling fan switched off, at no stated distance. Anycubic's 44 dB for the Kobra S1 has no stated distance or speed. Bambu owners report that Silent Mode runs at 50% speed. A 1 m vs 0.5 m difference alone is worth about 6 dB, more than the 44-vs-50 dB gap the ranking rests on.
angles.decides: It weakens ChatGPT's 'Kobra S1 is quietest' pick, which rests on unlike maker numbers. The only claim with a distance (P2S under 50 dB at 1 m) is not shown to be louder than Kobra S1's ≤44 dB or CC2's 45 dB, because those carry no distance, and Elegoo's has the part fan off. A fair page ranks on independent same-distance measurements, or says it can't. For a shopper it also says that every 'silent' figure costs print speed (Bambu Silent Mode is about half speed by owner reports). QIDI Q2, Plus5 and Max4, which Dealectric lists, publish no dB figure at all, so they can't enter a spec ranking.

pages.query: bluetti apex 200 vs apex 300 for home backup
pages.why_used: The cited BLUETTI comparison says only that panel use 'requires compatible integration or transfer equipment', and the cited product pages name no kit. None of them says that BLUETTI's single-unit panel kit fits only the Apex 300 ($699, 'Compatible Models: Apex300') or that the Apex 200 reaches a home backup kit only in a $5,699 two-unit Hub A1 bundle. This page names the kit, what it fits, what it contains and what it costs, and prices both routes today.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Apex 300's headline 0 ms UPS applies only to two front outlets in 240 V mode, and that in ordinary 120 V mode it is a 20 ms unit that StorageReview measured at 16 ms, which is no faster than the Apex 200's ≤15 ms (a mode that is off by default); none says either that the 7,680 W and 5,400 W 'Lifting Power' figures are not surge ratings.
angles.decides: The Apex 300 stays the pick for any 240 V load. For a shopper with only 120 V essentials, UPS speed is not a reason to pay more: in 120 V mode the Apex 300 is a 20 ms unit (16 ms measured), the same class as the Apex 200's ≤15 ms. Compared standalone, the output gap is 640 W (3,840 W vs 3,200 W), not 240 W, because the Apex 200's 3,600 W needs an expansion battery or live input. On BLUETTI's store today the Apex 200 is $400 cheaper ($1,099 vs $1,499), so it gets stronger for 120 V-only backup.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a price for the Apex 200 or a cost per Wh for either unit, and none includes measured idle draw in the runtime figures. BLUETTI lists the Apex 200 at $0.43/Wh against $0.54/Wh for the Apex 300 today. With the measured idle draws (12.8 W vs 19.5 W), the smaller Apex 200 runs longer than the Apex 300 at any average load under about 71 W.
angles.decides: This confirms that the Apex 200 is the pick for 120 V essentials only. It is 21% cheaper per Wh at today's early-bird price ($0.43 vs $0.54), and 30% more Wh/lb (43.0 vs 33.0). At typical overnight essentials loads under about 71 W it runs longer than the Apex 300, despite having 204.8 Wh less battery, because it idles at 12.8 W against 19.5 W. The Apex 300's extra $400 buys 240 V and 640 W more output, not runtime. So it only wins if the shopper needs 240 V loads or panel integration. The Apex 200 also cannot make 240 V when paired (The Solar Lab). Two caveats belong on the page. The Apex 200 early-bird price ends Nov 18; at its $1,399 compare-at price the two units cost about the same per Wh. And both product pages now say shipping in late January, so neither is a quick buy for this winter.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI sells a panel-connection kit for a single Apex 300 (Apex 300 Home Integration Kit, $699, 'Compatible Models: Apex300'), while the only home backup kit BLUETTI lists for the Apex 200 comes in a 2× Apex 200 + 2× B300K + Hub A1 bundle at $5,699, and the Hub A1 manual covers only the Apex 300.
angles.decides: For 'home backup' that means wiring into the house panel, the Apex 300 is the only one of the two with a maker-listed single-unit kit: one Apex 300 ($1,499) plus the Home Integration Kit ($699) comes to $2,198 on BLUETTI US today. On BLUETTI's store, the Apex 200 reaches a home backup kit only in a two-unit Hub A1 bundle ($5,699), and the Hub A1 manual (V1.2) and product page list only the Apex 300. That supports the Apex 300 for panel-connected backup. The Apex 200 ($1,099 early-bird, ends Nov 18) suits plug-in essentials over extension cords or its TT-30R. Both take B300K and B500K batteries, so capacity does not decide between them.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Apex 300's 0 ms UPS covers only its two left AC outlets, in 240V mode, fed from the 15A AC input (every other setup switches in 20 ms), or that a 120V-only unit like the Apex 200, which BLUETTI lists with no panel input and only a TT-30R RV outlet, leaves 'half your home' without power in BLUETTI's own words.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick and adds no new decider. If the plan is to feed a home panel through a transfer switch or 240V inlet, or to run any 240V load, only the Apex 300 works. The Apex 200 is 120V only, has a TT-30R RV outlet and no listed panel input, and BLUETTI says a 120V-only source means 'half your home' is cut off. The new nuance matters for CPAP or network gear: on the Apex 300, 0 ms needs the 15A input, 240V mode and the two left outlets, and anything else gets 20 ms. The Apex 200 is ≤15 ms, but only after UPS is turned on in the app. Separately, our page's 'Status' column is out of date. BLUETTI now says both units ship in late January.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, in named tests, the Apex 300's UPS transfer measured 16 ms rather than the 0 ms BLUETTI advertises (StorageReview). Nor does any state that the Apex 200 idles at 12.8 W against about 20 W for the Apex 300 and converts at 90% against 85% (The Solar Lab). Those measured numbers leave the two units within about 2% of each other in usable AC energy, even though the Apex 300's battery is 8% larger.
angles.decides: The measurements confirm the pick: choose by whether you need 240 V. They also remove two reasons to pay about $400 more for the Apex 300 when 120 V is enough. First, its 0 ms UPS claim measured 16 ms, the same range as the Apex 200's ≤15 ms spec. Second, its larger battery yields about the same usable AC energy because of higher idle draw and lower efficiency. For a 120 V fridge-and-router outage, the Apex 200 delivers about the same energy and lasts about 8.3 days on idle drain alone, against about 5.8 for the Apex 300. The Apex 300 stays the pick only for 240 V loads or for a 240 V home-integration setup.

This supports ChatGPT's pick of the Apex 300 for a panel-connected or 240 V home backup, and leaves the Apex 200 as the $400-cheaper choice for 120 V plug-in essentials. Both units now ship in late January, so neither is in stock. Our page's 'Ships from Nov 20' and 'In stock' cells are out of date.

None say that AIMS sells the same 4000 W 12V class in a 120 VAC-input version (70 A charger, $1,949) and a 240 VAC-input version (115 A charger, $1,695). A single Victron MultiPlus-II 12 V 2x120V is rated only 2,400 W (12/3000, its '3000' is VA) or 3,400 W (12/4k), at 25 °C. It also adds a catch: Sun Gold says its split-phase model 'requires 240VAC input', so a shopper with only 120 V RV shore power or a 120 V generator should check that before buying. angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much battery a 12 V split-phase inverter uses just sitting idle. The AIMS 4000 W 12 V split-phase unit that ChatGPT showed (Outbound Power, $1,949) is listed at 50 W idle. That is 50 W × 24 h ÷ 12.8 V ≈ 94 Ah a day, nearly a whole 100 Ah 12 V LiFePO4 battery gone with no load. Two Victron MultiPlus-II 12/3000 units, the pair needed for 240 V, use about 56 Ah a day (15 Ah in search mode).
angles.decides: For an off-grid cabin or RV bank that stays on all day, idle draw matters more than the 4,000 W rating. On paper the AIMS unit costs nearly a 100 Ah battery a day at idle, so its 21 W power-saver mode (≈39 Ah a day) is required. The Victron pair is the lowest-idle way to get true 120/240 V (8 W in search mode ≈ 15 Ah a day), but it takes two units weighing 100 lb. Sun Gold Power is the cheapest at $0.23 per watt today, but its idle draw is unsourced, so the lowest-drain claim can't be checked for it. Also, its price today is $936, not the $624 ChatGPT showed.
