pages.query: best 24v lifepo4 battery
pages.why_used: The cited rival covers only 12V packs with placeholder prices, and the main 24V comparison lists only 100A/2,560 W packs with no cost-per-Wh math. Neither shows that one 200A-BMS 24V pack costs less per Wh than the 24V 100Ah picks and also runs a 3,000 W inverter, which the 100Ah packs cannot.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Epoch's 24V 100Ah (B24100A-C) is rated 120 A continuous with a 200 A surge that lasts 60 seconds, not a one-second pulse. At 25.6 V with an assumed 90% inverter efficiency, that is about 2,765 W AC sustained and about 4,600 W for a full minute, compared with about 2,300 W AC from the 100 A BMS on the LiTime and Redodo cards. No result says either that Epoch's '11-year warranty' means free replacement only in years 1–3 and 40% off MSRP in years 4–11.
angles.decides: ChatGPT itself warned that a 100 A BMS gives about 2,560 W of DC, which falls short for a 3,000 W inverter. Measured that way, the 24V cards it showed differ in sustained power. LiTime and Redodo are 100 A. Epoch is 120 A continuous, which covers AC loads of roughly 2,300 to 2,765 W that would trip a 100 A BMS, and its 200 A surge lasts 60 s for motor or compressor starts. That supports Epoch as the pick for inverter-heavy or marine use. It does not support using Epoch with a fully loaded 3,000 W inverter: about 3,333 W of DC at 25.6 V is roughly 130 A, which is above 120 A. The case for paying $1,199 is also weaker than the headline suggests. The '11-year warranty' gives free replacement for only 3 years, against Redodo at $469.99. Epoch's own store also showed the battery as out of stock today.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a 24V inverter's DC capacitors can draw a spike at hook-up that the battery's BMS reads as a short circuit, so the battery shuts off before the inverter ever starts. Epoch's own guide gives the spike for a Victron MultiPlus-II 24/3000 as 'several hundred to over 1,000 A' and the fix as a 47 Ω pre-charge resistor (50 W minimum, 100 W recommended) held for 5 to 10 seconds.

It decides whether a 24V battery plus a 3,000 W-class inverter powers on at all, so any 24V pick paired with a big inverter needs a pre-charge step. It also supports Epoch's specs on paper: 120 A continuous and 200 A for 60 s against 100 A on the Redodo. But Epoch's 24V 100Ah is out of stock at $1,199, so it can't be the premium pick today, and its page lists Bluetooth only, with no CAN/Victron communication. I couldn't confirm a built-in pre-charge on the LiTime or Redodo 24V 100Ah, so a pick card shouldn't claim those batteries avoid the trip.

pages.query: best all in one solar inverter charger
pages.why_used: The cited pages (Current Connected's EG4 guide, Eco Solar Kits' EG4 vs Sol-Ark guide and EG4's 12000XP page) never say that EG4's GridBOSS whole-home interconnect pairs only with EG4 hybrids. So none of them tells the shopper that the off-grid 12000XP and 6000XP can grow only by stacking more of the same unit. They also don't say that the 12000XP uses the 6000XP battery list and that EG4 support won't troubleshoot batteries that aren't on it. This page sets out each unit's upgrade path and the batteries it takes, Sun Gold Power's included, and every figure has a source.

On that common basis the Sol-Ark costs about $479 per battery-only kW, against about $300 for the FlexBOSS21 and $175 for the 12000XP. The Sol-Ark is also the only one of the three with a published surge length that holds 2× its battery-only rating for 10 s; the 6000XP's 2× surge lasts about 3.5 s.

ChatGPT's cards frame the Sol-Ark 15K as '15 kW' and the FlexBOSS21 as '16 kW', but both figures need solar running. On battery at night, all three larger units deliver 12 kW. The Sol-Ark's $2,150 premium over the FlexBOSS21 buys a documented 10 s surge (24 kVA), 200 A pass-through and 275 A battery current. It also brings the highest published idle draw: 90 W, about 2.2 kWh/day. For an off-grid buyer, the 12000XP gives the same 12 kW on battery for $175/kW, with no export. Its surge is unpublished, so a motor-start claim cannot be compared.

pages.query: best integrated amplifier for vinyl
pages.why_used: The cited rivals list each amp's phono stage only as 'MM' or 'MM/MC'. The Luxman page gives raw sensitivities without converting them. None of them says how much power a low-output moving-coil cartridge actually gets from each phono stage at full volume: 100 W from the Marantz MODEL 30, about 69 W from the Luxman L-505Z, about 7.7 W from the Musical Fidelity A1, and nothing from the MM-only Rega. They also leave out each amp's MC load (the Marantz's switchable 33/100/390 Ω against fixed loads on the others, including the Yamaha's fixed 50 Ω, which Positive Feedback found dulled cartridges that want 100 Ω or more). This page works out the gain from the makers' figures and adds the loads. The pick, the Marantz MODEL 30, is not a product we list and has no earning route (Amazon returned nothing), so it is an outside row. None of our amplifiers has a phono input.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the four phono stages' MC specs side by side in common units. Marantz MODEL 30 is the only one whose MC input load can be changed (33, 100 or 390 Ω). Luxman L-505Z is fixed at 100 Ω and Musical Fidelity A1 at 1 kΩ, and Rega Elex Mk4 has no MC input at all. The A1 also needs 450 µV where the Marantz needs 250 µV, which is 5.1 dB more input from the cartridge.
angles.decides: This confirms the MODEL 30 for MC owners and adds a footnote to the other picks. The A1's fixed 1 kΩ MC load and 450 µV sensitivity suit higher-output MC cartridges better than low-output, low-impedance ones. The L-505Z gives a single 100 Ω load. The Elex Mk4 needs a separate phono stage for any MC cartridge. The phono S/N numbers shouldn't be ranked against each other: Luxman's 70 dB MC figure is IHF-A weighted, while Marantz (75 dB) and Musical Fidelity (70 dB) give no weighting or reference level on their pages.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how loud each amp's moving-coil phono input can play a low-output cartridge. With a 0.25 mV MC cartridge at full volume, the Marantz MODEL 30 reaches its full 100 W, the Luxman L-505Z about 69 W and the Musical Fidelity A1 only about 7.7 W. The Rega Elex Mk4 has no MC input at all.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's 'best for moving-coil' label for the Marantz MODEL 30: it has the most MC gain of the sourced amps (≈101 dB to the speaker terminals), three MC load settings (33/100/390 Ω) and about 30 dB of overload headroom on both MM and MC. It also shows that the Musical Fidelity A1's 'MM/MC' label is misleading for low-output MC owners. A 0.25 mV cartridge gets only about 7.7 W from it at full volume, so those owners should buy the Marantz or the Luxman, or add a step-up transformer or external phono stage. The Rega Elex Mk4 needs an external stage for any MC cartridge.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, from the makers' own documents, the moving-coil (MC) load each shortlisted amp gives a cartridge, or the Marantz matching rule. The Marantz MODEL 30 is the only one with a switchable MC load (33 / 100 / 390 Ω, and Marantz says to use MC LOW for cartridges under 50 Ω, MID for about 50 Ω and HIGH for 100 Ω or more). The Luxman L-505Z has a fixed 100 Ω load, the Musical Fidelity A1 has a fixed 1 kΩ nominal load, and the Rega Elex Mk4 takes moving-magnet (MM) cartridges only.

Low-impedance MC cartridges get 33 Ω and cartridges of 100 Ω or more get 390 Ω. The L-505Z (fixed 100 Ω) and the A1 (fixed 1 kΩ) give every MC cartridge the same load. An MC owner looking at the Elex Mk4 needs a separate MC phono stage, because Rega's page lists only an MM phono stage.

pages.query: cellular security camera with solar panel
pages.why_used: Buffalo Alarm, Reolink's 4G solar guide and the other ranked pages never say that charging stops below 0 °C (32 °F), so in a freeze these cameras run on the battery alone. None of them sets each model's rated cold limit next to its reserve without sun. This page does both, using Reolink's and eufy's support statements and Outdoor Tech Lab's northern Michigan winter log.

angles.name: Normalise

ANRAN tells G1 buyers who bring their own SIM to pick T-Mobile or AT&T.
angles.decides: Verizon is often the only usable signal on rural land, and that is the main use case here. If so, the eufy 4G LTE Cam S330 is the one candidate whose maker page states Verizon support without contradicting itself, and it is the only one with a solar panel built in (4.5 W). ChatGPT's 'best overall', the Reolink Go PT Ultra, has an unresolved Verizon contradiction on its own page, and ChatGPT's budget ANRAN G1 is limited to T-Mobile or AT&T when you use your own SIM. Where AT&T or T-Mobile coverage is strong, the pick doesn't change.

The makers' own figures put it at about 10 minutes for the Reolink Go PT Ultra and about 2 hours for the eufy S330, a 12× gap. By the makers' own figures it needs about one-twelfth the daily sun of the eufy S330 and runs about twice as long on one charge (about 2 months against about 1 month). The eufy is still the choice when Wi-Fi fallback matters, but it needs a spot with roughly 2 hours of direct sun a day.

Neither one gets local hub backup while it runs on LTE: eufy pairs with a HomeBase only over Wi-Fi, and Reolink's Home Hub does not support 4G cameras. The S330 is still the right pick for a site that sometimes has Wi-Fi, because there it can join a HomeBase S380, mini or Professional S1. It cannot join a HomeBase 2. For a bring-your-own SIM, Reolink names T-Mobile or AT&T prepaid data-only, while eufy's bundled EIOTCLUB SIM also uses Verizon. Both SIMs are tied to the region where you bought the camera, and the US bands are B2/B4/B5/B12/B13/B14/B66/B71. EU and Australian Reolink units use different bands, so a gray-import unit is a bad buy.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts these two things side by side. First, the 28, 32 and 40 MP figures on the FLEX-M, FLEX-M2 and FLEX-DARK never reach the phone on the free plan, which sends SD previews only. To get HD you need the Standard plan ($7/mo billed annually, 1,000 photos) or a pack at $0.10 per photo, and Hook & Barrel says even Full-HD transmissions are compressed, not the 32 MP originals. Second, the FLEX-M2's spec sheet says 'up to six months' on 8 AA, but Outdoor Life's camera ran out after about 1.5 months. Batteries, not a plan, are the cost that keeps coming back.
angles.decides: This confirms the FLEX-M at $59.99 as the pick for someone who wants it completely free. On the free tier, the extra $20 for the FLEX-M2 ($79.99) or $60 for the FLEX-DARK ($119.99) does not get sharper phone photos, because all three send the same 100 SD previews a month. The extra money buys hardware: the FLEX-DARK lists a 0.3 s trigger against 0.4 s, 100 ft detection against 90 ft, and no-glow flash. The page should tell the shopper two things. Once they want HD on the phone, the cheapest way is Standard annual: $84 a year for 1,000 HD photos a month, against $0.10 per photo in packs. And on AA batteries they should plan on swapping a set of 8 every couple of months, not twice a year.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which Apple-silicon Macs can feed both inputs of a dual-monitor DisplayPort KVM. Apple's documents show that an M2 MacBook Air drives only one external display. An M3 MacBook Air or MacBook Pro drives two only with the lid closed, and the second display tops out at 4K 100 Hz. An M4 or M5 MacBook Air drives two at up to 4K 144 Hz each. The M3 limit means a dual-4K-144 Hz KVM such as the TESmart DKS202-M24 cannot run both screens at 144 Hz from an M3 Mac.
angles.decides: For a MacBook user this decides which switch to buy. With an M1 or M2 MacBook Air, no dual-input switch will work: only one of the two inputs gets a signal, so a DisplayLink-type dock is the route. TESmart's FAQ says this for M1, and Apple's spec page confirms the one-display limit for the M2 Air. With an M3 MacBook Air or MacBook Pro, the switch works only with the lid closed, an external keyboard and mouse, and macOS 14.3 or later (14.6 on the Pro). The second screen is capped at 4K 100 Hz, so a dual 4K 144 Hz switch like the DKS202-M24 or StarTech gives no gain on screen 2. With an M4 or M5 MacBook Air, both screens can run at 4K 144 Hz, which suits the DKS202-M24. For anyone who weighs EDID, as ChatGPT told them to, the $149.99 CKL 622DP-4 drops out: its maker says it has no EDID emulation, and CKL's EDID version, the 622DP-5, is $379. The Level1Techs switch has no EDID emulation either.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the exact rule a shunt monitor uses to reset itself to 100%. In Victron's own words, sync needs pack voltage at or above the 'charged voltage' (55.6 V recommended for 48 V lithium) and charge current below the 'tail current' (default 4% of capacity) for the 'charged detection time' (default 3 minutes). The tail current 'must be set higher than the current at which the charger stops or reduces charging'. The defaults out of the box are lead-acid values: 200 Ah, Peukert 1.25, 50% discharge floor. Lithium should use Peukert 1.01. Without sync, 'the state of charge value will start to drift over time'.
angles.decides: This confirms rather than changes the pick. A shunt monitor (Victron SmartShunt on 36/48 V, or a 10 to 120 V monitor on 72 V) only stays accurate if it can tell when the pack is full. On a 48 V LiFePO4 cart that means setting charged voltage to about 55.6 V, which is below the 58.4 V the charger ends at. It also means setting tail current above the current at which the cart's charger shuts off, and changing Peukert from 1.25 to 1.01. If the monitor is left on lead-acid defaults, or the charger stops before current drops under 4% of capacity (4 A on a 100 Ah pack), the percentage drifts. That is the same failure the shopper is trying to escape. A battery whose own BMS reports state of charge (LiTime RS485 display, Redodo or Vatrer kit apps) needs no extra shunt calibration. That supports ChatGPT's advice to check for a maker BMS display first.

pages.query: home backup power supply
pages.why_used: The cited guides size backup batteries from nameplate kWh plus an assumed discharge efficiency. None of them gives a measured idle draw or a measured delivered energy for any named home-backup station. This page adds measured idle watts from The Solar Lab and pv magazine USA, and turns them into kWh lost over a 72-hour outage. That reorders the 5 kWh tier: the S5000 at about 10 W loses 0.72 kWh, and the Jackery 5000 Plus at 58 W loses 4.18 kWh.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power each 120 V leg gets when a split-phase power station feeds a transfer switch through its L14-30 port. Anker says the F3800 Plus's 6,000 W L14-30R is a 25 A port, which works out to 3,000 W per leg, and its TT-30R only gets power from leg L1. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3's 4,000 W total over 240 V works out to about 2,000 W per leg, and it runs its 120 V inverter or its 240 V inverter, not both at once.
angles.decides: Through a transfer switch most house loads (fridge, furnace blower, sump pump, microwave) are 120 V, and each one sits on one leg. So the per-leg figure, not the headline wattage, decides whether a fridge plus a microwave on the same leg trips the unit. On per-leg power the F3800 Plus (3,000 W per leg) beats the DELTA Pro 3 (about 2,000 W per leg), even though the DELTA Pro 3's 4,000 cycles to 80% is the only cycle-life figure I sourced with its end point. Anker gives the F3800 Plus as '3,000+ cycles' and the S5000 as '10,000 cycles', with no end point for either, so as published those two counts cannot be compared with EcoFlow's.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus, one of the two units it showed, works as a UPS only through its three leftmost NEMA 5-20R outlets, which have a 1,440 W bypass limit and a 20 ms switching time, or that its 240 V output cannot be used while the unit is charging from a 120 V wall outlet. angles.decides: This splits the shopper's two likely plans. (1) Leave the station plugged into the wall as an automatic UPS for the fridge and router: the F3800 Plus works if those loads stay on the three leftmost 5-20R outlets and under 1,440 W. (2) Use it for 240 V loads (well pump, transfer switch L14-30 feed) during an outage: that happens only on battery, after it is unplugged from 120 V charging, so it is not seamless. Before buying for a transfer switch, the shopper should check the station's neutral-ground bond against the switch. EcoFlow itself says an accidental neutral-ground connection can trip a GFCI. The finding confirms the F3800 Plus for 120 V essentials-UPS use and weakens it as a seamless 240 V backup. I could not get equivalent maker figures for the DELTA Pro 3 or Explorer 5000 Plus, so it does not yet rank them.

pages.query: stereo amplifier for home
pages.why_used: The rival pages count optical and coaxial inputs, but none of them says which TV audio formats those inputs accept. None reports that Denon's manual allows only Linear PCM into the PMA-600NE and warns that Dolby Digital, DTS or AAC 'could damage the speakers'. None notes that the WiiM Amp Pro takes Dolby Digital over HDMI ARC while the base WiiM Amp takes PCM only, or that the Marantz Model 50 has no digital input. Those facts decide the TV-and-music case and the vinyl case.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the '60W × 2' on the Yamaha A-S301 card and the '60W × 2' on the WiiM Amp Pro card are different kinds of rating. Yamaha's figure is full-band continuous power (20 Hz–20 kHz, 0.019% THD, 8 Ω). WiiM's product page and FAQ give 60 W/8 Ω and 120 W/4 Ω with no THD or bandwidth condition at all. At 4 Ω, none of the four picks is rated on the same basis.
angles.decides: The pick stays the same, but the reason a shopper might choose between ChatGPT's two '60W' cards goes away. The only figures on a shared basis are Yamaha 60 W against Denon 45 W, both full-band at 8 Ω. That gap is 10·log10(60/45) ≈ 1.25 dB, so power should not decide between them. The WiiM's 60 W cannot be ranked against either one from the maker's specs. Shoppers with 4-ohm or low-sensitivity speakers should not read Denon 70 W, Yamaha 140 W, WiiM 120 W or Marantz 100 W as a ladder, because each is a different measurement.

From the maker-rated 8 Ω power, the $2,000 Marantz Model 50 (70 W) plays only 0.67 dB louder than the 60 W Yamaha A-S301 or WiiM Amp Pro. The 45 W Denon PMA-600NE gives up 1.25 dB to the 60 W pair and 1.92 dB to the Marantz.

So the extra $1,570 for the Marantz over the Yamaha ($2,000 vs $429.95) buys under 1 dB at 8 Ω. That spend has to be justified by build or sound, not loudness. On rated 8 Ω power the Yamaha costs about half as much per watt as the Denon ($7.17 vs $13.31). The Denon is the only one of the four rated at 45 W, but that matters only with low-sensitivity speakers in a large room.

It gave no measured fridge consumption and did not mention that power stations deliver less at the low loads a fridge draws. This page uses ENERGY STAR's 363 kWh/yr fridge and the roughly 80% low-load yield two reviewers measured on the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2. From those it gives fridge-hours per charge and cost per fridge-day for each station.

angles.decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. For a fridge, Wi-Fi and lights, the 1 kWh LFP class delivers 85–87% at the AC outlets when measured, and the models differ by only 2 points: BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 890 Wh, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 890 Wh, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 910 Wh from 1,070 Wh, EcoFlow DELTA 3 870 Wh. BLUETTI's own calculator plans with about 0.76. The fine print also differs: Anker's '3,000 W peak' is a surge rating, while BLUETTI's '2,700 W Lifting Power' is a separate mode (see unsourced), so compare surge figures before planning on a fridge compressor start.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the EG4 6000XP's 6,000 W is split into two 120 V legs of 3,000 W each, with no balancing between them. One 120 V leg overloads at just over 3,000 W even when the total load is well under 6,000 W. ChatGPT's Growatt SPF 5000US card ($750) puts out 230/240 V only, so one unit cannot power a US 120 V panel without the Growatt ATS 5000T-ES transformer. That rules it out as a drop-in answer for a US cabin or home. The 6000XP stays the simplest single-box split-phase pick, but only when it is sized by leg, not by total watts.

pages.query: best split phase hybrid inverter
pages.why_used: The rival pages give only rated idle figures with no FlexBOSS21 row (liveoffthegrid) or no idle figure at all (both Eco Solar Kits guides). None gives a measured standby draw or turns it into battery kWh per day. This page adds The Solar Lab's measured idle for four split-phase units, including the Sol-Ark 15K at 97 W against its 90 W rating. It also prices the FlexBOSS21 + GridBOSS system that a 200 A whole-home install needs.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the EG4 FlexBOSS21's surge rating beyond half a second (18,000 W for 1 s, 15,000 W for 6 min, 13,200 W for 12 min), so its '24 kW' surge cannot be set beside the Sol-Ark 15K's 24,000 VA held for 10 s.
angles.decides: This confirms the order ChatGPT gave and puts a number on the Sol-Ark 15K's premium. Both inverters are 12 kW on battery alone. Read over the same window, though, the Sol-Ark holds 24,000 VA for 10 s while the FlexBOSS21 drops to 18,000 W by 1 s. A shopper starting large motors (well pump, central AC) off-grid should lean Sol-Ark 15K. For a grid-tied home with ordinary loads the FlexBOSS21 stays the value pick: 12 kW on battery, 16 kW with PV, at $3,599.99 against $5,650. Over about 10 minutes the FlexBOSS21 (15 kW at 6 min, 13.2 kW at 12 min) and the EG4 18kPV (13.5 kW for 10 min without PV) come out close.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each inverter burns just by staying on. Over 24 hours that comes to about 1.56 kWh/day (569 kWh/yr) for the EG4 FlexBOSS21, 2.16 kWh/day (788 kWh/yr) for the Sol-Ark 15K-2P, 1.44–1.68 kWh/day for the EG4 18kPV, 1.2 kWh/day for the EG4 6000XP and 2.59 kWh/day for the Sol-Ark 18K. angles.decides: It backs EG4 FlexBOSS21 and EG4 18kPV over Sol-Ark 15K for off-grid or battery-heavy buyers. They are cheaper per kW, and they also draw about 20–30 W less at idle, which saves roughly 0.5–0.7 kWh every day from the battery bank. For a grid-tied owner it doesn't change the pick, because the grid covers that small loss. EG4 6000XP has the lowest idle draw (about 1.2 kWh/day) for small off-grid builds.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Sol-Ark 15K-2P does generator, AC-coupled PV or smart load on its own '3-in-1 GEN Port' with 'No MID' and runs up to 12 units in parallel, while EG4's GridBOSS, which the FlexBOSS21 needs for the same three jobs, takes at most three inverters and EG4 names only the FlexBOSS21, 12kPV and 18kPV-v2 for it.

EG4's 6000XP manual lists 3,000 W max continuous line wattage against 6,000 W nominal, and a named reviewer writes that the unit cannot shift load between legs, so 4,000 W of 120 V appliances on one leg overloads it even though the house total is under 6 kW.

pages.query: best plug in solar inverter
pages.why_used: The cited guides list the EZ1-LV and HiFlow Pro LV ratings and certificates but mark input limits as 'not stated' and never say which panel suits which inverter. This page sets out each maker's panel size range and input current and voltage limits side by side, plus APsystems' own rule that the EZ1 runs from panels only (never a battery) and goes on a non-backup outlet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the plug-in inverters on the same footing for a two-panel 120 V setup: one APsystems EZ1-LV gives 900 VA, which works out to 7.5 A, for $325, while two Hoymiles HiFlow 360 Pro LV units give 720 VA, or 6.0 A, for $320.84. That is 25% more AC ceiling for about the same money. And EcoFlow's '1,200 W' is a cap on the whole STREAM system's grid output, not a figure that adds up per unit.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's EZ1-LV pick, with a reason it didn't give. For two panels, the EZ1-LV costs about the same as two Hoymiles 360 Pro LV units but has 180 VA more ceiling, so two 400 W panels (800 W DC) don't clip on it. Two 400 W panels would clip at 360 VA each on the Hoymiles. The Hoymiles stays the pick only for a single-panel setup or a state with a low wattage tier (Solar Waypoint reports Maine at 420 W and Colorado/Maryland around 391 W). It also undercuts ChatGPT's 'EcoFlow up to 1,200W' card: on EcoFlow's own page, 1,200 W is the most the STREAM system can feed to the grid in any configuration, and the microinverter adds solar input to a STREAM Ultra. EcoFlow's page doesn't say the microinverter can feed a wall outlet on its own.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the common 1,200 W state plug-in cap each inverter can use, or what each one would produce and save in a year. One APsystems EZ1-LV fills 75% of the cap (900/1,200). Paired with 900 W of tilted panels in Salt Lake City, it would make about 1,371 kWh a year and save about $182, so its $325 price pays back in about 1.8 years (inverter only, panels extra).
angles.decides: This supports the EZ1-LV as the one-unit pick: 900 VA uses 75% of a 1,200 W cap and pays for itself in about 2–3 years in a low-rate state like Utah. Only the EcoFlow STREAM Microinverter (1,200 W) fills the whole cap with one box, but its US maker price could not be checked today and its UL 3700 status is listed as 'in progress'. Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV needs 2–3 units to come close to the cap (one 500 VA unit uses 41.7%). That makes it a one-panel or budget choice, not an alternative to the EZ1 for filling the cap.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the panel limits for each plug-in inverter. For the APsystems EZ1-LV, APsystems lists a 27–45 V MPPT window, a 26–60 V operating range, 18 A per input and panels of 315–660 W+, and its US FAQ says the unit must be fed by panels, never a battery, and plugged into a non-backup outlet. For the Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV, Hoymiles lists a 64 V maximum, an input-current limit of 14–16 A depending on model, and a recommended panel range for each of the 360–500 VA models.
angles.decides: It confirms the EZ1-LV as the pick for a shopper with two modern 400–600 W panels: they fall inside its 315–660 W+, 27–45 V MPPT window, and one unit takes both panels. On the Hoymiles side it changes which model to buy. The HiFlow Pro LV is one panel per unit, so the model has to match the panel: Hoymiles lists 280–470 W+ panels for the HMS-360 and 400–670 W+ for the HMS-500. Its input-current limit is 14 A on the 360/391/420, 15 A on the 450 and 16 A on the 500, so for large high-current panels the HMS-450/500 fits better than the $149 HMS-360 ChatGPT quoted. It also rules out a pairing that matters to Dealectric's power-station readers: per APsystems' own FAQ, the EZ1 cannot be run from a battery and must go on a non-backup outlet, so it cannot be fed by, or plugged into the backup outlets of, the BLUETTI, Anker or EcoFlow stations we list.

angles.name: Mechanism

This page collects measurements from named reviewers of what actually comes out of the AC outlet on the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2, EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, Anker SOLIX C300X, EcoFlow RIVER 3 and Jackery Explorer 300 Plus. It also adds two figures no rival has: the Elite 30 V2's measured 19 W AC idle drain and the RIVER 3 Plus's measured 9 ms UPS switchover.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow's own US RIVER 3 Plus page gives battery life as time to 80% ('over 10 years before dropping to 80% capacity') with no cycle count, or that StorageReview measured its UPS switchover at 9 ms against EcoFlow's '<10 ms' rating.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus pick rather than changing it. The maker states 600 W rated output shared across three AC outlets, all UPS-protected. That is twice the 300 W of the C300X and Explorer 300 v2 on ChatGPT's cards, and the switchover was measured at 9 ms. The 1,200 W X-Boost figure should not be compared with 600 W surge ratings. I could not normalise cycle life across the three because I could not source the Jackery and Anker ratings.

angles.decides: It confirms rather than changes the pick. Among the 288 Wh AC units, the Elite 30 V2 costs about the same per usable AC Wh as the C300 ($1.26 vs $1.30) but has twice the AC rating (600 W vs 300 W), and it is in stock at BLUETTI US for $289.99. Two of ChatGPT's three cards may not be buyable from the maker: Jackery.com lists the Explorer 300 v2 at $299 but says 'We're sold out of Explorer 300 v2', and the Anker SOLIX US page for the C300X shows 'Sold Out' with no price. A page that says this and leads with the Elite 30 V2 (Dealectric lists it on awin:bluetti_us) would be backed by the derived cost and by the 600 W AC rating. The RIVER 3 Plus can't be ranked on cost per usable Wh, because I couldn't source its price or a measured AC output.

Jackery also excludes the 300 v2 and the Explorer 300 from charging with its SolarSaga 100 Air panel, so a camper who plans to use solar has to check the panel pairing. The EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus keeps the stronger compatibility story: EcoFlow sells EB300 (286 Wh) and EB600 (572 Wh) add-on batteries that connect by pogo pins and take it to 858 Wh. For Anker, the page should tell the shopper to buy the C300 or C300X, not the C300 DC, because Anker's own spec table lists no AC output for the DC model.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how the boost modes work. EcoFlow's X-Boost, which shares its trick with BLUETTI Power Lifting and Anker SurgePad, runs an appliance rated above the inverter by lowering the output voltage. A heating appliance therefore runs at reduced power, close to the rated continuous watts, rather than at its label wattage: Alex Kidman's RIVER 3 Plus measured 599 W on a fan heater's low setting, and the high setting tripped the overload. The real AC ceiling is the rated figure (600 W on the RIVER 3 Plus and Elite 30 V2, 300 W on the C300X and Explorer 300 Plus), not the 1,200 W or 1,500 W boost figure.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick and tightens it. ChatGPT's own table suggests coffee makers and kettles need 1,000–2,000 W+, and a shopper may think a '1,200 W X-Boost' or '1,500 W Lifting' unit can run them. On these boost modes, a heating appliance runs below its label wattage, and for loads that boost doesn't help, the rated continuous wattage is the limit. For anything above 300 W, choose a 600 W-rated unit (EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus, or BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 at $289.99 on bluettipower.com) over the 300 W C300X or Explorer 300 Plus. Treat a full-power kettle or hair dryer as out of reach for this class of unit.

pages.query: power station for outdoor camping

No page in the set says that Anker's own store charges the same $699.99 for the 2,010 Wh S2000 as for the 1,024 Wh C1000 Gen 2. That works out to $0.35 per Wh against $0.68, and it moves the car-camping pick. On 2026-11-13 I re-opened the maker pages to check the prices and specs, and Jackery's own help-center page confirmed its 70% cycle endpoint.

For multi-year camping use the Jackery's lifespan claim is the weakest of the three. The DELTA 3 Plus is the most expensive per Wh ($0.70) and is currently a pre-order. Its 1,000 W solar input only matters if the shopper carries more than 600 W of panels.

pages.query: power station for outdoor lights
pages.why_used: The cited results only give rated capacity and AC outlet specs (RIVER 3 Plus manual copies, EcoFlow and BLUETTI store pages, and a sizing rule in Wh). None says that power stations ship with a low-load auto-off that turns the AC off under the 10–30 W a string of LED lights draws, and none says how to switch it off. This page adds the BLUETTI AC180's ECO rule (on as shipped, 10–30 W, 1–4 h, switchable) and the Jackery 600 Plus rule (on by default, 25 W or less, 12 h). It also adds measured idle draw and runtime arithmetic.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a power station's low-load auto-off can switch off its AC outlets under small LED light loads: BLUETTI's AC180 manual says ECO mode turns AC output off when the load stays below a threshold the user can set from 10 to 30 W for 1, 2, 3 or 4 hours. ChatGPT's own table puts 10–30 W string lights inside that range.
angles.decides: For outdoor lights, low-load auto-off matters more than Wh. A unit whose AC turns off below 10–30 W after 1–4 hours will leave a 10–30 W string dark partway through the night unless ECO mode is turned off. The page should tell buyers to check for (and disable) ECO or energy-saving auto-off, or to run low-voltage LED strings from the 12 V DC port. It should also rank models by whether their low-load cutoff can be turned off. That auto-off rule is sourced here for the AC180 only. For the RIVER 3 Plus, Explorer 600 Plus and DELTA 3 Classic it is still unsourced and must be checked in each manual before the pick is made.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how long each recommended unit runs a lighting load: at ChatGPT's own 50 W × 6 h example, the River 3 Plus delivers about 249 Wh (286 Wh × 87% measured), which is about 5.0 h or 0.83 of a night, so it fails the example. The DELTA 3 Classic's measured 17 W inverter idle draw means a 20 W LED string runs about 28 h on it, not the 42 h that capacity × efficiency would suggest.
angles.decides: This changes the pick. On ChatGPT's own example load (50 W for 6 h), the River 3 Plus is not enough for one night, while the DELTA 3 Classic ($459 at EcoFlow US today) covers about 2.5 to 2.8 nights at about $0.54 per usable Wh. For small LED strings, the 17 W idle draw is the biggest loss, so the page should tell shoppers to add the idle draw to the light wattage before dividing.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Jackery Explorer 600 Plus, the pick it gave for 'several strings of lights running all evening', ships with Energy Saving Mode on. In that mode an AC load of 25 W or less counts as low power and the outputs shut off after 12 hours. Separately, the unit shuts itself down after 2 hours with no charging or discharging (the time can be changed in the Jackery app). So a small LED string, or lights on a plug-in timer, can be left dark unless the owner changes these settings.
angles.decides: This doesn't knock the Jackery 600 Plus out, but it adds a setup step to the recommendation. Light loads of 10–30 W, the bottom row of ChatGPT's own table, fall at or under Jackery's 25 W low-power line, so with default settings the AC goes off after 12 hours. That is shorter than a dusk-to-dawn winter night. A timer that removes the load during the day can also trigger the 2-hour standby shutdown. Before an overnight lighting setup, the page should tell the shopper to turn off Energy Saving Mode (hold the AC and Main Power buttons until the icon goes away) and lengthen the standby time in the Jackery app. The same check is needed for any EcoFlow pick (set the app's AC timeout to 'never'). The manual also says the unit must not be kept where rain or moisture can reach it, which supports ChatGPT's 'not waterproof' warning.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Jackery Explorer 600 Plus it recommended ships with Energy Saving Mode on by default, which shuts off all outputs after 12 hours of light load (the manual's table lists ≤25 W and ≤2 W thresholds). The 10–30 W LED strings in ChatGPT's own sizing table fall in that range. The same goes for lights on a dusk timer that draw almost nothing all day.
angles.decides: The finding doesn't change which model to buy. It decides whether the plan works out of the box. A 600 Plus running LED strings or timer-switched lights will cut power partway through the night unless the owner turns Energy Saving Mode off (long-press AC + Main Power) and then switches the unit off by hand afterwards. On the RIVER 3 Plus the owner has to set AC timeout to 'never' in the app. A unit with no app or button override for its low-load shutoff is a poor pick for small lighting loads.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that The Solar Lab measured the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic, one of ChatGPT's three picks, drawing about 17 W with its inverter on and nothing plugged in. For a 30–60 W string of patio lights, that is a large share of the energy used.
angles.decides: This changes how the unit should be sized rather than which unit to pick. ChatGPT's rule (50 W × 6 h = 300 Wh, so buy 400 Wh or more) leaves out inverter idle overhead. That overhead matters most at the small loads outdoor lights draw. With The Solar Lab's 17 W figure, the DELTA 3 Classic pulls about 67 W from the battery to run 50 W of lights. Using mybest's measured 950 Wh, that is roughly 14 hours, not the 19 hours a naive 950 ÷ 50 suggests. This is an estimate: the 17 W idle figure is added to the load directly. I found no measured idle draw for the RIVER 3 Plus or the Jackery 600 Plus, so I can't rank all three on it. The finding still says to size for idle loss, or to run DC/12 V lights where possible, rather than to pick a different unit.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Jackery sells an IP65-rated power station, the Explorer 1500 Ultra (1,536 Wh, $1,079 at Jackery US on 2026-11-13). ChatGPT's own answer only warned that most power stations are not waterproof and did not name one that is.
angles.decides: If the station stays outside next to the lights, the Explorer 1500 Ultra is the only IP65 unit I found, and its $1,079 price is the cost of that rating. If the station sits under cover, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is the value pick: $459 at EcoFlow US for 1,024 Wh, which is $20 less than the $479 Best Buy price ChatGPT showed and $40 less than the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2. For small string lights, the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 ($289.99, 288 Wh) is the only small unit whose maker states a standby draw (4.5 W). That figure matters when the load is 10–30 W for hours.

pages.query: portable power station for tv
pages.why_used: The only cited rival page (BLUETTI's AC70 listing) gives a maker runtime claim, and no result gives measured AC output at TV-size (50–100 W) loads or the inverter's idle draw. ChatGPT's 85% assumption overstates small-TV runtime, and the 768 Wh card it showed is sold out at BLUETTI US. This page has named low-load measurements and idle draws for five stations, plus in-stock prices checked today.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy each station actually delivers at TV-sized AC loads. Michael Barton at techtest.org measured 623 Wh (81% of rated) from the BLUETTI AC70 and 366 Wh (71.5% of rated) from the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max at a 50 W AC load, with the AC70 drawing about 8 W idle with an outlet on. ChatGPT's runtime calculator assumed a flat 85% usable for every station.
angles.decides: It changes the budget pick. At TV-sized loads the AC70 delivered 623 Wh against 366 Wh for the RIVER 2 Max, about 70% more energy, while ChatGPT's own cards price the two $50 apart ($359 vs $309; only the $359 is confirmed on bluettipower.com). For a 100 W TV that means roughly 6.2 h from the AC70 and about 3.7 h from the RIVER 2 Max. ChatGPT's 85% assumption gives about 4.3 h for the RIVER 2 Max, so it flatters the smaller EcoFlow most. On cycle life, Anker states its 4,000 cycles to 80% retention, but BLUETTI's AC70 page gives '3,000+' with no retention figure. So the normalised cycle-life column can only be filled for Anker.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many watt-hours a power station actually delivers through its AC outlets at a TV-sized load. At a 50 W AC load, Techtest.org measured 366 Wh from the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max (71.5% of 512 Wh) and 623 Wh from the BLUETTI AC70 (81% of 768 Wh). That works out to 7.3 h vs 12.5 h of a 50 W TV, or $0.84 vs $0.58 per usable Wh.
angles.decides: The measurement favours the BLUETTI AC70 over the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max for TV watching. For $50 more ($359 vs $309) it runs a 50 W TV about 1.7× as long (12.5 h vs 7.3 h). The RIVER 2 Max falls below ChatGPT's 8-hour minimum for a 500 Wh unit on a 32-inch TV, because its measured 71.5% AC efficiency at low load is well under the assumed 85%. Caveat: the AC70 shows as out of stock on BLUETTI's US store today. For the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, the measured 13.8 W idle draw means about 22% of the energy goes to inverter overhead with a 50 W TV, vs about 14% for the AC70. Its flat-85% runtime in ChatGPT's calculator is therefore optimistic for small TVs.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which of its three picks can take an add-on battery. Only the BLUETTI AC70 can: BLUETTI lists the B80, B230 and B300 for it. Anker's US page says the C1000 Gen 2 'does not include an expansion feature', and EcoFlow's US FAQ says the RIVER 2 series does 'not support an Extra Battery'.
angles.decides: If the shopper wants more TV hours later, for long outages or a bigger TV, the AC70 is the only one of ChatGPT's three picks that can grow. The AC70 page lists a B80 bundle at 1,574 Wh, and BLUETTI's AC70 page names B230 (2,048 Wh) and B300 (3,072 Wh) as compatible. The C1000 Gen 2 stops at 1,024 Wh and the RIVER 2 Max stays at its built-in capacity. Anker's BP1000 add-on battery is not a way out: its maker page lists only the C1000 and C1000X. For a fixed TV-runtime need that fits in 1 kWh, this changes nothing. The C1000 Gen 2 still has the faster UPS switchover (10 ms vs 20 ms), which matters if the TV or streaming box should stay on when the power cuts.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's AC70 manual adds a fixed ~15 W inverter self-consumption to every small load (runtime = 768 Wh × 90% DoD × 85% ÷ (TV W + 15 W)), or that the AC70's ECO Mode, on by default, turns the AC outlet off when the load stays under 40 W, a range that includes many 32-inch TVs.
angles.decides: This confirms the picks and corrects the sizing. On a small TV (30–50 W), the fixed 15–17 W inverter draw costs a quarter to a third of the runtime, so ChatGPT's '500Wh = 8–14 hours for a 32-inch' is too high. More importantly, the plan can fail at the default settings: AC70 ECO Mode is on out of the box and cuts AC below 40 W, and the Anker C1000 Gen 2's Smart AC Output shuts the inverter off after 15 minutes below 20 W (per Gidon, The Technology Man). The shopper must switch these modes off for a small or dimmed TV. A large TV (65 W and up) is not affected by the cut-off and feels the overhead less.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, at a TV-sized 50 W AC load, techtest.org measured only 366 Wh (71.5% of 512 Wh) from the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max and 623 Wh (81% of 768 Wh) from the BLUETTI AC70. Both are below the 85% usable energy ChatGPT's runtime calculator assumes. The Technology Man also measured about 17 W of inverter draw on an Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 with AC on and nothing plugged in.
angles.decides: It confirms that ChatGPT's capacity tiers point the right way, but its runtimes are too high at TV-level loads. A TV draws 50–100 W, which is where these inverters are least efficient. On techtest's 50 W numbers, a 50 W TV runs about 7.3 h on the RIVER 2 Max (366/50). That is below ChatGPT's own '8–14 hours' row for a 32-inch on a 500 Wh unit. The AC70 gives about 12.5 h (623/50). Measured usable energy per rated Wh favors the AC70 over the RIVER 2 Max for TV use. The C1000 Gen 2's roughly 17 W idle draw means a shopper watching TV in short sessions should switch AC off between sessions. One caveat: techtest and The Technology Man tested EU/UK 230–240 V units, and US 120 V inverters may measure differently.

pages.query: portable power station or generator
pages.why_used: The answer the shopper saw cited no pages and gave runtime only for the battery side (a 1,000 Wh station runs 100 W for 8–9 h). For the generator it said only 'can refuel', so a tank of fuel and a battery charge never appeared in the same unit. This page puts both in Wh: the maker's runtime gives 3,645 Wh per 0.95-gal Honda tank, and named reviewers measured 902–946 Wh per 1 kWh station charge. That makes one tank about 4 charges. It also shows that the generator's headline watts are a maximum, while the station's are continuous.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much AC energy one fill delivers. At the makers' own 25%-load runtimes, one tank of about 1 gallon gives 3.6–5.3 kWh (Honda EU2200i 450 W × 8.1 h = 3,645 Wh; Champion 201530 462.5 W × 11.5 h ≈ 5,319 Wh), and a 20-lb propane tank gives about 10.4 kWh. A full 1,024 Wh power station gave 907 Wh at the outlet in a reviewer's test, so one tank equals about 4–6 full station charges.
angles.decides: Divide your daily outage load by the stored energy. For essentials up to about 0.9 kWh a day (router, phones, CPAP, lights), one 1 kWh station charge lasts a day, and it's silent and safe indoors. If you need more than about 1 kWh a day for several days without sun (fridge, sump pump), one gallon of gas does the work of 4–6 station charges, and a 20-lb propane tank about 10. That points multi-day outages to an inverter generator, or to a station recharged by one. On watts the two classes are closer than the headlines suggest: Honda's '2200 W' is its maximum and its continuous rating is 1,800 W. That matches BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's 1,800 W continuous rating and sits just under the Anker C1000 Gen 2's 2,000 W, so continuous power shouldn't decide the pick.

At the same 450 W load, a 1 kWh station runs about 2.1 h, while one 0.95 gal tank in the generator runs 8.1 h and weighs less per Wh carried (76.9 vs 41.0 Wh/lb). For outages longer than a few hours or for heavy loads, the generator wins. For short outages, indoor use and cheap energy, the station wins: grid recharge costs about $0.18/kWh against about $1.01/kWh for gas at quarter load. The roughly 4-to-1 tank-to-charge ratio is the single figure a shopper can use to choose.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that 'power station or generator' doesn't have to be one or the other: each maker supports only specific pairings, with stated limits. EcoFlow's Smart Generator 3000 (Dual Fuel) can auto start and stop only with the DELTA 3, DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra Plus. angles.decides: This changes the pick for home-backup shoppers who need long runtime. Instead of buying either one, they can pair a battery with a generator the maker supports. For automatic hybrid backup at a low cost, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 or DELTA 3 Plus with the Smart Generator 3000 (Dual Fuel, $689 on EcoFlow US today) is the only listed pairing where the generator starts and stops itself, but it can't ship to California. For whole-home 240 V use through a transfer switch, the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus takes a 240 V generator through Anker's adapter. A shopper who wants a camping-size unit charged by a cheap open-frame generator should first check that the generator gives clean power and enough watts: Anker says pure sine under 5% THD for 120 V generators, and Jackery says at least 1,100 W for the Explorer 1000 v2.

Such a pump can only be powered by a source with a 120/240 V outlet, such as the L14-30R on a mid-size gas generator or the L14-30 on Anker's F3800 Plus. That can be a gas or dual-fuel generator (Champion 201077: 6,500 W running, 8,125 W starting, L14-30R) or a 240 V-capable power station (Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus: 120V/240V on NEMA L14-30R, up to 6,000 W), not a compact 1 kWh, 1,800 W 120 V unit. For 120 V-only loads (router, fridge, laptops) the choice stays open, and a power station works if its continuous and surge ratings exceed the load's.

Four named labs measured 850–910 Wh from 1,024–1,070 Wh units, which is 83–89% of the rating: Notebookcheck got 850 Wh from the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, OutdoorGearLab 890 Wh from the same model, StorageReview 910 Wh from the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, and nextpit 902 Wh from the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. angles.decides: The measurements confirm ChatGPT's runtime rule of thumb. 850–910 Wh measured works out to about 8.5–9 hours at 100 W. They also give a concrete side-by-side for the choice. Bob Vila ran a Honda EU2200i inverter generator with a full-size refrigerator for 4 hours on about half a tank of gas, so it keeps going as long as there is fuel. A 1 kWh power station holds about 0.9 kWh in total. For outages longer than a day with a fridge, that points to a generator or a much larger battery. For electronics and camping, the power station's measured 83–89% delivery and 30–47 dB noise make it the better choice. On noise, the measured figures contradict ChatGPT's table: power stations are quiet at light loads but not silent under heavy load.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the limit that decides each setup: an inverter is capped by the 12 V battery's BMS (Redodo 12V 100Ah: 100 A BMS, 1,280 W; Vatrer 12V 100Ah Group 24: 150 A BMS, about 1,920 W), and a power station like the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 recharges from a 12 V car socket only through its 11–28 V, 8.2 A input (about 100 W, so 10+ hours for its 1,024 Wh).

Buy an inverter only if your 12 V battery's BMS can supply its full draw: a 1,000 W inverter fits a 100 A or 150 A 100 Ah battery, but a 2,000 W inverter needs more than either can give. Buy a power station if you want to plug in and go, knowing that a car socket refills about 1 kWh overnight, not during a short drive, and that some models (C1000 Gen 2) cannot grow their capacity. For a battery you already own, the inverter is the pick: a Vatrer 1000 W pure sine inverter is $129.99 against $259.99 for the battery.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a car's 12 V accessory socket can only supply about 100–150 W. That limit applies both to a plug-in inverter and to a power station charging from the car. Above that, an inverter only works if it is wired to the battery with a 150–250 A fuse (Xantrex PROwatt SW), and it then runs off the car's own battery. A power station such as the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 delivers 1,800 W from its own battery with no wiring. Recharging it through the car socket is limited to about 100 W, though, unless you add a battery-wired charger like the 560 W BLUETTI Charger 1. So the pick comes down to the wattage the shopper needs and whether they will wire anything to the car battery.

The cheaper Aurzen ZIP ($259.99) does not; Gizmodo got about 45 min in Turbo and just over an hour in Eco. The Epson CO-W01 ($399.99) is a mains projector. pages.why_used: Victron's cited sizing article adds only '10-15% extra' for inverter losses on AC loads. Neither it nor the cited Renogy installation guide gives any inverter's no-load draw or turns it into Wh/Ah per day or panel watts. Victron rates its MultiPlus-II 12/3000/120-50 at 3,000 VA, which is 2,400 W at 25 °C, 2,200 W at 40 °C and 1,700 W at 65 °C, with a 5,500 W peak. On the Renogy store text I read, Renogy rates its 12V 3000W inverter at '3000W continuous / 6000W peak' and the REGO 12V 3000W at 'peak power up to 9000W', with no temperature or surge duration given.
angles.decides: It changes the sizing advice more than the brand pick. A 3,000-class inverter in a hot RV bay should be planned at about 2,200 W continuous, using Victron's 40 °C figure, because Renogy publishes no temperature basis. Someone running an RV air conditioner or a microwave plus a coffee maker on a 'starter 2,000W' unit is likely under-sized. The surge figures also don't compare: Renogy's 6,000 W and 9,000 W 'peak' carry no duration on the store text, while Victron's 5,500 W peak sits beside a continuous rating that drops with temperature. Idle draw matters for solar-only RV use. Victron states 13 W at zero load, 9 W in AES mode and 3 W in Search mode. That is about 312 Wh/day at 13 W versus 72 Wh/day at 3 W, roughly a third of a 100 W panel's daily yield. I could not source the Renogy equivalents, so the idle comparison is one-sided.

pages.query: best split phase inverter generator
pages.why_used: The cited pages give total watts and outlet types only. None says how much one 120 V leg can carry when a split-phase inverter runs in 120/240 V mode. That figure is in Honda's manual for the EU7000iS (22.9 A per circuit, so the load must be balanced) and can be worked out from Champion's 37.5 A at 240 V for the 201417 (4,500 W per leg). It decides which unit can run a panel through a transfer switch, and it shows that the most expensive unit has the least per leg.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much each 120 V leg of these split-phase generators can carry: Honda's manual limits each of the EU7000iS's two circuits to 22.9 A (about 2,750 W) in 120/240 V mode. That is less per leg than the Champion 201417's 4,500 W, worked out from Champion's 37.5 A at 240 V, even though the Honda costs about twice as much.
angles.decides: This supports Champion 201417 as the pick for running a 120/240 V panel through a transfer switch or interlock. On gasoline it has the most capacity per leg among ChatGPT's five picks: 4,500 W, or about 4,044 W on propane. It also undercuts the Honda EU7000iS as the premium pick. In the 120/240 V position that a panel hookup needs, the Honda's per-leg limit is 22.9 A (about 2,748 W). Only the WEN DF680iX is lower, at 21.25 A (2,550 W). So a 120 V load that the Honda's 5,500 W rating suggests will run can trip one Honda circuit while the other has spare capacity. WEN TF1050iX is the best pick for anyone who will run on propane, because WEN rates it at the same 8,550 running watts on propane as on gasoline.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the continuous 240 V current of the five recommended generators. Divided out, the $4,899 Honda EU7000iS gives the least at 22.9 A ($214 per amp), against 31.7 A for the Westinghouse ecoGen10000 ($41 per amp) and 37.5 A for the Champion 201417. Only the Champion and the WEN TF1050iX on gasoline or propane can sustain a 32 A load at 240 V (7,680 W).
angles.decides: This confirms the Champion 201417 and WEN TF1050iX for a heavy 240 V load: 37.5 A and 35.6 A continuous, and both clear a 32 A EV charge or a large well pump. It weakens ChatGPT's 'premium' Honda EU7000iS pick, which gives 22.9 A at 240 V, about 61% of the Champion's 37.5 A (22.9 ÷ 37.5), at the highest cost per amp ($214). For 240 V backup the Westinghouse ecoGen10000 is still the value pick at about $41 per continuous amp, but its 7,600 W is 80 W short of a 32 A EV charge (7,680 W). On fuel per day at quarter load, the Honda is lowest at 7.65 gal, then the Champion at 9.7 gal and the ecoGen at 10.6 gal. The ecoGen figure assumes its 'up to 12 hours' is at quarter load, which its page does not say.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, of its five picks, only the WEN units have a 240 V parallel path documented by the maker: WEN's GNA240i kit links two 240V WEN inverters through a transfer-switch-ready 14-50R rated 50 A / 12,000 W, and works only with 240V WEN models that have three parallel ports, not 120V-only units or 120V ports. WEN's other kit, the GNA50i, outputs 120 V only, and Champion lists 'Parallel capability: No' for the 201417, ChatGPT's 'best dual-fuel' pick.
angles.decides: For a shopper who may later need more 240 V power than one unit gives (well pump plus central AC, or a 50 A EV/panel feed), this changes the pick. The WEN TF1050iX or DF680iX can be doubled at 240 V with the $72.69 GNA240i (12,000 W through one 14-50R). The Champion 201417 cannot be paralleled at all per Champion's spec table. WEN's 120V kit (GNA50i) would drop a WEN pair to 120 V only, so buying the wrong kit loses split phase. WEN also states both of its units have a bonded neutral, which the installer needs to know when choosing the transfer switch or interlock. For one-generator buyers it confirms ChatGPT's watts-per-dollar ranking but adds a reason to prefer WEN over Champion if expansion matters. The Westinghouse ecoGen10000 is $1,299 and listed as unavailable on Westinghouse's own store, not the $1,149 ChatGPT showed.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, on a 120/240 V split-phase inverter generator such as the Honda EU7000iS, each 120 V leg is a separate power circuit. When the unit is set to 120 V/240 V, that leg can carry only half the rated current (22.9 A, about 2,750 W, of 5,500 W). Feeding a house panel therefore needs the 120 V loads balanced across both legs. Full 120 V power (45.8 A) is only available in the '120 V ONLY' position, and that position disables the 240 V receptacle.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. A split-phase unit is needed for a 120/240 V panel or a 240 V well pump, but the shopper has to size each 120 V leg, not just the total watts. On the EU7000iS, a fridge, a sump pump and a space heater on the same leg can trip that leg at about 2,750 W while the unit as a whole is under its 5,500 W rating. A generator whose rating gives about 2,750 W or more per leg covers a typical leg of essential circuits. A 5,100 W unit such as the WEN DF680iX would have roughly 2,550 W per leg if it splits the same way. That figure is my inference, not sourced. This page should tell shoppers to divide 120 V loads across both legs, and to treat the 120 V-only mode as something that cannot be used while the 240 V receptacle is in use.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Consumer Reports' lab verdicts on the 120/240 V inverter generators it tested. The Honda EU7000iS 'handled surges very well' and was 'fairly quiet from a distance of 23 feet'. The Westinghouse iGen8200TFc 'could not handle surges well'. The Champion 201176 was 'fairly noisy from a distance of 23 feet; we recommend hearing protection'. CR found all three gave 'especially clean power'.
angles.decides: CR's lab backs the Honda EU7000iS as the premium split-phase pick: more than enough power, surges handled very well, clean power, fairly quiet at 23 ft. Among the cheaper split-phase inverters CR tested, the Westinghouse iGen8200TFc is quiet but 'could not handle surges well', which matters for well pumps and AC compressors. The Champion 201176 handles surges but CR rates it 'fairly noisy' at 23 ft. ChatGPT's value picks (ecoGen10000, 201417, TF1050iX, DF680iX) have no named lab or reviewer measurement I could find, so their THD and noise rest on maker claims alone. The page can say: if you need proven surge handling at 240 V, the only CR-verified choice is the Honda (or the louder Champion 201176).

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Audio-Technica preamp puts out about 5 dB more line level than the Fluance one: Audio-Technica's manual gives 252 mV for the AT-LP70XBT and Fluance gives 140 mV for the RT81/RT81+. Fluance's own phono and line figures work out to about 31–32 dB of preamp gain, against Audio-Technica's 36 dB.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Both preamps reach normal consumer line level, so either one drives powered speakers or an AUX input. On the same input, the Audio-Technica plays about 5 dB louder at the same volume setting, so the Fluance may need the volume turned up a bit, especially on low-gain powered speakers. The noise specs can't rank the two directly. Fluance's 67 dB is A-weighted and Audio-Technica's 55 dB has no stated weighting. Neither maker gives a wow-and-flutter method that can be compared: Audio-Technica says <0.25% 'WTD' and Fluance says 0.2% with no method.

Each one has a PHONO/LINE selector, so the shopper sets LINE for powered speakers or an AUX input and PHONO only when feeding a receiver's PHONO jack. It also tilts the pick slightly. Wrongly plugging 252 mV into a PHONO input that expects about 4 mV overdrives it by about 36 dB, which is the distortion the rivals only describe in words.

pages.query: battery backup with power conditioner
pages.why_used: The sources shoppers see for this question are maker datasheets and retailer listings that carry rated figures only. None has Custom PC Review's oscilloscope switchover measurements (CP1500PFCLCD 8–11 ms against a 4 ms rating; SMT1500 0.8–9.4 ms), and none has the ENERGY STAR certified idle draw, which shows that always-on double-conversion conditioning (SRT1500XLA) burns 34.64 W against 4 W for line-interactive AVR units.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got lines up the three makers' 'AVR' and 'noise filtering' claims on one scale: CyberPower's own spec lists its AVR as 'Single Boost' (it raises low voltage but lists no buck/trim step) and gives only 'EMI/RFI Filtration: Yes' with no dB or let-through figure. So the pick ChatGPT named 'Best overall' for 'power conditioning' has the least specific conditioning spec of the three, and only the CyberPower side of that comparison could be sourced from a page I opened.
angles.decides: If it can be sourced, it confirms ChatGPT's closing caveat and sharpens it: for a shopper who asked specifically for a 'power conditioner', CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD's 'AVR' only boosts low voltage, and its filtering is a yes/no claim with no number. That weakens calling it 'Best overall' for conditioning, though it is still the pure-sine pick on price. As it stands I can't change the pick, because the APC and Tripp Lite figures that would decide it come only from search snippets.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the candidates side by side at the same load: at 500 W the APC SMT1500C runs about 23.1 min against 10 min for the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD (2.3×), and at 1000 W it runs 6.5 min against 2.5 min (2.6×).

The CyberPower gives 10 min at 500 W for $239.99 (Dell), which is enough for a desktop PC to shut down cleanly. The APC's extra cost buys 2.3× the runtime at the same load, which only matters if the shopper needs to ride out outages longer than about 10 minutes. The Tripp Lite can't be placed on the same scale because I couldn't open a page with its runtime figures.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that CyberPower's own CP1350PFCLCD/CP1500PFCLCD manual (K01-0000162-00) forbids plugging laser printers, paper shredders, copiers, space heaters, vacuums or sump pumps into the battery outlets, says the warranty prohibits using extension cords, outlet strips and surge strips, and names RB1280X2A as the replacement battery where current listings name RB1290X2 for units with serial numbers beginning CXX.
angles.decides: This confirms the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD as the budget pick for a PC or AV rack with Active PFC power supplies, and it adds limits the page should state. Plug the conditioner straight into the wall, not into a power strip or surge strip, or you lose warranty cover. Keep laser printers and large motor or heater loads off the five battery outlets and use the five surge-only outlets for them. Before buying a replacement battery, check the serial number: RB1290X2 is for serials starting CXX, and older units list RB1280X2A. The APC SMT1500C keeps its premium place for anyone who wants a network card later: Schneider lists a SmartSlot and graceful shutdown over USB or serial through PowerChute Serial Shutdown. I couldn't open any Eaton or Tripp Lite document, so I have no compatibility facts on the SMART1500LCDT.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says what CyberPower's 'Single Boost' AVR means for the CP1500PFCLCD: the unit can raise low line voltage but cannot trim high voltage. CyberPower's own manual says it switches to battery once input exceeds 140 V. APC's support FAQ says that boost-only Smart-UPS units go to battery on high voltage and that loads needing both boost and trim belong on an SMT or SMX. APC's double-conversion SRT1500XLA delivers power with zero transfer time.
angles.decides: A shopper who wants a 'power conditioner' expects both high and low voltage to be corrected while the battery stays out of use. The CP1500PFCLCD only boosts, so if the line runs above 140 V it falls back to battery (4 ms typical transfer) and wears the battery. It is still the value pick for brownout-prone homes, but not for homes where high voltage is the problem. On APC's own wording, the SMT1500C line is the boost-and-trim choice among line-interactive units. Only a double-conversion online unit such as the APC SRT1500XLA (zero transfer time) actually conditions the power all the time.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Custom PC Review (Sam Chen, 2017) put the CP1500PFCLCD on an oscilloscope and measured its switch to battery at about 8–11 ms against CyberPower's 4 ms rating, while the APC Smart-UPS 1500 measured 0.8–9.4 ms, so the best-overall and premium picks switch over in about the same time in practice.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The CP1500PFCLCD's measured transfer time (8–11 ms) is close to the APC Smart-UPS 1500's measured range (0.8–9.4 ms), and Custom PC Review saw both put out a sine wave on battery that looked the same as utility power. So the $748.99 'premium' APC buys no measured advantage in switchover or waveform over the $239.95 CyberPower for a PC or audio load. ENERGY STAR data adds that all three units draw under 4 W at no load and are 97.8–99.5% efficient in normal mode. The conditioning layer costs almost nothing to run, and efficiency doesn't separate them. Tripp Lite has no named measurement, and ChatGPT's own card says it puts out a simulated sine wave on battery, which keeps it third.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, together with a price on a retailer page opened today, that its 'best overall' CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD costs $239.99 at Dell on 2026-11-14 and offers only single-boost AVR (Dell lists an 88–144 V input range, a 4 ms transfer to battery, and 10 minutes of runtime at half load or 2.5 at full). pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "can a 1000 wh power station run a 1500 w space heater". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Can a 1000 wh power station run a 1500 w space heater?
pages.why_used: All four cited rival pages work out heater runtime from rated Wh × an assumed 85%. None names a lab or gives a measured AC output for any 1 kWh model. This page gives the measured output for each candidate, from OutdoorGearLab, Notebookcheck, StorageReview, The Solar Lab and The Technology Man (850–950 Wh, and 37.5 min at a 1,479 W load). It also adds the two tests run at heater-level loads.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got explains that the 'Power Lifting', 'X-Boost' and 'Lifting Power' numbers makers print next to continuous output (2,200–2,700 W on the 1 kWh units) work by lowering the output voltage, so a heater running on them gets less power and gives less heat; and BLUETTI sells a 600 W station with a printed '1,500W Lifting Power' that looks like it matches a 1,500 W heater but does not.
angles.decides: This backs the current pick: the 1,800–2,000 W continuous units (AC180, Elite 100 V2, DELTA 3, C1000 Gen 2) run a 1,500 W heater at full power without using any lifting mode. A unit that only reaches 1,500 W through Lifting, X-Boost or surge (for example the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2: 600 W rated, '1,500W Lifting Power') would run the heater at lowered voltage and noticeably less heat, so it is out. The Jackery 1000 v2 is rated exactly 1,500 W, and I found no lifting mode on its page, so it has no margin. The page should keep it marked 'at its limit'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured runtime at a heater-sized load. Every rival's 34–36 minutes comes from an assumed 85% efficiency. Two reviewers measured it: The Solar Lab ran the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at 1,479 W for 37.5 min (about 924 Wh), and The Technology Man ran the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 on a 1 kW electric heater for just over 54 min (907 Wh). From those and other measured capacities, each ~1 kWh candidate gives about 36–38 min on high.
angles.decides: The measurements confirm the headline answer of about half an hour (36–38 min measured or derived, against the 34–35 min rivals assume). They also weaken the 'at its limit; not recommended' cell our page gives the Jackery 1000 v2: The Solar Lab held 1,479 W for 37.5 min and 1,500–1,560 W for 10 min without a trip. For value, the BLUETTI AC180 at $499 is the cheapest candidate per minute of heat that I could price: about $13 per minute against about $16 for the EcoFlow DELTA 3. There is also a caution for the C1000 Gen 2: The Technology Man's UK unit overheated after 26 min on a 2 kW heater, so it can't be assumed to run safely right at the inverter limit.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own AC180 page pairs the 1,152 Wh AC180 with its B80 (806 Wh), B230 (2,048 Wh) or B300 (3,072 Wh) battery packs, 'for a total of up to 4,224Wh', and says the AC180's 2,700 W Power Lifting Mode is meant for resistive heaters.
angles.decides: It strengthens the case for the BLUETTI AC180 (which Dealectric lists under awin:bluetti_us) as the roughly 1 kWh pick for someone who wants to run a heater. It is the only one of our listed roughly 1 kWh units with a maker-sourced add-on battery path. That path takes it from about 39 min to about 2.4 h of runtime by the arithmetic with a B300 (4,224 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 1,500 W = 2.39 h), with a caveat on how the packs feed power, explained in the notes. Power Lifting itself doesn't change the answer for a 1,500 W heater, because the AC180's 1,800 W rated output already covers it. I could not source expansion support for the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 or the EcoFlow DELTA 3 / 3 Plus from maker pages, so the page must not claim they can't expand.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, the one 1,000 Wh-class candidate rated at exactly 1,500 W, carried a heater-sized 1,479 W load for 37.5 minutes and 1,560 W for 10 minutes in The Solar Lab's bench test, and shut off only on a 2,200 W surge after a couple of seconds.
angles.decides: This settles ChatGPT's rule that the station needs 'at least 1,500 W continuous', which leaves the Jackery 1000 v2 in an unclear spot. Measured, it holds a 1,479 W load for 37.5 minutes, so it can run a heater that draws at or slightly under its label. That matches the roughly 35-minute figure on our page and the rivals' pages, now backed by a measurement. Above 1,500 W it has little margin: The Solar Lab ran 1,560 W for 10 minutes and stopped the test, so a longer run was not shown, and 2,200 W tripped it within seconds. The pick stays the same. Recommend a station with 1,800 W or more continuous (EcoFlow DELTA 3, BLUETTI AC180, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2). Change the Jackery's 'not recommended' to 'works on a heater drawing 1,500 W or less, about 37 minutes measured, no headroom'. For the 1,800 W stations, EcoFlow's manual says its voltage-lowering X-Boost mode is 'more suitable for heating devices'. A heater over the rating there runs at lower heat instead of shutting off.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named lab's measured AC output for the 1 kWh candidates. Those measurements are 850–950 Wh (Notebookcheck 850 Wh for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2; OutdoorGearLab 870 Wh for the EcoFlow DELTA 3, 890 Wh for the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, 910 Wh for the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and 950 Wh for the BLUETTI AC180), which works out to about 34–38 minutes on a 1,500 W heater.

The candidates land within about 4 minutes of each other on high (34–38 min, or about 41 min on StorageReview's AC180 figure), so runtime doesn't decide the pick. The deciding facts stay AC headroom and weight. The AC180 tested highest in measured Wh (950 Wh at OutdoorGearLab, 1,030 Wh at StorageReview), so it gets the longest run, but it is also the heaviest. The Jackery 1000 v2 measured a respectable 910 Wh but is still rated at only 1,500 W continuous. If the heater has to run on high, the cheapest workable 1 kWh unit is $459 (DELTA 3 Classic). The BLUETTI AC180 at $499 gives the most minutes in the 1 kWh class (about 39 min). Spending about $420 more on a 2 kWh unit doubles the time at no extra cost per minute. pages.query: can a nas host a minecraft server for friends and which one is best
pages.why_used: The two cited rivals (racksandwatts.com and esp32.co.uk) give CPU names, and in esp32's case mixed clock claims. Neither gives a single-thread benchmark or says that the DXP4800 Plus's 4.4 GHz applies to only one of its five cores, and neither mentions Minecraft. This page ranks each NAS on PassMark single-thread rating (3,197 vs 1,879 / 1,492 / 1,151 / 1,136). It shows Intel's 1 P-core + 4 E-core split, and it ties both to the single-threaded server tick using PaperMC's own wording.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus's advertised 4.4 GHz applies to only one of its five cores (1 P-core at 4.4 GHz; the four E-cores top out at 3.3 GHz), or that this one core gives it a PassMark single-thread rating of 3,197, against 1,879 for the DXP2800's N100, 2,032 for the 8-core i3-N305 and 1,136 for the DS925+'s V1500B. Single-thread speed is the figure that matters for Paper's single-threaded tick.
angles.decides: It confirms the DXP4800 Plus as the pick on a number rather than a clock claim. Its one P-core scores 1.70× the N100 (3,197 / 1,879), 2.81× the DS925+ (3,197 / 1,136) and 1.57× the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro's i3-N305 (3,197 / 2,032). The F4-424 Pro's 8 cores look stronger on a spec sheet, and its multithread score is in fact slightly higher (9,337 vs 8,997), but Paper ticks the world on one thread, so the 8505 wins for Minecraft. The DS925+ costs about the same ($639.99 list vs $619.99) and has the slowest single thread in the table except the DS225+'s J4125. The F2-425 Plus's N150 scores the same as the N100 (1,889 vs 1,879, 0.5% apart), so its '3.6 GHz' buys nothing over the DXP2800's '3.4 GHz'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the DXP4800 Plus's Pentium Gold 8505 scores 3,197 in PassMark single-thread. That is 2.8× the Synology DS925+'s Ryzen V1500B (1,136) and 2.1× the QNAP TS-464's Celeron N5095 (1,492), and single-thread speed is the figure Minecraft's tick loop depends on.
angles.decides: It confirms the DXP4800 Plus as the pick and pushes the Synology DS925+ down. The DS925+ costs about as much as the DXP4800 Plus, but its CPU has the lowest single-thread score of the four, below even the cheaper DXP2800's N100 (1,879 vs 1,136, 1.65×). It rules out the cheaper ARM boxes (UGREEN DH4300 Plus at $399.99, Pi 5) when friends play Bedrock, because there the Mojang server runs only under box64 emulation; a Java server with Geyser is the arm64-native route. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that since Bedrock 26.50 (September 2026) the Bedrock Dedicated Server uses Mojang's WebRTC-based NetherNet transport by default, and that since 26.60 (27 October 2026) Bedrock clients no longer connect over RakNet. The old 'forward UDP 19132' setup therefore stops working: you now need TCP 19132 for signaling plus a range of UDP ports with one port per player (or TCP+UDP on 19132 for Geyser). playit.gg also says Bedrock Dedicated Server 'can't connect to playit by itself', so it needs a WaterdogPE proxy.
angles.decides: This doesn't change which NAS wins, because the transport works the same on any x86 Docker NAS (DXP2800, DXP4800 Plus, TS-464, DS925+). It does decide whether the shopper's plan works if any friend plays Bedrock (phone, Windows, console via Geyser). Two setups now work. (1) A Java server (itzg/minecraft-server, TCP 25565) plus Geyser build 1237 or later with transport set to nethernet, and 19132 open on both TCP and UDP. On Docker, Geyser also needs -DgeyserAdvertiseAddresses, because GeyserMC says it is for servers 'in containers or behind a NAT'. (2) Bedrock Dedicated Server with TCP 19132, a UDP range of at least max-players ports (default 10) and the public IP set in SERVER_UDP_PORTS. On playit.gg, that means adding WaterdogPE with online-mode=false. Either way the page should keep the 'Java server + Geyser on an x86 NAS' route as the main recommendation and correct the Bedrock port row.

pages.query: can a nas replace google drive for a 5-person remote team
pages.why_used: The Synology Drive spec page that was cited says the recommended number of client connections 'varies by Synology model' but gives no figures for any model. None of the rival pages gives Google's limit of 500,000 items per shared drive or its 30-day / 100-version retention rule. This page puts Synology's per-model Drive ratings next to Google's limits: 100,000 hosted files on the DS225+ against 500,000 on the DS425+. That tells the reader which model to buy. It also shows that Synology's version history stops at 32 versions per file, which covers fewer days than Google's history when a file is saved often.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Synology's per-model Drive ratings. The DS225+ is rated for 10 Drive users and only 100,000 hosted files, the DS425+ for 20 users and 500,000 files, and Google allows 500,000 items in one shared drive. So for the same five people, the 2-bay box holds one-fifth as many files as the Google setup it would replace. Its '32 versions' is also a count cap, while Google's limit is time-or-count (30 days or 100 newer versions).
angles.decides: This changes the Synology pick depending on file count. Five users is within the DS225+'s rated 10, but a team bringing over a Google Drive with more than 100,000 files and folders goes past what Synology rates the DS225+ to host. That is only 20,000 per person. The DS425+ is rated for 500,000, the same as one Google shared drive, and has the same Celeron J4125 and 2 GB of RAM, so the extra bays are not the only difference. The page should say: count your files first. Under 100k, the DS225+ is fine. Over 100k, pick the DS425+ (or DS925+, rated 80 users and 500,000 files). On versions, Synology and UGREEN both cap at 32 per file, and UGREEN keeps only 8 unless an admin raises it. A file saved 10 times a day uses up 32 versions in about 3 days. Google keeps up to 100 versions for up to 30 days, and Nextcloud/Hetzner thins versions over time (hourly for a day, daily for 30 days, weekly after). So 'version history' is not the same feature across these products. For heavily edited files, use Synology Intelliversioning plus snapshots.
