angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what a self-hosted NAS means for a 5-person remote team in time and money. At the US median upload speed of 68.31 Mbps, one 1 GB file takes about 2 minutes to reach one remote user and about 10 minutes when all five pull it at once. A DS225+ running all day costs about $27 a year in electricity. Power plus 1 TB of Backblaze B2 offsite backup comes to about $1.84 per user per month, against $14 for Google Workspace Business Standard. That leaves about $2,190 for the NAS and its drives before three years of the NAS cost more than Workspace.
angles.decides: This supports 'yes, for file storage and sync' for a 5-person team. Running costs are about an eighth of a Business Standard seat, and the DS225+ is rated for 10 Drive users, so five fit with room to spare. The real limit is the upload line where the NAS sits. At a median 68 Mbps, five people pulling large video or design files at the same time wait about 10 minutes per GB. That points large-file teams toward fiber or a high-split cable plan, or toward hosted storage. Teams that mostly share small documents are not affected.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that existing Google Docs, Sheets and Slides only leave Google as .docx, .xlsx and .pptx files. Synology's Active Backup for Google Workspace converts them, and Cloud Sync converts them only in download-only tasks. Synology Office then has to import those files, and on the 2 GB DS225+ it caps a spreadsheet at 2,000,000 cells instead of the 5,000,000 it allows with 4 GB or more.
angles.decides: This confirms Synology over UGREEN for a team leaving Google Drive. Synology has an official, free path out of Google: Active Backup for Google Workspace or Cloud Sync produces Office files, Synology Office imports them, and up to 10 users can edit them on a DS225+. UGREEN offers only Nextcloud and Collabora in Docker. It also sharpens the model choice. On a stock 2 GB DS225+, spreadsheets are capped at 2 million cells and Drive is rated for 10 users. The DS925+ comes with 4 GB, which lifts the cap to 5 million cells, and it is rated for 80 Drive users and 80 Office users. So a team with big Sheets should take the DS925+ or put 4 GB or more in the DS225+. Two setup rules follow. Keep shared work in Team Folders, which are ordinary shared folders, because the homes folder can't be rolled back to a snapshot. And install Tailscale from Tailscale's own package, not from Package Center.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that if the internet line hosting the NAS uses carrier-grade NAT (a WAN address in 100.64.0.0/10, which RFC 6598 calls 'not globally routable'), the direct port-forwarded or DDNS route that keeps Drive sync fast cannot be set up from home. That leaves the five remote laptops on Synology's QuickConnect relay, which Synology says 'may be slower than port-forwarded connections', or on Tailscale, which falls back to its slower DERP relays when both ends are behind a hard NAT.
angles.decides: This is a go/no-go check before buying any NAS, not a choice between Synology and UGREEN. Look at the WAN IP on the office or home router where the NAS would sit. If it is a public address, set up port forwarding/DDNS for Synology Drive, or Tailscale, and the NAS plan works within that line's upload speed. If it falls in 100.64.0.0/10 (CGNAT), every remote sync goes through a relay: QuickConnect for Synology, UGREENlink for UGREEN, or Tailscale DERP if a direct path fails. In that case, either buy a public IPv4 from the ISP or switch to a hosted option such as Hetzner Storage Share or Google Workspace, which removes the problem. This firms up the hosted rows as the fallback for CGNAT connections.

pages.query: can a nas replace icloud 2 tb for a family of iphones and a mac
pages.why_used: The pages ChatGPT cited are Apple and Synology pages on features and setup, and none of them gives a price. None sets iCloud+ 2 TB at $119.88 a year against the cost of the off-site copy a NAS needs: Synology C2 at $155.98, Backblaze B2 at $166.80 or BeeProtect at $119.99 for 2 TB. ChatGPT said a separate copy is needed but never priced it, so this page shows that a NAS does not lower the yearly bill once that copy is paid for.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the yearly cost of an off-site copy of 2 TB from a NAS: $119.99 for BeeProtect, $155.98 for Synology C2 and $166.80 for Backblaze B2. Each is the same as or more than the $119.88 a year for iCloud+ 2 TB, which already covers six people, and the NAS hardware comes on top.
angles.decides: A NAS lowers the yearly bill only if the family gives up a paid off-site copy. If they keep one, as both ChatGPT and our page advise, BeeProtect ($119.99) costs about the same as iCloud+ 2 TB ($119.88), and C2 or B2 for 2 TB costs about $36–47 a year more. So the NAS is a choice for control and capacity, not for saving money. Among the NAS candidates, BeeStation Plus is the cheapest way to get an off-site copy, because BeeProtect is a flat fee whatever the amount of data. A DS225+ or DXP2800 costs more each year as the library grows. Second footnote: if iCloud Photos uses Optimize Storage, UGREEN tells you to switch to 'Download and Keep Originals' before the NAS copy can be a full-resolution archive. That means the iPhones need room for the whole library, so a family that wants iCloud Photos off-loading plus a NAS archive still needs iCloud.

That is longer than the 2-year UGREEN warranty and longer than Synology's 3-year warranty. Of the NAS boxes, the DH2300 at $239.99 pays back fastest. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got explains why iPhone photo backup to a NAS is less reliable than iCloud Photos. iOS decides when a third-party app may run in the background. Apple added a system-managed background photo-upload extension in iOS 26.1. That extension needs the upload server's base URL written into the app's Info.plist (its settings file). A self-hosted NAS has a different address in every home, so NAS photo apps can't easily use it. Synology Photos' iOS release notes through version 2.4.2 don't mention it, and an Immich maintainer said in October 2025 that adding it is not likely 'anytime soon'.
angles.decides: This confirms the plan works only in part, and the deciding limit is in iOS, not in the NAS hardware. Synology Photos, Immich and the UGREEN NAS app all depend on iOS background scheduling or on someone opening the app. A DS225+, DXP2800 or BeeStation doesn't change that. For a family: 1) keep a small iCloud plan, or have each person open the photo app regularly; 2) don't use a NAS app's 'free up space' while iCloud Photos is still on; 3) each iPhone's Finder backup is written to the Mac's internal drive before Time Machine copies it to the NAS (Apple supports Time Machine to a NAS over SMB; AFP is not supported from macOS 27). So the Mac needs free internal space for every phone's backup. Picking the NAS should come down to the photo app and price, not CPU.

pages.query: can a portable power station charge an ev enough to get home in an emergency
pages.why_used: The two pages ChatGPT cited are Jackery's FAQ, which covers only Jackery's adapter, and ryzzun.com, which covers Jackery and the Anker F3800 EV mode. Neither names EcoFlow's grounding adapter or the EcoFlow models it lists, and neither warns that EcoFlow's EV X-Stream Adapter charges the station from an EV charger and cannot charge a car. This page shows which stations have a route their maker documents for charging a car, what that route costs, and how many miles each one gives.

EcoFlow's car-charging accessory is a separate $49 Portable Power Station Grounding Adapter, and its US listing names the DELTA Pro, DELTA 2, DELTA 2 Max, DELTA Max and DELTA 3 family but not the DELTA Pro 3. So 'EV support' means three different things: built into the stock firmware (Anker F3800 EV mode), a maker's grounding accessory (EcoFlow $49, Jackery $49 plus a firmware update on the Explorer 5000 Plus), or charging the station from an EV charger, which is useless when you are stranded.
angles.decides: It overturns our own page's DELTA Pro 3 row, which reads 'Level 2 with the $99 adapter'. That $99 adapter is a way to charge the station, not the car, and EcoFlow's car-charging grounding adapter does not list the DELTA Pro 3. Among the stations whose maker documents a car-charging route, we list the DELTA 3 Ultra and DELTA 2 Max (each with the $49 adapter), the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus ($49 adapter plus firmware update) and the Anker F3800 Plus (EV mode in stock firmware). These should be the picks. Stations with no maker-documented route should be marked 'no maker-supported way to charge a car'. That covers the BLUETTI models we list: I found no BLUETTI output accessory, and I could not read what its two '$99 EV' items do.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a cold EV can use the plug-in power to keep its own pack warm instead of storing it: Tesla's manual says that when plugged in, the car 'uses the charging system, rather than the Battery itself, to keep your Battery warm'. InsideEVs reported that a Model 3 at -15 °F on a 9 A Level 1 cord for 14 hours gained only 1.14 kWh, about 7% of what the outlet supplied. At that rate a 2–3 kWh power station would add well under 1 mile in deep cold.
angles.decides: This confirms that the plan works only in mild weather. In freezing conditions, a 120 V / 12 A session from any station in the current table (BLUETTI Elite 300, ALLPOWERS R4000 and so on) may add almost no range, because the car's own heater takes the power first. That favours 240 V output, which delivers more power per minute beyond what heating takes: Anker SOLIX F3800 / F3800 Plus EV mode, or Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus with its Grounding Adapter. The rebuilt page should also add a cold-weather caveat to its miles columns. Separately, the current page's 'Level 2 with the $99 adapter' cell for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is wrong. EcoFlow's own FAQ describes the EV X-Stream Adapter as a way to charge the DELTA Pro 3 from EV charging stations, not to charge an EV. That cell has to be removed or corrected.

pages.query: can a portable power station be a ups for a gaming pc
pages.why_used: The answer the shopper got gave only illustrative switchover figures (0/4/10/20/30 ms) and called ATX hold-up 'limited' without a number; no cited page sets a lab-measured station switchover beside a lab-measured gaming-PSU hold-up and PWR_OK time. This page sets StorageReview's measured 8 ms (DELTA 3 Plus, Elite 300) against Cybenetics' 14.1 ms AC-loss-to-PWR_OK on an 850 W gaming PSU and gives every candidate's margin.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a PC power supply's hold-up time is specified at full load: ATX 3.1 requires 12 ms at 100% load and recommends 17 ms at 80% load. Measured that way, the power stations rated at 10 ms or faster (EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, BLUETTI Elite 300) fall inside even the minimum. Ratings of 15 ms (Elite 200 V2) or 'under 20 ms' (Jackery v2 line) are longer than the ATX 3.1 full-load minimum, so they only work when the PSU does better than spec or runs well below full load.
angles.decides: It supports the 10 ms-or-faster group (DELTA 3 Plus, which StorageReview measured at just over 8 ms; C1000 Gen 2; Elite 300) as the picks for a gaming PC, because their ratings are below the 12 ms minimum a compliant ATX 3.1 PSU must reach even at 100% load. It moves Elite 200 V2 (15 ms) and the Jackery v2 line (under 20 ms) to 'only if your PSU does better than spec'. HWBusters measured 20.2 ms on one 850 W ATX 3.1 unit, but its AC-loss-to-PWR_OK time was 16.5 ms, so even that example is tight against 20 ms. It also adds a second normalisation footnote: in UPS mode the C1000 Gen 2 load limit is its 1,800 W bypass, not its 2,000 W inverter rating. Elite 200 V2 shares 1,800 W between charging and bypass. Neither limit matters for a 500–700 W gaming PC.

Once a unit passes that test, about 1.5 h at 600 W from a 1 kWh unit is enough to finish a match and shut down. A shopper who wants long runtime pays less per Wh at 2 to 3 kWh: Elite 300 $0.40, Elite 200 V2 $0.43, AC180 $0.48, DELTA 3 Plus $0.71 per measured Wh. For the C1000 Gen 2, keep the protected load under 1,800 W, the pass-through rating on Anker's 120 V page. The 2,000 W figure is the inverter rating.

pages.query: can you host a wordpress site on a nas at home instead of paying for hosting

This page turns each NAS maker's own power figures into a yearly bill at the EIA's 18.16¢/kWh. It sets that bill against Hostinger, Bluehost and DigitalOcean prices, which shows that a NAS bought just for the site costs more than intro-rate hosting for about 7 years.

At the August 2026 US residential rate of 18.16¢/kWh, running one of these NAS units 24/7 costs about $10 to $46 a year in electricity, depending on the model and on whether the disks ever sleep.

Electricity alone for a 2-bay NAS running 24/7 is about $27 a year for the DS225+ and about $46 a year for the TS-264 at their 'access' or 'typical' figures. That is about as much as, or more than, a year of the cheapest shared hosting before renewal. Ranked by power, the DS225+ is the lowest-cost NAS choice and the TS-264 the highest. The TS-264's figures are about 70% higher, but QNAP tested with every bay filled and didn't name the drives.

Electricity alone costs about as much as intro-rate shared hosting or a $4 VPS, and the hardware takes about 4 years to pay back even against renewal prices. The QNAP TS-264-8G draws the most power, so it costs the most to run as a web host.

pages.query: cheapest nas to use as a remote hyper backup target for a synology at a relatives house
pages.why_used: The cited Synology pages give Hyper Backup's destination rules, and the rival answer gives two purchase prices. None of them gives a power draw, a yearly running cost or a payback time against cloud storage for a box left on all year at someone else's house. This page prices each candidate's waiting-state draw at the EIA August 2026 rate and works out how many months each box takes to beat Backblaze B2. On that basis the cheapest box to buy, the DS124, is also the cheapest to run.

Switching from a Synology running Vault to a cheaper non-Synology target loses entire-system and LUN backup (Synology's spec), not version history.

A DS124 or DS223j running Vault is needed only if the shopper wants entire-system or LUN backup, or Vault's task monitoring. Our current page says the UGREEN row is a 'single-version copy: no .hbk, no version history'. On this evidence that is wrong and should be corrected, or at least sourced. On power, Synology's official 'Access' figures and NASCompares' measured idle cannot be compared directly. Both Synology boxes publish hibernation figures (DS124 3.44 W, DS223j 4 W) that matter for a backup target that sits idle most of the day, and no source I opened measured DH2300 hibernation.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the yearly electricity cost of leaving the target running at a relative's house, or how many months the box takes to pay for itself against cloud backup. Worked out from spec-sheet or reviewer wattage and the August 2026 EIA residential rate (18.16¢/kWh), the cheapest box to buy is also the cheapest to run: a DS124 costs about $5.47 a year with its drive asleep and pays back its $159.99 price against Backblaze B2 in about 6 months at 4 TB. A UGREEN DH2300 costs about $15.91 a year at its measured idle and takes about 9 months.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's DS124 pick on total cost as well as sticker price. It is the cheapest to buy and to run: about $176 over 3 years for the box plus power, against about $189 for the TerraMaster F2-212, $229 for the DS223j and $288 for the UGREEN DH2300, all with drive asleep except the DH2300. At 4 TB stored, every NAS box pays itself back against B2 within a year, so cloud only wins for very small backups (around 2 TB-years or less for the DS124). This favors the Synology Vault pick over the UGREEN rows in our current page on cost as well as features.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which Synology model generations can still run Hyper Backup Vault as a target: Vault 4.2.x (current 4.2.2-4262, 2026-07-07) needs DSM 7.3 or later. The DS223j, DS118 and DS120j reach DSM 7.4, but a used DS216j stops at DSM 7.1, so it can't run Vault 4.2.x.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's 'used Synology' route but adds a cut-off. A used DS118 or DS120j (maximum DSM 7.4) can run the current Vault 4.2.2. Avoid used models capped at DSM 7.1 (for example the DS216j), which can't run Vault 4.2.x because it needs DSM 7.3. The new DS223j also reaches DSM 7.4, so it qualifies. For non-Synology targets (UGREEN DH2300 / DXP2800, QNAP): Synology's spec lists rsync servers for folder and package backup but not for entire-system backup. Hetzner's rsync guide recommends client-side encryption and offers a retention setting. Both of those exist only in multi-version tasks, which suggests multi-version .hbk to an rsync target works. QNAP's own documentation shows only single-version. Our page's statement that a UGREEN target is single-version only with no .hbk is therefore weakly sourced and should be softened to 'single-version is the documented path; multi-version .hbk over rsync is not documented by the NAS maker'.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Hyper Backup on DSM 7 has a multi-version rsync task, separate from 'rsync copy (single-version)'. That task writes the same versioned, client-side-encryptable .hbk backup to any rsync/SSH server that a Synology running Hyper Backup Vault would hold, and the .hbk can be restored without any Synology using Hyper Backup Explorer or the open-source hbkit.
angles.decides: If it holds, the cheapest box with a working rsync/SSH server gives the same versions, Smart Recycle and AES-256 client-side encryption as a DS124 or DS223j running Vault. That makes non-Synology targets real contenders on price, including the UGREEN DH2300, a cheap TerraMaster or a Pi with a USB disk. The current page's 'single-version, no .hbk' cells for the UGREEN rows should change to 'multi-version .hbk via rsync (SSH)'. A Synology target is still required in two cases: entire-system backup (Synology lists only a remote Synology NAS or C2), and Vault's view of the vaults a NAS hosts plus its concurrent-task limit.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured power draw for any candidate. PC-WELT measured the Synology DS223j at 16.4 W idle, 3.1 W with the drives asleep and 22.3 W under load. NASCompares measured the UGREEN DH2300 at 9.5 W idle with two 4 TB IronWolf drives. That matters for a box left running all year at a relative's house.
angles.decides: The finding confirms that a Synology J or value model with drive hibernation suits an always-on remote target, and it adds a running cost no rival gives. PC-WELT's 3.1 W sleep figure for the DS223j is about a third of the DH2300's 9.5 W idle (NASCompares). If the DS223j's drives sleep about 23 hours a day between nightly runs, it uses roughly 34 kWh a year, against about 83 kWh for a DH2300 that never spins down. The DH2300's lower idle draw (9.5 W vs 16.4 W) only wins if the Synology's drives never sleep. It does not change the case for the DS223j or DS124 as the Hyper Backup Vault pick, which rests on features, not power.

pages.query: cheapest nas for infuse on an apple tv 4k
pages.why_used: The Firecore pages that were cited list the share protocols and one SMB3 tip. They give no measured speed for any NAS and no 4K remux bitrate, so a shopper can't tell how much NAS is enough. This page sets a named measurement for each cheap box against the 144 Mbit/s Ultra HD Blu-ray peak. It also shows that the Apple TV's own Gigabit port, or the 64 GB model's missing Ethernet port, is the real limit.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: None of the results ChatGPT got turns a NAS's network rating into the bitrate Infuse needs. A gigabit NAS measured at about 112 MB/s (896–944 Mbit/s) has roughly 7× the headroom of the 128 Mbit/s Ultra HD Blu-ray maximum. The Apple TV 4K's own port is only Gigabit Ethernet, and the 64 GB model has no Ethernet port at all, so a 2.5GbE NAS gives no benefit to a single Infuse stream.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick: buy the cheapest 1GbE box with SMB/NFS (Synology DS124 or DS223j, TerraMaster F2-212, UGREEN DH2300). It rules out paying more for 2.5GbE (UGREEN DXP2800, Asustor AS1102TL) just for Infuse, because the Apple TV caps the link at 1 Gb/s. Owners of the 64 GB Wi-Fi-only Apple TV 4K have Wi-Fi 6 as their only link, so for them the router matters more than the NAS port. A second normalisation note for the page: makers' low power figures are 'HDD hibernation' numbers, not idle numbers. Synology lists 3.44 W (DS124) and 4 W (DS223j) for hibernation, while ocinside measured 9–11 W idle on the DH2300. Compare idle against idle.

angles.decides: It confirms that the cheapest gigabit ARM box is the right pick and rules out paying more for 2.5GbE or Intel N100/J4125 models when the only goal is Infuse direct play. Gigabit has about 7× headroom over the highest UHD Blu-ray bitrate, and the Apple TV 4K can't go past 1 Gb/s anyway. Within that tier, running cost separates the 1-bay DS124 (about $17 a year at Synology's rated access power) from the 2-bay DS223j (about $26 a year), so the extra bay costs about $9 a year in electricity.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Apple TV 4K's wired port tops out at Gigabit (and the 64 GB Wi-Fi-only 3rd-generation model has no Ethernet port at all), so a 2.5GbE NAS adds nothing for Infuse. It adds two warnings that apply whatever NAS is bought: shoppers with the 64 GB Wi-Fi-only Apple TV 4K (3rd gen) are limited to Wi-Fi, and Profile 7 remuxes will play as HDR10, not Dolby Vision, so a transcoding NAS will not fix that.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the bottleneck for direct-playing a 4K remux in Infuse is the link from the Apple TV to the network, not the NAS. Ultra HD Blu-ray tops out at 128 Mbit/s (about 16 MB/s), and any gigabit NAS can deliver that roughly 7 times over. Firecore staff recommend a wired Gigabit connection for high-bitrate files, but Apple's spec page shows the cheaper 64 GB Apple TV 4K (3rd gen) Wi-Fi model has no Ethernet port at all.
angles.decides: It confirms the cheapest-NAS pick and points the money at a different part of the setup. 1GbE ARM boxes (Synology DS124, DS223j, TerraMaster F2-212, UGREEN DH2300) are enough because 128 Mbit/s uses about a seventh of gigabit. Paying extra for 2.5GbE or an Intel CPU (DXP2800, DS225+) does nothing for Infuse direct play. What decides whether remuxes play without buffering is whether the Apple TV can be wired. A shopper with the 64 GB Wi-Fi-only 3rd-gen model has to rely on Wi-Fi and should use 5 GHz: Apple lists the 2.4 GHz link rate as 195 Mbit/s, close to the 128 Mbit/s peak. Owners of the 128 GB model or the 2nd/4th gen should plug in Ethernet. If SMB3 transport encryption is on, turning it off (Firecore's own advice) keeps a weak ARM CPU from becoming the limit.

Vortex Radar measured buffered parking recording at 300–600 mA, which is 15–30 times VIOFO's 20 mA rating at 12 V. So a buffered setup has to be sized in hours, not days.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's framing and sharpens it. The impact-only low-power modes that stretch parking over days (the A329S's 0.24 W mode, the N4 Pro S 'Power Savings' mode) record after the hit: VIOFO says within 2 seconds, and one N4 Pro S owner reports 7–8 seconds. A driver who taps a bumper and leaves can be gone by then. For hit-and-runs the pick should be a camera running buffered or radar-triggered recording (Thinkware U3000 Pro radar: 7 s before and 13 s after; Vantrue N4 Pro S motion: 10 s before and 30 s after, per Milewitness). The shopper should budget a battery pack or a hardwire cutoff that allows about 13–25 hours of buffered recording per charge, not a week. I couldn't source the parking draw of our linked cameras (Vantrue N5S, N4 Pro S, DDPAI Z90 Pro, N5 Pro, Botslab G980H), so this angle alone doesn't move the pick toward or away from them.

pages.query: which kvm switch holds 4k 144 hz between a macbook pro and a gaming pc on one monitor
pages.why_used: The cited TESmart and Level1Techs pages only tell Mac buyers to 'confirm the external-display limits of the exact Mac model', or to use a USB-C-to-DisplayPort cable. None of them gives Apple's limits for each port. This page now does, from Apple's own documents: on M2 Pro to M4 Max MacBook Pros, 4K 144 Hz is rated only on the HDMI port and Thunderbolt only to 6K 60 Hz. The M1 Pro/Max HDMI port is limited to 4K 60 Hz, and only the M5 Pro/Max and M6 are rated for 4K 144 Hz on any port. That splits buyers between the HDMI route and the USB-C-to-DP route those pages recommend, and it corrects our old top row, which put the Mac on the monitor's USB-C.

A DP 1.4 KVM fed by USB-C-to-DP (Level1Techs, TESmart DKS202-M24) has no Apple 4K144 rating on those Macs and needs DSC at 4K144 in any case. With a 2021 M1 Pro/Max, an HDMI KVM caps the Mac at 4K60. M5 Pro/Max is rated for 4K144 over Thunderbolt or HDMI, so either KVM type is possible. The current page's 'use the monitor's KVM' advice still holds, because a direct HDMI cable avoids the middle device, and Apple says to 'Connect displays directly to your Mac for best results'.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the arithmetic: uncompressed 4K at 144 Hz and 8-bit colour needs 31.35 Gb/s, which is 121% of the 25.92 Gb/s a DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) KVM can carry (151% at 10-bit). 4K at 120 Hz and 8-bit fills 99.6% of that link. That link has the headroom for 4K144 without compression. One catch: TESmart's HKS201-M24 page lists 4K144/165 as running 'through DSC' and makes no Mac claim, so no switch is proven to carry 4K144 uncompressed. angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which MacBook Pro chips can send 4K 144 Hz into an HDMI 2.1 KVM. Apple's own spec pages limit the HDMI port to 4K 60 Hz on the 2021 M1 Pro MacBook Pro and to 4K 120 Hz on the base M3 (Nov 2023). The M2 Pro (2023) and later reach 4K 240 Hz. Apple also says adapters aren't supported at those HDMI rates, so the Mac's own HDMI port has to go straight into the switch.
angles.decides: The Mac's chip decides the switch type. With an M2 Pro/Max (2023) or later, base M4/M5/M6, or M3/M4/M5 Pro/Max, the Mac's built-in HDMI port can feed an HDMI 2.1 KVM such as the TESmart HKS201-M24 at 4K 144 Hz alongside the PC. It must be a direct HDMI cable, not a USB-C-to-HDMI adapter. With an M1 Pro/Max or base M3 MacBook Pro, the HDMI side stops at 4K 60 Hz or 4K 120 Hz. Those Macs need the USB-C DP Alt Mode route into a DisplayPort KVM, using a DP Alt Mode USB-C-to-DP cable (Cable Matters says its switch 'is not natively compatible with computers with a USB-C port'). On that route, 4K 144 Hz depends on DSC working end to end (Cable Matters FAQ; L1Techs FAQ: 'Without DSC, no'), and Level1Techs officially rates its switch only to 4K 120 Hz. This keeps our page's verdict of using the monitor's built-in KVM for M1 Pro and base M3 owners, and it allows an HDMI 2.1 KVM for M2 Pro and later.

For MacBook Pros with M2 Pro/Max, M3 Pro/Max and M4/M4 Pro/M4 Max, Apple documents 4K at 144 Hz only on the HDMI port, and lists the Thunderbolt/USB-C ports at 6K 60 Hz. angles.decides: For an M2 Pro through M4 MacBook Pro, the only Apple-documented 4K 144 Hz output is the HDMI port. So the Mac's side of the switch should be HDMI 2.1, either through an HDMI 2.1 KVM such as the TESmart HKS201-M24 or into the monitor's own HDMI 2.1 input when using the monitor's KVM, with the PC on DisplayPort. A DP 1.4 KVM such as the Level1Techs depends on a USB-C-to-DP plus DSC path that Apple does not document for those chips. On top of that, Level1Techs' own spec is 4K 120 Hz, with 144 Hz only through DSC. This also corrects our current top row. It puts the Mac on the monitor's USB-C (DP Alt Mode), which Apple documents only to 6K 60 Hz on these chips, so the Mac should go on the monitor's HDMI 2.1 input instead. For an M1 Pro/Max (2021), Apple documents no 4K 144 Hz output at all, so no switch fixes it. For the M5 Pro/Max and M6, Apple lists 4K 144 Hz or more on any port, including Thunderbolt, so DP and USB-C paths are documented too.

The Trio 3 Pro, and probably the three-panel FOPO S788 (driver required per our records), win only for shoppers who accept a DisplayLink-style driver or whose laptop has two DP-enabled USB-C ports and drives two external displays (M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max, any M4/M5 per Macworld). pages.query: battery charger with jump starter
pages.why_used: The cited Schumacher and Advance Auto pages and the top roundups put a plug-in combo's 100–200 A engine start next to a pack's 1,000 A or more peak. None of them says these are different kinds of rating. This page explains the plug-in figure: it is a capped current from the wall, limited to 7 seconds per crank and under 3 seconds on a hard crank, with a 180 s cool-down after repeated cranks, and it needs a battery installed in the car. It then compares that with the pack combos that jump-start without an outlet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Schumacher's plug-in 'engine start' amps are not the same kind of rating as a lithium pack's 'peak amps'. The SC1281/SC1309 rate is a capped current fed from the wall. It flows for up to 7 seconds per crank, and if the starter draws more than that rate the crank can last less than 3 seconds. Repeated cranks then trigger a 3-minute cool-down. A pack's '1,000 A peak' is a brief maximum, so 100 A vs 1,000 A is not a 10× difference in starting power.
angles.decides: This confirms that the plug-in Schumacher combos (SC1281 at 100 A, SC1309 at 200 A) suit a shopper who has an outlet and time. The charger gives a capped, timed boost with a 2-minute wait before cranking, and on a hard-to-turn engine the crank can drop below 3 seconds. A shopper who needs a strong start away from an outlet should not choose by comparing the 100 A or 200 A figure with a pack's peak amps. They should choose a lithium pack or a pack-plus-charger unit such as the Battery Tender CNS 4120. The page should footnote the amp column as 'charger engine-start rate (AC, capped, 7-second crank) vs pack peak (instantaneous)'.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives hours to recharge: Schumacher's own manual chart says a 6 A combo like the SC1281 or SC1309 needs 10 h to refill a half-flat 1000 CCA truck battery and 4 h for a 300 CCA car battery (30 h and 12 h on the 2 A maintain rate), and a 10 A timer-wheeled unit like the SC1446 delivers at most 22.5 Ah per full 135-minute timer turn.
angles.decides: This confirms rather than overturns ChatGPT's picks. Every plug-in combo it showed charges at 6 A, so all of them refill a battery equally slowly, about 10 h for a large truck battery. They differ only in engine-start amps and price, so the shopper should choose on cranking amps (100 A for cars, 150–200 A for trucks) rather than expect any of them to charge faster. If faster recharging matters, a 10 A unit cuts the 1000 CCA case to 7 h, but the manual-timer wheeled models (SC1446, SC1667) need the 135-minute timer reset about 4 times to get there. A shopper who wants a hands-off overnight recharge should pick an automatic 6 A unit (SC1281L or SC1309) over a timer-wheeled one.

So nobody shows that the 38% label lead the XTAR 4150 has over the EBL 3000 shrinks to 0.5–4.5% when measured, that the EBL beats its own label while the XTARs reach 82–86% of theirs, or that the label that looks biggest (PUJIMAX 4,255 mWh) measured the least. The page also adds Gough Lui's mAh × voltage check, which explains the gap, and his cycle-wear test, which Charge-Test says it did not do.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that once you swap printed ratings for measured energy, the 38% capacity lead the XTAR 4150 mWh AA has over the EBL 3000 mWh AA on the label shrinks to roughly 0.5–4.5%: XTAR measured 3,420 mWh (82% of its rating) and EBL measured 3,273–3,404 mWh (109–113% of its rating).
angles.decides: ChatGPT called the XTAR 4150 'best overall' for 'high capacity' and the EBL 3000 mWh 'budget'. On measured energy the two are close: within about 5%, or 6–11% if you use XTAR's own 0.25 A figure (3,605 mWh). So the pick between them should rest on price per pack, charger fit and high-current behaviour, not on the mWh printed on the label. The XTAR CLR 4300 is still the measured capacity leader at 3,703 mWh. Its lead shrinks at high drain: about 2,300–2,440 mAh at 2 A against 2,676 mAh at 1 A. Caveat: the XTAR and EBL figures come from different test rigs (charge-test averaged 0.1/0.4/1 A; Light And Matter used an XTAR VX4 V2 with no current stated). This is directional, not a head-to-head test.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states cost per measured watt-hour. At the maker stores on 2026-11-10, the XTAR CLR 4300 costs $1.82 per measured Wh as a 4-pack ($26.99 ÷ 4 × 3.703 Wh) and $1.69 as an 8-pack, while the EBL 3000mWh that ChatGPT called the 'budget option' costs $2.31–2.40 per measured Wh at EBL's own store.
angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick on value as well as capacity, and it challenges ChatGPT's 'budget' label for the EBL: at the maker stores the EBL costs about 30% more per measured Wh than the CLR 4300 (4-pack against 4-pack: $2.36 vs $1.82). There is one catch for first-time buyers. XTAR says the CLR series needs a compatible charger (the VX4 V1 cannot charge it), and the L4 Pro + 4 × CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99 works out to $2.70 per Wh for the first purchase.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that XTAR's 1.5 V AA cells have their own charge-management chip and take 4.75–5.5 V only from a charger that supports XTAR's 1.5 V Li-ion protocol. That means a NiMH charger won't do it, and XTAR's own store says its VX4 V1 charger cannot charge the CLR 4300 that ChatGPT made its top pick.
angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick only if it's bought with a charger XTAR lists as compatible: the L4 Pro, MX4, L4 or L8, or a VX4 V2 but not a V1. The cheapest sure route is XTAR's USA L4 Pro + 4× CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99, against $26.99 for the batteries alone. Someone who already owns a NiMH charger, such as the Tenergy TN480U that Dealectric lists, can't charge these cells with it. The same mechanism explains each candidate's low-battery behaviour: the EBL holds 1.5 V and then cuts off, the XTAR 4150 steps down to 1.1 V, and the CLR 4300 declines linearly to about 1.0 V. In devices that judge charge by voltage, only the stepped and sloped designs give a warning before the device dies.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how fast a 1.5V lithium AA actually wears out: Gough Lui ran the XTAR 4150mWh AA through 100 lab cycles and measured a loss of 0.85–0.89 mWh per cycle, which projects to 80% of its energy at about 843 cycles against XTAR's 1,200-cycle rating, with only about 63% of the charging energy coming back out.

It is the only candidate with a published cycle-wear measurement, and the projection of about 770–840 cycles to 80% is honest life data, about 30–35% short of the 1,200-cycle claim. Gough Lui's I-V testing also suggests keeping loads below 1.25 A, which matters for flashes and other high-drain devices.

None says which mechanical combos use one dongle and which need two (Redragon's own HORUS combo needs two). None says that sharing works only between a maker's listed models, with at most two devices on Logitech's keyboard receiver. And none quotes Logitech and Razer advising separate receivers for full performance and polling above 1 kHz. This page counts the USB ports each combo uses, from the makers' own text, and explains the trade-off.

pages.query: nd filter for camera
pages.why_used: The only text the shopper saw names ND8, ND64 and ND1000 and the split between fixed and variable ND. It never says how many stops a given aperture needs in daylight, so the shopper can't tell whether a 1–5 stop variable ND is enough. This page gives the stop count for each aperture at 1/50 s and the widest aperture each filter allows in full sun, worked from the makers' own ranges.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that ND numbers and stop counts are not on the same scale. Stops = log2(ND number), so an ND2-400 variable ND tops out at 8.64 stops, yet makers list the same ND400 end as '8.6' (Urth), '9' (Hoya) or 'OD 2.7, 9 stops' (K&F, where OD 2.7 is really about ND500). Hoya says that near or at its maximum a cross-shaped dark pattern appears 'and cannot be eliminated', so the darkest stops on these labels can't be used cleanly. 1–5-stop VNDs (ND2-32) and PolarPro's preset 2–5 / 6–9-stop ranges are built so that the cross never shows.
angles.decides: For video, where you can't fix a cross pattern later, it supports a 1–5-stop VND (ND2-32) such as the K&F Concept ND2-32 True Color that Dealectric already lists, or a preset range like PolarPro's 2–5 / 6–9 stops, over a wide 'ND2-400, 9-stop' filter. The extra headline stops on ND2-400 fall at the end that Hoya says shows an uncorrectable cross, and Urth says its ND2-400 is not recommended for wide-angle or telephoto lenses. A shopper who needs more than 5 stops should add a fixed ND, such as ND64 for 6 stops or ND1000 for about 10, rather than buy a wider VND.
products: K&F Concept ND2-32 True Color Variable ND (Nano-Xcel) 67mm

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many stops the shopper actually needs. For 24p video at 1/50 s in direct sun at ISO 100 (sunny-16 baseline), that is about 5 stops at f/4, 6 at f/2.8 and 7.3 at f/1.8. A 1–5 stop ND2-32 variable ND therefore can't open up wider than f/4 in sun, while a 1–9 stop ND2-400 reaches f/1.2 and costs $8.89 per stop against $20.70.
angles.decides: This changes the pick for the most common video use. Dealectric's listed K&F ND2-32 True Color (67 mm or 77 mm) only works in bright sun at f/4 or narrower at 1/50 s and ISO 100. Shoppers with f/2.8 zooms or f/1.8 primes need the K&F ND2-400 (1–9 stops), which also costs less ($79.99 vs $103.49). Keep the ND2-32 for f/4 zooms, or for people who care most about colour and reflection (0.1% vs 0.2%). Log profiles with a higher minimum ISO push the need further toward the ND2-400.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a variable ND is two polarizing layers rotated against each other, so near its darkest setting it shows an X-shaped dark pattern, worse on wide lenses. Makers cap the range for that reason: K&F's ND2-32 stops at 5 stops 'with reduced "X" effect', and Kenko advises staying at ND128 or below at 24mm. A 1–5 stop VND is therefore about 1 stop short of 1/50 s at f/2.8 in full sun at ISO 100.
angles.decides: This settles whether a VND alone works. On lenses of about 24mm and longer with a moderate need (up to about 5 stops), the listed K&F ND2-32 True Color VND (67mm or 77mm) works: its 1–5 stop cap keeps it out of the worst-X zone. Wide-open daylight video at a 180° shutter needs about 6 stops at f/2.8 (about 7.3 at f/1.8, for example on the listed Meike 85mm F1.8), which is more than the ND2-32 gives. Those shoppers need a fixed ND (K&F's own advice) or a stronger VND kept at ND128 or below on wide lenses (Kenko's limit at 24mm). Ask the shopper's focal length and aperture before recommending the K&F VND.

pages.query: best off grid solar system packages
pages.why_used: The cited guides list each kit's panel watts and battery kWh. Ecosolarkits works out cost per kWh for SunGoldPower kits only. None of them works out how many peak-sun hours each kit's own panels need to refill its own battery, and none compares that across brands. That figure is what shows the 6.5 kW SGM-6510M (4.6 h) and Renogy's 400 W kit (9 h) can't refill in one day, while the $4,949 SGR-8K10E refills in 2.8 h. Every kit price was rechecked on the seller's store on 2026-11-09.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power the kit inverters draw when idle (the EG4 6000XP draws about 50 W, which is roughly 1.2 kWh a day or about 12% of the 10.2 kWh kit battery before any appliance runs), or that the rated surge figures can't be compared: EG4's 12,000 W claim lasts about 3.5 s and The Solar Lab measured 7.3–7.5 kW, SunGoldPower gives 13,000 VA with no duration, and ECO-WORTHY gives 6,000 W with no duration.
angles.decides: The finding mostly changes how to size the kit. It only partly changes which kit to pick. On a 10.2 kWh kit like the EG4 6000XP package ChatGPT ranked first, about 12% of the battery goes to the inverter idling each day, so a cabin buyer should plan for about 1.2 kWh a day before any load. ChatGPT's surge ranking favours EG4 6000XP (12 kW), then SunGoldPower (13 kVA), then ECO-WORTHY (6 kW), but that ranking isn't sound: the units differ (W vs VA), no durations are given except EG4's, and EG4's measured surge was 7.3–7.5 kW. That makes the 3.5 kW ECO-WORTHY kit look weaker for well pumps than the headline numbers suggest, and it makes EG4 vs SunGoldPower a tie on what can actually be checked. One more fix: ECO-WORTHY's $2,499.99 1560W kit includes one 48V 100Ah (5.12 kWh) battery, which answers the 'confirm battery capacity' caveat ChatGPT left open.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how many peak-sun-hours each kit's own panels need to refill its own battery from empty. On the same 10.24 kWh battery, SunGoldPower's 6.5 kW SGM-6510M needs 4.6 h, while the $4,949 SGR-8K10E needs 2.8 h. Renogy's 400 W / 3.6 kWh kit needs 9.0 h, which is more than one day even at Renogy's own 5–6 sun-hour basis.
angles.decides: This changes ChatGPT's cabin picks. Its 'SunGoldPower 6.5kW Complete Kit' card says 3.6 kW of panels. The maker's own 6.5 kW kit with 10.24 kWh (SGM-6510M, $4,703) ships only 2,220 W, so it needs 4.6 sun-hours to refill: more than one day at SunGoldPower's own 4 h/day basis. SunGoldPower's SGR-8K10E has 3,600 W, the same 10.24 kWh and an 8 kW inverter for $4,949, and refills in 2.8 h. It is the better buy at nearly the same price. The ECO-WORTHY 1560W budget pick does include a 5.12 kWh battery (ChatGPT told the shopper to confirm this) and refills in 3.3 h for $488/kWh, which supports it as the budget pick. The Renogy 400W complete kit needs 9 h of sun per full charge, so it suits weekend use but not daily cycling.

Pick the EG4 6000XP kit if the shopper will stay on EG4 48V batteries and wants room to grow: up to 16 inverters and a 7 kW generator port. pages.query: best plug in solar inverter
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give inverter output only in VA or W. I opened Solar Waypoint, PluginSolarCheck, Solar United Neighbors and APsystems' pages, and none of them converts those ratings to amps on the house circuit. None checks the totals against the EZ1-LV's dedicated 10 A circuit condition or works out how much current breaker masking can let through. None points out that APsystems' own claim of '2 units on a standard 15A circuit' (15 A) is more than that condition allows. This page adds the current figures from the makers and retailers, the arithmetic, Hoymiles' plug and shutdown timings, and the CEC efficiencies.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the VA ratings into amps on the house circuit: APsystems EZ1-LV 900 VA = 7.5 A and Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV 360–500 VA = 3.0–4.17 A, so one EZ1 uses 75% of the 10 A dedicated circuit that rivals cite as its install condition, and the two-unit '1,800 W on a standard 15A circuit' setup on APsystems' own consumer page adds 15 A, the full rating of a 15 A circuit.
angles.decides: This confirms the EZ1-LV as the two-panel pick, but only as a single unit: one unit at 7.5 A fits a 10 A dedicated circuit, while two units add 15 A. For a shopper who can't add a dedicated circuit, the HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0–4.17 A per unit. That makes it the low-load choice for one panel, which ChatGPT's 'budget' label doesn't explain.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives each inverter's yearly output in kWh or its price per yearly kWh. In NREL PVWatts v8 for Kansas City, a 900 VA APsystems EZ1-LV with matched panels makes about 1,288 kWh a year at a 20° tilt and about 865 kWh hung flat (vertical) on a balcony. That works out to $0.25 to $0.38 of inverter price per yearly kWh. A 360 VA Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV makes about 515 kWh (20° tilt) or 346 kWh (vertical), which is $0.31 to $0.46 per yearly kWh.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the EZ1-LV. It gives 2.5× the yearly energy of a 360 VA HiFlow Pro LV (1,288 vs 515 kWh) at a lower inverter cost per yearly kWh ($0.25 vs $0.31). At the US average rate that is about $234 vs $94 a year. It also matters for balcony buyers: hanging the panels vertically cuts yearly output by about a third. From November to January, though, a vertical array makes more than one at 20° (December: 98.4 vs 80.6 kWh per kW), so railing mounts lose mostly in summer. Caveats: the APsystems page carries a 5-unit order limit, and two rival pages say the EZ1-LV is sold out. I could not source the EcoFlow STREAM's AC rating, so it is left out of the comparison.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which solar panels each plug-in microinverter can take: the APsystems EZ1-LV accepts 18 A per input across two inputs (25 A short-circuit) with a 27–45 V tracking range and recommended 315–660+ Wp modules, while each Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV takes one module at 14–16 A and 64 V max, so a large modern panel above 14 A fits the EZ1-LV but is current-limited on the smaller HiFlow models.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's EZ1-LV pick for a two-panel build. It is the only candidate with two 18 A inputs and a published 315–660+ Wp module range, so one unit can run two current large-format panels. The HiFlow Pro LV is one panel per unit, and the model has to match the panel: the 360/391/420 models allow 14 A, the 450 allows 15 A and the 500 allows 16 A. A shopper pairing a high-current panel with the $149 HMS-360 would lose output. Panels must stay under the 60–64 V input ceiling. That rules out series-wiring two panels into one input, and it rules out high-voltage rooftop strings.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the breaker-masking current. A plug-in inverter's output goes onto the branch wiring without passing through the breaker, so one APsystems EZ1-LV (7.5 A nominal) on a shared 15 A circuit can let part of that wiring carry up to 22.5 A without tripping. APsystems' own consumer page still advertises two EZ1s, 1,800 W or 15 A, 'on a standard 15A circuit', while the CSA UL 3700 conditions reported by Solar Waypoint and Plugin Solar Check allow only a dedicated 10 A circuit. The Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0 A (360 VA model) and drops its plug to 34 V or less within 1 second of unplugging.
angles.decides: Confirms the EZ1-LV for one unit on its own dedicated circuit: 7.5 A fits a 10 A circuit. It rules out ChatGPT's implied path of stacking two EZ1s for 1,800 W on an ordinary shared 15 A outlet, because 15 A of backfeed exceeds the certificate's 10 A dedicated-circuit condition. For a shopper who must use a shared outlet, the Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV is the safer pick: it adds 3.0 to about 4.2 A per unit, plugs into a GFCI outlet, and its plug goes dead within 1 s. Either way, the deciding question is which circuit the outlet is on, not the inverter's VA rating.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the California Energy Commission's lab-tested weighted efficiency for the US 120 V plug-in microinverters: APsystems EZ1-LV 95%, Hoymiles HMS-360/391/420-1WM-LV (HiFlow Pro LV) 95.5%, NEP BDM-1200-LV 96.5%, with no 120 V EcoFlow entry on the list.
angles.decides: It mostly confirms the EZ1-LV pick rather than changing it. The EZ1-LV is on California's grid-support list, where its 95% weighted efficiency is a point below the 96% peak on the APsystems datasheet. The Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV sizes ChatGPT recommended are 0.5 point higher, but only the 360, 391 and 420 W models are listed, not the 450 or 500. ChatGPT's 'higher-output option to watch', the EcoFlow STREAM Microinverter, has no 120 V entry on the list. NEP's BDM-1200-LV, which turned up in ChatGPT's results but was never recommended, lists 1.2 kW at 96.5%, the highest of the plug-in-class 120 V microinverters. The gaps are small: 1.5 points is about 15 kWh a year per 1,000 kWh of DC input. So the finding mainly tells shoppers which inverters a US state lab list covers, rather than ranking them by efficiency.

For a shopper doing sub-2-hour workouts, the 10-day vs 1-day gap is about charging habit, not whether a workout gets tracked, so the Apple Watch Series 12 at $399 and the Versa 4 are fully competitive. None quotes Newport's own store line that the Smart Battery Box is 'not compatible with lithium batteries'. angles.decides: The 'breaker' line on these boxes means different things. On Newport and Minn Kota it is a 60 A breaker on the motor circuit. On LiTime it is a 16 A breaker on the accessory sockets only. So LiTime ($84.99 today) is not a breaker-equipped alternative to Newport ($69.99): it still needs an inline motor breaker sized to the motor. For the lead-acid shopper, Newport stays the pick, though most Newport motors under 62 lb also need Newport's recommended 50 A or 40 A breaker. For a LiFePO4 shopper, Newport's store listing rules its box out. LiTime ('suitable for Lithium') plus a separate 50–60 A breaker becomes the pick, or the discontinued Minn Kota Power Center, where Minn Kota says lithium works but the meter always shows full.

angles.decides: Choosing the box comes down to the motor's thrust. Minn Kota 50–55 lb motors and the Newport 62 lb motor match the Newport box's built-in 60A breaker, so the Newport box ($69.99) works as sold. Minn Kota 30–45 lb motors (30–50A) and Newport 36–55 lb motors (40–50A) are a different case. With the Newport box they need a second breaker of the correct size, and Newport warns that skipping it 'can damage your motor'. pages.query: turntable with preamp
pages.why_used: None of the cited guides gives the built-in preamp's actual line-output voltage for any deck. One of them says outright that no output is stated for any pick. Angle A puts maker figures on five decks: AT-LP70X 252 mV, AT-LP120XUSB 240 mV, Sony PS-LX3BT 180 mV and the Fluance RT81 and RT81+ at 140 mV each. That shows the AT-LP70X is about 5 dB hotter into powered speakers, and that the RT81+ upgrade adds no line level. Angle C's Sony finding goes in as a supporting detail. None of the site's products is a turntable, and Amazon blocked the ASIN lookup, so the pick (Audio-Technica AT-LP70X) is a product we don't list and its link goes to the maker's page.

That is about 5 dB less signal into the same powered speakers, from a preamp with about 4–5 dB less implied gain (32 dB and 31 dB, against A-T's stated 36 dB).
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the AT-LP70X for a shopper who will plug straight into powered speakers. Its line out is about 1.8× the voltage of the RT81 and RT81+ (20·log10(252/140) ≈ 5.1 dB). All of them sit below the −10 dBV (316 mV) consumer line reference, and the Fluance pair sits furthest below it. The Fluance therefore needs more volume from the speakers or amp to play as loud. The RT81+'s stronger cartridge (4.0 mV against 3.5 mV) does not raise its stated line output, which stays at 140 mV. As a result, upgrading from the RT81 to the RT81+ gives no extra level at the LINE output, going by Fluance's own figures.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that, of its four picks, only the Epoch 24V 100Ah publishes a surge figure (200 A for 60 seconds) or a continuous rating above 100 A (120 A, about 3,072 W at 25.6 V). angles.decides: This mostly confirms the picks and adds one real limit. At the 25.6 V nominal voltage, a 100 A BMS (LiTime, Redodo) caps a single battery at about 2,560 W. That's below a 3,000 W inverter even before inverter losses. Epoch's 120 A continuous gives about 3,072 W. That still falls short once you allow about 10% inverter loss (a 3,000 W load then draws about 130 A), but Epoch's 200 A for 60 seconds covers motor starts and compressor kicks. Epoch is the premium pick for high-draw or cold-weather installs, and a single LiTime or Redodo fits loads up to about 2,000 W unless you add a second battery in parallel. On cycle life, Epoch's 3,500+ looks lower than LiTime's 4,000+ at 100% depth of discharge. Neither states end-of-life capacity, and Epoch's page puts its test conditions in a datasheet I couldn't read, so the headline numbers shouldn't decide between them.

pages.query: 3d printer with tool changer
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages (3dtoolchangers.com/printers, 3dprinteray.com/toolchanger-printers) give only maker swap-time claims and prices. This page has them: CNC Kitchen's 4-colour cube took under 4 h on the U1 and Prusa XL and about 7 h on the Bambu H2C, and a colour change took about 40 s on the H2C against 10–15 s on a toolchanger. It also has Notebookcheck's Creator 5 Pro waste and prep-time figures and today's prices: U1 $699, Creator 5 Pro $849. The pick, the Snapmaker U1, is not a product we list. Snapmaker isn't in our programs and amzcheck found no U1 on Amazon. Our QIDI and Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro printers have a single nozzle and win no segment of this question, so the page adds no product of ours.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the U1's 5-second swap and the INDX's 12-second swap are measured differently. Prusa's ~12 s runs from the last extrusion on one tool to the first extrusion on the next, while Snapmaker's 5 s is an undefined 'typical' lab result. A hands-on reviewer timed the U1 at 10–12 s per colour change, which is about the same as the INDX, not 2.4× faster.
angles.decides: It removes the U1's apparent speed edge over the INDX. Measured the same way, both swap in about 10–12 s, so the $749-vs-$1,999 choice comes down to enclosure and chamber heat (INDX up to 55 °C, U1 only an optional unheated Top Cover), waste per swap (INDX 0.013 g claimed with no prime tower, U1 about 0.049 g measured from its prime tower), and the INDX's smaller Y travel. Swap speed doesn't separate them. This confirms the U1 as the value pick but not as a faster one.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much tool-change time and waste a full job adds. Per 1,000 tool changes, the Prusa CORE One+ INDX spends about 3.3 h swapping (12 s each) and wastes about 13 g of filament (0.013 g each). The Snapmaker U1 spends about 1.4 h (5 s each). So on a print with many colour changes, the INDX's low-waste nozzle swap adds about 1.9 h per 1,000 changes.
angles.decides: For dense multicolour work (thousands of changes per plate), this favours the U1 or Creator 5 Pro on time, since a full toolhead swaps in about 5 s. The INDX makes sense when the buyer cares more about nozzle or material variety and near-zero waste (13 g per 1,000 changes) than about speed. Its 8-tool configuration also brings the price per tool close to the budget machines: $281 assembled, $244 as a kit.

pages.query: smart plug with timer
pages.why_used: The two cited TP-Link FAQs (947 and 83) explain how to set up schedules and Auto-Off. Neither says what happens when the internet or power goes out. TP-Link's own FAQ 2463 does: schedules, timers and Away Mode run on the plug with the internet down, there is a 32-rule cap per plug, the timers stop after a power cut until the plug goes back online to reset its clock, the priority order is Timer > Schedule > Away, and Tapo's Away Mode can run past midnight while Kasa's can't. The product pages add the 1/6 HP motor limit behind the '15 A' rating, against 1/2 HP on the EP40. Angle A is the only one that is fully sourced from the maker for every row, and it changes the pick for outdoor/motor loads and for cabins with no internet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that TP-Link's Kasa and Tapo plugs keep running their schedules and timers when the internet is down but stop running them after a power cut until they get back online to reset their clocks, or that the plugs' '15 A' rating covers only 1/6 HP for motors.
angles.decides: This confirms Kasa or Tapo for the usual lamp-or-fan schedule: the schedules are stored on the plug and run with the internet down. It changes the pick in two cases. (1) If the timer must recover by itself after a power cut while the internet is also out, as in a cabin, a holiday house or an aquarium during a storm, these plugs stop running schedules until they're back online. That points to the plain programmable timer ChatGPT offered as its 'No Wi-Fi required' option. (2) For a motor load such as a pump, dehumidifier or compressor, the '15 A' headline drops to a 1/6 HP motor rating on both the EP10 and the P125M. Within TP-Link, Tapo beats Kasa for overnight away/vacation lighting, because Tapo Away Mode can run past midnight and Kasa's can't. For 'shut off X minutes after every turn-on', the P125M has a built-in Auto-Off setting on every Tapo plug. On the EP10, TP-Link's own FAQs only show it done as a Smart Action, and automations need the internet.

pages.query: best security camera solar panel
pages.why_used: Both of ChatGPT's searches ended in 'solar panel compatibility', and its answer told shoppers to 'choose a panel explicitly compatible with your exact model' without naming any. The cited rivals (SafeWise, Bob Vila, HomeGearLab, RottenWiFi) give no panel model numbers or generation exclusions, apart from HomeGearLab's one Blink line and its mention of USB-C for Ring. This page adds a maker-sourced fit chart (Reolink, eufy, Ring, Arlo VMA by camera model number, Blink), each maker's exclusions, Reolink's 0 °C charging floor and its 9 m extension limit.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' sunlight claims into one comparable figure. eufy's '2 hours of sun' for the SoloCam S340 rests on a harvest of 800–1,200 mAh a day against 100–200 mAh of use, so it carries a 4–12× margin. Reolink's '20 minutes with the 3 W panel' (Argus PT Ultra) works out to only about 1 Wh at the panel's rated output, and Tapo's '50 minutes' (C465) is measured at lab standard sun of 1,000 W/m² with up to 100 events a day. The gap between 2 hours and 20 minutes comes from how each maker builds its claim, not from a 6× difference in panels. Also, every maker's charging floor is 32°F, even where the camera is rated to run at -4°F.
angles.decides: This backs the S340 and Argus 4 Pro picks. It removes a false tie-breaker: a shopper shouldn't choose the Argus PT Ultra over the S340 because '20 minutes' sounds better than '2 hours'. The claims are built on different margins and conditions. On the same 300 s/day basis that both makers use, the S340 (10,000 mAh, 3 months) lasts longer on battery alone than the Argus 4 Pro (5,000 mAh, about 2 months), and that reserve is what matters when the panel can't charge. For buyers where winters freeze, the 32°F floor from eufy, Reolink and TP-Link means no panel size will charge a frozen camera. Battery reserve and a sunny, south-facing mount matter more than panel watts.
products: Reolink Argus 4 Pro + Solar Panel 2 (6 W)

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how long a drained kit takes to refill from its own panel, or how many days the battery can carry the camera with no sun. Worked out from the makers' own figures: a fully drained eufyCam S3 Pro needs about 16–52 days of optimal sun to refill (13,000 mAh at a net 250–800 mAh per day). A drained Reolink Argus PT Ultra needs about 22 days of eufy-style 'claimed minimum' sun (21.6 Wh at 1 Wh per day from 20 minutes on its 3 W panel). So the battery reserve (about 60–130 days) is what gets these cameras through winter, not the panel's wattage.
angles.decides: This backs the eufyCam S3 Pro kit for shady or northern sites: its own figures give at least 2.25× surplus on a sunny day (450 ÷ 200) and 65–130 days on battery alone. It counts against the Reolink Argus 4 Pro for those sites. Its maker claims only about 2 months per charge at 300 s of recording a day, about half the 4 months Reolink claims for the 21.6 Wh Eco Ultra and PT Ultra. For the shopper who 'just needs a panel', it shows that a bigger panel shortens refills but does not add reserve days. Reserve is the battery's job.
products: Reolink Argus 4 Pro + Solar Panel 2 (6 W)

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a maker-sourced chart of which solar panel fits which camera generation. For example: Arlo's Pro (6th Gen) VMC4070 and Ultra (3rd Gen) VMC5050 are listed only for the VMA7600 Universal panel, not the magnetic VMA5600. The VMA3600 is for 1st-gen Essential only and the VMA6600 is for 2nd-gen Essential only. Ring's USB-C panel excludes the 1st-gen Stick Up Cam. Blink's Solar Panel Mount works only with Outdoor (3rd Gen) and not with Outdoor 4, XT or XT2. Reolink's 3/6/12 W panels fit every Reolink battery camera except the original Argus and Keen, and charge only from 0 to 45 °C.
angles.decides: This mostly settles the second branch ChatGPT offered, 'just a solar panel for my existing camera'. The right panel is set by brand and generation, not by watts, and buying the wrong Arlo or Blink generation means a connector or mount that doesn't fit. It confirms Reolink's 6 W Solar Panel 2 (USB-C) as the right add-on for the Argus 4 Pro and Argus Eco Ultra that ChatGPT showed. For the eufy S340 and S3 Pro, it points to eufy's own 3 W panel ($29.99, sold as certified for both) rather than a third-party panel, because eufy warns non-certified panels may damage the battery. Ring Outdoor Cam/Spotlight owners can buy the $59.99 USB-C panel unless they own a 1st-gen Stick Up Cam.
products: Arlo VMA6600 Essential Solar Panel (2nd Gen)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states, from the maker's own pages, that the cameras it recommended stop taking solar charge at 0 °C (32 °F) even though they are rated to keep running far colder: eufy SoloCam S340 charges at 0–40 °C but operates down to −20 °C, and Reolink's Solar Panel 2 charges at 0–45 °C while the Argus 4 Pro operates down to −10 °C. It also isn't stated that Reolink's Solar Panel 2S, which has a built-in 5,900 mAh battery, keeps the camera powered from 0 °C down to −20 °C.
angles.decides: For shoppers where winter days stay below freezing, the 6 W Solar Panel 2 bundled with the Argus 4 Pro and Argus Eco Ultra, and the S340's built-in panel, put no charge into the camera on sub-freezing days. The camera runs down its own battery until a day above 0 °C. That doesn't change the pick for mild climates, where the Argus 4 Pro or S340 is fine. For cold climates it changes which panel to buy: for a Reolink camera, choose the Solar Panel 2S, whose internal battery recharges down to −10 °C and powers the camera from 0 °C to −20 °C. The Argus 4 Pro itself is rated only to −10 °C (14 °F), so the camera, not the panel, is the cold limit there. Reolink also lists the original Argus, Keen and Doorbell (Battery) as unsupported by its panels. eufy has no equivalent in what I read, so S340 owners in cold areas get no solar charge below freezing.

pages.query: best split phase inverter
pages.why_used: The cited guides give each split-phase inverter a single 240 V total and never say how much one 120 V leg can carry. This page adds EG4's own manual limit of up to 8 kW of L1/L2 imbalance for the 18kPV, and the 6000XP's 3,000 W ceiling per leg (25 A × 120 V, SolarTech). That limit is the catch behind the usual 'budget off-grid' pick.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the headline split-phase rating you can draw on one 120 V leg. EG4's 6000XP manual caps output current at 25 A, which works out to about 3,000 W on a single 120 V leg, half its 6 kW label. EG4's 18kPV manual says that unit can take up to 8 kW of imbalance between L1 and L2.
angles.decides: This matters most for ChatGPT's 'best budget off-grid' pick. If a cabin or shop runs mostly 120 V loads, the EG4 6000XP behaves like a 3 kW inverter per leg, not 6 kW, so the shopper may need two units or a different inverter. The EG4 18kPV handles up to 8 kW of imbalance, which supports keeping it as the value pick for whole-home backup where loads are rarely balanced. I couldn't open a source for the Sol-Ark 15K's per-leg rating, so the comparison table has to footnote it as missing rather than fill it in.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the yearly energy the inverter burns just by being switched on (idle W × 8,760 h): about 788 kWh/yr for the Sol-Ark 15K, 613 kWh/yr for the EG4 18kPV, 438 kWh/yr for the EG4 6000XP and 70 kWh/yr for the Schneider XW Pro 6848. None works the 18kPV's daily idle draw (1.68 kWh) out as about 12% of a 14.3 kWh battery.
angles.decides: It backs the EG4 18kPV as the value pick for whole-home hybrid use: about $333–$408 per battery-only kW against the Sol-Ark 15K's $471–$479, and it idles 20 W lower (613 vs 788 kWh/yr). For off-grid cabins the EG4 6000XP is cheapest per kW ($250). The Schneider XW Pro costs the most per kW ($544) but wastes about 1/9 the 18kPV's idle energy, about 1/11 the Sol-Ark 15K's and about 1/6 the 6000XP's. That matters on a small battery with little winter sun. Dealectric's own Sun Gold Power 6000W unit is cheap at $203/kW but has no MPPT, so it needs a separate solar charge controller, and every variant showed as sold out on 2026-11-10.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EG4's own warranties for the 18kPV (10-year) and the 6000XP (5-year) exclude 'damages incurred from voltage or current spikes due to open-loop lithium battery communications'. So the battery has to talk closed-loop with the inverter or the inverter's warranty doesn't cover that damage, and EG4's product pages only promise closed-loop with EG4 48V batteries.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's 'best overall value' pick, the EG4 18kPV, still stands. But the page should say it suits buyers who use EG4 batteries, or another closed-loop battery on EG4's list, because pairing it with an open-loop battery leaves spike damage outside the 10-year warranty. A buyer who wants to mix battery brands should look at the Sol-Ark, whose warranty rule is similar but tied to its own approved list. The finding also separates the two EG4 cards: the 6000XP has half the warranty term (5 years against 10). And a whole-home build through EG4's GridBOSS is limited to three inverters, even though the 18kPV parallels up to 10 on its own.
products: Sun Gold Power 6000W 48V Split Phase Inverter Charger

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the EG4 6000XP, its 'best value' and 'budget off-grid' pick, can deliver only about 3,000 W on each 120 V leg and does not shift load between legs. Its 6,000 W rating is a 240 V total, so a house with 4,000 W of 120 V loads on one leg overloads the inverter even though the total is under 6,000 W.
angles.decides: The finding qualifies the 6000XP pick. The shopper typed 'split phase', which suggests a house panel full of 120 V circuits. On the 6000XP, any single leg above about 3,000 W trips the inverter, so the shopper has to balance circuits between L1 and L2 or choose another unit. Choose a bigger hybrid like the 18kPV or Sol-Ark 15K, with higher per-leg headroom, or a low-frequency transformer unit like the Sun Gold Power 6000W LF or Schneider XW Pro. The page should tell shoppers to add up the 120 V loads on each leg before buying, not to compare only the headline wattage.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named tester's measured idle draw. The Solar Lab measured the Sol-Ark 15K at 97 W in standby and the EG4 18kPV at 60–70 W idling on battery, about 0.65–0.89 kWh a day more for the Sol-Ark. SunForgeLab measured the EG4 6000XP at 55–65 W idle and 94.2% battery-to-AC efficiency.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's EG4 18kPV pick over the Sol-Ark 15K for off-grid and battery-heavy use. pages.query: which nas can you reach from your phone behind cgnat
pages.why_used: ChatGPT's answer marks every brand 'Yes' behind CGNAT and says only 'install Tailscale on a compatible NAS' without naming the models that can. This page states for each model whether Tailscale runs and how: the DH2300 cannot (no Docker), Synology needs Tailscale's hand-installed .spk because the Package Center copy is unsupported, and Asustor's package is a community Docker build. It also cites QNAP's 1–2 Mbps relay figure to the QNAP page that actually states it.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that QNAP is the only one of the five NAS makers to put a number on its CGNAT relay speed: myQNAPcloud Link relay traffic is 'usually limited to 1-2 Mbps', so 1 GB of phone video takes about 67–133 minutes. Synology, Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN only say their relays are slower or bandwidth-limited, and give no figure.
angles.decides: This partly settles the pick. QNAP's built-in relay is out for phone photo and video backup behind CGNAT, because its own stated 1–2 Mbps (0.125–0.25 MB/s) works for browsing files but not for moving video. QNAP owners on CGNAT need Tailscale in Container Station or a direct route. The other four makers publish no relay cap, so they can't be ranked on speed. The real split is direct path versus relay. Synology tries a hole-punched direct path before falling back to its relay. UGREEN tries IPv6 P2P first, which matters on Starlink and 5G home internet where IPv6 is often present. For heavy phone backup, the safe recommendation on any brand is Tailscale, whichever maker it is. The page should stop presenting 'Works behind CGNAT: Yes' as if it meant the same thing for every brand.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts a number on how slow the relay fallback is. QNAP's own figure for its myQNAPcloud Link relay is 1–2 Mbps. At that speed one 1 GB phone video takes about 67–133 minutes to pull. Tailscale measured about 2.2 Mbps through its DERP relay, which is about 61 minutes per GB. Neither Synology, UGREEN nor Asustor publishes a relay speed at all.
angles.decides: This confirms that the pick should depend on getting a direct path, not on which brand's relay you use. Every vendor relay that publishes a number or has been measured runs at about 1–2 Mbps. That works for opening a document or a single photo. It is not workable for pulling video or catching up a photo backup. Behind CGNAT, favor a NAS that can run Tailscale (UGREEN DXP2800 through Docker, Synology DS225+/DS223j through the official package, QNAP through Container Station) or that offers an IPv6 direct path, and treat the vendor relay as a last resort. The DH2300 has no Docker, so it is weaker here unless you add a separate Tailscale device.

For the pick: on UGREEN, Synology or QNAP, use a stick that has been reported working under VM passthrough (Sonoff ZBDongle-E on UGREEN). Avoid the ConBee II. If buying a ZBT-2, flash its firmware on another computer before passing it through. Expect to restart the VM, not just HAOS, after the stick drops. The DS223j moves from 'verify adapter' to 'also 12 V, per retailer listings of Synology's Adapter 60W_1', so it becomes a real 12 V option. It costs about 2.6 Ah more each day. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the hard-drive limit that decides whether a 12 V NAS can be wired to a van's house battery. NAS drives are specified at 12 V ±10% (10.8–13.2 V). A 12 V LiFePO4 bank charges at up to 14.6 V, which is 1.4 V above that limit. So a 12 V-input NAS needs a regulated DC-DC converter set to 12 V, such as Victron's Orion-Tr 12/12, which accepts 8–17 V in and gives an adjustable 10–15 V out.
angles.decides: This confirms the plan rather than changing which NAS to buy. Every 2-bay candidate (QNAP TS-233, Synology DS124/DS223j, UGREEN DH2300/DXP2800) runs from a 12 V brick, so all of them work in a van, but only behind a regulated 12 V DC-DC converter, not wired straight to the house battery. During charging (14.6 V from a LiFePO4 charger like Redodo's) the bus is 1.4 V, or about 11%, above the 13.2 V ceiling the drives are specified for. The converter's own losses add to the NAS's spec-sheet watts in the Ah/day column. The 19–20 V UGREEN models (DXP4800 Plus, DXP480T Plus) need a boost converter anyway. An all-SSD build doesn't avoid the issue, because SATA SSDs take 5 V from the NAS's own regulator.

With SSDs, LANOC measured 3.7 W idle, about 7 Ah a day from a 12.8 V battery, against QNAP's 10.81 W 'typical', about 20 Ah a day. pages.query: bluetooth speaker for pc

TechRadar, Tom's Hardware, Tom's Guide and PC Gamer returned only their titles, and Wired blocked the fetch, so the angle agents could not rule them out. Microsoft's driver docs say that once any app opens the speaker's mic, playback switches to mono at 8 or 16 kHz, and on Windows 10 the stereo stream is thrown away. This page gives each candidate's Bluetooth profile or mic listing and its wired fallback, and picks the A2DP-only Creative Pebble Pro, which plays USB audio.

The mains-powered Creative T60 gives 30 W RMS while taking USB-C audio.

In that setup the Pebble Pro ($66.49) gives 10 W RMS and the Pebble X Plus ($123.49) gives 15 W RMS. The T60 ($94.99, with its own 18 V 2 A adapter) gives 30 W RMS while playing USB-C audio. ChatGPT's 'best overall value' Pebble Pro is a third as loud as the T60 in the mode ChatGPT recommended, unless the shopper buys a 30 W PD brick and moves to Bluetooth SBC or AUX. The Pebble Pro is still the right pick for a small desk where 10 W RMS is enough. For more volume over USB, the T60 is the better buy, and it costs less than the X Plus.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Windows switches a Bluetooth speaker that supports the Hands-Free Profile to mono playback at 8 kHz or 16 kHz as soon as any app opens that speaker's microphone input. Microsoft says this happens on Windows 11 and that Windows 10 discards the stereo stream outright. Microsoft also lists only SBC, AAC, aptX Classic and aptX Adaptive (aptX Adaptive only on select Qualcomm radios) as Windows A2DP codecs, so a mic-less, A2DP-only speaker such as the Creative Pebble Pro, or a wired USB-C connection, avoids the problem.
angles.decides: For a PC used for both media and calls, pick a speaker that is A2DP-only with no built-in mic, or one with a wired USB-C audio input. That confirms the Creative Pebble Pro (A2DP only, SBC, USB audio, no built-in mic) as the safe default. A single portable speaker with a hands-free mic, such as the Marshall Emberton III, is a poor PC choice when calls matter. The moment Teams or Discord opens its mic, Windows drops the speaker to mono 8 kHz or 16 kHz, and the Emberton III has no wired audio input to fall back on (its USB-C is listed only for charging). The Creative T60 lists HFP alongside A2DP, so Windows 11 creates a mic input for it. Over Bluetooth, keep the PC's default mic set to something else, or use the T60's USB-C audio. A further point for the Pebble Pro: the 30 W RMS figure needs a separate 30 W USB PD adapter, which is not included. Powered from a PC port it is 10 W RMS.

pages.why_used: The rival pages only give a generic Bluetooth lag figure (about 150 ms, credited to PCWorld) and say plainly that they have no per-model measurement. None of them gives a measured delay for any recommended bar, converts it to film frames or checks it against the ITU lip-sync limit. None notes that the portable Bose Flex (2nd Gen) has no wired input. This page gives the HT-S100F's measured 62 ms (ARC) and 70 ms (optical), which is 1.5–1.7 frames and inside the ITU's 125 ms limit. It also sets out a wired-input check for every candidate.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Sony's own US manuals rate the 120 W HT-S100F and the 330 W HT-SD40 at the same 20 W per channel minimum RMS (FTC, ≤1% THD). The headline totals are sums of 'reference' figures measured at a single frequency, and both bars receive Bluetooth over SBC only.
angles.decides: This confirms the cheap pick and changes why you'd pay more. The $229 HT-SD40's 330 W against the HT-S100F's 120 W does not mean a louder bar. Both are rated 20 W per channel minimum RMS under FTC rules. The difference is mostly the SD40's 130 W (reference) subwoofer, so pay the extra only for bass. Both use SBC-only Bluetooth receivers, and the Samsung B630F's 'Bluetooth TV Connection' works only with Samsung TVs. For a lag-free TV link, use the HDMI ARC or optical input, which every candidate has. Don't count on Bluetooth from the TV. Samsung's own spec page lists no output wattage, only 24 W (bar) + 48 W (sub) operating power consumption. That makes the 370 W retail claim impossible to compare with the Sony figures.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured wired delay for any picked soundbar: the Sony HT-S100F measures 62 ms over HDMI ARC and 70 ms over optical (Gadget Review). That is 1.5–1.7 film frames at 24 fps, under the ITU-R BT.1359 lip-sync detectability limit of 125 ms audio lag. The portable pick, Bose SoundLink Flex (2nd Gen), has no AUX input, and its measured 7 h 03 min battery covers only 2 full 3-hour TV evenings per charge.
angles.decides: It confirms ChatGPT's soundbar-over-portable advice and makes it measurable. On the budget pick (HT-S100F), connecting by cable keeps the delay at 1.5–1.7 frames, inside the ITU detectability limit. Portable speakers like the Bose Flex 2 have no AUX input, so they must use the TV's Bluetooth output (if the TV has one), and they need charging every 2 evenings. The page should recommend the cable (ARC) route on the soundbar, and treat a portable speaker as a second option only for TVs with Bluetooth audio out.

A shopper who answers ChatGPT's follow-up with 'Bluetooth only' loses the soundbar's lip-sync correction. A portable speaker such as the Bose SoundLink Flex 2nd Gen has no such control to begin with.
