pages.query: cd player for stereo
pages.why_used: Every page ChatGPT cited compares the Yamaha CD-S303, Onkyo C-7030 and Denon DCD-600NE on the makers' own 105 / 107 / 112 dB claims; none carries a bench measurement. This page adds Audio Science Review's and Hi-Fi News' lab figures, which put the Yamaha and Denon at the same 95 dB noise floor and give the output-level gap, so the choice falls to outputs and USB, where the Yamaha wins.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the three makers' noise, distortion and output figures on one line and says that the Yamaha CD-S303's Pure Direct mode switches off the optical and coaxial outputs that are its main hardware edge over the optical-only Denon DCD-600NE, nor that Denon's own manual (12 W, 4.3 kg) and US product page (13 W, 4.0 kg) disagree with each other.
angles.decides: On the makers' own numbers the Denon leads on S/N (112 dB) and dynamic range (101 dB) but has no coaxial output; the Onkyo is the only one with a headphone jack and is the cheapest; the Yamaha is the only one with USB playback but loses both digital outputs whenever Pure Direct is on. For a shopper feeding an external DAC the Yamaha's advantage is conditional, which confirms the Onkyo as the practical pick and the Denon as the analog-only pick.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a Denon DCD-600NE left powered but idle draws 12 W against 0.3 W in standby, that its 30-minute Auto Standby ships switched off, or that the Yamaha-vs-Denon running-cost gap works out to about 1.5 kWh a year at 2 h of play a day.
angles.decides: Running cost cannot separate the Yamaha CD-S303 and Denon DCD-600NE: 11 W vs 12 W playing and 0.2 W vs 0.3 W in standby is about 1.5 kWh a year apart at 2 h/day. What does matter is behaviour: the Denon ships with Auto Standby off, so a forgotten unit burns 12 W around the clock (about 105 kWh/yr) until the owner holds POWER 5 s to enable the 30-minute timer. Both put out 2.0 V RMS on RCA, so neither needs a different amp input gain; the FiiO DM13 line out is 2.5 V RMS, about 1.9 dB hotter, which matters if the shopper is weighing the portable FiiO against a full-width deck for the same stereo.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Onkyo C-7030's one-remote/auto-input RI link works only with Onkyo RI-equipped amplifiers and still needs an analog RCA connection even when you use the digital output, or that the Denon DCD-600NE's rear IR CONTROL jacks are for Denon network audio players, not an amplifier link.
angles.decides: Confirms the Onkyo C-7030 only as the pick for a shopper who owns an Onkyo RI amp or receiver (one remote, auto input switch); for any other brand of stereo amp the RI jack is dead weight and the Onkyo should be connected only by RCA/optical/coaxial. The Denon DCD-600NE has no amplifier link jack and no coaxial output, so it suits an amp with an optical input or RCA only. Yamaha CD-S303 remains the pick for USB/FLAC playback (rival-stated), but maker confirmation of its USB limits was not reachable.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Denon DCD-600NE and Onkyo C-7030 both put out a fixed 2.0 V RMS analog line level (Onkyo rated into 600 Ω), so the stereo must offer a line-level CD/AUX/TAPE input and the player cannot drive volume itself, nor that the Denon caps data discs at 512 files/256 folders, 48–320 kbps MP3/WMA, refuses non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA, and outputs digital on optical only.
angles.decides: For a stereo with a spare analog CD/AUX/TAPE input the mechanism does not separate the three: each delivers a fixed ~2.0 V RMS line level over RCA, so any of them works and the player has no volume control of its own (a PHONO input is the wrong place). The mechanism only decides the pick when the stereo's free input is digital: a coaxial-only input rules out the Denon DCD-600NE (optical only); any digital link needs Pure Direct off on the Yamaha CD-S303 or Mode 1 on the Denon, else silence. For shoppers with burned discs, the Denon manual says non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA will not play and caps a data disc at 512 files and 320 kbps.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states an independently measured noise, distortion or jitter figure for any candidate: Hi-Fi News measured the Denon DCD-600 at 95.3 dB A-weighted S/N, 0.0013% THD and 480 psec jitter, and an Audio Science Review member measured the Yamaha CD-S303 at 95.7 dB dynamic range, 0.0022% THD+N and 1.74 V output.
angles.decides: It confirms rather than overturns the pick: both of the two most-cited budget players measure to roughly the same 95 dB noise floor, well below the makers' 105 dB (Yamaha) and 110 dB (Denon) claims, so neither has a measurable sound-quality edge and the choice can rest on price, outputs and features. Two usable details: the Denon's 1.92 Vrms output is near the 2 V standard while the Yamaha's 1.74 Vrms sits 1.2 dB low (the Yamaha will sound quieter at the same volume setting), and the Yamaha was verified bit-perfect as a transport over optical, which matters for anyone feeding an external DAC. No independent measurement exists for the Onkyo C-7030, so its 107 dB claim stays unverified.

None of them explains that AM comes in through an antenna inside the case and that you aim it by turning the whole unit. This page sorts every candidate by the bands listed in its maker spec or manual, adds today's prices and says which models skip AM.

Their headline watts are not comparable: Sony's honest US figure is 1.1 W/ch, and Jensen publishes no measured rating on a maker page. So pick on battery count and band coverage, not on watts. The battery-life claims are also on different bases. Sony states about 10 h of CD play at volume 23 on Sony alkaline cells. Jensen's '50 hours' comes from a brand rep's Target Q&A answer, with no mode or volume given.

pages.query: electric coolers for camping
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (OutdoorGearLab, plus GearJunkie's one BougeRV CRD45 bundle) list which cords each cooler ships with. None of them says which maker battery fits which cooler: BougeRV's 240 Wh internal battery fits neither the 23 qt nor the CRPRO30, ICECO's bank is external on the VL45, and Dometic's PLB40 costs $539.99. None of them adds up cooler plus battery for each pick, so a shopper who answers 'need a built-in battery' gets no priced path.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the US Dometic CFX5 45 (R1234yf, SKU 97000050755) is rated at 1.05 Ah/h (about 302 Wh/day at 90°F ambient, 39°F inside), 38% more than the 0.76 Ah/h Dometic gives for the AU/NZ R600a version. They also don't say that the other makers state power on bases you can't compare: Anker gives runtime at 77°F with an empty cooler in Eco mode, and ICECO gives kWh per 24 h with no ambient temperature.
angles.decides: This keeps Dometic as the premium pick but changes the power-station sizing. Converted to Wh/day, the US CFX5 45's own rating is about 302 Wh/day at 90°F, so a 500 Wh station covers about 1.7 days before DC-conversion losses. Anker's claim works out to about 134 Wh/day, but that is at 77°F, so it doesn't mean the Anker is more than twice as efficient. On the one common basis we have (OGL's 75°F lab), the measured gap is small: 5.8 W vs 6.8 W. In the table, the footnote is the finding: makers quote power at 77°F, at 90°F and at no stated temperature, and the US and AU versions of the same Dometic carry different ratings.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a hot-weather daily energy figure or days on a power station. Dometic's own spec for the US CFX5 45 is 1.05 Ah/h at 32 °C (90 °F) outside and 4 °C (39 °F) inside. That works out to about 302 Wh a day, so a 1,024 Wh station (EcoFlow DELTA 3, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2) lasts about 3.4 days in summer heat. OutdoorGearLab's 75 °F lab draw of 6.8 W gives about 6.3 days, so heat almost doubles the draw.
angles.decides: It doesn't change which cooler to pick. It changes what to pair with it. For summer car camping, size the station at about 300 Wh per day for a 45 L compressor cooler, not the 160–200 Wh/day the 75 °F lab numbers suggest. A weekend in the heat needs about 600 Wh, which rules out 245–300 Wh stations (RIVER 3, Tenergy T320, ALLPOWERS R600) for anything past one night. The 1,024 Wh class is the right pairing for a 3-day trip. ChatGPT's '500 Wh ≈ 1–2 days' holds in heat (500/302 = 1.7 days) but undersells mild weather (500/163 = 3.1 days).

Dometic's battery for the CFX5 45 is the external PLB40 at $539.99, which almost doubles the cost of the $997 fridge. What it changes is the advice that goes with it: the shopper can run the BougeRV, ICECO VL45 or Dometic CFX5 straight off the car, as long as the battery protection is set to HIGH. A built-in-battery model (Anker SOLIX EverFrost 2) or a power station (Dealectric lists several) is what makes overnight off-grid use work without touching the starter battery. pages.query: 3d printer with enclosure
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (firstlayerlab, 3dprintgearlab) list the P2S chamber only as 'passive' or 'no active heating listed' and give the Q2's 65 °C without its heater wattage. None of them places the P2S's 50 °C passive ceiling and CNC Kitchen's measured 50.3–54.1 °C next to the Q2's separate 280 W heater, and none shows that the $349 Q2C drops that heater for $100 less on the same frame. This page covers all three.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Bambu Lab P2S's own '50 °C chamber' figure is a passive limit with no heater: it comes from bed heat held in by an automatic air flap, and owners log about 37–52 °C depending on the aux-fan setting. The QIDI Q2's '65 °C' is a setpoint held by a dedicated 280 W chamber heater. The two figures look comparable but are not.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split pick. For PLA and PETG, the P2S's passive chamber is enough. For ABS, ASA and nylon, the Q2 at the same $449 has a 280 W heater that holds 65 °C. The P2S's 50 °C is a best case that one owner logged at 37–42 °C with the right aux fan at 100% in heating mode. It also warns shoppers off the QIDI Q2C ($349): it has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm build volume, but its US store blurb doesn't list chamber heating, while the Q2's blurb does.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of a heated chamber in dollars per liter of build space. On QIDI's own US store, the QIDI Q2 costs $449 for 18.66 L ($24.06 per liter). The QIDI Q2C has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm volume for $349 ($18.70 per liter), and its listing does not mention the Q2's 65 °C active chamber heating. On QIDI's own figures, the heated chamber costs $100. The Q2's 280 W heater can use up to 2.8 kWh over a 10-hour ABS print, on top of the printer's 350 W rating.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split: the QIDI Q2 for ABS, ASA and nylon, where an actively heated chamber matters, and a cheaper passive printer otherwise. It also adds an option ChatGPT never mentioned. A shopper printing only PLA or PETG can buy the QIDI Q2C for $349, the same build volume as the Q2 for $100 less ($18.70 vs $24.06 per liter). The extra $100 for the Q2 only pays off for engineering filaments. Dealectric already lists the qidi-q2 (awin:qidi), so a Q2 vs Q2C section would point to a product we can link.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the add-on multicolor units for two of its recommended enclosed printers are tied to specific models: the QIDI Box comes in separate Plus4, Q2 and Max4 versions (different Box Hub and signal cable, $40.99 kit to move it to another printer), and Creality's K1-series CFS upgrade kit for the K1C works only with the integrated-nozzle hotend and keeps the top cover from closing fully, so the K1C stops being fully enclosed for ABS unless you print the height-extension part.
angles.decides: This backs the QIDI Q2 as the pick for a shopper who wants an enclosed printer for ABS/ASA now and multicolor later. QIDI's US Q2 page says it works with the QIDI Box, and QIDI says the Box can dry and print at the same time (up to 65 °C) and chain up to 4 units. Buy the Q2 version of the Box, or plan $40.99 for the upgrade kit if you move it to another printer. It counts against the Creality K1C for the same shopper. ChatGPT pitched it as 'enclosed', but adding Creality's CFS means an integrated-nozzle hotend, a top cover that no longer closes fully (Creality supplies height-extension files for ABS), and a smaller 220 × 215 × 250 mm print volume. The finding doesn't change the pick for a shopper printing PLA/PETG in one color.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the P2S's chamber ceiling. It has no chamber heater: its only heat is the bed, held in by a motorized airflow flap that switches to recirculation, which tops out at about 50 °C. The QIDI Q2 adds a separate 280 W PTC chamber heater (rated 350 W + 280 W) that holds up to 65 °C whatever the bed is doing.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's split. If the shopper mostly prints PLA, PETG or small ABS/ASA parts, the P2S works: its bed heat, held in by the flap, reaches about 50 °C, and in cooling mode it pulls in outside air so PLA can print with the door shut. If they print large ABS/ASA parts, PC or nylon, they need a heater that works independently of the bed, and among the cards shown only the QIDI Q2 has one (65 °C, 280 W PTC). The P1S, K1C and Adventurer 5M Pro all rely on bed heat alone. The Q2 heater pushes the rated draw to 630 W, which does not affect a standard 15 A US outlet. For a PLA-only buyer the Q2's heater is no advantage. QIDI's own blog lists heat creep among the risks of too much chamber heat.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured chamber temperature for any of these printers. CNC Kitchen's thermocouples read 50.3 °C and 54.1 °C inside the Bambu Lab P2S's passive chamber, with the bed at 100–110 °C. Clever Creations timed the Creality K1C's chamber at 30 minutes to rise from 25 °C to its 38 °C maximum.
angles.decides: The measurements back ChatGPT's split pick and make it more precise. The P2S's passive chamber was measured at about 50–54 °C, which is far warmer than the K1C's measured 38 °C maximum. That makes the P2S a fair choice for occasional ABS/ASA. It also weakens the K1C as a choice for ABS. The case for the QIDI Q2's 65 °C active heater rests only on QIDI's own claim, because I found no independent measurement of it. So the Q2 pick for engineering filaments stays plausible but is not measured.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the cheapest way to get both an actively heated chamber and multicolor printing is the QIDI Q2 at $449 plus the QIDI Box at $228, $677 in total from qidi3d.com on 2026-11-08. That is $112 less than the $789 Bambu X2D AMS Combo, the only other heated-chamber multicolor pair priced in the cited pages.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's choice of the QIDI Q2 for engineering materials and stretches it to shoppers who also want multicolor. At $677 the Q2 + Box costs $112 less than the X2D AMS Combo, and both have a 65 °C heated chamber. The Q2 alone is the same $449 that 3dprintgearlab gives for the P2S, but it adds active heating and about 11% more build volume (18.66 L vs 16.78 L). The P2S stays the pick only for mostly-PLA buyers who want Bambu's ecosystem. The $349 Q2C has the same build volume, but its store listing does not name the heater, so it is not a substitute for ABS/ASA.

pages.query: camera flash with diffuser
pages.why_used: The cited B&H AK-R11 page and the cameraegg dome roundup price only the diffusers and assume the shopper already owns a V1. Neither gives a flash's output, its full-power flashes per charge or its cost per flash. This page compares watt-seconds, flash count, light per charge and price across the four Godox round-head flashes that take the dome directly. None of them is a product we list or an approved brand, and Amazon blocked amzcheck, so the page has no earning link.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Godox V1's guide number in its own manual is 42 m at ISO 100, with a head that only zooms to 105 mm. Shop tables list it as '92' or '76' next to the TT685 II's '60' without units or zoom settings, and '76' is the V1's flash energy in watt-seconds (76 Ws), not a guide number.
angles.decides: This supports the V1 + AK-R11 pick for diffused, bounced or close-range light: the V1 makes 76 Ws, recycles in about 1.5 s and gives about 480 full-power flashes from its Li-ion pack. It does not support picking it over a 20–200 mm square speedlight because of a bigger 'GN 92'. That figure has no stated conditions, and the V1's own manual says GN 42 m (ISO 100). For long-range direct flash, a 200 mm zoom head is the comparison to make, and I could not put both flashes at the same zoom setting from an opened page.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 100 Ws Godox V100 gives about 0.4 stop more light per pop than the 76 Ws V1Pro, yet both flashes deliver about the same total light per charge (V100 40,000 J vs V1Pro 38,000 J, from the same 7.2 V/2980 mAh ≈ 21.5 Wh battery). That works out to $0.66 per full-power flash for the V1Pro and $0.87 for the V100.
angles.decides: A dome diffuser costs light, so a flash with more power per pop helps. The V100 gives about 0.4 stop more per pop (log2(100/76) = 0.40) for $20 more, but it delivers 100 fewer full-power flashes per charge (400 vs 500), recycles slower (1.7 s vs 1.3 s) and weighs 616 g with its battery. For event shooting with a dome, the V1Pro stays the pick: more pops, faster recycle, lower cost per flash. The V100 is the pick only if the shopper bounces off high ceilings or uses the larger AK-R22 dome and needs the extra 0.4 stop.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Godox's newer V1 mid round-head flash takes the AK-R1 magnetic round-head accessories (whose dome is the one the AK-R11 matches) but comes only in C/N/S/F/O versions, so Panasonic (P) shooters still need the V1-P. None of them says that a flash for one camera brand will not do TTL on another.
angles.decides: The answer holds: a Godox round-head flash plus the magnetic dome is the simplest diffuser setup, because the dome mounts with no adapter. Godox names the V1 (C/N/S/F/O/P) and the V1 mid (C/N/S/F/O) as round-head flashes for its AK-R1 accessories. The newer V1 mid is the current option for Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and Olympus/OM bodies. Panasonic users should pick the V1-P. A TT685II or V860III owner needs the separate S-R1 adapter before any round dome will fit. ChatGPT asked 'What camera do you use?', and the camera brand is what decides which flash version to buy.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a flash only widens its zoom for a dome if it can detect the dome: Nikon's SB-5000 senses its own Diffusion Dome and sets the zoom head to 12, 14 or 17 mm on FX (8, 10 or 11 mm on DX). The Godox V1 manual says nothing about detecting accessories, and its zoom only goes down to 28 mm.
angles.decides: This confirms how the plan works more than it changes the pick. A dome only softens light by spreading it wide and bouncing it off nearby surfaces. Nikon's own manual pairs the dome with bounce flash ('can be further diffused during bounce flash photography') and says the flash zooms to its widest setting by itself when the dome is fitted. On a Godox V1 with an AK-R11, the flash doesn't do this, so the shopper should set the zoom to 28 mm with the ZOOM button and point the head up or to the side. If they leave auto zoom on, the flash follows the lens focal length and sends a narrower beam into the dome. For a shopper who wants it to just work, a system flash that ships with its own dome and senses it (the Nikon SB-5000 with its SW-15H) is the hands-off choice. A Godox V1 plus AK-R11 does the same job at much lower cost but needs that manual step.
products: Nikon SB-5000 + Nikon SW-15H Diffusion Dome

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named meter reading for the Godox V1. Fstoppers (Dylan Goldby, 2019-07-01) measured the bare V1 at f/8.8 against f/8.7 for the V860II, and f/8.5 against f/8.7 inside a 173 cm umbrella. Fstoppers (Alex Coleman, 2024-04-05) reports that the original V1 reached its overheat zone after 20–30 full-power pops at 90–100 °F; the V1Pro's spec sheet allows 100.
angles.decides: This supports the V1 or V1Pro as the flash to pair with a dome. Fstoppers' meter shows the V1's round head matching a conventional 76 Ws speedlight bare (f/8.8 vs f/8.7), so the round head costs no output before a dome goes on. The thermal finding is a tie-breaker: a dome usually means turning the power up, and Coleman saw the original V1 hit its heat limit after 20–30 full-power pops in hot conditions. Shoppers who shoot events at high power should pick the V1Pro (rated for 100 pops at 1/1; Coleman did not test it in that heat). No named lab has measured how much light the AK-R11 or AK-R22 domes cost, so the page cannot rank the domes by light loss.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got prices the flash and the diffuser together. A Godox TT685 II ($129), the S-R1 round-head adapter ($9) and the AK-R1 magnetic kit, which includes a diffusion ball ($59), cost $197 at MoLight on 2026-11-08. The V1 ($258.99) plus the AK-R11 dome ($11.90) costs $270.89 at Pro Photo Supply. The newer V1 Pro ($329) and V100 ($349) cost $70–$90 more than the V1 before any dome.
angles.decides: The V1 + AK-R11 pick ChatGPT gave holds for someone who wants a round head that takes the dome directly. For a budget shopper it does not hold: the TT685 II + S-R1 + AK-R1 route is $73.89 cheaper and includes a grid, snoot and barn doors. The V1 Pro and V100 only make sense if the sub-flash (V1 Pro) or the 100 Ws output (V100) is worth $70–$90 more.

pages.query: best lifepo4 battery 12v
pages.why_used: BatteryTrail tabulates 100 A continuous for five brands and ExploringOffGrid says a 100 A BMS is about 1,280 W, but neither names a Group 24 100Ah battery with a 150 A BMS, neither lists Vatrer or Redodo, and neither converts the amp rating into the inverter size one battery can carry. This page does all three with maker-page figures dated today.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that LiTime's 4,000-cycle figure is at 100% DoD to about 80% remaining capacity while its 15,000-cycle headline applies only at 60% DoD, so on a full-discharge basis LiTime (4,000) sits inside Battle Born's 3,000-5,000 band and the $490 price gap buys pack-level listing and warranty, not cycle life.
angles.decides: Confirms ChatGPT's LiTime-for-value pick but on a different basis: once cycle counts are put on the same 100% DoD footing, LiTime and Battle Born claim the same order of life, so the premium is paying for ETL pack listing and a 10-year warranty, not longevity. It also flags that Redodo's '4000-15000 cycles' spans undeclared DoD tiers, and that the Dealectric-listed Vatrer Group 24 at $259.99 is the only sub-$300 pack here with a 150 A BMS (1,920 W continuous) and a UL 1973 claim, which matters for inverter loads.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Wh per pound or dollars per Wh for the 12V 100Ah candidates; on those two derived figures the Redodo 12V 100Ah Group 24 Bluetooth ($0.203/Wh, 58.7 Wh/lb) and the Vatrer 12V 100Ah Group 24 150A ($0.203/Wh) both beat ChatGPT's value pick, the LiTime Group 24 Bluetooth ($0.243/Wh, 57.8 Wh/lb), and the LiTime Xtra-Mini is the Wh/lb leader at 66.9.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's 'best overall value' is the LiTime Group 24 Bluetooth at $311.09. At the same 1,280 Wh, 100A-class BMS, Bluetooth, low-temp cutoff and 5-year warranty, the Redodo Group 24 Bluetooth costs $51 less ($0.203 vs $0.243 per Wh) and is 0.36 lb lighter, and the Vatrer Group 24 at the same $259.99 adds a 150A BMS (1,920 W continuous vs 1,280 W, i.e. 7.4 W per dollar vs 4.1). If weight is the shopper's number, the LiTime Xtra-Mini (19.13 lb, 66.9 Wh/lb) wins for $8 more than the Group 24 Bluetooth. Battle Born stays a 3x-the-price premium pick ($0.62/Wh, about 41 Wh/lb) whose only derived advantage is warranty length.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the LiTime 12V 100Ah Group 24 Bluetooth and LiHeat Self-Heating batteries it recommended top out at 4P4S (16 batteries, 51.2 V, 20.48 kWh), ship switched off and need a charger connected to turn on, and carry no CAN/RS485 inverter communication (LiTime reserves that for its ComFlex line), while Redodo's otherwise identical 4P4S Group 24 battery is excluded by the maker from golf-cart, water-pump, electric-jack and mower duty.
angles.decides: Confirms the LiTime 12V 100Ah Group 24 Bluetooth ($311.09) as the value pick for a 12 V bank that may later grow to 24 V or 48 V, since LiTime, Redodo and (per the maker) the LiTime LiHeat all allow 4S4P where Renogy Pro is parallel-only and Dakota stops at 2S. It adds two conditions none of the rival pages give: a buyer must have a LiFePO4 charger on hand to switch a new LiTime Bluetooth battery on, and anyone wanting the battery to talk to a Victron GX / inverter should not buy any of ChatGPT's three picks, because none of them has CAN or RS485. For cold climates the LiTime LiHeat ($368.99) is the only candidate whose maker says it can heat from its own stored energy before charging; Vatrer's heated model heats only while a charger is connected.
products: LiTime LiHeat 12V 100Ah Group 24 Dual-Mode Self Heating

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BMS continuous-discharge rating is the hard cap on the inverter one battery can feed, and that Vatrer's Group 24 100Ah carries a 150A BMS (150 A × 12.8 V = 1,920 W) where LiTime and Redodo Group 24 batteries stop at 100 A (1,280 W) and Epoch's 105Ah at 105 A, so a 1,500 W inverter runs on one Vatrer but trips a single LiTime, Redodo or Epoch.
angles.decides: For a shopper who will run a 12 V inverter: 100 A BMS batteries (LiTime Group 24 Bluetooth, Redodo Group 24 Bluetooth) are limited to 1,280 W from a single unit and Redodo's own page excludes water pumps, electric jacks and mowers; the Vatrer 12V 100Ah Group 24 (150A BMS, $259.99, UL 1973) is the only Group 24 100Ah candidate confirmed on the maker's page to carry a 1,500 W inverter alone, and it is cheaper than the LiTime pick ChatGPT led with ($311.09). For shoppers without an inverter the 100 A batteries are fine and the finding confirms LiTime/Redodo as value picks. Every candidate stops charging at 32°F; only the Epoch Essential and the Vatrer/LiTime heated versions can charge below that, and Epoch's heater only works while a charger is connected.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured capacity for any of its picks: techtest.org's electronic-load tests put the LiTime 12V 100Ah Group 24 Bluetooth at 102.46 Ah average (100.92 to 103.33 Ah, 30 to 40 A discharge), the standard LiTime 12V 100Ah at 106.06 Ah, Vatrer 12V 100Ah at 104.2 Ah and Redodo 12V 100Ah at 107.7 Ah, all above the 100 Ah rating, while Will Prowse's controlled test of a Battle Born 75 Ah had the BMS repeatedly disconnecting after 14 cycles at 49 A.
angles.decides: Confirms LiTime as the value pick with a number instead of a spec sheet: every LiTime 100Ah variant techtest measured delivered 101.6 to 106.1 Ah, and the Group 24 Bluetooth model ChatGPT led with delivered 102.5 Ah average even at 30 A and 100.9 Ah at 40 A. It undercuts the 'premium, buy for support' framing of Battle Born: Will Prowse's teardown of a 100 Ah unit found the positive terminal loosely attached to the bus bar with a melted spacer, and his controlled 49 A cycling of a 75 Ah unit produced repeated BMS disconnects after 14 cycles, with Dragonfly Energy (Battle Born's parent) now suing him over the videos. The cheapest candidate in Dealectric's catalog, Redodo 12V 100Ah, has the highest measured capacity of the group at 107.7 Ah, and Vatrer 12V 100Ah measured 104.2 Ah, so both can be recommended on measured data rather than brand reputation.

angles.name: Whole category, priced

pages.query: low profile or mechanical keyboard
pages.why_used: Neither chat ran a search or cited a page. Its answer only called low-profile customization 'more limited' and travel 'shorter', with no figure. This page puts a number on the travel difference (about 3 mm on Gateron's low-profile 2.0 against 4.0 mm on Cherry MX). It also says which switch and keycap family each board ties you to: Keychron's MX-style low-profile on the RGB hot-swap version only, Lofree's Kailh low-profile that isn't MX pin-compatible, and full-size switches on the Q1 Max.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the makers' headline battery figures assume the backlight is off. With the lights on, the full-height Keychron Q1 Max is rated for only about 30 h, at its lowest RGB brightness (it claims up to 180 h unlit), and the low-profile NuPhy Air75 V2 is rated for 35–57 h (it claims up to 220 h unlit). That is a cut of roughly 4 to 6 times that neither headline shows.
angles.decides: It doesn't change the pick between low-profile and full-height, but it corrects a hidden assumption. ChatGPT named the Q1 Max and the Air75 V2. Their headline battery claims (180 h and 220 h) are both lights-off figures. Measured the same way, with the backlight on, the 4,000 mAh in each lasts about one to two working weeks, not a month or more. The full-height Q1 Max is also 22.6 mm tall at the front and 35.8 mm at the back before keycaps, by KitGuru's figures. That supports ChatGPT's ergonomic point: a full-height board like this will likely need a wrist rest.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much taller a full-height board sits at the wrist edge. Without keycaps, Keychron's figures put the front edge of the Q1 Max at 22.6 mm and the low-profile K3 Max at 11 mm. That is 11.6 mm higher, or 2.05×. The Q1 Max also weighs 3.3× as much (1,724 g vs 525 g) and costs $120 more at Keychron's own store today.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's lean for laptop and desk typists. The low-profile K3 Max starts 11.6 mm lower at the front edge, 1.16 lb against 3.80 lb, and $89.99 against $209.99. That is why the full-height Q1 Max needs a wrist rest and the K3 Max mostly doesn't. On rear height without keycaps the difference grows to 20.8 mm (35.8 vs 15). The Q1 Max is the pick only if the shopper wants full-height keycaps and switch choice and doesn't mind a wrist rest. Lofree's Flow84 claims a 10 mm thickness, which fits the same low-profile range.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Keychron's own low-profile keyboards accept only low-profile parts, and only some of them: K3 Max hot-swap applies 'for RGB Backlight Hot-Swappable Version only' with Gateron low-profile MX-style switches, and Keychron's low-profile LSA keycap set 'is not compatible with the Keychron K1 versions 1 to 5, K1 SE, K3, K5, K5 SE, and K7'. A full-height board like the Q1 Max instead takes ordinary full-size switches (Gateron Jupiter, sold by Keychron at $13.99 a set).
angles.decides: This supports the low-profile pick for laptop-style typists, with one condition: a low-profile board ties you to low-profile switches and keycaps, and in Keychron's case to particular versions. If the shopper wants to change switches on a K3 Max, they must buy the RGB hot-swappable version. Low-profile keycaps from Keychron's current sets will not fit the original K3, K1 v1–5, K5 or K7. Shoppers who want to swap keycaps and switches freely should buy a full-height board (Q1 Max class). This matches ChatGPT's 'enthusiasts → standard' line, but gives the actual reason.
products: Keychron Low Profile Double Shot PBT LSA Keycap Set Version 2
Keychron Low Profile ABS LSA Full Set Keycap Set
Gateron Low Profile 2.0 Mechanical Switch (Keychron store)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a low-profile board's hot-swap sockets only take that board's own low-profile switch family, with less travel than MX. Lofree's Kailh-based switches are not pin compatible with MX low-profile switches, and full-height Cherry or SA keycaps tend to stick on them. Gateron's KS-33 low-profile switch travels 3.0 mm against Cherry MX's 4.0 mm. So ChatGPT's 'customization: more limited' is really a lock-in to one switch and keycap ecosystem.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's split. A shopper who wants to swap switches or keycaps later should buy full-height MX, such as the Keychron Q1 Max. A low-profile board such as the Lofree Flow 2 84, Keychron K3 Max or NuPhy Air75 V2 suits someone happy with the switches it ships with or the same maker's replacements. It also puts a number on the feel difference: 3.0 mm of travel on Gateron KS-33 against 4.0 mm on Cherry MX.

pages.query: best portable projector screen
pages.why_used: I opened the ranked guides: ProjectorVerdict (both pages), iTechGuides, Austin Gallery and Projector Reviews. This page uses Elite's foot-lambert formula and the SMPTE 16 fL target to give the lumens each screen needs and the screen size that suits each projector.

pages.query: which solar generator recharges fastest from solar panels in one day
pages.why_used: The cited rivals (Solar Waypoint's spec comparisons, the maker pages, the best-of lists) give only rated maximum solar input and theoretical Wh-divided-by-W times; none uses a named reviewer's measured energy-to-fill (StorageReview 1,180 Wh for the DELTA 3 Plus, Notebookcheck 1,110 Wh for the C1000 Gen 2, StorageReview 1,360 Wh for the AC180), and none shows that the big stations' one-hour figure needs a 3-5 kW array while the same 800 W of panels refills a two-input 1 kWh station four to five times sooner.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the makers' refill claims on the same basis. Every claim assumes the station's full solar input. Anker's own spec splits the C1000 Gen 2 input into two bands: 11–28 V at 8.2 A (about 230 W at most) and 29–60 V at 14.5 A. So two low-voltage panels wired in parallel get well under half of the 600 W behind its '1.8 hours' figure. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 claims the same 70-minute full refill as the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. The difference is that the BLUETTI takes its 1,000 W through one 12–60 V, 20 A input, while EcoFlow splits its 1,000 W across two 500 W inputs.
angles.decides: This mostly confirms the DELTA 3 Plus pick for 'two panels', because it takes one panel per input and two panels need no series or parallel wiring. The Elite 100 V2 makes the same 70-minute claim for $499, but only when both panels are wired into one string that sits between 50 V working and 60 V open-circuit. Wired in parallel, it is capped at 20 A times the panels' working voltage. On the Anker C1000 Gen 2, the '1.8 hours' needs a string above 41 V. Two small panels in parallel at about 18–20 V stay inside the 8.2 A band and reach only about a third of that rate.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out that with the same pair of 400 W panels (EcoFlow's FAQ example: 37.1 V open-circuit, 12.9 A each), only the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus can take both: one panel per input gives 800 W and a refill in 1,024 / 800 = 1.28 h. Wired either way, the pair falls outside the stated input limits of the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2: in series 74.2 V is over the 60 V maximum, and in parallel 25.8 A is over 14.5 A (Anker) or 20 A (BLUETTI).
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's pick, the DELTA 3 Plus, for the stated question, and it rules out the strongest-looking alternative. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 makes the same '1,000W … Full in 70 Minutes' claim at $499, but it has one 12–60 V, 20 A input. Two common 400 W panels go over that limit in series and in parallel. A 1,000 W refill would need a single string working at 50 V or more (1,000 W / 20 A) while staying at or under 60 V open-circuit. With two panels, the fastest refill of the five candidates is the DELTA 3 Plus with one panel on each input.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what Anker's own split current limit means for its 600 W / 1.8-hour solar claim on the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: the station takes only 8.2 A at 11–28 V, so a two-panel setup running at 28 V or less tops out near 230 W, and the full 600 W needs the panels working at 41.4 V or more on its single XT60i input.
angles.decides: This supports the DELTA 3 Plus as the pick. It is the only candidate where EcoFlow states a second solar input ('from 1 input to 2 inputs'), so each of the two panels can have its own input. On the C1000 Gen 2, Anker's 1.8-hour figure only holds when the two panels together work at 41.4 V or more and stay at 60 V or less open-circuit on one input. Anker's own two-panel recipe for 600 W is a mismatched 400 W + 200 W pair, not two equal panels. The BLUETTI AC180 is capped at 500 W on one input with a hard 60 V open-circuit limit. That rules out wiring two higher-voltage panels in series, so the AC180 ranks below both.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 has a single solar input whose current limit drops to 8.2 A whenever the array works below 29 V. If two panels on that one input run below 29 V, the station takes about 230 W at most (28 V × 8.2 A), not its rated 600 W. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus gives each of the two panels its own 500 W MPPT input.

The Anker C1000 Gen 2, ChatGPT's runner-up, puts both panels on one input. It reaches its 600 W ceiling only if that array works at about 41 V or more (600 W ÷ 14.5 A) while staying at or under 60 V open-circuit. A pair of panels working below 29 V is limited to roughly 230 W, which stretches the advertised 1.8 h refill to about 4.5 h or more (1,024 Wh ÷ 230 W, before losses). The page should tell C1000 Gen 2 buyers to check their panels' working voltage (Vmp) and combined open-circuit voltage (Voc) before trusting the 1.8 h figure.

pages.query: which power station keeps a wifi router running the longest
pages.why_used: The cited rivals give the Anker C300X DC only as a 272.9 Wh average with no port or load, quote the TRAIL 300 DC only at EcoFlow's 0.01 W claim, and work out router hours from rated Wh. This page has techtest.org's 277.6 Wh (96%) at a router-sized 24 W on 12 V, The Solar Lab's measured 2 Wh a day idle for the TRAIL 300 DC, and router hours on DC vs AC worked out from each station's measured own draw, which moves the DELTA Pro 3 from the 8 to 10 days shown elsewhere to about 6.1 days on DC and 2.7 on AC.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' 'standby' and 'self-consumption' figures and the testers' '% lost per hour' results into one number: watts drawn with only the DC side on. Measured that way by the same reviewer, BLUETTI's own Elite 30 V2 draws about 11 W with DC on, not the 4.5 W BLUETTI advertises. The BLUETTI EB3A, which ChatGPT told DC-only shoppers to avoid, draws about 3.6 W.
angles.decides: It changes the DC-only pick and corrects ChatGPT's advice. With a 15 W router on the 12 V port, the Elite 30 V2's measured 11 W of DC-on draw nearly doubles the load: about 11 h from 288 Wh (288 ÷ 26 W). Its own 4.5 W claim would suggest about 15 h (288 ÷ 19.5 W). For low DC loads, the advertised standby number can't be used to rank stations. DC-on draw measured by a reviewer is the column that decides it. The EcoFlow TRAIL '0.01 W no-load' figure is a storage/sleep figure, not DC-on draw: EcoFlow gives it with no condition, next to '≤5% a month'. So it can't be ranked against the others either. The Anker C300 DC's 94.8% is an AC-port test of the C300X DC with no load stated, so it doesn't support ChatGPT's 'best for DC-only' claim.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of the battery each station's own DC-on draw uses up at a 15 W router load, worked out from measured no-load drain. The estimates come to about 46% for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 (13 W), 42% for the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (10.9 W), 19% for the BLUETTI EB3A (3.6 W) and under 1% for the EcoFlow TRAIL 300 DC (about 0.08 W). On those figures a 288 Wh TRAIL 300 DC would run a 15 W router for about 19 h, against about 11 h for the 288 Wh Elite 30 V2.
angles.decides: For the 'loses the least on USB and 12 V' question, the pick moves to a DC-only unit (EcoFlow TRAIL 300 DC, 2 Wh a day measured idle). Among stations with an inverter, the older EB3A beats the newer Elite 30 V2. For the 'longest router runtime' question, the big station's lead is smaller than it looks: DELTA Pro 3 works out to about 6.1 days on DC and about 2.7 days on AC at 15 W. ChatGPT showed 8–10 days and outagemath showed 9.7 days. Its own 13–49 W draw can be up to three times the router's load.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' UPS promise covers only the AC outlets. EcoFlow's US RIVER 3 Plus page says 'All three AC outlets have UPS protection' and says nothing about the USB or car ports. BLUETTI's Elite 30 V2 page gives '≤10ms' and '980W bypass' without naming any outputs. So the shopper who saves energy by running the router from USB or 12 V gets no written switchover promise from the maker for that port.
angles.decides: This narrows the pick rather than overturning it. If the router must survive a power cut with no blip, the only route the makers document is AC with UPS on, which gives up the DC savings. If the shopper goes DC-only to lose the least power, which is question pm015, they should treat the station as a battery they switch over to by hand, or test the DC port themselves, until the maker confirms DC pass-through. On the Anker SOLIX C300 DC, a 12 V router needs one of the 140 W ports (USB-C1 to C3). USB-C4 is limited to 15 W and shares 20 W with USB-A.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the auto-off threshold that decides whether a router survives an outage on a given port. The likely example is Jackery's Energy Saving Mode, on by default on the Explorer 240 v2. Search results quote its manual as switching every output off after 12 hours when the AC load is at or below 25 W or the USB and car-port load is at or below 2 W. That would cut a 10–20 W router on AC but leave it running on the 12 V car port. I could not open a Jackery page to confirm these figures.
angles.decides: It confirms the DC-port route. On stations whose default auto-off uses a high AC threshold and a very low DC threshold, a 10–20 W router stays up on the 12 V or USB-C port but gets switched off on AC unless the shopper disables the mode. On BLUETTI Elite V2 units with DC-ECO on by default, the shopper has to turn DC-ECO off first. For the 'least loss on USB/12 V' question, DC-only units with no inverter (EcoFlow TRAIL 300 DC, rated 0.01 W no-load) beat stations that run their DC side through a control board that stays on (Elite 30 V2: about 7–11 W with DC on, as measured by reviewers our page cites).

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that techtest.org measured 277.6 Wh out of 288 Wh (96%) from the Anker SOLIX C300X DC's 12 V socket at 2 A (about 24 W, a router-plus-modem-sized load) and 271.5 Wh (94%) on USB-C at 9 V/3 A (about 27 W). It also does not state that The Solar Lab measured the inverter-free EcoFlow TRAIL 300 DC using about 2 Wh in 24 hours switched on with no load, while Gough Lui measured 1.14 W idle on the EcoFlow RIVER 2 and The Technology Man saw a BLUETTI EB3A lose 16% in 12 hours with DC on and nothing plugged in.

At a router-sized 24 W on its 12 V socket, techtest.org measured it losing about 4% (277.6 of 288 Wh), the low-load test ChatGPT said it was missing. That works out to about 11.5 h at 24 W, or about 13.9 h at 20 W if efficiency holds. The EcoFlow TRAIL 300 DC is the runner-up for standby loss (about 2 Wh a day measured idle), but nobody has measured how much energy it delivers. Hobotech, as reported by wattpowerstation, measured about 13 W DC-only idle on the DELTA Pro 3, and at a 15 W router load that idle draw almost doubles the drain. This page puts those side by side with prices read on 2026-11-26.

angles.decides: It confirms the UGREEN Nexode 20,000 mAh 130 W as the pick for an Air charged alongside a phone: it is the only one of our two unrecorded 20K candidates whose laptop port stays above Apple's 70 W line when shared. The Baseus FC41 20K 100 W honestly wins the built-in-cable, lightest (428 g), laptop-only segment. Anker Prime (140 W port, 100 W input, $119.99) and Cuktech 15 Ultra (140 W port, 165 W input, 590 g) win on recharge speed, but their extra port power does nothing for an Air. On capacity, the makers' own usable figures (55-60 Wh) say one 13-inch Air charge (53.8 Wh) and not a full 15-inch (66.5 Wh), which is tighter than the 85-105% and 70-85% ChatGPT told the shopper. One caveat belongs on the page: Best Batteries reports the UGREEN's 100 W port falls to 45 W on laptops after 18-22 minutes, so 100 W is a peak figure.

This page maps each bank's one-port watts to Apple's fast-charge list (140 W for a 16-inch MacBook Pro, 96 W for a 14-inch, 70 W for an Air), including that Baseus's 140 W sits on a fixed USB-C cable while UGREEN's is on a port that takes a MagSafe 3 cable.

UGREEN's spec gives 140 W from one port; the INIU gives 100 W that smartzone saw drop to 65 W after 30-35 minutes or as soon as a second device is plugged in, and it needs a 5 A cable bought separately. The INIU keeps the weight segment only. pages.query: best 40000mAh power bank for laptop
pages.why_used: The rival pages give rated mAh and Wh only (powerbanks.fyi) or a single laptop-recharge count for the UGREEN (Macworld). None carries a bench-measured delivered capacity for a 40,000 mAh bank. This page sets ChargerLAB's 121.6 Wh at 100 W for the AOHi Starship 40K beside the roughly 125 Wh Macworld's test implies for the UGREEN 48K, with the weight each costs.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that UGREEN's "48,000 mAh" is counted at 3.2 V LiFePO4 cells (153.6 Wh), so on the 3.6 V scale the 40,000 mAh rivals use it is about 42,700 mAh: 6.7% more energy than a 144 Wh Cuktech 30, not 20%, at about 46% more weight; and that every "300 W" or "140 W" bank in this size gives one laptop the same 140 W.
angles.decides: It reframes the pick rather than flipping it. The UGREEN 48,000 mAh should be sold as the long-life desk and camping bank (3,000 cycles to 80%, maker claim), not as "20% more capacity". Its real energy lead over a 40,000 mAh bank is about 4-7%, and it weighs about 0.5 kg more than the Cuktech 30. For one laptop, the 300 W label adds nothing over a 140 W bank, because the most one port gives is 140 W on the UGREEN and on the Cuktech 30. The 300 W only matters for two or three laptops at once (UGREEN: 100 W on each of three USB-C). That supports a split: the UGREEN for longevity and several laptops at a desk, a lighter 40,000 mAh 140 W bank (the AOHi Starship) when it gets carried. The Cuktech 30 is unavailable on its maker's store today.

UGREEN 48K wins for a desk, car or campsite: it is the cheapest per Wh of the banks priced ($0.77 per rated Wh at $118.99) and the only one with a named laptop test (Macworld, 1.8 charges, about 126 Wh delivered). It does not win on capacity by the 20% its mAh label suggests, only 6.7%, and it weighs 3.6 lb. AOHi Starship 40K wins if the bank is carried: 72.6 Wh per lb against 42.7, about 1.6 lb lighter for 9.6 Wh less, at about $0.99 per Wh through our link. Cuktech 30 sits between them on weight (57.8 Wh/lb) but its maker's US store shows it unavailable today, so it cannot be the pick to buy. Both of ours place in the top three on these figures.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "what size power station and solar panel run an off-grid cabin for a weekend". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: What size power station and solar panel run an off-grid cabin for a weekend?
pages.why_used: The cited cabin guides give sizing formulas, sun-hour ranges and a two-day storage figure, but none works out how many days a specific kit's panel needs to refill its battery or what the kit costs. This page does that for each priced kit. One 200 W panel needs 5.2 poor-sun days to refill a 2 kWh station, against 2.4–2.6 days with 400 W. Of the kits priced here, only the 3,168 Wh kit meets SolutionEnergy's 2.5–3 kWh two-day storage figure without any sun.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says how much power the stations use just by keeping the AC inverter on all weekend for the fridge. Normalised to a 44-hour Friday-evening-to-Sunday-afternoon weekend, the drain is about 420 Wh on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (9.5 W, The Solar Lab) and about 600 Wh on the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max (13.6 W, The Solar Lab). On the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus it is about 4.9 kWh (112 W, Zelpio), which is more than its 3,840 Wh battery, so the inverter alone empties it in about 34 hours.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the pick at about 2 kWh. Its idle draw is the lowest sourced here (9.5 W, about 420 Wh over the weekend). APH Networks also measured 2,028 Wh usable from it at a 987 W load, 97.8% of rated. The DELTA 2 Max has the same nominal capacity but loses about 180 Wh more to idle over the weekend. It also rules out ChatGPT's F3800 Plus suggestion for a fridge weekend. Zelpio measured 112 W with the inverter on and nothing plugged in. Anker's own firmware post claims only a 50% cut, which would still be about 56 W and about 2.5 kWh over 44 hours. The page should put idle watts × 44 h in the table as a line in the energy budget, with a footnote naming who measured each figure and the firmware caveat.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how many December days a kit's own panel needs to refill its battery. Using SolutionEnergy's figure of 2 kWh per kW of panels on a December day, the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit ($1,199) needs 5.2 sunny days to refill, so its panel cannot top it up within a weekend. The ALLPOWERS R2500 V2 + SP037 400 W kit ($948) needs 2.4 days, supplies about 3,330 Wh over a two-day December weekend and has the lowest cost per usable Wh of the kits checked ($0.55).
angles.decides: The panel bundled with a kit decides the pick more than the battery size does. A single 200 W panel on a 2 kWh station refills it only every 2.4 summer days or 5.2 December days, so for a weekend the battery has to carry nearly all the load. With 400 W, a kit adds about 1.6 kWh over a December weekend. That moves the pick to a 2 kWh-class station with 400 W of panels: the ALLPOWERS R2500 V2 + SP037 at $948 if it can be confirmed in stock, or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 2× 200 W at $1,499. It moves away from the Elite 200 V2 + 350 W, which now costs $1,449 and ships from Dec 25, and from the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W. The AC180 + 200 W ($769) supplies about 1.8 kWh over a December weekend, which covers SolutionEnergy's 2 kWh weekend load on that page's numbers. It falls well short of ChatGPT's 2,270 Wh fridge example.

Two in series reach 66 V, over the Elite 200 V2's 12–60 V solar input, and two in parallel are held to the station's 20 A limit, which caps them below 660 W (20 A × 33 V). So the $2,148 Elite 200 V2 + 2×350 W bundle cannot put 700 W into the station. Two SP200L 200 W panels (24.6 V Voc each, 49.2 V in series) do fit under the 60 V limit.

In parallel the two panels' 21.6 A short-circuit current is over the 20 A input limit. It argues against stepping up to the 2×350 W bundle ($2,148). Series wiring is ruled out by the 60 V limit, and in parallel the 20 A limit keeps the input under 660 W. So the extra $649 buys less than its 700 W nameplate. Separately, the single 350 W kit price on BLUETTI's store is now $1,449, not the $1,249 on our page.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that BLUETTI stations ship with ECO mode turned on, and that ECO cuts the AC outlets after a stretch of low or no load. The BLUETTI manual itself says to turn ECO off for refrigerators. A fridge that cycles off can drop below the threshold and lose power overnight, and that can happen on an otherwise correctly sized weekend setup.

On the Elite 200 V2 and AC180, which are both on our page, ECO must be turned off before leaving the fridge plugged in. This is a setup step the answer should state. For a November trip there is a second check: the Elite 200 V2 manual lists charging at 0–40°C (32–104°F). If the station is below freezing, solar can't refill it, so the battery has to cover the whole weekend on its own. That points to the larger-battery option (3 kWh or more), or to keeping the station inside the heated part of the cabin.

The Solar Lab measured 9.5 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and 13.6 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max with AC on and nothing plugged in. Over 48 hours that is about 456 Wh (22 % of 2,073.6 Wh) and about 653 Wh (32 % of 2,048 Wh). Load-tested usable capacity also differs by product: APH Networks got 2,028 Wh from the Elite 200 V2, StorageReview got 1,800 Wh from the DELTA 2 Max, and StorageReview got 920 Wh from the S2000 Pro.
angles.decides: It supports the Elite 200 V2 + 350 W kit as the pick and strengthens the case against the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max as an equal. Elite 200 V2: 2,028 Wh measured (APH Networks) minus about 456 Wh of idle over 48 h (The Solar Lab's 9.5 W) leaves about 1,570 Wh for loads. DELTA 2 Max: 1,800 Wh measured (StorageReview) minus about 653 Wh (The Solar Lab's 13.6 W) leaves about 1,150 Wh. The two are rated almost the same (2,073.6 vs 2,048 Wh), but the BLUETTI keeps about 420 Wh more for the fridge. Without solar, neither covers a 2.3–4.0 kWh fridge weekend, so the panel is not optional. Switching the AC inverter off when nothing needs it, or running a 12 V fridge on DC, saves roughly 0.45–0.65 kWh per weekend. The AC180 measured 950–1,030 Wh (OutdoorGearLab, StorageReview), which keeps it at 'marginal with a fridge'. pages.query: which portable power station can be a ups for a nas and send a usb shutdown signal
pages.why_used: The cited rivals cover NUT 2.8.3, the usbhid-ups driver and the RIVER 3 Plus low-battery bug, but none says EcoFlow's USB link cannot switch the station's AC off and back on after the NAS shuts down (NUT #2735: 'Shutdown does nothing', AC live 60+ s), so the NAS stays off after a short outage. None says EcoFlow's Power Manager lists only the RIVER 3 Plus, or that EcoFlow's Synology package needs port and device-name edits. This page puts those findings in the table and gives a separate pick for each segment, including a UPS that does restart the NAS (UGREEN US3000).

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that stock Synology DSM 7.3.2 does not see an EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus as a USB UPS (it shows "No USB UPS Connected"). It only works through EcoFlow's Power Manager NAS package, after hand-editing its port (3496 to 3493) and device name (nutdev1 to ups) and switching DSM to Synology UPS Server mode. Even then, several owners report that the NAS never shut down. So "NUT 2.8.3+ support" means support for anyone who runs current NUT, not for the NAS firmware people actually have.
angles.decides: It confirms that no portable power station is a plug-and-play USB UPS for a Synology or QNAP on stock firmware. The RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus only make sense if the NAS can run current NUT itself (2.8.3 or later, which on Debian means forky or sid, not Debian 12 or 13) or can poll a separate NUT server. For a Synology or QNAP owner who wants an automatic shutdown, the pick is a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1, CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD). The EcoFlow is then a long-runtime source that you shut down on a timer, not one that sends a low-battery signal.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of adding NAS runtime while keeping the USB shutdown link. EcoFlow's DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery adds 1,024 Wh for $388 ($0.38/Wh). The RIVER 3 Plus EB300 adds 286 Wh for $149 ($0.52/Wh), and the RIVER 3 Plus stops at 858 Wh. Measured DELTA 3 Plus output is 910 Wh per 1,024 Wh, so DELTA 3 Plus plus one extra battery gives about 57 h on a 32 W 2-bay NAS and about 31 h on a 59 W 4-bay NAS.
angles.decides: The USB shutdown requirement leaves only EcoFlow units with a data port: RIVER 3 Plus (USB-B), DELTA 3 Plus (USB-C) and DELTA 3 Ultra / Ultra Plus (USB-C UPS-HID). Among those, the pick depends on how many NAS hours you need. Up to a few hours: RIVER 3 Plus. Overnight or more: DELTA 3 Plus, adding the $388 extra battery if needed. That costs less per added Wh than stacking RIVER 3 Plus EB300s, and the RIVER 3 Plus tops out at 858 Wh. If you need 2 days or more on a 4-bay NAS, the DELTA 3 Ultra at $1,299 for 3,072 Wh ($0.42/Wh nominal) has the lowest cost per hour of any unit with a data port. This supports ChatGPT's RIVER 3 Plus / DELTA 3 Plus split and adds a price-based reason to choose the Ultra.
products: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus + DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery
EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus + EB300 Smart Extra Battery

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow's USB HID link cannot cut the station's AC output after the NAS shuts down. NUT's open issue #2735 for the RIVER 3 Plus (firmware V1.33.81.61, Oct 2026) says 'Shutdown does nothing' and that the AC output 'stays live for 60+ seconds', so the NAS stays off when mains power returns. Nor does any result state that EcoFlow's own Power Manager software lists only the RIVER 3 Plus as a supported device, which leaves the DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra without it.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus as the only power station with a maker-documented NAS shutdown path: EcoFlow names it as the only device Power Manager supports, and the cable is in the box. It also limits what the RIVER 3 Plus can do. It can tell a NAS to shut down, but it cannot switch its AC off and back on, so the NAS will not restart by itself after an outage. DSM also needs manual config edits, and commenters on a DS920+ report it hanging instead of shutting down. Shoppers who need unattended recovery should get a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1 or CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD) or UGREEN's US3000 for NASync. The DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra only work through generic NUT 2.8.3 or later, without EcoFlow software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus give NUT no command to switch their AC output off and back on (no load.off, load.off.delay or shutdown.return), so after the NAS shuts itself down the station keeps its outlets live. If mains returns before the battery runs flat, the NAS never sees a power loss and stays off until someone presses its power button.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus as the only stations here that can signal a shutdown, but it adds a limit to the pick. They can shut a NAS down cleanly, yet they cannot bring it back by themselves after a short outage, because the 'restart after power failure' setting only fires when the NAS really loses power. A NAS the shopper needs to reach remotely, such as one serving a VPN, will stay off. Two things avoid that: a conventional HID UPS (the APC class), which exposes load-off-with-delay commands, or a timer or Wake-on-LAN workaround. The table's 'What a NAS sees' column should add 'won't power the NAS back on after a short outage'.
products: APC Back-UPS ES (BE650G2, same family as BE600M1)

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy the EcoFlow units with a UPS data port actually delivered when StorageReview measured them: 910 Wh from the DELTA 3 Plus (88.9% of its 1,024 Wh) and 2.61 kWh from the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus (about 85% of 3,072 Wh). Those figures put real numbers on NAS runtimes, roughly 28 h for a 2-bay NAS and 15 h for a 4-bay NAS on the DELTA 3 Plus.
angles.decides: This backs the DELTA 3 Plus as the long-runtime pick with a data port. Two separate measurements (StorageReview 910 Wh, nextpit 950 Wh) support our page's runtimes of about 28 h at 32 W and 15 h at 59 W. They are an upper bound, though: one owner found NUT's low-battery point equals the app's discharge limit, so a 30% limit leaves about 637 Wh, or roughly 20 h at 32 W. For the RIVER 3 Plus, the October 2026 owner report means our cell 'an open NUT bug never reports low battery' should change. In that report on Ubuntu, upsmon did start a low-battery shutdown, but NUT has no shutdown command for the unit and the AC output stayed on for 60+ seconds. A NAS set to power back on when AC returns may therefore not restart. Measured switchover adds nothing new: all the data-port EcoFlows test at 8 to 9 ms (StorageReview), and computingforgeeks already has most of those numbers.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives today's maker-store prices for the units it named: the only EcoFlow pick with a documented USB UPS data link that we could price on us.ecoflow.com today is the DELTA 3 Ultra series at $1,299 (Ultra Plus $1,599). angles.decides: This keeps the AC180 as the pick, but adds a condition. ChatGPT's 7–9 nights assume the AC180 runs the CPAP all night through the 12 V port with the humidifier off. Willitrunpower puts that draw at about 7 W, inside the AC180's DC ECO range of 5–10 W. If ECO is on with a 10 W threshold, the port can switch off 1–4 hours into the night. Using AC instead doesn't avoid this, because the AC ECO range is 15–30 W. So the page should tell AC180 buyers to turn ECO off in Setting mode, or set it to 5 W, and test a full night at home. The table footnote should list each station's low-load cutoff next to its capacity. Also, the ResMed converter draws up to 10 A at 12 V, which is exactly the AC180's 12 V/10 A port rating. That leaves no headroom if the humidifier and heated tube run on DC.

A humidifier-off AirSense 11 (about 7 W) on the AC180's AC outlet is under the lowest AC ECO threshold (15 W), so with ECO on, the outlet will switch off within the 1–4 hour window every night. This also backs up the DC route, since it's the only one that can stay on with ECO enabled.

The Technology Man measured about 11 W with nothing plugged in on the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 (100% to 24% in 20 hours). angles.decides: It backs the AC180 as the one-charge pick, with a condition. Four named tests put its usable energy at 950–1,030 Wh. With the CPAP alone at 7 W × 8 h = 56 Wh a night, that covers 7 nights easily. If the DC port idles at an Elite-30-V2-like 11 W and stays on, a night costs (7 + 11) × 8 = 144 Wh, and 7 nights need about 1,008 Wh, which is right at the AC180's measured ceiling. Left on 24 hours a day, the port alone would eat about 264 Wh a day and the AC180 would not last the week. So the page should say: switch the 12 V port off in the morning (or use ECO mode), or step up to the Elite 200 V2. APH Networks measured 2,028 Wh for the Elite 200 V2, which leaves a week with margin even with the humidifier on via AC at 19 W. It also rules the Elite 30 V2 out of anything more than 1–2 nights.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which power station gets a farmers-market booth". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which power station gets a farmers-market booth?
pages.why_used: Two pages were cited. Both give only label capacities or size ranges. Neither compares named-lab measured output for the 1 kWh stations (DELTA 3 Plus, Jackery 1000 v2, Elite 100 V2, S2000 Pro and AC180) with a 1.0 kWh, 6-hour booth day. That comparison shows every 1 kWh unit at or just below the day, and only the Elite 200 V2 keeps a reserve. The Elite 200 V2 also costs the least per measured Wh at today's BLUETTI prices. Angle C (the AC180's 1,500 W cap in heat) scored higher, but it is sourced for only one candidate. I folded it into the page as the AC180's caveat instead.

For a motor load like a blender plus a mini fridge, the comparable limit is therefore the 1,800 W continuous rating, and BLUETTI publishes no separate figure above that for motor start-up.
angles.decides: This confirms the AC180 rather than changing the pick, and it tightens the wording. The blender verdict has to rest on the 1,800 W continuous rating, not on '2,700 W surge'. A 1,500 W blender plus a running mini fridge (roughly 60–100 W) and lights leaves about 200 W of headroom under 1,800 W. If a vendor might start the blender while the fridge compressor is starting, the Elite 200 V2 (2,600 W continuous) is the safer choice. Separately, the AC180 is $499 at BLUETTI US today, not the $449 that our page and ChatGPT quoted from Nov 3.

angles.decides: This changes the pick for warm-season markets. Above 86 °F the AC180's AC limit drops from 1,800 W to 1,500 W, so a 1,500 W blender alone uses the whole limit, and the fridge (plus anything else on AC) pushes it over. That leaves no headroom; it's not a thin margin. In summer the AC180 is only safe with a blender rated well under 1,500 W (about 1,300 W or less, leaving room for the fridge), or with the fridge unplugged while blending. Otherwise the Elite 200 V2 (2,600 W) is the pick, though I couldn't find its own heat limit. The AC180's battery can be extended with a B230/B300 through a P090D-to-DC7909 cable ($89). That adds stored energy for the day but adds no inverter power, so it doesn't fix the blender problem.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which power station can run a home oxygen concentrator in a power outage and for how long". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which power station can run a home oxygen concentrator in a power outage and for how long?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals list 10–20 ms switchover times but leave out the concentrator side. The Philips EverFlo manual documents only a 0.5-cycle (8.3 ms) total dropout and tells users who need uninterrupted running to use a UPS or battery. No rival names the one station rated for a 0 ms path, and none shows that lab-timed switchovers land at 8–16 ms. This page pairs those facts with reviewer-measured watt-hours.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much AC energy each station actually delivered when reviewers measured it. Every page applies a flat 85% to the rated Wh, and that hides the fact that the BLUETTI Elite 300 measured 2,670 Wh: short of the roughly 2,800 Wh an 8-hour night on a 350 W EverFlo needs, so it gives about 7.6 h rather than covering the night.
angles.decides: It confirms the pick structure and corrects one implied promise. Measured AC output runs from 85% of rated (DELTA 3, Jackery 1000 v2) to 92% (Elite 200 V2), so the flat 85% rule is fair to slightly pessimistic. At 350 W, though, even the largest station on our page, the Elite 300 at 2,670 Wh measured, falls about 25 minutes short of 8 hours. For overnight cover the shopper needs an expandable unit plus a battery: AC200L + B300K, or DELTA 3 + extra batteries. The 1 kWh units (DELTA 3, C1000 Gen 2, Jackery 1000 v2) land within 0.1 h of each other, about 2.5 to 2.6 h, so capacity doesn't separate them; switchover and price have to.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a live price for each hour of runtime on a 350 W EverFlo-class concentrator, or names the cheapest maker-store setup that covers a full 8-hour night (3,294 Wh needed at 0.85). On 2026-11-14 that was the EcoFlow DELTA Pro at $1,799 for about 8.7 h. The BLUETTI Elite 300 at $1,199 is the cheapest per hour (about $164/h) but runs out about 40 minutes short of 8 hours, and the BLUETTI Apex 200 + B300K at $2,199 gives about 12.9 h at about $170/h.
angles.decides: The finding splits the pick by need. For an evening outage up to about 7 hours, the BLUETTI Elite 300 ($1,199, about 7.3 h) is the best value at about $164 per runtime hour. For a full 8-hour night on a 350 W unit, the Elite 300 is not enough. The cheapest single box that covers it is the EcoFlow DELTA Pro ($1,799 at us.ecoflow.com, about 8.7 h). The BLUETTI Apex 200 + B300K bundle ($2,199, about 12.9 h) costs $400 more but gives about 4 more hours and a lower cost per hour ($170 vs $206). The BLUETTI AC200L, our current expandable row, was sold out at BLUETTI US on 2026-11-14, and so was the Anker F3800 Plus at ankersolix.com. A backup oxygen tank from the supplier comes first, whatever station the shopper picks.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Philips EverFlo's own EMC table only covers a total power dropout of 0.5 cycle (about 8.3 ms at 60 Hz). Every UPS switchover in those results is 10–20 ms, which is longer. The manual's own advice for anyone who needs the unit to keep running through mains interruptions is to power it from 'an uninterruptible power supply or a battery'.
angles.decides: Batteries are compared on Wh, but the deciding question is whether the concentrator stays on when the grid drops. Every station on our page publishes a 10–20 ms switchover, which is 0.6–1.2 cycles at 60 Hz. That is longer than the 0.5-cycle dropout the EverFlo manual documents, so in UPS mode the shopper should expect the concentrator to stop and sound its power-failure alarm (the alarm is per our page's citation of the EverFlo manual), not run through. Two ways around it: (a) put the concentrator on the left two AC outlets of a BLUETTI Apex 300, set to 240 V mode and fed from the grid through the 15 A AC input, which BLUETTI rates at 0 ms; or (b) plan for a restart plus backup tanks. The page should make the Apex 300 (0 ms outlets, 2,764.8 Wh, about 6.7 h at 350 W) the pick for anyone who needs no interruption. It should present the 10–20 ms stations as runtime-only choices.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much energy the candidate stations actually delivered at concentrator-like loads, as measured by a reviewer. Notebookcheck measured 2,905 Wh from the Anker SOLIX F3800 at a constant 260 W load, which is 75% of its 3,840 Wh rating. At 350 W that works out to about 8.3 hours, not the 9.3 hours ChatGPT gave. Notebookcheck also measured about 2,650 Wh from the BLUETTI Elite 300 at about 200 W, or about 7.6 hours at 350 W.

The F3800 delivered only 75% of its rating, so measured, it clears an 8-hour night only just (about 8.3 h). The Elite 300 falls short whether you use measured energy (about 7.6 h from 2,650–2,670 Wh) or rated energy (about 7.3 h). The DELTA Pro 3 measured 3,790 Wh, about 10.8 h, which is the only comfortable overnight margin. At 280 W, both the Elite 300 (about 9.5 h) and the F3800 (about 10.4 h) clear 8 hours. The 1 kWh class measured 850–910 Wh, about 2.4–2.6 h at 350 W, which confirms they cover only a short outage. Two independent labs measured the Elite 300's switchover at 8 ms and 8.9 ms, under BLUETTI's 10 ms claim. That supports, but does not prove, that a concentrator would ride through the switch.

pages.query: Run one web search with exactly this query: "which portable power station keeps a 75-gallon tropical aquarium alive through a 24-hour outage". Then answer my question the way you normally would, from what you found: Which portable power station keeps a 75-gallon tropical aquarium alive through a 24-hour outage?
pages.why_used: The cited rivals guess a heater duty cycle (15–30%) or leave the heater out, and none turns a 75-gallon tank's cooling times into heater watts. This page works out the heater load from the tank's heat loss: about 52 W wrapped and 184 W with a glass lid in a 59 °F room. That shows insulation decides whether any station lasts 24 hours, and it gives measured runtimes for each station.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the Elite 300's measured AC-on idle draw (19 W, which is 456 Wh a day) or points out that its 94% efficiency was measured at a 1 kW load. A 75-gallon tank's 27 W filter and air pump load at night is a very different case, so the real 24-hour budget at 20% heater duty is about 2,544 Wh against the 2,819 Wh it measurably delivers.
angles.decides: It confirms the BLUETTI Elite 300 as the pick and leaves less room to spare. With 19 W measured idle instead of the 15 W assumed, the 20% heater-duty budget rises from 2,448 Wh to 2,544 Wh. That is about 90% of the 2,819 Wh The Technology Man measured it delivering. At 30% duty (3,264 Wh) it falls short. The Elite 200 V2's idle draw is lower (10 W per The Gadgeteer, or 240 Wh a day), but that does not make up its 940 Wh capacity deficit. The page should fold the measured idle draw into the duty-cycle table instead of a flat 15 W.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the 75-gallon tank's own heat loss into a heater load. AquariumToolbox's cooling times for a 75-gallon tank at 77 °F in a 59 °F room work out to about 52 W wrapped in a blanket (17% duty on a 300 W heater), 184 W with only a glass lid (61%) and 323 W open (more than a 300 W heater can supply). That makes a wrapped tank about a 2 kWh day: the Elite 300 lasts about 31 h, the Elite 200 V2 about 24 h and the DELTA 2 Max about 22 h. With only a lid, no candidate passes about 12 h.
angles.decides: The heater's duty cycle comes from how well the tank is insulated, not from the shopper's guess, so insulation decides the pick before capacity does. In a 59 °F room, a blanket-wrapped tank (≈69.5 W of equipment plus the station's own draw) is covered for 24 h by the BLUETTI Elite 300, with about 7 h to spare. The Elite 200 V2 ($899) just reaches 24 h, and the DELTA 2 Max falls short at about 22 h. A tank with only a lid needs about 5.2 kWh, which no single candidate holds; the Elite 300 lasts about 12 h. An open tank loses more heat than a 300 W heater can replace, so no battery holds temperature. In a 68 °F room with only a lid, the Elite 300 lasts about 21 h. This supports the Elite 300 pick, with the condition that the tank is wrapped. It also makes the Elite 200 V2 the cheaper pick when wrapped, at $0.47 per measured usable Wh against $0.45 for the Elite 300.

The B300K list names AC200L, AC200MAX, AC300 and AC500. The B500K list names Apex 300, AC300, AC500, AC200L and AC200MAX, and the store sells it as 'B500K for Apex 200 & Apex 300'. The Apex 200 + B300K bundle (5,324.8 Wh, about 4.5 kWh usable at 85 %) covers 30 % duty with room to spare and nearly covers 50 % duty (4.6 kWh). It costs $0.41/Wh against the Elite 300's $0.40/Wh. In a warm room at 15–20 % duty the Elite 300 still wins: the Apex 200 alone (about 2.2 kWh usable) has less energy than the Elite 300 for $100 less. The AC200L also takes B300K/B500K, but BLUETTI US shows it unavailable today.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 300 ships with AC-ECO turned on, that it shuts off its AC outlets after a period of low or no load, or that BLUETTI tells owners to disable it for critical appliances. The setting only becomes active once wall power is lost, so a station tested on the wall looks fine and can then cut the filter and air pump a few hours into the outage.

Once the heater's thermostat stops calling for heat, the station's load is only the filter and air pump, about 27 W. That is a 'low load' under BLUETTI's own wording, and the AC180's adjustable AC threshold of 10–30 W covers it. The same applies to the filter-and-air-pump-only setup the page suggests for the AC180 and Elite 200 V2. The page should tell readers to switch it off with the AC button or in the app, as BLUETTI's manual says to for critical appliances. It's a setting, not a hardware limit, so the ranking doesn't change.

pages.query: which power station can run a cpap for the most nights on one charge
pages.why_used: The cited CPAP pages rank stations by rated Wh × 0.85 and leave out what each station draws just to keep its inverter on. At CPAP loads that idle draw is as large as the CPAP itself. With it added, every nights figure drops by about half, the 5,040 Wh Jackery falls from 13.4 to 4.3–5.5 nights, and the 5,024 Wh Anker SOLIX S5000 (about 10 W idle, measured by pv magazine USA) runs about twice as many nights as the larger DELTA Pro Ultra or Explorer 5000 Plus.

angles.name: Normalise

Counting that draw roughly halves every nights-per-charge figure the rivals publish. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X still comes out on top, at about 20 nights rather than 32, while the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus falls from 13.4 nights to 5.0–6.4.
angles.decides: It confirms the DELTA Pro Ultra X as the most-nights pick, because it has the lowest idle draw measured among the giants (about 36 W, The Solar Lab). It also shows the 'nights' rankings everyone publishes are about 2× too high. Ranked by nights after idle draw, the Explorer 5000 Plus (58–85 W idle) and the original DELTA Pro Ultra (45–60 W idle) fall from about 13–16 nights to about 5–9. That makes idle draw, not capacity alone, the spec to compare. The table footnote should read: nights = rated Wh ÷ (8 h × (CPAP W + station idle W)). The Ultra X also has no USB ports, and no DC or 12 V output was found in what I read, so it can't use a CPAP's 12 V DC lead to skip the inverter. The Explorer 5000 Plus does list a 12 V car socket.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that once each station's measured inverter idle draw is added to a 40 W CPAP, the ranking changes: the Anker SOLIX S5000 (about 10 W idle, pv magazine) gives about 10.7 nights from 5,024 Wh, while the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra gives 6.5–7.7 nights from 6,144 Wh (45–60 W idle) and the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus gives 5.5 nights from 5,040 Wh (58 W idle). At a CPAP's low load, idle draw is roughly as large as the CPAP's own draw on the big inverters (45–60 W on the DELTA Pro Ultra, 58 W on the 5000 Plus, against a 40 W CPAP), so the biggest battery does not give the most nights. Among single-box stations the Anker SOLIX S5000, which Dealectric lists via rakuten:ankersolix, comes out on top at about 10.7 nights at 40 W and 17.8 nights at 20 W with the humidifier off. Only the much pricier 12,288 Wh DELTA Pro Ultra X does better, at about 17.2 nights. Among stacks we list, the BLUETTI Apex 300 + 2× B300K (8,294.4 Wh) works out to about 14.7 nights, but only if its idle stays near 20 W with packs attached, which nobody has measured.

ChatGPT's capacity-first table ranks units that fail this.
